L00_welcome.title: A Computer Engineering Degree, Re-Taught
L00_welcome.file: Lecture - 00 Welcome - A Computer Engineering Degree, Re-Taught.mp4

say: Welcome. This series re-teaches a complete computer engineering bachelor's degree, one course at a time, following the curriculum of the computer engineering program at California State University, Fullerton. It's meant for anyone who wants to learn this material properly: current students who want a second explanation, graduates who want to refresh what didn't stick, and curious people starting from scratch. Every lecture assumes nothing was retained, explains why each idea matters in the real world, and works through concrete examples with diagrams.

pts: Bridge hardware and software
Design chips, boards, embedded systems and the code that runs them
From ENIAC (1945) to billions of transistors per chip
Phones, cars, medical devices, robots, data centers
say: Computer engineering sits between electrical engineering and computer science. Computer engineers design the hardware that computes, and write the software that runs closest to it. This is ENIAC, one of the first general purpose electronic computers, built in the nineteen forties with about eighteen thousand vacuum tubes. It filled a room.
Today, a single chip holds billions of transistors, and computer engineers design them, often in hardware description languages on boards like this F P G A, which you'll learn to program.

They also build embedded systems, computers hidden inside other products, from phones and cars to pacemakers and robots like this one. Every one of those systems needs people who understand both the transistors and the code. That's what this degree trains you to do.

slides.h: The map: thirty courses in five tracks
say: Here's the whole degree on one slide, grouped into five tracks. Math and physics come first. They're the language everything else is written in: calculus, discrete math, differential equations, linear algebra, probability, mechanics, and electricity and magnetism.
The software track runs from a first programming course through object oriented programming and data structures, to operating systems, software engineering and databases.
The circuits and devices track starts with circuit laws, moves to diodes and transistors, and ends inside the chip with CMOS design, plus signals and systems, the math of filters and frequencies.
The digital systems track is the heart of computer engineering: digital logic, microcontrollers, hardware description languages, processor design, embedded systems and hardware security.

And finally, engineering economics and ethics, and a two semester senior design project that ties it all together. The lectures follow roughly the order a student takes them, so each builds on the ones before.

slides.h: The big idea: layers of abstraction
pts: Every layer hides the details of the one below
This degree climbs the whole stack
Physics → transistors → logic → processors → software
Engineers who understand several layers solve the hardest bugs
say: One idea organizes the entire degree: abstraction. A computer is built in layers. Physics explains how electrons move. Transistors use that physics to make switches. Switches make logic gates, gates make processors, processors run instructions, and instructions build operating systems and applications. Each layer hides the details of the one below, so a programmer doesn't need to think about electrons. This degree is unusual because it climbs every one of those layers, from physics at the bottom to applications at the top. That's its real value: when something goes wrong at the boundary between layers, like a timing bug, a power glitch or a slow program caused by the cache, the engineer who understands more than one layer is the one who can fix it. Keep this picture in mind. At the end of the series, we'll come back to it.

pts: Each course: one lecture video + a slide deck
Watch in order, or jump to what you need (chapters)
Pause on the worked examples and try them first
Re-derive, don’t just re-watch: write it out by hand
Every image is credited at the end of the series
say: Each course has its own lecture video and a matching slide deck.
You can watch in order, which is how the material builds, or jump straight to a course using the chapter markers.
When a worked example appears, pause and try it yourself before listening to the answer. That's where real learning happens.
And don't just re watch. Write things out by hand: derive the formula, draw the circuit, trace the code. Retention comes from doing, not from watching.
The photographs come from Wikimedia Commons under free licenses, and every one is credited. Let's begin, with calculus.

L01_math150a.title: Calculus I
L01_math150a.file: MATH-150A Calculus I/Lecture - MATH 150A Calculus I.mp4

say: Welcome to Calculus one. Calculus is the mathematics of change: how fast something is changing right now, and how much it adds up to over time. Every engineering course you'll take later leans on it. Circuits, signals, physics, even machine learning. So in this lecture we'll build it from scratch: limits, then derivatives, then integrals, with lots of examples and pictures. If you've forgotten all of it, that's fine. Start here.

pts: Speedometer: rate of change of position
Odometer: speed added up over time
Derivative ↔ integral: two sides of one idea
say: Look at a car dashboard. The speedometer tells you how fast your position is changing right now, in miles per hour. That's a rate of change, and in calculus it's called a derivative.
The odometer does the opposite job. It adds up your speed over every moment of the trip to get the total distance. That running total is called an integral.

So calculus asks two big questions. On the left: how steep is a curve at one exact point? That's the derivative, the slope of the tangent line. On the right: how much area is under a curve? That's the integral. The amazing discovery, which we'll reach at the end of this lecture, is that these two questions are inverses of each other. In engineering you'll see this everywhere. Current is the rate of change of charge. The current through a capacitor is proportional to how fast its voltage changes. Energy is power added up over time.

Calculus was invented twice, independently, in the late sixteen hundreds. Isaac Newton in England developed it to explain motion and gravity. Gottfried Leibniz in Germany developed it on his own a few years later, and published first.

The two men argued bitterly about who deserved credit. But Leibniz's notation won, and we still use it today. d y over d x for the derivative, and the tall S shaped integral sign, which is a stretched letter S for sum. Keep that in mind: an integral is a sum of infinitely many tiny pieces.
Part one. Limits. Everything in calculus is built on this one idea.

slides.h: A limit is where a function is heading
pts: sin(x)/x is undefined at x = 0 (zero over zero)
Written: lim x→0 of sin(x)/x = 1
say: Here's the function sine of x divided by x. Try to plug in zero, and you get zero divided by zero, which is undefined. There's literally a hole in the graph at zero.

But watch what happens as x gets close to zero. At x equals point one, the value is point nine nine eight three. At point zero one, it's point nine nine nine nine eight. The closer we get, the closer the output gets to one.

So we say the limit as x approaches zero of sine x over x equals one. A limit doesn't care what happens exactly at the point. It asks where the function is heading as you get closer and closer. That's the key idea, because the derivative is going to be exactly this kind of zero over zero situation.

pts: Plug in first. If you get a number, done
If you get 0/0: factor, cancel, try again
say: How do you actually compute a limit? Step one: just plug the number in. If the function is well behaved there, you get a number, and that's the limit.
If you get zero over zero, the function is hiding something. Usually a common factor in the top and bottom.

Example: x squared minus four, over x minus two, as x goes to two. Plugging in gives zero over zero. But x squared minus four factors into x minus two times x plus two. Cancel the x minus two, and you're left with x plus two, which is four when x is two. So the limit is four. The graph is just the line y equals x plus two, with a single hole punched out at the point two comma four.

slides.h: Worked example: a limit that needs a trick
pts: (written on the whiteboard) lim_xto 0\ fracsqrtx+4 - 2x
(written on the whiteboard) plug in x = 0: (2 − 2)/0 = 0/0
(written on the whiteboard) = fracsqrtx+4-2xcdotfracsqrtx+4+2sqrtx+4+2
(written on the whiteboard) = frac(x+4)-4x (sqrtx+4+2)
(written on the whiteboard) = fracxx (sqrtx+4+2)
(written on the whiteboard) = frac1sqrtx+4+2
(written on the whiteboard) to (1)/(2+2) = (1)/(4)
say: Let's work one together, step by step. Find the limit as x goes to zero of the square root of x plus four, minus two, all over x. First, always try plugging in. The top is root four minus two, which is zero, and the bottom is zero. Zero over zero, so there's a hole hiding here.

Factoring won't work with a square root, so we use a different trick: multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate, root x plus four, plus two. On top, that's a difference of squares: x plus four, minus four, which is just x. So we get x over x times root x plus four plus two.

Now the x on top cancels the x on the bottom. That leaves one over root x plus four, plus two. Plug in zero: one over two plus two, which is one quarter. On the graph, the curve heads smoothly toward one quarter, with a single missing point exactly at zero.

slides.h: When a limit does NOT exist
pts: (written on the whiteboard) f(x) = (|x|)/(x)
(written on the whiteboard) lim_xto 0^- f(x) = -1
(written on the whiteboard) lim_xto 0^+ f(x) = +1
(written on the whiteboard) left ≠ right → limit does not exist
(written on the whiteboard) (1)/(x^2) to infty : no finite limit
say: A question students always ask: does every function have a limit? No. Look at f of x equals the absolute value of x, divided by x. For any negative x, that's negative one. Approach zero from the left, and the function is stuck at negative one.

For any positive x, it's positive one. So approaching from the right gives a different answer. The little minus and plus signs on the zero mean from the left and from the right. These are called one sided limits.

The rule: the limit exists only if both one sided limits exist and agree. Here they disagree, so the limit does not exist. That's a jump. A function that blows up to infinity, like one over x squared at zero, also has no limit as a number. We just write that it goes to infinity.

slides.h: Continuity: no holes, jumps, or blow-ups
pts: Continuous at a: f(a) exists, the limit exists, and they match
Intermediate Value Theorem: a continuous function crossing from − to + must hit 0
Bisection: halve the interval again and again
say: A function is continuous at a point if you can draw through it without lifting your pen. Formally, three things must be true: f of a exists, the limit exists, and they're equal. These three pictures show the three ways that fails: a hole, where the point is missing or misplaced, a jump, and an infinite blow up called an asymptote.

Continuous functions have a very useful property called the intermediate value theorem. Look at f of x equals x cubed minus x minus one. At x equals one it's negative one. At x equals two it's positive five. Since it's continuous, it must cross zero somewhere in between. There has to be a root.

And that gives us an algorithm that computers actually use: bisection. Check the midpoint, one point five. It's positive, so the root is between one and one point five. Check one point two five, it's negative, so the root is between one point two five and one point five. Each step cuts the interval in half, and after about twenty steps you know the root, one point three two four seven, to six decimal places. That's math turning directly into code.
Part two. Derivatives.

slides.h: The derivative: zooming in until a curve looks straight
say: Here's the problem. Slope is rise over run, and that needs two points. But we want the slope of the curve y equals x squared at one point, x equals three. So we cheat: take a second point a distance h away, and draw the line through both. That's called a secant line. With h equals two, the second point is at five, twenty five, so the slope is twenty five minus nine, over two: eight.
Move the second point closer. With h equals one, the slope is seven.

With h equals one half, it's six and a half. Do the algebra in general: the slope is three plus h, all squared, minus nine, all over h. Expand, and you get six h plus h squared, over h, which is six plus h.

Now let h shrink to zero. That's a limit! Six plus h heads to six. So the slope of the tangent line at x equals three is exactly six. That's the derivative: f prime of x is the limit, as h goes to zero, of f of x plus h minus f of x, over h. It's the instantaneous rate of change. Notice we needed limits, because plugging in h equals zero directly gives zero over zero.

slides.h: Worked example: a derivative from the definition
pts: (written on the whiteboard) f(x)=(1)/(x)
(written on the whiteboard) f'(x)=lim_hto 0(f(x+h)-f(x))/(h)
(written on the whiteboard) =lim_hto 0frac(1)/(x+h)-(1)/(x)h
(written on the whiteboard) =lim_hto 0(x-(x+h))/(x (x+h) h)
(written on the whiteboard) =lim_hto 0(-h)/(x (x+h) h)
(written on the whiteboard) =lim_hto 0(-1)/(x (x+h))
(written on the whiteboard) f'(x) = -(1)/(x^2)
(written on the whiteboard) f'(2) = -(1)/(4)
say: Let's use the definition ourselves, on a new function: f of x equals one over x. Write the definition first: the limit as h goes to zero of f of x plus h, minus f of x, over h. Substitute our function: one over x plus h, minus one over x, all over h.

Combine the two fractions on top over a common denominator, x times x plus h. The numerator becomes x minus x plus h, which is just negative h. So the whole thing is negative h over x times x plus h times h.

The h's cancel, which is exactly what removes the zero over zero. Now let h go to zero: we get negative one over x squared. At x equals two, the slope is negative one quarter, and you can see that tangent line on the graph, gently sloping downward.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) f'(x)\ =\ y'\ =\ (dy)/(dx)\ =\ (d)/(dx) f(x)
(written on the whiteboard) all mean: the slope of f at x
(written on the whiteboard) f' : short and handy
(written on the whiteboard) (dy)/(dx) : tiny change in y over tiny change in x
(written on the whiteboard) (d)/(dx) : an instruction, "differentiate"
(written on the whiteboard) (dy)/(dx) = (dy)/(du)cdot(du)/(dx) (looks like cancelling!)
say: Before we go on, let's clear up the notation, because textbooks mix it freely. If y equals f of x, its derivative can be written f prime of x, y prime, d y d x, or d d x of f of x. These all mean exactly the same thing: the slope of f at x.

Prime notation, from Lagrange, is short and handy. Leibniz notation, d y over d x, reminds you it came from a tiny change in y over a tiny change in x. And d over d x, on its own, is an instruction: take the derivative of whatever comes next, with respect to x.
One warning. d y d x is not really a fraction, because it's a limit. But in the chain rule it behaves like one, which is exactly why Leibniz's notation won.

slides.h: Shortcut rules (so you never use the limit by hand again)
say: Computing limits every time would be painful, so we derive rules once and reuse them. The power rule: the derivative of x to the n is n times x to the n minus one. So x to the fifth becomes five x to the fourth, and our x squared becomes two x, which is six at x equals three, matching what we found. Constants just come along for the ride. Derivatives of sums are sums of derivatives. Products need the product rule: derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times the derivative of the second. Quotients have the quotient rule: low d high minus high d low, over low squared. And the most important one, the chain rule, for functions inside functions. Let's look at that one more closely.

slides.h: Worked example: product and quotient rules
pts: (written on the whiteboard) y = x^2 sin x
(written on the whiteboard) (fg)' = f'g + fg'
(written on the whiteboard) y' = 2x sin x + x^2cos x
(written on the whiteboard) y = (x)/(x^2+1)
(written on the whiteboard) (f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/(g^2)
(written on the whiteboard) (fg)' neq f' g'
(written on the whiteboard) test f = g = x: f'g' = 1, but (x^2)' = 2x
say: Let's actually use the product rule. y equals x squared times sine x. Call the first factor f, x squared, and the second g, sine x. The rule: f prime g plus f g prime.
f prime is two x, so the first term is two x sine x. g prime is cosine x, so the second term is x squared cosine x. Add them.
Now a quotient: x over x squared plus one. Low d high, minus high d low, over low squared. The low is x squared plus one, d high is one. The high is x, d low is two x.

And the most common mistake on every first exam: the derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives. Test it on x times x. The product of the derivatives is one times one, which is one. But x times x is x squared, whose derivative is two x. Wrong.

pts: Function inside a function: y = sin(3x²)
Inner rate × outer rate
Gears: if A turns B 3× as fast, and B turns C 2× as fast, C turns 6× as fast as A
say: The chain rule handles composition, a function inside another function. Take y equals sine of three x squared. There's an inner function, u equals three x squared, and an outer function, y equals sine of u.
Each stage has its own rate. The inner one changes at six x. The outer one changes at cosine of u. The chain rule says: multiply them. So d y d x equals cosine of three x squared, times six x.

Think of gears. If gear A turns gear B three times as fast, and B turns C twice as fast, then C turns six times as fast as A. Rates multiply through the chain. You'll use this constantly, including in machine learning, where training a neural network is the chain rule applied millions of times. That algorithm is called backpropagation.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) y = (3x^2+1)^5
(written on the whiteboard) inside: u = 3x^2+1,  outside: y = u^5
(written on the whiteboard) (dy)/(du) = 5u^4
(written on the whiteboard) (du)/(dx) = 6x
(written on the whiteboard) (dy)/(dx) = (dy)/(du)cdot(du)/(dx) = 5u^4cdot 6x
(written on the whiteboard) (dy)/(dx) = 30x (3x^2+1)^4
(written on the whiteboard) at x=1: 30cdot 1cdot 4^4 = 30cdot 256 = 7680
say: Let's differentiate y equals three x squared plus one, all to the fifth power. Don't expand it! Instead, name the inside: u equals three x squared plus one. Then y is just u to the fifth.
Find each rate separately. The outer rate, d y d u, is five u to the fourth. The inner rate, d u d x, is six x.
The chain rule says multiply them. Five u to the fourth times six x. Now put u back in terms of x: thirty x times three x squared plus one, to the fourth.

Let's get a number. At x equals one, the inside is four, four to the fourth is two hundred fifty six, and thirty times two hundred fifty six is seven thousand six hundred eighty. Expanding the fifth power by hand would have taken a page. The chain rule took three lines.

pts: (sin x)′ = cos x  ·  (cos x)′ = −sin x
(eˣ)′ = eˣ — its own slope
(ln x)′ = 1/x
say: Some derivatives you just memorize. Look at the sine wave on top. At zero it's climbing steeply, slope one. At pi over two it's flat at the peak, slope zero. At pi it's falling, slope negative one. Plot those slopes on the bottom and you trace out the cosine wave. So the derivative of sine is cosine.

The derivative of cosine is negative sine. This pair is why sine waves are everywhere in electrical engineering: differentiate a sine wave and you get another sine wave of the same frequency, just shifted.

The exponential function, e to the x, is the only function that's its own derivative. Its slope at every point equals its height. That's why it describes anything whose growth is proportional to its size, like populations, compound interest, and, with a negative sign, a capacitor discharging.
And the natural log, ln x, has derivative one over x.
Part three. What can you do with derivatives? A lot.

pts: Throw a ball up at 20 m/s:  s(t) = −4.9t² + 20t
a(t) = v′(t) = −9.8 m/s² (gravity)
Top of flight: v = 0 → t = 2.04 s, height 20.4 m
say: Here's the classic example. Throw a ball straight up at twenty meters per second. Its height is s of t equals negative four point nine t squared plus twenty t.
Velocity is the derivative of position. Using the power rule: negative nine point eight t plus twenty.
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity: a constant negative nine point eight meters per second squared. That's gravity.

Where is the ball highest? At the top it stops for an instant, so the velocity is zero. Solve negative nine point eight t plus twenty equals zero: t is about two point zero four seconds. Plug back in: the height is about twenty point four meters. Look at the three graphs lined up. The slope of each graph is the height of the next one down.

slides.h: Linear approximation: the tangent line as a shortcut
pts: Near a point, a curve ≈ its tangent line
f(x) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)(x − a)
say: Zoom in far enough on any smooth curve and it looks like a straight line, its tangent line. So near a point, we can replace a complicated function with a simple line.
The formula: f of x is approximately f of a, plus f prime of a times x minus a.

Example: estimate the square root of four point one without a calculator. We know the square root of four is two, and the derivative of root x is one over two root x, which is one quarter at x equals four. So root four point one is about two plus one quarter of point one, which is two point zero two five. The true value is two point zero two four eight five. Very close! Engineers use this idea constantly. In electronics, transistors are wildly nonlinear, but for small signals we replace them with their tangent line. That's called small signal analysis, and it's how amplifiers are designed.

pts: Always true: x² + y² = 100
Differentiate in time: 2x·x′ + 2y·y′ = 0
y′ = −0.75 ft/s (top slides down)
say: Related rates problems connect how fast different quantities change. A ten foot ladder leans against a wall, and the bottom slides away at one foot per second. How fast is the top sliding down when the bottom is six feet from the wall? First, write an equation that's always true: x squared plus y squared equals one hundred, by Pythagoras. Then differentiate both sides with respect to time, using the chain rule: two x times d x d t, plus two y times d y d t, equals zero. Why do d x d t and d y d t appear? Because x and y both change with time. y squared is a function of y, and y is a function of t, so the chain rule multiplies by d y d t. This step is called implicit differentiation. When x is six, y is eight. Plug in: d y d t equals negative x times d x d t over y, which is negative six over eight, or negative point seven five feet per second. The negative sign means the top is moving down. The recipe always works: relate the quantities, differentiate with respect to time, then plug in numbers last.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) Given: dr/dt = 2 cm/s.  Find dA/dt when r = 5
(written on the whiteboard) A = pi r^2
(written on the whiteboard) (dA)/(dt) = 2pi r (dr)/(dt)
(written on the whiteboard) = 2pi (5)(2)
(written on the whiteboard) (dA)/(dt) = 20pi approx 62.8\ mathrmcm^2/s
say: Here's another related rates problem, worked from scratch. A stone drops into a pond and a circular ripple spreads out. The radius grows at two centimeters per second. How fast is the area growing when the radius is five centimeters?

Step one: write an equation that's always true. The area of a circle is pi r squared. Step two: differentiate both sides with respect to time. Using the chain rule, d A d t equals two pi r, times d r d t.

Step three, and only now, plug in the numbers: two pi times five times two. That's twenty pi, about sixty three square centimeters per second. Notice the area grows faster as the ripple gets bigger, even though the radius grows at a steady rate.

pts: Maximum or minimum → slope is zero
Box from a 12×12 sheet: V = x(12 − 2x)²
Best box: 2 × 8 × 8 = 128 in³
say: Engineering is full of optimization: least material, lowest power, maximum range. Calculus finds the best design, because at a maximum or minimum, the curve is momentarily flat. The derivative is zero.

Example: take a twelve by twelve inch sheet of cardboard, cut an x by x square from each corner, and fold up the sides into an open box. The base is twelve minus two x on each side, and the height is x. So the volume is x times twelve minus two x, squared.
Take the derivative and factor it: twelve minus two x, times twelve minus six x. Set it to zero: x equals six, which gives a flat box with no volume, or x equals two.

So cut two inch squares. The box is two by eight by eight, for a volume of one hundred twenty eight cubic inches. The graph confirms it: the volume peaks exactly where the slope is zero. One more habit: when x is limited to a range, here between zero and six, also check the two endpoints. Both give zero volume, so x equals two really is the best.

slides.h: Worked example: the biggest pen by a river
pts: (written on the whiteboard) 100 m of fence, river on one side.
(written on the whiteboard) Maximize the area.
(written on the whiteboard) A(x) = x (100-2x) = 100x - 2x^2
(written on the whiteboard) A'(x) = 100 - 4x
(written on the whiteboard) 100 - 4x = 0 Rightarrow x = 25
(written on the whiteboard) 25 times 50 = 1250\ mathrmm^2
(written on the whiteboard) check: A''(x) = -4 < 0 so it's a maximum
say: Let's do a full optimization problem on the board. You have one hundred meters of fence to build a rectangular pen along a straight river. The river side needs no fence. What dimensions give the largest area?
Draw it. Call the two sides that touch the river x. The fence covers x, plus x, plus the far side, so the far side is one hundred minus two x. The area is x times one hundred minus two x.
At the maximum, the slope is zero. The derivative is one hundred minus four x. Set it equal to zero, and x equals twenty five.

So the sides are twenty five meters and the far side is fifty meters, for an area of twelve hundred fifty square meters. Check that it's a maximum: the second derivative is negative four, so the curve bends downward. It's a peak, not a valley.

slides.h: Curve sketching: reading a function from its derivatives
pts: f ′ > 0: rising · f ′ < 0: falling
f ′ = 0: possible max or min
f ′′ > 0: cupped up (min) · f ′′ < 0: cupped down (max)
f ′′ changes sign: inflection point
say: The derivative tells you the shape of a graph without plotting a single point. Where f prime is positive, the function is rising. Where it's negative, it's falling.

Where f prime is zero, the graph is flat: a possible peak or valley. For f of x equals x cubed minus three x, f prime is three x squared minus three, which is zero at x equals plus and minus one. But careful: a zero slope doesn't guarantee a peak or a valley. x cubed is flat at zero and keeps rising straight through it. So we need one more test.

The second derivative tells you which way the curve bends. Here f double prime is six x. At x equals negative one it's negative, so the curve is cupped downward: a local maximum, at height two. At x equals one it's positive, cupped upward: a local minimum, at negative two.
And where the second derivative changes sign, at x equals zero, the curve switches its bend. That's called an inflection point.

slides.h: Newton's method: how calculators find roots
pts: Guess → follow the tangent line to zero → repeat
√2: 1 → 1.5 → 1.41667 → 1.414216 (correct digits double each step)
say: How does a calculator compute the square root of two? Often with Newton's method, which uses tangent lines. Start with a guess, follow the tangent line down to where it hits zero, and use that as your next guess.
The formula is: the next x equals the current x minus f of x over f prime of x.

To find root two, solve x squared minus two equals zero. Start at one. The next guess is one minus negative one over two, which is one point five. Then one point four one six six seven. Then one point four one four two one six, which is already correct to six digits. Each step roughly doubles the number of correct digits. Bisection, from earlier, is slower but never fails. Newton's method is fast but needs a decent starting guess. Choosing between reliable and fast is a trade off you'll make again and again.
Part four. Integrals.

pts: Approximate area with rectangles
More, thinner rectangles → better answer
Limit of infinitely many → the integral ∫
say: How do you find the area under the curve y equals x squared, from zero to two? There's no formula from geometry for that shape. So we approximate it with rectangles. Four rectangles, each half a unit wide, with each height taken from the curve at the rectangle's right edge, give a total area of three point seven five. That's too big, because the rectangles poke above the curve.
Use eight thinner rectangles, and the total drops to about three point one nine. Closer.

With thirty two rectangles, we get about two point seven nine. As the number of rectangles goes to infinity, the sum approaches the exact area, eight thirds, about two point six six seven. That limit is the definition of the definite integral. The integral sign really does mean sum: a sum of infinitely many infinitely thin rectangles.

pts: Antiderivative F: a function whose derivative is f
∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a)
∫₀² x² dx = [x³/3]₀² = 8/3 exactly
Distance = ∫ speed dt
say: Adding up infinitely many rectangles sounds impossible to do by hand. Here's the miracle that makes it easy. First, an antiderivative of f is a function F whose derivative is f. Run the derivative backwards.
The fundamental theorem of calculus says: the integral of f from a to b equals F of b minus F of a. Find an antiderivative, evaluate at the two ends, and subtract.

Let's check our rectangle problem. An antiderivative of x squared is x cubed over three, because its derivative is x squared. Evaluate from zero to two: eight thirds minus zero. Exactly eight thirds, the number our rectangles were creeping toward.

Here's what it means physically. If your speed is three t meters per second, the distance you travel in six seconds is the area under the speed graph. The antiderivative is three halves t squared. At six seconds that's fifty four meters. The speedometer and the odometer, the derivative and the integral, are two sides of the same coin. That's why it's called fundamental.

slides.h: Why '+ C'? Indefinite vs definite integrals
pts: (written on the whiteboard) (d)/(dx) (x^3)/(3) = x^2
(written on the whiteboard) (d)/(dx)((x^3)/(3) + 5) = x^2
(written on the whiteboard) int x^2 dx = (x^3)/(3) + C
(written on the whiteboard) int_0^2 x^2 dx = ((8)/(3) + C) - (0 + C) = (8)/(3)
(written on the whiteboard) indefinite → a family of functions (+ C)
(written on the whiteboard) definite → a number (an area)
say: Every student asks where the plus C comes from. Differentiate x cubed over three, and you get x squared. But add five, or subtract seven, and the derivative is still x squared, because a constant has slope zero.

So going backwards, we can't know which constant was there. The answer is a whole family of curves, each shifted up or down, all with the same slope at every x. We write the family as x cubed over three, plus C.

The d x at the end means: with respect to x. It's the width of those thin rectangles. Now a definite integral, from zero to two. The C appears at both ends, and cancels when we subtract. That's why definite integrals never need it.
So remember: an indefinite integral, with no limits, is a function, really a family of functions, so it needs plus C. A definite integral, with limits, is a number, an area.

slides.h: Worked example: an exact area in three lines
pts: (written on the whiteboard) int_0^2 (3x^2 + 2x) dx
(written on the whiteboard) F(x) = x^3 + x^2
(written on the whiteboard) check: F'(x) = 3x^2 + 2x
(written on the whiteboard) = F(2) - F(0) = (8 + 4) - 0
(written on the whiteboard) = 12
say: Let's use the fundamental theorem on a fresh example. Find the area under y equals three x squared plus two x, from zero to two.

First, find an antiderivative, term by term, using the power rule backwards. Three x squared comes from x cubed, and two x comes from x squared. So F of x is x cubed plus x squared. Check it: the derivative is three x squared plus two x.

Now evaluate at the top and the bottom and subtract. At two: eight plus four, which is twelve. At zero: zero. So the area is exactly twelve. That shaded region would take thousands of rectangles to approximate, and we got it exactly in three lines.

slides.h: u-substitution: the chain rule in reverse
slides.code:
∫ 2x·cos(x²) dx

let u = x²   →   du = 2x dx

= ∫ cos(u) du
= sin(u) + C
= sin(x²) + C

check: d/dx sin(x²) = cos(x²)·2x  ✓
say: Not every integral is a simple power. A common trick is substitution, which is the chain rule run backwards. Look at the integral of two x times cosine of x squared. The inside function is x squared, and its derivative, two x, is sitting right there. So let u equal x squared. Then d u equals two x d x, and the whole integral becomes the integral of cosine u d u. That's sine u, plus a constant. Put x back in: sine of x squared, plus C. Always check by differentiating. The derivative of sine of x squared is cosine of x squared, times two x. It matches.

And here's an everyday engineering integral. On the right is the current drawn from a phone battery: two amps for half an hour, then one amp for half an hour. The total charge used is the integral of current over time, which is just the area under this graph. Two times one half, plus one times one half: one point five amp hours, or fifteen hundred milliamp hours. That's exactly the unit printed on every battery you own.

slides.big: Derivative = rate right now. Integral = total over time. The Fundamental Theorem says they undo each other.
say: Let's wrap up. A limit tells you where a function is heading. The derivative is the instantaneous rate of change, the slope of the tangent line, built from a limit. Derivatives find velocities, approximations, maximums and minimums. The integral adds up infinitely many tiny pieces to find areas and totals. And the fundamental theorem of calculus says derivatives and integrals undo each other. Every later course will use these tools, so if anything felt shaky, rewatch that section and work the examples yourself with pencil and paper. Next up, Calculus two. See you there.

L02_math150b.title: Calculus II
L02_math150b.file: MATH-150B Calculus II/Lecture - MATH 150B Calculus II.mp4

say: Welcome to Calculus two. In Calculus one, we learned what derivatives and integrals are. In Calculus two, we get good at integrals, we use them to compute real quantities like volume and work, and then we take a fascinating detour into infinite sums, which turn out to be how your calculator computes sine, cosine and e to the x. Let's go.

slides.h: Where Calculus II shows up in engineering
pts: Volumes, work, energy: tanks, springs, capacitors
Series: how calculators and computers evaluate sin, cos, eˣ
Euler's formula → phasors, the language of AC circuits
say: Here's why this course matters. Engineers compute volumes, like how much water a tank like this holds. They compute work and energy, like the energy stored in a spring or a capacitor. All of those are integrals.
Your calculator, and every computer math library, evaluates functions like sine and e to the x using polynomials built from infinite series. You'll see exactly how by the end of this lecture.

And infinite series give us Euler's formula, e to the i theta equals cosine theta plus i sine theta. That one formula is the foundation of how electrical engineers analyze AC circuits and signals. So this course quietly sets up half of your later degree.
Part one. Integration techniques. Integration is harder than differentiation, because there's no product rule or chain rule that always works. Instead, we have a toolbox.

slides.h: Integration by parts: the product rule in reverse
slides.code:
∫ u dv = u·v − ∫ v du

Example:  ∫ x·eˣ dx
  u  = x      dv = eˣ dx
  du = dx     v  = eˣ

= x·eˣ − ∫ eˣ dx
= x·eˣ − eˣ + C

Pick u by LIATE:
Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic,
Trig, Exponential
say: The first tool is integration by parts. It comes from the product rule, run backwards, and it says the integral of u d v equals u times v, minus the integral of v d u. The idea is to trade an integral you can't do for one you can. Example: the integral of x times e to the x. Choose u equals x, because its derivative is simpler, just one. Then d v is e to the x d x, so v is e to the x. Plug in: x e to the x, minus the integral of e to the x, which gives x e to the x minus e to the x, plus C. To choose u, a handy rule is LIATE: logs first, then inverse trig, then algebraic, then trig, then exponentials. Pick whichever comes first in that list as u. You'll use this exact technique in signals and systems to compute Laplace and Fourier transforms.

slides.h: Worked example: parts with a logarithm
pts: (written on the whiteboard) int x ln x dx
(written on the whiteboard) LIATE: log first, so u = ln x,  dv = x dx
(written on the whiteboard) du = (1)/(x) dx,   v = (x^2)/(2)
(written on the whiteboard) = (x^2)/(2)ln x - int (x^2)/(2)cdot(1)/(x) dx
(written on the whiteboard) = (x^2)/(2)ln x - int (x)/(2) dx
(written on the whiteboard) = (x^2)/(2)ln x - (x^2)/(4) + C
(written on the whiteboard) from 1 to e:  ((e^2)/(2)-(e^2)/(4) ) - (0-(1)/(4) ) = (e^2+1)/(4) approx 2.097
say: Let's do one where the choice of u really matters: the integral of x times the natural log of x. LIATE says logs come first, so u is ln x. That means d v is x d x.

Now apply the formula: u v minus the integral of v d u. That's x squared over two times ln x, minus the integral of x squared over two times one over x. Look what happened: the log is gone, and x squared over x is just x.

The last integral is easy: x squared over four. So the answer is x squared over two ln x, minus x squared over four, plus C. As a numerical check, from one to e it comes out to e squared plus one, over four, about two point one. If we'd picked u equals x instead, we'd have needed the integral of ln x, which is harder. The right choice of u makes the problem collapse.

slides.h: Trig integrals — and why your outlet says 120 volts
pts: Half-angle identity: sin²t = ½ − ½cos 2t
Average of sin² over a cycle = ½
RMS voltage: V_rms = V_peak / √2
US outlet: 120 V rms → peaks at ≈ 170 V
say: Integrals of powers of sine and cosine use trig identities. The most useful is the half angle identity: sine squared t equals one half minus one half cosine two t.

Integrate that over a full cycle. The cosine part averages to zero, so the average of sine squared is exactly one half. You can see it in the graph: the blue sine squared wave bounces between zero and one, centered on one half.

Here's why engineers care. The power delivered by an AC voltage depends on the voltage squared. So the effective voltage, called R M S for root mean square, is the square root of the average of the square. For a sine wave, that's the peak times the square root of one half, which is the peak divided by root two.

That's why a U S wall outlet labeled one hundred twenty volts actually swings up to about one hundred seventy volts at its peak. One twenty times root two is about one seventy. That label comes straight from this integral.

slides.h: Trig substitution: proving the area of a circle
pts: √(r² − x²) → let x = r sin θ
Then √(r² − r²sin²θ) = r cos θ
Area = 2r²∫cos²θ dθ = πr²
say: When you see a square root like root of r squared minus x squared, substitute x equals r sine theta. Here's a beautiful use: proving the area of a circle.

Slice the circle into thin vertical strips. A strip at position x has height two times root r squared minus x squared. With x equals r sine theta, that square root becomes r cosine theta, because one minus sine squared is cosine squared.

The integral turns into two r squared times the integral of cosine squared, and using the half angle identity from the last slide, it comes out to exactly pi r squared. The formula you memorized in grade school, proved with calculus.

slides.h: Partial fractions: break a fraction into simple pieces
pts: Factor the bottom, split into simple fractions
Plug in the roots to find A and B instantly
Used constantly in circuits & signals (inverse Laplace transforms)
say: For rational functions, one polynomial over another, we use partial fractions. Take one over x plus one times x plus two. Write it as A over x plus one, plus B over x plus two. Multiply through by the denominator: one equals A times x plus two, plus B times x plus one. Now a shortcut: plug in x equals negative one, and the B term vanishes, leaving one equals A. Plug in x equals negative two, and you get one equals negative B. So the integral splits into one over x plus one, minus one over x plus two, and each piece integrates to a natural log. Remember this one, because in signals and systems, the response of almost every circuit comes out as a fraction like this, and partial fractions is how you turn it back into a time signal. Two cautions for exams. The plug in shortcut works when the bottom splits into different linear factors and the top has a lower degree. If the top's degree is as big as the bottom's, do long division first. And a repeated factor, like x plus one squared, needs one term for each power: A over x plus one, plus B over x plus one squared.

slides.h: Improper integrals: area out to infinity
pts: Replace ∞ with b, then take the limit
∫ 1/x² from 1 to ∞ = 1 (finite!)
∫ 1/x from 1 to ∞ = ∞ (diverges)
Key in probability and Laplace transforms
say: Can an infinitely long region have a finite area? Surprisingly, yes. An improper integral has an infinite limit. To handle it, replace infinity with a variable b, integrate, then let b go to infinity.
For one over x squared from one to infinity, the antiderivative is negative one over x. From one to b, that's one minus one over b. As b goes to infinity, that heads to one. Finite area!
But one over x, which looks almost the same, has antiderivative ln x, which grows forever. Its area is infinite. The difference is how fast the curve drops.

You'll use improper integrals all the time. In probability, the total area under a probability curve, over the whole number line, must equal one. And the Laplace transform, the main tool of signals and systems, is an integral from zero to infinity.

slides.h: Worked example: a decaying signal has finite area
pts: (written on the whiteboard) int_0^infty e^-2t dt
(written on the whiteboard) = lim_btoinftyint_0^b e^-2t dt
(written on the whiteboard) = lim_btoinfty [-(1)/(2)e^-2t ]_0^b
(written on the whiteboard) = lim_btoinfty (-(1)/(2)e^-2b + (1)/(2) )
(written on the whiteboard) e^-2bto 0
(written on the whiteboard) = (1)/(2)
say: Here's an improper integral you'll meet again in signals and systems: the integral of e to the minus two t, from zero to infinity. This curve decays like a capacitor discharging, and we want the total area under it, all the way out.
Step one: replace infinity with b and write a limit. Step two: the antiderivative of e to the minus two t is negative one half e to the minus two t. Evaluate from zero to b.

Now let b go to infinity. E to the minus two b shrinks to zero, so the whole limit is one half. An infinitely long region, with an area of exactly one half. This exact calculation, with a general s in place of the two, is the Laplace transform of a constant.

slides.h: When there is no formula: numerical integration
pts: Some integrals have no elementary antiderivative
Trapezoid rule: connect the dots with lines
Simpson's rule: fit parabolas — far more accurate
This is what computers actually do
say: Here's a secret: many integrals have no formula at all. The integral of e to the minus x squared, which is the bell curve you'll meet in probability, can't be written with ordinary functions.
So we compute it numerically. The trapezoid rule splits the area into slices and connects the tops with straight lines. With just four slices, we get point seven four two nine eight.

Simpson's rule fits little parabolas instead of straight lines. With the same four slices, it gets point seven four six eight six. The true value is point seven four six eight two, so Simpson is already correct to four decimal places.
This is how engineering software, from circuit simulators to MATLAB, really computes integrals. Not with clever antiderivatives, but with smart sums.

slides.h: Which technique? A checklist for any integral
pts: (written on the whiteboard) 1. basic form? int x^5 dx, int e^x dx to just integrate
(written on the whiteboard) 2. inside + its derivative? int 2xcos(x^2)dx to u-sub
(written on the whiteboard) 3. product of two kinds? int x e^x dx to by parts
(written on the whiteboard) 4. powers of sin, cos? → identities
(written on the whiteboard) 5. sqrta^2 - x^2 ? to x = asintheta
(written on the whiteboard) 6. polynomial / polynomial? → partial fractions
(written on the whiteboard) 7. nothing works? → numerical (Simpson)
say: The question every Calculus two student asks: how do I know which technique to use? Here's the checklist I give my students. Go down it in order. One: is it a basic form you already know, like a power, e to the x, or sine? Then just integrate.

Two: is an inside function sitting there with its own derivative beside it? Use u substitution. Three: is it a product of two different kinds of function, like x times e to the x? Use integration by parts, with LIATE to pick u.
Four: powers of sine and cosine? Use identities, like the half angle formula. Five: a square root of a squared minus x squared? Trig substitution. Six: one polynomial over another? Partial fractions.
And seven: if nothing works, the integral may have no formula at all. Compute it numerically. With practice you'll spot the right tool in seconds, but this list never fails you on an exam.
Part two. Applications. Integrals add up tiny pieces, so whenever a quantity is made of pieces that vary, you integrate.

slides.h: Volumes of revolution: the disk method
pts: Spin a curve around an axis → a solid
Slice into disks: area π·r(x)²
V = π∫ r(x)² dx
y = √x from 0 to 4: V = π∫x dx = 8π ≈ 25.1
say: Spin a curve around an axis and you sweep out a solid, like a vase on a pottery wheel. Many real parts are made this way, on a lathe.
To find the volume, slice the solid into thin disks. A disk at position x has radius equal to the height of the curve, so its face has area pi times r squared.
Add up all the disks: the volume is pi times the integral of r of x squared, d x.

Example: spin y equals root x from zero to four. The radius squared is just x, so the volume is pi times the integral of x from zero to four, which is pi times eight, about twenty five point one cubic units. Tank designers, engine designers and anyone shaping parts on a lathe use exactly this.

slides.h: Worked example: proving the cone's volume formula
pts: (written on the whiteboard) Cone: radius R, height H
(written on the whiteboard) edge: y = (R)/(H) x
(written on the whiteboard) V = int_0^H pi ((R)/(H)x )^2 dx
(written on the whiteboard) = (pi R^2)/(H^2)int_0^H x^2 dx
(written on the whiteboard) = (pi R^2)/(H^2)cdot(H^3)/(3)
(written on the whiteboard) V = (1)/(3)pi R^2 H
say: Where does the cone formula, one third pi R squared H, come from? Let's derive it. Lay the cone on its side. Its edge is a straight line through the origin, rising to radius R at length H, so its equation is y equals R over H times x.
Slice it into thin disks. A disk at position x has radius R over H times x, so its volume is pi times that radius squared, times d x. Add them up from zero to H.

Pull the constants out: pi R squared over H squared, times the integral of x squared. That integral is x cubed over three, which at H is H cubed over three. Two powers of H cancel, and we're left with one third pi R squared H. The cone holds exactly one third of the cylinder around it.

slides.h: Work and energy: springs and capacitors
pts: Work = ∫ F dx (force can change along the way)
Spring: F = kx → W = ½kx²
k = 200 N/m, stretch 10 cm → W = 1 J
Same math: capacitor energy = ½CV²
say: Work is force times distance, but only when the force is constant. When the force changes, you integrate: work equals the integral of F d x.
A spring pushes back harder the more you stretch it: F equals k x. Integrate from zero to x and you get one half k x squared. Geometrically, it's the area of the triangle under the force line.
Example: a spring with k equals two hundred newtons per meter, stretched ten centimeters. The work is one half times two hundred times point one squared, which is one joule.

And here's the connection to electronics. Charging a capacitor is the same math. The voltage grows in proportion to the charge, so the energy stored is one half C V squared. Same integral, same triangle, different physics. Once you see these patterns, a lot of engineering becomes the same few ideas reused.
Part three. Infinite series. Can you add up infinitely many numbers and get a finite answer?

pts: Geometric series: a + ar + ar² + … = a / (1 − r) if |r| < 1
Ball dropped 10 m, bounces to 60%: total distance = 10 + 2·(6/0.4) = 40 m
say: Look at this square. Shade half of it. Then half of what's left, a quarter. Then an eighth, a sixteenth, and so on forever. You never run out of square, and you never go past it either. So one half plus one quarter plus one eighth, forever, equals exactly one.

That's a geometric series, where each term is the previous one times a fixed ratio r. If the ratio is between negative one and one, the sum is the first term divided by one minus r. Here that's one half over one minus one half, which is one. Notice how much easier the formula is than adding forever.

Real example. Drop a ball from ten meters, and each bounce reaches sixty percent of the previous height. The total distance is the first ten meters down, plus twice each bounce height, up and down. The bounces form a geometric series: six, three point six, two point one six, and so on, summing to six over point four, which is fifteen. So the total is ten plus two times fifteen: forty meters, even though the ball bounces infinitely many times.

slides.h: Worked example: a repeating decimal is a geometric series
pts: (written on the whiteboard) 0.272727ldots = ?
(written on the whiteboard) = 0.27 + 0.0027 + 0.000027 + ldots
(written on the whiteboard) a = 0.27,  r = 0.01
(written on the whiteboard) |r| < 1, so the sum converges
(written on the whiteboard) S = (a)/(1-r) = (0.27)/(0.99) = (27)/(99)
(written on the whiteboard) = (3)/(11)
say: Here's a neat use of the geometric series formula. Write zero point two seven two seven repeating, forever, as a fraction. Split it into pieces: point two seven, plus point zero zero two seven, plus point zero zero zero zero two seven, and so on.
Each piece is the previous one times one hundredth. So it's geometric, with first term a equals point two seven and ratio r equals point zero one. The ratio is less than one, so it converges.

Use the formula, a over one minus r: point two seven over point nine nine, which is twenty seven over ninety nine, which reduces to three elevenths. Check it on a calculator: three divided by eleven is point two seven two seven, repeating. Every repeating decimal is a geometric series in disguise, which is why every repeating decimal is a fraction.

slides.h: But some sums blow up — testing convergence
pts: Terms shrinking to 0 is NOT enough
Harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … diverges
Use convergence tests
say: Here's the trap. The harmonic series, one plus one half plus one third plus one fourth and so on, has terms that shrink to zero. Yet the sum grows forever. Slowly, like the natural log of n: a hundred terms gives about five point two, a thousand terms gives about seven point five, but it never stops growing. Meanwhile, one plus a quarter plus a ninth, the sum of one over n squared, settles down to pi squared over six. A famous and surprising result.

So how do you know whether a series converges? We use tests. If the terms don't go to zero, it diverges, period. Geometric series converge when the ratio is less than one. P series, one over n to the p, converge when p is greater than one. The ratio test compares each term to the one before, so for n over two to the n the ratio heads to one half, and it converges. Comparison tests bound your series by one you already know. And alternating series, with signs flipping and terms shrinking, converge too. For example, one minus a half plus a third minus a quarter equals the natural log of two.

slides.h: Sequences vs series, and the ratio test
pts: (written on the whiteboard) sequence: (1)/(2),\ (1)/(4),\ (1)/(8),\ ldots  (a list)
(written on the whiteboard) series: (1)/(2)+(1)/(4)+(1)/(8)+ldots  (a sum)
(written on the whiteboard) sum (n)/(2^n)
(written on the whiteboard) fraca_n+1a_n = fracn+12^n+1cdot(2^n)/(n) = (n+1)/(2n)
(written on the whiteboard) to (1)/(2) < 1  so it converges
(written on the whiteboard) L < 1 converges,  L > 1 diverges
(written on the whiteboard) L = 1 : the test is silent!
(written on the whiteboard) sum(1)/(n) diverges,  sum(1)/(n^2) converges,  both give L = 1
say: First, two words students mix up. A sequence is a list of numbers: one half, one quarter, one eighth. A series is what you get when you add the list up. The sequence can go to zero while the series still diverges, like the harmonic series.
Now the ratio test, worked out. Take the sum of n over two to the n. Divide each term by the one before it: n plus one over two to the n plus one, times two to the n over n.
As n grows, n plus one over two n heads to one half. The rule: if that limit is less than one, the series converges. More than one, it diverges.

And here's the trap. If the limit equals exactly one, the test tells you nothing. The harmonic series gives one, and diverges. One over n squared also gives one, and converges. When you get one, switch to another test, like the p series or comparison test.

slides.h: Power series: a polynomial that never ends
pts: Works only inside the radius of convergence (|x| < 1)
More terms → better match, but only inside that interval
say: Now the big idea. What if the terms of a series contain x? Then the series is a function. Take the geometric series one plus x plus x squared plus x cubed and so on. By our formula, that equals one over one minus x.
But only when x is between negative one and one. That interval is called the interval of convergence, and half its width is the radius of convergence.

Look at the graph. Inside the green band, adding more terms makes the polynomial hug the true curve, in black, more and more closely. Outside the band, the polynomials fly off. A power series is like an infinitely long polynomial, and polynomials are easy for computers, because they only need multiplication and addition.

slides.h: Taylor series: how your calculator computes sin x
say: Taylor series let you write almost any smooth function as a power series. The recipe: match the function's value, slope, curvature, and every higher derivative at one point. For sine around zero, start with just the first term, x. That's the tangent line, the small angle approximation. It's good near zero, but drifts away quickly.
Add the next term, minus x cubed over three factorial. Now the curve bends back the right way and matches much farther out.
Add plus x to the fifth over five factorial, and it hugs the sine wave across nearly a full hump.

With the seventh degree term, it's accurate to the eye from about minus four to four. Let's test it numerically. Sine of point five: point five, minus point five cubed over six, plus point five to the fifth over one twenty. That gives point four seven nine four two seven. The true value is point four seven nine four two five five. Three terms, six correct digits.

This is genuinely how computers do it. A math library first uses symmetry to shrink the angle into a small range, then evaluates a short polynomial like this one. Similar series give e to the x as one plus x plus x squared over two factorial plus x cubed over three factorial and so on, and cosine as one minus x squared over two factorial plus x to the fourth over four factorial.

slides.h: The Taylor formula: where the factorials come from
pts: (written on the whiteboard) f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + (f''(a))/(2!)(x-a)^2 + (f'''(a))/(3!)(x-a)^3 + ldots
(written on the whiteboard) n-th term: fracf^(n)(a)n! (x-a)^n
(written on the whiteboard) x^3 to 3x^2 to 6x to 6 = 3!
(written on the whiteboard) divide by n! so the derivatives match
(written on the whiteboard) sin,\ cos,\ -sin,\ -cos,\ ldots at 0: 0,\ 1,\ 0,\ -1,\ ldots
(written on the whiteboard) sin x = x - (x^3)/(3!) + (x^5)/(5!) - ldots
say: Let's write the recipe as a formula, because it's on every exam. Around a point a, f of x equals f of a, plus f prime of a times x minus a, plus f double prime of a over two factorial, times x minus a squared, and so on. The n th term uses the n th derivative, divided by n factorial.

Why factorials? Differentiate x cubed three times: three x squared, then six x, then six, which is three factorial. Each power leaves a factorial behind when you differentiate it down to a constant. Dividing by n factorial cancels it, so every derivative of the polynomial matches the function exactly.

Now build sine around zero. Its derivatives repeat in a cycle: sine, cosine, minus sine, minus cosine. At zero, those are zero, one, zero, minus one. So only odd powers survive, with alternating signs, and that's exactly the series we just graphed.

slides.h: Worked example: computing e by hand
pts: (written on the whiteboard) f(x)=e^x:  f(0)=f ^prime(0)=f ^primeprime(0)=ldots=1
(written on the whiteboard) e^x = 1 + x + (x^2)/(2!) + (x^3)/(3!) + (x^4)/(4!) + ldots
(written on the whiteboard) e = 1 + 1 + (1)/(2) + (1)/(6) + (1)/(24) + (1)/(120) + ldots
(written on the whiteboard) = 2 to 2.5 to 2.667 to 2.708 to 2.717
(written on the whiteboard) true: e = 2.71828ldots
say: Let's use a Taylor series to compute the number e itself, the way a computer might. Every derivative of e to the x is e to the x, and at zero they all equal one. So the Taylor series around zero is one, plus x, plus x squared over two factorial, plus x cubed over three factorial, and so on.
Set x equal to one. Then e is one, plus one, plus one half, plus one sixth, plus one twenty fourth, plus one over one hundred twenty, and so on.

Add them up as decimals. One plus one is two. Plus point five is two point five. Plus point one six seven is two point six six seven. Plus point zero four two is two point seven zero eight. Plus point zero zero eight is two point seven one seven. The true value is two point seven one eight two eight. Six terms, already three correct decimals, and each new term adds about one more, because factorials grow so fast.

slides.h: Euler's formula: the bridge to electrical engineering
pts: Put iθ into the series for eˣ
Real terms → cos θ, imaginary terms → sin θ
e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ
A rotating arrow = a sine wave → phasors
say: Now something remarkable. Take the Taylor series for e to the x, and plug in an imaginary number, i theta, where i squared is negative one.
The powers of i cycle: i, negative one, negative i, one. Sort the terms, and all the real ones form exactly the series for cosine theta, and all the imaginary ones form the series for sine theta.
So e to the i theta equals cosine theta plus i sine theta. This is Euler's formula. Geometrically, e to the i theta is an arrow of length one, rotated by angle theta, on the complex plane.

Let theta increase with time, and the arrow spins around the circle, while its shadow on the horizontal axis traces out a cosine wave. That's the key insight behind phasors in your circuits course, where every sine wave voltage becomes a rotating arrow, and calculus turns into algebra. We'll come back to this many times.

slides.h: Polar coordinates: describing shapes by angle
pts: Point = (distance r, angle θ) instead of (x, y)
x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ
Antenna and microphone patterns are polar plots
say: One more tool. Some shapes are easier to describe by angle and distance than by x and y. In polar coordinates, a point is given by its distance r from the origin and its angle theta. Converting is easy: x is r cosine theta, and y is r sine theta.

Here's where engineers see it. Microphones like this one are described by a polar pickup pattern. This one is a cardioid, a heart shape, with r equals one half times one plus cosine theta. Sound from the front, at zero degrees, gets full sensitivity. Sound from the back, at one hundred eighty degrees, gets zero. That's why a singer's monitor speaker is placed behind the microphone. Antenna engineers describe radiation patterns exactly the same way.

slides.big: Integrals add up pieces — volumes, work, energy. Series turn functions into polynomials computers can evaluate.
say: Let's recap. Integration techniques, by parts, trig identities, substitution and partial fractions, let you handle most integrals, and numerical methods handle the rest. Integrals compute real quantities: area, volume, work and energy, including RMS voltage and capacitor energy. Infinite series can converge to finite values, and convergence tests tell you when. Taylor series turn functions into polynomials, which is how computers evaluate them. And Euler's formula links exponentials to sines and cosines, which will power your circuits and signals courses. Next, we switch gears completely and learn to program. See you there.

L03_cpsc120.title: Introduction to Programming
L03_cpsc120.file: CPSC-120 Introduction to Programming/Lecture - CPSC 120 Introduction to Programming.mp4

say: Welcome to C P S C one twenty, Introduction to Programming. Every one of those blinking servers is running programs that people wrote, one line at a time. In this lecture, you'll learn how a computer actually runs code, and the five building blocks behind every program ever written: variables, decisions, loops, functions and collections of data. We'll use C plus plus, the language this course uses, but the ideas carry over to every language.

pts: A precise list of instructions
Computers do exactly what you say — not what you mean
Compiler: source code → machine code
say: A program is a precise list of instructions for a computer. The idea is older than electronics. In the eighteen forties, Ada Lovelace wrote what's often called the first computer program, an algorithm for Charles Babbage's mechanical Analytical Engine, which was never fully built.

In the nineteen forties, the first general purpose electronic computer, ENIAC, was programmed by a team of women who set thousands of switches and plugged cables by hand. Changing the program could take days. Here's the most important lesson they learned, which is still true: a computer does exactly what you tell it, not what you meant.

Today we write programs as text, called source code, in a language like C plus plus. A program called a compiler translates that text into machine code, the ones and zeros a C P U can execute. The compiler translates once, and then the processor runs billions of simple instructions every second.

pts: Created by Bjarne Stroustrup (1979–85) as "C with classes"
Fast, close to the hardware, yet high-level
Game engines, web browsers, databases, robotics, trading systems
Embedded C/C++ runs in cars, medical devices, appliances
say: Why C plus plus? It was created by Bjarne Stroustrup, pictured here, starting in nineteen seventy nine, as C with classes: the speed of the C language plus tools for organizing big programs. It gives you control over memory and hardware, which is why performance critical software is written in it. Most major game engines, the core of web browsers like Chrome and Firefox, databases, robotics software and high speed trading systems all rely on C plus plus. And its close cousin C runs inside the embedded computers in cars, medical devices and appliances. For a computer engineer, that closeness to the hardware is exactly the point. You'll write C for microcontrollers in later courses.

Here's the classic first program. The include line pulls in the input output library, so we can print. Every C plus plus program starts running at the function called main. Inside, s t d colon colon c out, with the two less than arrows, sends text to the screen. The backslash n is a newline. Return zero tells the operating system that the program finished successfully. Notice the details: curly braces group statements, and every statement ends with a semicolon. Leave one out and the compiler will refuse to build your program. To run it, you compile in a terminal with g plus plus, which produces an executable file, and then run that file. In this course, students do all of this on Linux, in a terminal, which is how professional developers work.

pts: A variable = a name + a type + a value
The type decides size and meaning of the bits
int: about ±2.1 billion (4 bytes)
Exceed it → overflow wraps to negative!
say: A variable is a named box in memory that holds a value. Every variable has a name, a type and a value.

The type tells the computer how many bytes to reserve and how to interpret the bits inside. An int holds whole numbers, a double holds decimals, a char holds one character, a bool holds true or false, and a string holds text.
An int is usually four bytes, thirty two bits, so it holds numbers from about negative two point one billion to positive two point one billion.

Go past the top and it wraps around to a large negative number. That's called overflow, and it's the same two's complement wheel you'll study in digital logic. It's not just a classroom problem: in two thousand fourteen, a video's view count on YouTube passed the maximum of a thirty two bit integer, and YouTube had to upgrade to sixty four bit counters.

pts: int / int throws away the fraction
% gives the remainder — great for clocks, even/odd, digits
Never compare doubles with ==
say: Arithmetic has a few traps. Seven divided by two, with both numbers as ints, gives three, not three point five. Integer division throws the fraction away. The percent sign is the modulo operator, which gives the remainder: seven mod two is one. These two operators together are incredibly useful. Here's an example: convert three thousand seven hundred twenty five seconds into hours, minutes and seconds. Hours: divide by thirty six hundred, giving one. Minutes: take the remainder after removing the hours, which is one hundred twenty five, and divide by sixty, giving two. Seconds: the total mod sixty, giving five. So it's one hour, two minutes, five seconds. Last trap: decimals are stored in binary, which can't represent point one exactly. So point one plus point two is actually point three zero zero zero, with a tiny error at the end. Never compare two doubles with double equals. Check whether they're close enough instead.

slides.h: The equals sign is not algebra
pts: (code on the board) int x = 5;
(code on the board) x = x + 1;      // x is now 6
(written on the whiteboard) read = as "becomes"
(code on the board) x += 3;         // same as x = x + 3
(code on the board) x++;            // same as x = x + 1
(code on the board) for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++)
(code on the board) int total;          // garbage!
(code on the board) total += 10;        // ??? + 10
(code on the board) int total = 0;      // always initialize
say: Here's the line that confuses every math student on day one: x equals x plus one. In algebra that's impossible. In C plus plus, the single equals sign is not a statement of fact. It's a command: compute the right side, then store the result in the box on the left.

So read it as: x becomes x plus one. The old value, five, is read first, one is added, and six is written back into the same box. Programmers do this so often that there are shortcuts. Plus equals adds to a variable. Plus plus adds exactly one.

That's what the i plus plus in a for loop means: step i up by one. Whether you write plus plus i or i plus plus doesn't matter on a line by itself. It only matters when the expression's value is used inside a bigger expression, which beginners should simply avoid.

One more trap. A variable you create but never give a value holds whatever bits were left in that memory. Here, total starts as garbage, so the sum is garbage too. The compiler may not even warn you. Always initialize: int total equals zero.

pts: if (condition) { … } else { … }
Comparisons: <  <=  >  >=  ==  !=
Combine with && (and), || (or), ! (not)
Order matters: check the strictest case first
say: Programs make decisions with if and else. If a condition is true, run one block. Otherwise, run another. Here's a flowchart for assigning a letter grade.

Conditions use comparison operators: less than, less than or equal, greater than, equal, and not equal. Careful: a single equals sign assigns a value, and double equals compares. Mixing them up is one of the most common beginner bugs.

You can combine conditions with and, written as two ampersands, or, written as two vertical bars, and not, written as an exclamation point. These are exactly the AND, OR and NOT gates you'll build in hardware. Software logic and hardware logic are the same logic.
And order matters. We check ninety or above first, then eighty. If we checked eighty first, a ninety five would get a B. An else if chain stops at the first true condition.

pts: (code on the board) int score;
(code on the board) std::cin >> score;
(code on the board) if (score >= 90) {
(code on the board)     std::cout << "A\n";
(code on the board) } else if (score >= 80) {
(code on the board)     std::cout << "B\n";
(code on the board) } else if (score >= 70) {
(code on the board)     std::cout << "C\n";
(code on the board) } else {
(code on the board)     std::cout << "F\n";
(code on the board) }
(program output) $ ./grade
(program output) 85
(program output) B
(written on the whiteboard) Order matters: the first true condition wins.
(written on the whiteboard) Check the strictest case first.
say: Let's write a real program together, one line at a time. It reads a test score and prints a letter grade. First, we make a variable called score to hold a whole number, and then we read it from the keyboard with c in.
Now the decision. If the score is at least ninety, print A. Else, if it's at least eighty, print B. Else, if it's at least seventy, print C. And if none of those were true, print F.

Let's run it and type eighty five. The computer checks the conditions in order, top to bottom. Is eighty five at least ninety? No. Is it at least eighty? Yes. So it prints B, and skips every remaining branch.

Here's the lesson hiding in this example. If we had written the seventy check first, a score of ninety five would pass it immediately and print C. In an else if chain, the first true condition wins, so always check the strictest case first.

pts: while (condition) { … }  — repeat while true
Trace it by hand: i, sum after each pass
Classic bugs: off-by-one, infinite loop
say: Computers are great at repetition. A while loop repeats its body as long as a condition stays true. Here, we start with sum equals zero and i equals one, and keep adding i to sum while i is at most one hundred.
The for loop packs the three parts, start, condition and step, into one line. This is the most common loop you'll write.

Trace it by hand. After the first pass, sum is one. After the second, three. Then six, then ten. After one hundred passes, sum is five thousand fifty. Fun fact: the mathematician Gauss supposedly found that answer as a child by pairing one with one hundred, two with ninety nine, and so on: fifty pairs of one hundred one.

Two classic loop bugs. Off by one: writing less than instead of less than or equal, and silently skipping the last value. And the infinite loop: forgetting to change the variable, so the condition never becomes false, and your program hangs forever.

slides.h: Worked example: tracing a loop by hand
pts: (code on the board) int sum = 0;
(code on the board) for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
(code on the board)     sum += i * i;
(code on the board) }
(code on the board) std::cout << sum << "\n";
(program output) $ ./squares
(program output) 30
say: Programmers trace loops by hand to see exactly what they do. Here's a loop that adds up the squares of one through four. Sum starts at zero. The loop variable i starts at one, keeps going while i is at most four, and goes up by one each pass. Each pass adds i times i to the sum.
Now we trace it, one row per pass. Pass one: i is one, i times i is one, and sum becomes one. Pass two: i is two, its square is four, and sum becomes five.
Pass three: nine more makes fourteen. Pass four: sixteen more makes thirty. Then i becomes five, the test five is at most four is false, and the loop ends.

So the program prints thirty. If you ever can't figure out why a loop gives the wrong answer, make this exact table on paper. Off by one bugs, like writing less than instead of less than or equal, show up immediately.

slides.h: Functions: build big programs from small, tested pieces
pts: A function takes inputs (parameters) and returns an output
Name it, test it, reuse it
Each call gets its own frame on the call stack
say: As programs grow, we split them into functions. A function is a named black box: it takes inputs, called parameters, does some work, and returns an output. Here, CircleArea takes a radius of two and returns about twelve point five seven. Once it's written and tested, you can call it from anywhere, and you don't have to think about how it works inside. That's called abstraction, and it's how million line programs stay manageable.

How does the computer keep track of function calls? With the call stack. When main calls CircleArea, a new frame is pushed on top, holding CircleArea's own variables. If that calls Square, another frame goes on top. When a function returns, its frame is popped off and its variables disappear. That's why a variable declared inside a function isn't visible outside it. It's called the variable's scope. And if a function calls itself forever, the stack overflows, which is where the famous website name comes from.

slides.h: Worked example: what happens when you call a function
pts: (code on the board) double Area(double w, double h) {
(code on the board)     return w * h;
(code on the board) }
(code on the board) int main() {
(code on the board)     double a = Area(3.0, 4.5);
(code on the board)     std::cout << a << "\n";
(code on the board) }
(program output) $ ./area
(program output) 13.5
say: Let's write a small function and watch what the computer does when it's called. The function is named Area. It takes two doubles, a width and a height, and returns their product.
Main calls it with three and four and a half, and stores the result in a. When main starts, it gets a frame on the call stack, a little block of memory for its variables.
When main calls Area, a new frame is pushed on top. The parameter w gets a copy of three, and h gets a copy of four and a half.

Area computes three times four and a half, thirteen point five, and returns it. Its frame is popped off the stack, so w and h disappear, and the value lands in main's variable a. Finally main prints thirteen point five. Every function call in every program works this way.

pts: (code on the board) int SquareR(int x) { return x * x; }
(code on the board) void SquareP(int x) { std::cout << x * x; }
(written on the whiteboard) return → a value for the PROGRAM
(written on the whiteboard) cout → text for a HUMAN
(code on the board) int y = SquareR(3) + 1;   // y = 10
(code on the board) int z = SquareP(3) + 1;   // compile error: void
(written on the whiteboard) compute + return; let main print
say: Here's the confusion I see on every first exam: the difference between returning a value and printing it. These two functions look like they do the same thing. The first returns x times x. The second prints x times x.

Return hands a value back to whoever called the function, silently. Nothing appears on the screen. The caller can store it, add to it, or pass it on. Print sends characters to the screen, for a human to read, and the program can't use them afterwards.

So this line works: y becomes the square of three, plus one, which is ten. But the same line with the printing version won't even compile, because a void function returns nothing. There's no value to add one to.
The rule: functions should usually compute and return. Let main decide what to print. That way the same function can be tested, reused, and combined.

slides.h: Pass by value vs. pass by reference
pts: By value: the function gets a copy
By reference (&): the function gets the original
Use & to change the caller’s variable (e.g. swap)
const & for big objects you only read
say: When you pass a variable to a function, C plus plus normally makes a copy. That's pass by value. The function can change its copy, and the caller's variable is untouched.
If you add an ampersand to the parameter type, you pass by reference. Now the parameter is just another name for the caller's variable. One box, two names.
That's how you write a function that changes its arguments, like a swap function that exchanges two variables. With pass by value, swap would only swap the copies, and nothing would happen.
And for big objects like long strings or vectors, copying is slow. So professionals pass them as const reference: no copy, and the const keyword promises the function won't modify it.

pts: (code on the board) void AddOneCopy(int x) { x = x + 1; }
(code on the board) void AddOneRef(int& x) { x = x + 1; }
(code on the board) int n = 5;
(code on the board) AddOneCopy(n);   // n is still 5
(code on the board) AddOneRef(n);    // n is now 6
(written on the whiteboard) value: a private copy  ·  &: the original
say: Here are two functions that look almost identical. Both add one to their parameter. The only difference is the ampersand in the second one.

Main makes n equal to five and calls the first one. The function gets its own copy of five in a new box called x. It changes the copy to six, then the box disappears when the function returns. So n is still five.
Now call the reference version. This time x isn't a new box. It's just another name for n itself. So adding one to x adds one to n, and n becomes six.

Rule of thumb: pass by value when the function only needs to read a small value. Pass by reference when the function must change the caller's variable, like a swap. And pass large objects by const reference, which avoids the copy without allowing changes.

pts: Many values under one name, in a row in memory
Index from 0 to size − 1
std::vector grows as needed: push_back()
Out-of-bounds access = undefined behavior (a top security bug)
say: Usually you have many values, like the scores of a whole class. A vector stores them in one row in memory under a single name.
