Each element has an index, and indexes start at zero, not one. So six scores live at indexes zero through five.

A standard vector can grow: call push back to add an item to the end, and size to ask how many there are. To find the maximum, loop through every element and remember the largest you've seen. Here, that's ninety nine, at index four.

And here's a serious danger. Index six doesn't exist, but C plus plus won't stop you from reading it. You'll get garbage, or a crash, or worse. Reading or writing past the end of an array, called a buffer overflow, has been behind many of the most serious security vulnerabilities in history. Use the at function, or check your bounds.

slides.h: Putting it together: average and maximum
say: Let's combine everything. The Average function takes the vector by const reference, so nothing is copied. It loops over every element with a range based for loop, adding to a sum. Then it divides by the number of elements. Notice the static cast to double. Without it, we'd do integer division, and the average of these scores, which is about eighty three point two, would come out as just eighty three. The Max function starts by assuming the first element is the best, then walks through the rest, replacing best whenever it finds something larger. These two patterns, accumulate and keep the best so far, show up in almost every program you'll ever write. One question to always ask: what happens if the vector is empty? Here, both functions would fail. Testing edge cases like empty inputs is what separates working code from fragile code.

slides.h: Text: strings are just numbers in disguise
pts: Each char is stored as a number: 'H' = 72
Strings: length(), indexing, +, comparisons
Example: count vowels by looping over characters
say: Computers only store numbers, so text is stored as numbers too. Each character has a code. In the ASCII table, capital H is seventy two, lowercase e is one hundred one, and so on.

Capital letters run from sixty five to ninety, lowercase from ninety seven to one twenty two. So converting lowercase to uppercase is just subtracting thirty two. Modern systems use Unicode, which extends this to every language and emoji.
A string is a sequence of characters. You can ask its length, read a character by index, join strings with plus, and compare them alphabetically.
A classic exercise: count the vowels in a sentence. Loop over each character, and if it's a, e, i, o or u, add one to a counter. It's the same accumulate pattern as before, just on text.

slides.h: Worked example: counting the vowels in a word
pts: (code on the board) std::string word = "engineering";
(code on the board) int vowels = 0;
(code on the board) for (char c : word) {
(code on the board)     if (c == 'a' || c == 'e' || c == 'i' || c == 'o' || c == 'u') {
(code on the board)         vowels++;
(code on the board)     }
(code on the board) }
(code on the board) std::cout << vowels << "\n";
(code on the board) e n g i n e e r i n g     vowels: 5
(program output) $ ./vowels
(program output) 5
(written on the whiteboard) "Engineering" prints 4! Capital E is a different code (69 vs 101).
(code on the board)     char lower = std::tolower(c);   // fix: then test lower
say: Let's process text. Our goal: count the vowels in the word engineering. Start with a string variable holding the word, and a counter set to zero.
Then loop over every character. This kind of for loop reads: for each character c in word. Inside, if c is an a, or an e, or an i, or an o, or a u, add one to the counter.
Trace it: e, yes. n, no. g, no. i, yes. n, no. e, yes. e, yes. r, no. i, yes. n, no. g, no. Five vowels, and the program prints five.

One thing to test: capital letters. The word Engineering, with a capital E, would print four, because a capital E is a different number than a lowercase e. The fix is to convert each character to lowercase first, with tolower. Thinking of these edge cases is what testing is all about.

pts: Read the FIRST compiler error first
Print values or use a debugger (gdb) to see what really happens
Write small tests for each function
git: save snapshots, undo mistakes, collaborate
say: Every programmer spends a lot of time debugging, so let's talk about bugs. There are three kinds. Compile time errors, like a missing semicolon, are the easiest: the compiler tells you exactly where. Always fix the first error first, because one mistake can cause dozens of follow on messages. Run time errors crash the program, like dividing by zero or using a bad index. Logic errors are the hardest: the program runs perfectly and gives the wrong answer. To find those, print out values at key points, or step through the program line by line in a debugger like g d b, and compare what's happening to what you expected. And write small tests for each function.

Finally, version control. Git saves a snapshot of your project every time you commit, with a message describing the change. If you break something, you can go back. If you work on a team, everyone's changes can be merged together. This course uses Git and GitHub for assignments, and every software company in the world uses something like it. Commit early, and commit often.

pts: Plan in plain English (or a flowchart) before coding
Meaningful names: total_seconds, not ts
Small functions that do one thing
Test the edge cases: 0, 1, empty, negative, huge
Follow a style guide; let tools format and check your code
Commit often; read error messages carefully
say: Let's finish with the habits that make programming much less painful.
Plan before you type. Write the steps in plain English or draw a flowchart. Most bugs are thinking bugs, not typing bugs.
Use meaningful names. Code is read far more often than it's written, including by you, six months from now.
Keep functions small. If a function does one thing, it's easy to test, and easy to reuse.
Test the edge cases: zero, one, an empty list, negative numbers, very large numbers. That's where bugs hide.

Follow a consistent style guide, and let tools like formatters and linters check your code automatically. This course follows a professional style guide, the same kind used at large software companies.
And commit your work often, and read error messages slowly. They usually tell you exactly what's wrong.

slides.big: Every program is built from variables, decisions, loops, functions and data. Master these five and you can learn any language.
say: To wrap up: a program is a precise list of instructions that a compiler turns into machine code. Variables hold typed values in memory. If statements make decisions, loops repeat work, functions break problems into small tested pieces, and vectors and strings hold collections of data. Those five building blocks appear in every programming language, from Python to the assembly language you'll write for microcontrollers. Next up, object oriented programming, where we learn to organize larger programs. See you there.

L04_cpsc121.title: Object-Oriented Programming
L04_cpsc121.file: CPSC-121 Object-Oriented Programming/Lecture - CPSC 121 Object-Oriented Programming.mp4

say: Welcome to C P S C one twenty one, object oriented programming. In the last course, you learned the building blocks of programs. In this one, you learn how to organize big programs, by bundling data and the code that works on it into objects, like snapping together Lego bricks. We'll cover classes and objects, encapsulation, how memory really works with pointers, and the two big ideas of object orientation: inheritance and polymorphism.

slides.h: Why objects? Because programs got big
pts: Real software: millions of lines, hundreds of developers
Procedural: any function can touch any data → chaos
OOP: each object owns its data and guards it
Model the problem’s nouns: Player, Enemy, Account, Sensor
say: Real software is enormous. A web browser or a car's infotainment system can have tens of millions of lines of code written by hundreds of people over many years.

In a purely procedural style, the data lives in one place and many functions reach in and change it. When something goes wrong, any of those functions might be guilty. Look at the tangle of red lines on the left.

Object oriented programming bundles data together with the functions allowed to touch it. Each object guards its own data. If an enemy's health goes negative, you only need to look inside the Enemy class.
A good rule of thumb: the nouns in your problem become classes. In a game: Player, Enemy, Bullet. In a bank: Account, Customer, Transaction. In embedded systems: Sensor, Motor, Display.

slides.h: Classes and objects: blueprint vs. house
pts: Class = blueprint (a new type)
Object = one instance built from it
Each object has its own data; all share the same methods
say: This photo shows a nineteen fifties suburb where thousands of houses were built from the same few blueprints. That's exactly the relationship between a class and its objects. A class is the blueprint. It defines a new type: what data each instance holds, and what operations it supports.

An object is one house built from that blueprint. Here, the class BankAccount says every account has an owner and a balance, and supports deposit, withdraw and checking the balance. Alice, Bob and Carol are three separate objects. Each has its own owner and its own balance, but they all share the same code for depositing and withdrawing. The diagram on top is written in U M L, the unified modeling language, which engineers use to sketch designs before coding. Minus means private, plus means public.

slides.h: Worked example: writing a class and making objects
pts: (code on the board) class Rectangle {
(code on the board)  public:
(code on the board)   Rectangle(double w, double h)
(code on the board)       : width_(w), height_(h) {}
(code on the board)   double Area() const {
(code on the board)     return width_ * height_;
(code on the board)   }
(code on the board)  private:
(code on the board)   double width_;
(code on the board)   double height_;
(code on the board) };
(code on the board) Rectangle door(0.9, 2.1);
(code on the board) Rectangle window(1.2, 1.0);
(code on the board) std::cout << door.Area() << " " << window.Area();
(program output) $ ./rect
(program output) 1.89 1.2
say: Let's write a complete class. A Rectangle has two pieces of private data, its width and its height. By convention, private member names end in an underscore.

The constructor, the function with the same name as the class, fills in the data when an object is created. Area is a const method: it promises not to change the object. Now let's build two objects from this one blueprint: a door, point nine by two point one meters, and a window, one point two by one.

Each object carries its own width and height. But the code for Area exists only once, shared by every Rectangle. When we call door dot Area, the method runs on the door's data, and window dot Area runs on the window's.

The output: one point eight nine for the door, and one point two for the window. And because width and height are private, no other code can accidentally set a negative width. That protection is encapsulation.

Here's the class in C plus plus. The data members, owner and balance, are private. Code outside the class cannot touch them directly. The only way in is through the public methods. Why? Because the class can now guarantee a rule, called an invariant: the balance never goes negative. Deposit ignores negative amounts. Withdraw refuses to take out more than you have, and returns false to say so. If balance were public, any line in the whole program could set it to minus a million, and the bug could be anywhere. Notice three more details. The constructor, the function with the same name as the class, initializes a new object, using a member initializer list after the colon. The const after Balance promises that method doesn't change the object. And the underscore at the end of member names is a common style convention so you can tell members from local variables at a glance.

slides.h: Using objects, and splitting code into files
say: Using an object looks like this. Create alice with an opening balance of one hundred. Call Deposit with the dot operator, adding twenty. Try to withdraw five hundred: the method refuses and returns false, so we print insufficient funds. The balance is still one hundred twenty. In real projects, each class is split into two files. The header file, dot h, declares the interface: what the class can do. The source file, dot c c, defines the implementation: how it does it. Other code only includes the header. That separation means you can change how something works internally without breaking anyone who uses it, and it lets the compiler build each file separately, which matters a lot when a project has thousands of files. One symbol to decode: in the source file, BankAccount colon colon Deposit means the Deposit method that belongs to BankAccount. The double colon is called the scope resolution operator, and it's the same one in s t d colon colon c out.

slides.h: How memory really works: stack, heap and pointers
pts: Stack: local variables, freed automatically
Heap: objects created with new, live until delete
Pointer = a variable holding an address
&x → address of x · *p → the thing p points to
say: Now let's look under the hood, because computer engineers need to know where data lives. A program's memory has two main areas. The stack holds local variables. They're created when a function starts and destroyed automatically when it returns.
The heap is for objects that must outlive the function that created them, or whose size isn't known until run time. You create them with new, and they stay until someone calls delete.
How do you find something on the heap? With a pointer: a variable whose value is a memory address. Here, p lives on the stack and holds the address of a Circle object on the heap.

Two operators: ampersand x gives you the address of x, and star p follows the pointer to the thing it points at. Pointers are how linked lists, trees, operating systems and device drivers work. In embedded systems, you'll even use pointers to specific addresses to control hardware registers directly.

slides.h: Worked example: pointers, step by step
pts: (code on the board) int x = 42;
(code on the board) int* p = &x;      // p holds x's address
(code on the board) *p = 7;           // follow the arrow
(code on the board) int* q = new int(99);
(code on the board) std::cout << x << " " << *q;
(code on the board) delete q;
(program output) $ ./ptr
(program output) 7 99
say: Pointers confuse almost everyone at first, so let's draw memory as we go. int x equals forty two creates a box on the stack holding forty two. Every box has an address. Let's say this one lives at hex one thousand.
Next, int star p equals ampersand x. The ampersand means: the address of x. So p is a box that holds the number hex one thousand. We draw that as an arrow from p to x.
Star p equals seven means: follow the arrow, and store seven there. We never mentioned x, but x is now seven.
New int of ninety nine asks for a box on the heap instead. Heap boxes don't disappear when the function ends. We only get to them through a pointer, here q.

Printing x and star q shows seven and ninety nine. Finally, delete q gives the heap box back. Forget that delete, and the memory leaks. Use q after it, and you're reading memory you no longer own, a dangling pointer. That's why modern C plus plus prefers unique pointer, which deletes for you.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) In a DECLARATION (part of the type):
(code on the board) int* p = &x;    // p is a pointer to int
(code on the board) int& r = x;     // r is a reference: another name for x
(written on the whiteboard) In an EXPRESSION (an operator):
(code on the board) p = &x;         // address of x
(code on the board) *p = 7;         // the thing p points to
(code on the board) Circle c(1.0);   c.Area();
(code on the board) Circle* pc = &c; pc->Area();   // same as (*pc).Area()
(written on the whiteboard) declaring a name? yes: type  no: operator
say: Here's why pointers feel so confusing: C plus plus uses the same two symbols for different jobs, depending on where they appear. The rule is simple once you see it. In a declaration, where a new name is being created, the symbol is part of the type.
In an expression, where a value is being used, the same symbols are operators. Ampersand x means the address of x. Star p means follow p to the thing it points at.
And one more pair you've already seen. For an object, you call a method with a dot. For a pointer to an object, you use the arrow. The arrow is just shorthand: follow the pointer, then use the dot.
So when you read code, ask one question: is a new name being declared here? If yes, star and ampersand describe the type. If no, they're doing something.

slides.h: Memory bugs — and the modern fix
pts: Leak: forgot to delete → memory slowly runs out
Dangling: used after delete → random crashes
RAII: tie a resource’s lifetime to an object
std::unique_ptr deletes automatically
say: Manual memory management causes three classic bugs. A memory leak: you new an object and never delete it. Each leak is small, but a server that leaks a little on every request will eventually run out of memory.

A dangling pointer: you delete an object but keep using the pointer. The memory may already belong to something else, so you get random, hard to reproduce crashes. Deleting twice is just as bad. Studies by Microsoft and Google have found that around seventy percent of serious security vulnerabilities in their large C and C plus plus code bases are memory safety bugs like these.

Modern C plus plus fixes this with an idea called RAII: resource acquisition is initialization. Tie the lifetime of a resource to an object on the stack, and let its destructor clean up automatically.

The standard library's unique pointer does exactly this. When the unique pointer goes out of scope, it deletes the object for you. No leaks, no double deletes. The rule in modern code: avoid raw new and delete, and use smart pointers or standard containers instead.

pts: “Has-a” relationship
A Car has an Engine and four Wheels
Each part is tested on its own
Usually the first tool to reach for
say: Objects can contain other objects. That's composition, a has a relationship.
A Car has an Engine and four Wheels. In U M L, the filled diamond on the Car side shows that the car owns its parts.
Each part is its own class, designed and tested on its own. The Car just coordinates them: Drive starts the engine and rotates the wheels.

Composition is usually the first tool to reach for, because the pieces stay independent and easy to swap. Want an electric car? Replace the Engine class with an ElectricMotor that has the same interface.

pts: A derived class inherits data and methods from a base class
class Circle : public Shape { … };
Override behavior that differs (Area)
Abstract base: Area() = 0 means “every shape must define this”
say: The second relationship is inheritance, an is a relationship. A circle is a shape. A rectangle is a shape.
In C plus plus, you write class Circle, colon, public Shape. Circle automatically gets everything Shape has, like its name, and adds its own data, like a radius.
Each derived class can override behavior that differs. Every shape can report its area, but a circle computes pi r squared, and a rectangle computes width times height.

In the base class, Area is declared virtual and set equal to zero. That makes it a pure virtual function, and Shape an abstract class. You can't create a plain Shape, only specific shapes. It's a contract: every shape must define its area.

pts: Store different shapes in one container of Shape pointers
s->Area() calls the RIGHT version at run time
Add a Triangle later — the loop never changes
say: Now the payoff. We can keep a single vector of pointers to Shape, holding circles and rectangles mixed together.

When the loop calls Area on each one, C plus plus figures out at run time which version to call, based on the object's real type. A circle of radius one gives three point one four. The two by three rectangle gives six. A circle of radius two gives twelve point five seven. The total is about twenty one point seven one. This is called polymorphism, Greek for many forms. Under the hood, each object carries a hidden pointer to a table of its class's virtual functions, called the v table, and the call looks up the right entry.

Here's why that's powerful. Next month, someone adds a Triangle class. The loop that totals the areas doesn't change at all. Code written today works with types invented tomorrow. That's how plugin systems, graphics engines and device driver frameworks are built.

pts: (code on the board) class Shape  { public: std::string Name() { return "shape"; } };
(code on the board) class Circle : public Shape { public: std::string Name() { return "circle"; } };
(code on the board) Circle c;  Shape* s = &c;
(code on the board) s->Name();   // prints "shape"  (pointer type decides)
(code on the board) virtual std::string Name() { return "shape"; }
(code on the board) s->Name();   // prints "circle"  (object type decides)
(code on the board) virtual ~Shape() = default;
(written on the whiteboard) virtual = decide at RUN time by the real object
say: Students always ask why the keyword virtual is needed. Let's take it away and see. Shape has a Name method that is not virtual. Circle defines its own Name.

Now call it through a pointer to Shape that really points at a circle. Without virtual, C plus plus decides at compile time, using the pointer's type, Shape. So it prints shape. The circle's version is silently ignored.
Add virtual to the base method, and the decision moves to run time, using the object's real type. Now it prints circle. That run time lookup, through the v table, is polymorphism.
That's also why a base class with virtual functions needs a virtual destructor. When you delete a circle through a Shape pointer, the circle's destructor must run too, or its resources leak.

slides.h: Worked example: one loop, many shapes
pts: (code on the board) class Shape {
(code on the board)  public:
(code on the board)   virtual double Area() const = 0;
(code on the board)   virtual ~Shape() = default;
(code on the board) };
(code on the board) class Circle : public Shape {
(code on the board)   double r_;
(code on the board)  public:
(code on the board)   explicit Circle(double r) : r_(r) {}
(code on the board)   double Area() const override {
(code on the board)     return 3.14159 * r_ * r_; }
(code on the board) };
(code on the board) // Square: same idea, returns s_ * s_
(code on the board) std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>> shapes;
(code on the board) shapes.push_back(std::make_unique<Circle>(1.0));
(code on the board) shapes.push_back(std::make_unique<Square>(2.0));
(code on the board) for (const auto& s : shapes)
(code on the board)   std::cout << s->Area() << "\n";
(program output) $ ./shapes
(program output) 3.14159
(program output) 4
say: Let's build the shape example in code. The base class Shape declares Area as pure virtual: equals zero means every kind of shape must provide its own.
Circle inherits from Shape, stores a radius, and overrides Area with pi r squared. Square does the same with side squared.

Now the payoff, on a fresh board. We keep a vector of pointers to Shape, holding a circle of radius one and a square of side two. One loop calls Area on each, and C plus plus picks the right version at run time.

It prints three point one four one five nine, then four. Here's why this matters: add a Triangle class next year, and this loop doesn't change by a single character. New behavior is added by adding classes, not by editing working code.

slides.h: Operator overloading: making your types feel built-in
say: C plus plus lets you define what operators mean for your own types. Here's a Fraction class. We define operator plus, so you can add fractions with a normal plus sign. To add a over b and c over d, the numerator is a d plus c b, and the denominator is b d. So one half plus one third is one times three plus one times two, over two times three: five sixths. The constructor calls Reduce, which divides the top and bottom by their greatest common divisor, so two fourths automatically becomes one half. That's encapsulation again: every Fraction object is always stored in lowest terms. The standard library uses operator overloading everywhere: strings use plus to join, streams use the arrows for input and output, and complex numbers, which you'll use in circuits, overload all the arithmetic operators.

pts: Unit test: small code that checks one behavior
EXPECT_EQ(account.Balance(), 120.0);
Test the rules: can’t withdraw more than you have
Red → green → refactor
say: How do you know a class works? You write unit tests: small pieces of code that create an object, do something, and check the result. Frameworks like Google Test run hundreds of these in seconds.
A test might create an account with one hundred, deposit twenty, and expect the balance to equal one hundred twenty.
The most valuable tests check the rules. Try to withdraw more than the balance, and expect false, with the balance unchanged. Try to deposit a negative amount, and expect nothing to happen.

Many teams follow the red, green, refactor cycle. Write a test that fails, which is red. Write just enough code to make it pass, green. Then clean up the code, with the tests protecting you from breaking anything. Tests are what let professional teams change big programs without fear.

slides.h: Worked example: a unit test for the bank account
pts: (code on the board) void TestWithdraw() {
(code on the board)   BankAccount acct("test", 100.0);
(code on the board)   assert(acct.Withdraw(30.0));        // allowed
(code on the board)   assert(acct.Balance() == 70.0);
(code on the board)   assert(!acct.Withdraw(500.0));      // refused
(code on the board)   assert(acct.Balance() == 70.0);     // unchanged
(code on the board)   std::cout << "all tests passed\n";
(code on the board) }
(program output) $ ./test_account
(program output) all tests passed
(written on the whiteboard) Remove the balance check? Test fails at once.
say: Let's test the BankAccount class from earlier. A unit test sets up an object, does something to it, and checks the result. Start with an account holding one hundred dollars.
Test the normal case. Withdrawing thirty should succeed, and the balance should drop to seventy. Assert stops the program with an error message if its condition is false.
Now test the rule that matters most: you can't withdraw more than you have. Withdrawing five hundred must return false, and the balance must still be seventy. Untested rules quietly break.

Run it, and it prints all tests passed. Now suppose someone later deletes the check for amount greater than balance. This test fails immediately, before any real customer is overdrawn. Real projects use frameworks like Google Test, but the idea is exactly this.

pts: Encapsulate: keep data private; expose a small, clear interface
Single responsibility: one class, one job
Prefer composition over deep inheritance trees
Program to an interface: depend on Shape, not Circle
DRY: don't repeat yourself — factor out shared code
RAII: let objects clean up after themselves
say: Let's collect the design principles from today.
Encapsulate. Keep data private and expose a small, clear interface, so every object can protect its own rules.
Single responsibility. Each class should have one job. If you describe a class with the word and, it's probably two classes.
Prefer composition. Inheritance is powerful, but deep hierarchies become rigid. Building objects from parts is usually more flexible.
Program to an interface. Write code that depends on the general Shape, not the specific Circle, so new types plug right in.
Don't repeat yourself. If you copy and paste code, factor it into a function or a base class instead.
And RAII. Let objects clean up their own resources: memory, files, locks. You'll see the same pattern in operating systems, where a lock guard automatically releases a lock.

slides.big: Bundle data with the code that protects it. Composition builds things from parts, inheritance + polymorphism let new types plug in.
say: To wrap up. A class is a blueprint, and objects are instances of it. Encapsulation keeps data private behind methods that enforce the rules. Memory lives on the stack or the heap, pointers hold addresses, and smart pointers prevent leaks. Composition builds objects from parts, inheritance models is a relationships, and polymorphism lets one piece of code work with many types, including ones that don't exist yet. These ideas show up in every large codebase, and you'll use them in software engineering, operating systems and embedded firmware. Next, we switch to physics. See you there.

Welcome to physics two twenty five, mechanics. This is the physics of things that move: rockets, cars, robot arms, and the tiny vibrating structures inside your phone. We'll build up from describing motion, to Newton's laws, energy, momentum and rotation, with real numbers at every step. Grab a calculator.

slides.h: Why does a computer engineer need mechanics?
pts: Robots & drones: motors, torque, balance
Sensors: your phone’s accelerometer is a tiny mass on a spring
Control: software that steers physical things
say: Computer engineers increasingly build things that move. A robot arm like this one has to be programmed knowing how much torque each motor can supply and how heavy the payload is. Drones, self driving cars and warehouse robots are the same story.

Sensors too. This tiny chip is an accelerometer and gyroscope, the same kind of part inside your phone and game controllers. Inside is a microscopic mass on springs etched in silicon. When the chip accelerates, the mass lags behind, and the circuit measures that tiny shift. It's literally F equals m a, on a chip.

And control. This rocket booster landed itself, with software reading sensors and steering the engine hundreds of times per second. Software that controls physical things has to be built on mechanics.

pts: Scalar: just a size (mass, time, speed)
Vector: size + direction (displacement, velocity, force)
Add vectors tip-to-tail, or by components
3 km east + 4 km north = 5 km at 53.1°
say: Some quantities only have a size, like mass or temperature. Those are scalars.
Others have a size and a direction, like displacement, velocity and force. Those are vectors. Push a box with fifty newtons, and it matters a lot whether you push left or right.
To add vectors, place them tip to tail, or more practically, break each into x and y components and add the components separately.

Example: walk three kilometers east, then four kilometers north. Your net displacement has length square root of three squared plus four squared, which is five kilometers, at an angle of inverse tangent of four over three, which is fifty three point one degrees north of east. Breaking things into components is the single most useful trick in this course.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) 3 km east, then 4 km north
(written on the whiteboard) |vecd| = sqrt3^2 + 4^2 = sqrt25
(written on the whiteboard) = 5\ mathrmkm
(written on the whiteboard) tantheta = (4)/(3)
(written on the whiteboard) theta = tan^-1(4/3) approx 53° north of east
say: Let's add two vectors by hand. You walk three kilometers east, then four kilometers north. Where do you end up, and in what direction? Draw them tip to tail: first the east arrow, then the north arrow starting where the first one ends.

The total displacement is the arrow from the start to the finish. It's the hypotenuse of a right triangle, so use Pythagoras: the square root of three squared plus four squared, which is the square root of twenty five, five kilometers.

For the direction, use the tangent: opposite over adjacent is four over three. The inverse tangent gives fifty three degrees north of east. Notice you walked seven kilometers, but you're only five kilometers from where you started. Distance and displacement are different things.

pts: v = v₀ + at
x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at²
v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀)
Car 0 → 60 mph (27 m/s) in 6 s: a = 4.5 m/s², 81 m
say: Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. For constant acceleration, three equations do almost everything. Velocity grows linearly: v equals v naught plus a t.
Position follows x equals x naught plus v naught t plus one half a t squared. That should look familiar from calculus: position is the integral of velocity.
And when you don't know the time: v squared equals v naught squared plus two a times the distance.

Example: a car goes from zero to sixty miles per hour, about twenty seven meters per second, in six seconds. The acceleration is twenty seven divided by six, four point five meters per second squared. That's the slope of the velocity graph. The distance covered is the area under it: one half times six times twenty seven, which is eighty one meters.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) v = v_0 + at
(written on the whiteboard) x = v_0 t + (1)/(2)at^2
(written on the whiteboard) v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ax
(written on the whiteboard) quantities: v_0,\ v,\ a,\ t,\ x
(written on the whiteboard) no x   no v   no t
(written on the whiteboard) v_0 = +20,\ v = 0,\ a = -9.8,\ x = ?
(written on the whiteboard) choose up = + , then a = −9.8
(written on the whiteboard) 0 = 20^2 + 2(-9.8) x Rightarrow x approx 20.4\ mathrmm
say: Students always ask which of the three equations to use. Here's the trick. There are five quantities: v naught, v, a, t, and the distance x. Each equation leaves exactly one of them out.

The first has no x. The second has no final v. The third has no t. So list what you know, find the one quantity the problem doesn't mention and doesn't ask for, and pick the equation that leaves it out.
Example: a ball is thrown up at twenty meters per second. How high does it go? We know v naught is twenty, v at the top is zero, and a is gravity. Time isn't asked for, so use the equation with no t.

Now the signs. Pick up as positive and stick with it. Then gravity is negative nine point eight, because it points down. Zero equals twenty squared plus two times negative nine point eight times x, so x is about twenty point four meters, matching what we found in calculus. Mixing sign conventions halfway through is the most common way to lose points.

pts: Horizontal: constant velocity
Vertical: constant acceleration (−9.8 m/s²)
20 m/s at 45°: range 40.8 m, peak 10.2 m, 2.9 s
30° and 60° land at the same spot
say: Throw something, and its motion splits into two independent problems. Horizontally, nothing pushes it, so it moves at constant velocity, ignoring air resistance.
Vertically, gravity accelerates it downward at nine point eight meters per second squared, exactly like the ball we threw straight up in calculus.

Launch at twenty meters per second at forty five degrees. The vertical speed is twenty times sine forty five, about fourteen point one. It stays in the air for two times fourteen point one over nine point eight, about two point nine seconds, and in that time travels about forty point eight meters horizontally, peaking at ten point two meters.

Notice that thirty and sixty degrees land at the same spot, about thirty five meters, because the range depends on sine of twice the angle. Forty five degrees gives the maximum range, at least without air resistance.

slides.h: Worked example: a ball thrown off a cliff
pts: (written on the whiteboard) v_x = 15\ mathrmm/s,  v_y0 = 0,  drop = 20\ mathrmm
(written on the whiteboard) vertical: 20 = (1)/(2)(9.8) t^2
(written on the whiteboard) t = sqrt40/9.8 approx 2.02\ mathrms
(written on the whiteboard) horizontal: x = v_x t = 15 times 2.02
(written on the whiteboard) x approx 30.3\ mathrmm
(written on the whiteboard) v_y = 9.8 times 2.02 approx 19.8
(written on the whiteboard) v = sqrt15^2 + 19.8^2 approx 24.8\ mathrmm/s
say: Here's a new projectile problem, worked on the board. A ball is thrown horizontally at fifteen meters per second from the top of a twenty meter cliff. How far from the base does it land?

Split it into two problems. Vertically, it's just falling from rest. So twenty equals one half times nine point eight times t squared. Solve: t squared is about four point zero eight, so t is about two point zero two seconds.
Horizontally, nothing slows it down, so the distance is speed times time: fifteen times two point zero two, about thirty point three meters.

And how fast is it going when it hits? The vertical speed is nine point eight times two point zero two, about nineteen point eight. Combine the two components with Pythagoras: about twenty four point eight meters per second.

pts: 1. Objects keep doing what they’re doing unless a net force acts
2. F_net = m a
3. Every force has an equal and opposite partner
say: Now, what causes motion? Isaac Newton's three laws. First: an object at rest stays at rest, and an object moving stays moving in a straight line at constant speed, unless a net force acts on it. Motion doesn't need a cause. Changes in motion do.
Second: the net force equals mass times acceleration. Double the force, double the acceleration. Double the mass, half the acceleration. This one equation is the engine of all of mechanics.

Third: forces come in pairs. If A pushes on B, B pushes back on A equally hard in the opposite direction. A rocket pushes hot gas down out of its engines, and the gas pushes the rocket up. It doesn't need air to push against, which is why rockets work in space.

slides.h: Third-law pairs act on different objects
pts: (written on the whiteboard) W and N: equal & opposite
(written on the whiteboard) a 3rd-law pair?
(written on the whiteboard) NO: both act on the book
(written on the whiteboard) they cancel by the 2nd law (a = 0)
(written on the whiteboard) pairs: Earth ↔ book, table ↔ book
(written on the whiteboard) pairs never cancel each other
(written on the whiteboard) mass: kg · weight W = mg: newtons
say: The third law causes more confusion than the other two combined. Here's the classic puzzle. A book rests on a table. Two forces act on it: its weight, the Earth pulling it down, and the normal force, the table pushing it up. They're equal and opposite. Is that a third law pair?

No! Both of those forces act on the same object, the book. They cancel because of the second law: the book isn't accelerating, so the net force on it is zero. A third law pair always acts on two different objects.

The real partner of the weight is the book pulling the Earth up, just as hard. And the partner of the normal force is the book pushing down on the table. Each pair is the same kind of force, between the same two objects.

That also answers the horse and cart puzzle. If the cart pulls back on the horse as hard as the horse pulls the cart, how does anything move? Because the forces act on different objects. The cart moves if the pull on it beats the friction on it. And one more fix: mass, in kilograms, is how much stuff there is. Weight, in newtons, is a force, m times g.

slides.h: Free-body diagrams: a box on a ramp
pts: Draw every force on ONE object
Tilt the axes along the slope
a = 32.0 / 10 = 3.2 m/s² down the ramp
say: To use F equals m a, draw a free body diagram: the object alone, with an arrow for every force acting on it. Here's a ten kilogram box sliding down a thirty degree ramp, with a friction coefficient of point two. Gravity pulls straight down with m g, ninety eight newtons. The ramp pushes back perpendicular to its surface with the normal force. And friction opposes the sliding.
Trick: tilt your axes so x runs along the slope. Then the normal force and the perpendicular part of gravity cancel: N equals m g cosine thirty, eighty four point nine newtons.

Along the slope, gravity's component is ninety eight times sine thirty, forty nine newtons. Friction is the coefficient times the normal force: point two times eighty four point nine, about seventeen newtons, pointing up the slope. The net force is about thirty two newtons down the slope.

Divide by the mass: the box accelerates at about three point two meters per second squared. Every mechanics problem, from bridges to robot joints, follows this same recipe: isolate the object, draw the forces, pick smart axes, apply F equals m a. One detail: point two is the kinetic friction coefficient, for a box that's already sliding. Static friction, which holds a resting box in place, is usually a little larger. That's why it takes more force to start something moving than to keep it moving.

slides.h: Worked example: two blocks and a pulley
pts: (written on the whiteboard) Find a and T (no friction)
(written on the whiteboard) table block: T = 4a
(written on the whiteboard) hanging block: 2g - T = 2a
(written on the whiteboard) add: 2g = 6a
(written on the whiteboard) a = (2(9.8))/(6) approx 3.27\ mathrmm/s^2
(written on the whiteboard) T = 4a approx 13.1\ mathrmN
(written on the whiteboard) check: T < 2g = 19.6\ mathrmN
say: Now a problem with two objects. A four kilogram block sits on a frictionless table. A string runs over a pulley at the edge to a two kilogram block hanging below. What's the acceleration, and what's the tension in the string?

Draw a free body diagram for each block. The table block feels only the tension T pulling it sideways. The hanging block feels T pulling up and its weight, two g, pulling down. The string keeps them moving together, so they share the same acceleration a.
Add the two equations, and the tension cancels: two g equals six a. So a is two times nine point eight over six, about three point two seven meters per second squared.

Then the tension is four times a: about thirteen point one newtons. Sanity check: that's less than the hanging block's weight of nineteen point six newtons, which makes sense, because the hanging block is accelerating downward. If the tension equaled its weight, nothing would move.

slides.h: Apparent weight: what your phone’s accelerometer feels
pts: Scale reads the normal force N, not mg
N = m(g + a)
Going up faster: you feel heavier
Free fall: N = 0 — "weightless"
say: Stand on a bathroom scale in an elevator. The scale doesn't measure gravity directly. It measures how hard it has to push up on you: the normal force.
Apply Newton's second law: N minus m g equals m a, so N equals m times g plus a.

A seventy kilogram person reads six hundred eighty six newtons at rest. Accelerating upward at two meters per second squared, the reading jumps to eight hundred twenty six newtons. You feel heavier. Accelerating downward, it drops to five hundred forty six.

And in free fall, the reading is zero. That's why astronauts in orbit float: they're falling around the Earth continuously. An accelerometer works exactly like this scale. That's why a phone lying still on a table reports about one g pointing up, and how it knows which way is up to rotate your screen.

slides.h: Circular motion: why cars slide on curves
pts: Moving in a circle = constantly changing direction
Centripetal acceleration a = v²/r, toward the center
Something must supply that force: friction, tension, gravity
say: Even at constant speed, moving in a circle means your velocity keeps changing direction. And a change in velocity is an acceleration.

That centripetal acceleration points toward the center, with size v squared over r. A car at twenty meters per second, about forty five miles per hour, on a curve of radius fifty meters needs eight meters per second squared toward the center.

Something has to supply that force. For a car, it's friction between the tires and the road. The friction coefficient must be at least eight over nine point eight, about point eight two. Dry pavement can do that. A wet road, with a coefficient around point five, can't, and the car slides outward. That's why curve speed limits exist, and why highway curves are banked. The same equation sizes the spin speed of hard drive platters and the forces in a centrifuge.

pts: Kinetic energy ½mv² · potential energy mgh
Without friction, the total never changes
Drop 30 m: v = √(2gh) = 24.2 m/s (87 km/h)
Work W = F·d changes energy
say: Forces and accelerations can get messy. Energy is often a much faster route. Moving objects have kinetic energy, one half m v squared. Raised objects have gravitational potential energy, m g h.

Without friction, energy just converts between these forms, and the total stays constant. Look at the roller coaster. At A, it's all potential energy, the blue bar. At B, the bottom, most of it has become kinetic, orange. At C, it's partly back to potential.

So how fast is a coaster after dropping thirty meters? Set m g h equal to one half m v squared. The mass cancels, and v is the square root of two g h, about twenty four point two meters per second, or eighty seven kilometers per hour. No forces, no time, no calculus. Just bookkeeping.

Work, force times distance, is how energy enters or leaves. Friction does negative work, turning motion into heat. In electronics, you'll see the same conservation idea: energy delivered by a battery ends up as heat in resistors, light in LEDs, or stored in capacitors.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) k = 800\ mathrmN/m,  x = 0.1\ mathrmm,  m = 0.05\ mathrmkg
(written on the whiteboard) E_spring = (1)/(2)kx^2 = (1)/(2)(800)(0.1)^2 = 4\ mathrmJ
(written on the whiteboard) (1)/(2)mv^2 = 4
(written on the whiteboard) v = sqrt(2(4))/(0.05) = sqrt160 approx 12.6\ mathrmm/s
(written on the whiteboard) mgh = 4 Rightarrow h = (4)/(0.05(9.8)) approx 8.2\ mathrmm
say: Let's use energy bookkeeping on a spring launcher. A spring with stiffness eight hundred newtons per meter is compressed ten centimeters, with a fifty gram ball on top. How fast does the ball leave, and how high does it go?
The energy stored in the spring is one half k x squared: one half times eight hundred times point one squared, which is four joules.

All four joules become kinetic energy as the ball leaves. One half m v squared equals four, so v squared is eight over point zero five, one hundred sixty, and v is about twelve point six meters per second.

At the top, it's all potential energy: m g h equals four. So h is four over point zero five times nine point eight, about eight point two meters. We never needed the time or the acceleration. Energy skipped straight to the answer.

pts: Momentum p = mv; total is conserved in collisions
1000 kg at 20 m/s hits 1500 kg at rest, they stick: 8 m/s
Kinetic energy: 200 kJ → 80 kJ (rest crushes metal)
Impulse: F·Δt = Δp → airbags stretch Δt, cut the force
say: Momentum is mass times velocity. When objects collide, the forces between them are equal and opposite, so the total momentum before equals the total after.

A thousand kilogram car at twenty meters per second hits a fifteen hundred kilogram car at rest, and they stick together. Momentum before: twenty thousand. After, two thousand five hundred kilograms share it, so they move at eight meters per second.

But kinetic energy is not conserved here. It drops from two hundred kilojoules to eighty. The missing one hundred twenty kilojoules went into crushing metal, heat and sound. Car crumple zones are designed to absorb exactly that energy. Two names to know: a collision that keeps kinetic energy, like billiard balls bouncing, is called elastic. One where the objects stick together, like these cars, is perfectly inelastic, and loses the most energy possible. Momentum is conserved in both.

And impulse explains safety design. Force times time equals the change in momentum. Your momentum has to drop to zero in a crash either way. An airbag stretches the stopping time from a few milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, so the force on you drops by roughly the same factor. Electronics borrowed a related trick: many laptops with spinning hard drives used an accelerometer to detect a fall and park the drive's read head before impact.

pts: Torque τ = r F sin θ: the “twisting force”
0.3 m wrench × 50 N = 15 N·m
Every linear idea has a rotational twin
say: Spinning things are described by rotational versions of everything we've done. The rotational version of force is torque: how hard you twist. Torque equals the distance from the pivot times the force times the sine of the angle between them. Push at the end of a thirty centimeter wrench with fifty newtons, at a right angle, and you apply fifteen newton meters. Use a longer wrench and you need less force for the same torque. That's why it's easier to open a door by pushing far from the hinges.

Every linear quantity has a twin. Position becomes angle. Velocity becomes angular velocity. Mass becomes moment of inertia, which depends on how far the mass is from the axis. F equals m a becomes torque equals I alpha. And kinetic energy becomes one half I omega squared. Learn one column, and the other comes almost for free.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) 30 kg at 2 m. 40 kg at d = ?
(written on the whiteboard) balance: tau_left = tau_right
(written on the whiteboard) (30g)(2) = (40g) d
(written on the whiteboard) 60 = 40 d
(written on the whiteboard) d = 1.5\ mathrmm
say: Here's torque on the board. A thirty kilogram child sits two meters from the pivot of a seesaw. Where must a forty kilogram child sit to balance it?
Balance means the torques cancel: the counterclockwise torque equals the clockwise torque. Each torque is weight times distance from the pivot.

The g cancels from both sides, so sixty equals forty d, and d is one and a half meters. The heavier child sits closer to the pivot. This is exactly how a balance scale, a crane's counterweight, and the robot arm on the next slide are designed.

slides.h: Engineering example: sizing a robot arm motor
pts: Holding torque = weight × horizontal distance
2 kg at 0.5 m → 9.8 N·m (+ the arm itself)
Small motors give ≈ 0.5 N·m → need ≈ 25:1 gearing
Worst case: arm fully extended
say: Here's mechanics doing real engineering work. A robot arm holds a two kilogram object at the end of a half meter arm, held horizontal. The payload's weight is nineteen point six newtons.

The motor at the shoulder must supply a torque of nineteen point six times point five, about nine point eight newton meters, just to hold still. Add the arm's own weight, acting at its middle, and the requirement is closer to twelve.
A typical small hobby motor might deliver around half a newton meter. So you'd need a gearbox of roughly twenty five to one, trading speed for torque.

And notice that the worst case is the arm stretched out horizontally, when the lever arm is longest. Engineers always size motors for the worst case, plus a safety margin. Robot arm projects, like the one in this degree's senior design course, start exactly with this calculation.

slides.h: Gravity and orbits: how GPS satellites stay up
pts: F = G m₁m₂ / r²
Orbit: gravity supplies the centripetal force
v = √(GM/r) — no fuel needed to stay in orbit
GPS: ~26,600 km radius, 3.9 km/s, 12-hour orbit
say: Newton's law of gravitation says every two masses attract with a force G m one m two over r squared. At the Earth's surface, that gives the familiar nine point eight meters per second squared.

Now combine it with circular motion. A satellite in orbit is falling toward Earth the whole time, but it's moving sideways so fast that it keeps missing. Gravity provides exactly the centripetal force: G M m over r squared equals m v squared over r. The satellite's mass cancels, and the orbital speed is the square root of G M over r. No engine needed to stay up. GPS satellites like this one orbit at a radius of about twenty six thousand six hundred kilometers, moving at about three point nine kilometers per second, and circle the Earth every twelve hours. Your phone finds your position by timing signals from several of them, which you'll appreciate more after the electromagnetism and signals courses.

slides.big: Draw the forces, apply F = ma — or skip straight to energy and momentum conservation. Rotation is the same physics, spinning.
say: Let's recap. Vectors are broken into components. Kinematics describes motion with three equations for constant acceleration. Newton's laws explain what causes motion, and free body diagrams are how you apply them. Energy and momentum conservation are shortcuts that skip the details. And rotation, with torque and moment of inertia, mirrors everything linear. You'll see these ideas again in robotics, sensors and control, and the math patterns, like conservation and equal and opposite pairs, come back in circuits. Next up, discrete mathematics, the math of logic and computing. See you there.

L06_math170a.title: Mathematical Structures I
L06_math170a.file: MATH-170A Mathematical Structures I/Lecture - MATH 170A Mathematical Structures I.mp4

say: Welcome to Math one seventy A, Mathematical Structures, often called discrete mathematics. Calculus is about smooth, continuous change. But computers are discrete: bits, steps, finite states. This course gives you the math of that world: logic, proofs, sets, counting and number theory. The machine on screen is an Enigma, a World War Two cipher machine, and breaking it took exactly this kind of mathematics, plus some of the first electronic computing machines.

Here's where you'll use it. Logic is the language of if statements in software and of logic gates in hardware, and it's how engineers formally verify that a chip design is correct. Counting tells you how strong a password is, how many cases a test must cover, and how long an algorithm takes. Number theory, the study of whole numbers and remainders, is the foundation of encryption, error checking codes and hash tables. And graphs, dots connected by lines, model road maps, computer networks, and the dependencies in a build system. Let's start with logic.

pts: Proposition: a statement that is true or false
AND ∧, OR ∨, NOT ¬, XOR ⊕
Truth table: list every combination
p → q is false only when p is true and q is false
say: A proposition is a statement that's either true or false. It is raining. Two plus two equals four. We'll write them as letters, like p and q, and represent true as one and false as zero.

We combine them with connectives. AND is true only when both are true. OR is true when at least one is true. NOT flips the value. And exclusive or, X O R, is true when exactly one is true. These are exactly the gates you'll build in digital logic.
A truth table lists every combination of inputs. With two variables there are four rows. With n variables there are two to the n rows, which is why exhaustive testing of a big circuit is impossible.

The trickiest connective is implication, p implies q. Think of it as a promise: if it rains, I'll bring an umbrella. The promise is only broken in one case: it rains and I don't bring the umbrella. If it doesn't rain, I haven't broken my promise either way. That's the highlighted row: true implies false is false, and every other row is true.

slides.h: Worked example: proving an equivalence with a truth table
pts: (written on the whiteboard) Claim: (p to q) equiv (neg p vee q)
(written on the whiteboard) every row matches,
(written on the whiteboard) so the formulas are equivalent
say: Let's build a truth table by hand and use it to prove something. Claim: p implies q means exactly the same thing as not p, or q. Set up columns: p, q, p implies q, not p, and finally not p or q.

Row one: p true, q true. The promise is kept, so p implies q is one. Not p is zero, and zero or one is one. Row two: p true, q false. That's the broken promise: zero. Not p is zero, and zero or zero is zero.
Rows three and four: whenever p is false, the implication is automatically true. And not p is one, so not p or q is one as well.

Now compare the two highlighted columns: one, zero, one, one, and one, zero, one, one. They match in every row, so the two formulas are equivalent. That's a complete proof. Checking every row is exactly how chip verification tools prove two circuits do the same thing.

pts: Contrapositive: (p → q) ≡ (¬q → ¬p)
Converse (q → p) is NOT equivalent
De Morgan: ¬(A ∧ B) ≡ ¬A ∨ ¬B
Simplify code and circuits
say: Two formulas are equivalent if they have the same truth table. The most useful equivalence for proofs: p implies q is equivalent to not q implies not p, the contrapositive. If it rains, the ground is wet, is the same as: if the ground isn't wet, it didn't rain.

But the converse, q implies p, is not equivalent. If the ground is wet, it rained? No, maybe the sprinklers were on. Confusing a statement with its converse is one of the most common reasoning errors, in math and in life. There's also the inverse, not p implies not q: if it didn't rain, the ground isn't wet. That fails for the same reason, sprinklers. The inverse is actually equivalent to the converse, and neither is equivalent to the original.

De Morgan's laws tell you how to push a NOT through an AND or an OR: flip each piece and swap AND with OR. Not A and B equals not A or not B. In hardware, that means a NAND gate is the same as an OR gate with inverted inputs.

And in code, not open parenthesis a and b equals not a or not b. Programmers use this constantly to simplify conditions, and chip design tools use it to rearrange logic into whatever gates are cheapest.

slides.h: Worked example: simplifying code with De Morgan
pts: (written on the whiteboard) if not (x > 5 and y < 3):
(written on the whiteboard) neg(A wedge B) equiv neg A vee neg B
(written on the whiteboard) if not (x > 5) or not (y < 3):
(written on the whiteboard) not (x > 5) → x <= 5
(written on the whiteboard) not (y < 3) → y >= 3
(written on the whiteboard) if x <= 5 or y >= 3:
(written on the whiteboard) test x = 7, y = 1:  original → False,  new → False
say: Here's De Morgan in real code. Suppose a program has this condition: if not, open parenthesis, x is greater than five and y is less than three. It's correct, but hard to read. Let's simplify it.
De Morgan says: push the not inside, negate each piece, and swap and with or. So it becomes: not x greater than five, or, not y less than three.

Now negate each comparison. Not greater than five means less than or equal to five. Not less than three means greater than or equal to three. Be careful with the equals signs, because that's where most bugs hide.

So the final condition is: if x is at most five, or y is at least three. Test it with x equals seven and y equals one. The original: seven is greater than five and one is less than three, so the and is true, and not makes it false. The new version: seven at most five, false. One at least three, false. False or false is false. They agree.

pts: ∀x P(x): P is true for every x
∃x P(x): P is true for at least one x
Negation flips them: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x)
"Not every test passes" = "some test fails"
say: Statements about whole collections use quantifiers. For all, written as an upside down A, means the statement holds for every element. There exists, written as a backwards E, means it holds for at least one. For all integers x, x squared is at least zero: true. There exists an integer x with x squared equal to two: false. Negating a quantified statement flips the quantifier and negates the inside. Not every test passes is the same as: there exists a test that fails. To disprove a for all claim, you only need one counterexample. To prove it, you need an argument that covers every case, and that's what proofs are for.

pts: Direct: even + even = 2a + 2b = 2(a + b) → even
Contrapositive: n² even → n even  ⇔  n odd → n² odd
Contradiction: assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms … impossible
say: A proof is an argument that leaves no case uncovered. The direct method: start from what you know and march to the conclusion. Claim: the sum of two even numbers is even. Any even number is two times some integer, so write them as two a and two b. Their sum is two times a plus b, which is even. Done.

Sometimes the contrapositive is easier. Claim: if n squared is even, then n is even. Prove the contrapositive instead: if n is odd, then n squared is odd. Odd n is two k plus one. Squaring gives four k squared plus four k plus one, which is two times something, plus one. Odd. Done.

And proof by contradiction: assume the opposite and derive something impossible. The classic: the square root of two is irrational. Assume it equals a over b in lowest terms. Then a squared equals two b squared, so a squared is even, so a is even, using the result we just proved. Write a as two c: four c squared equals two b squared, so b squared is even, and b is even too. But then a over b wasn't in lowest terms. Contradiction. So root two can't be a fraction.

pts: Base case: true for n = 1
Step: if true for k, then true for k + 1
Example: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2
Same idea proves loops and recursion correct
say: Induction proves a statement for every positive integer at once. Picture an infinite row of dominoes. First, show the first domino falls. That's the base case.
Then show that whenever domino k falls, it knocks over domino k plus one. That's the inductive step. Together, every domino falls.

Example: one plus two plus up to n equals n times n plus one over two. Base case: n equals one, and one equals one times two over two. Inductive step: assume it's true for k. Then the sum up to k plus one is k times k plus one over two, plus k plus one. Factor out k plus one, and you get k plus one times k plus two, over two, which is the formula for k plus one. Done, for every n. Students often worry that this is circular: aren't we assuming what we want to prove? No. We assume it for one particular k, and show that this forces it to hold for the next one. On its own, that proves nothing. Only together with the base case, the first domino, does the chain reach every n.

Computer scientists use induction to prove programs correct. A loop invariant is a statement that's true before the loop starts, the base case, and stays true after each pass, the step. And a recursive function is correct if its base case is right and each call correctly uses smaller calls.

slides.h: Worked example: an induction proof you can see
pts: (written on the whiteboard) Claim: 1 + 3 + 5 + ldots + (2n-1) = n^2
(written on the whiteboard) Base, n=1:  1 = 1^2
(written on the whiteboard) Assume: 1 + 3 + ldots + (2k-1) = k^2
(written on the whiteboard) Add next: k^2 + (2k+1)
(written on the whiteboard) = (k+1)^2
(written on the whiteboard) true for all n
say: Let's write out a complete induction proof. Claim: the sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared. One plus three plus five, up to two n minus one, equals n squared. Look at the picture: each new odd number is an L shaped layer that grows the square by one.
Base case: n equals one. The left side is just one. The right side is one squared, also one. True.
Inductive step: assume it's true for k, so the first k odd numbers add up to k squared. Now add the next odd number, two k plus one. The sum becomes k squared plus two k plus one.

But k squared plus two k plus one factors as k plus one, squared. That's exactly the formula for k plus one. So the statement holds for one, and each case pushes over the next, like dominoes. True for every n. And the picture agrees: one plus three plus five plus seven is sixteen, a four by four square.

pts: Union A ∪ B, intersection A ∩ B, complement
Inclusion–exclusion: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|
100 students: 60 C++, 45 Python, 25 both
→ 80 take at least one, 20 take neither
say: A set is an unordered collection of distinct things. The union of A and B contains everything in either one. The intersection contains only what's in both. The complement is everything not in the set.
To count a union, add the sizes, then subtract the overlap, because the overlap got counted twice. That's the inclusion exclusion principle.
Example: in a group of one hundred students, sixty take C plus plus, forty five take Python, and twenty five take both.

Sixty plus forty five minus twenty five is eighty students taking at least one, so twenty take neither. Databases do this all day: a SQL query with AND and OR conditions is set intersection and union, and you'll see it again in the databases course.

pts: Function: every input maps to exactly one output
One-to-one: no two inputs share an output
Onto: every output is hit
Bijection = both → it can be inverted (e.g. encryption)
say: A function assigns each input exactly one output. Mathematicians care about two special properties.
One to one, or injective: different inputs always give different outputs. No collisions.
Onto, or surjective: every possible output is actually produced by some input.

A function that's both is a bijection, a perfect pairing, and only bijections can be undone. That's why an encryption function must be a bijection: every ciphertext has to decrypt to exactly one message. A hash function, on the other hand, squeezes huge inputs into a small range of outputs, so it can't be one to one. Collisions are guaranteed, and the next slides show why.

slides.h: Counting: how strong is your password?
pts: Product rule: k choices, n times → kⁿ
8 lowercase letters: 26⁸ ≈ 2.1 × 10¹¹
8 letters+digits mixed case: 62⁸ ≈ 2.2 × 10¹⁴
Length beats complexity: 62¹² ≈ 3.2 × 10²¹
say: The basic tool of counting is the product rule. If you make a sequence of choices, multiply the number of options at each step. A license plate with three letters and four digits has twenty six cubed times ten to the fourth, about a hundred seventy six million possibilities.

Passwords. Eight lowercase letters gives twenty six to the eighth, about two hundred billion. A modern graphics card can try around ten billion guesses per second against a weakly protected password file, so that falls in about twenty seconds.
Use upper case, lower case and digits, sixty two choices per character, and eight characters gives about two times ten to the fourteen. Now it takes about six hours. Better, but not good.

Now go to twelve characters: sixty two to the twelfth, about three times ten to the twenty one, which takes roughly ten thousand years. Length matters more than anything, because it's in the exponent. And six words chosen at random from a list of seven thousand seven hundred seventy six are even stronger, hundreds of thousands of years at this rate, while being much easier to remember.

pts: Order matters → permutations: P(n,k) = n!/(n−k)!
Order doesn’t → combinations: C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!)
Pick 2 of 6 teammates: C(6,2) = 15
say: When order matters, you're counting permutations. How many ways can first, second and third place be awarded among ten runners? Ten times nine times eight, seven hundred twenty. In general, n factorial over n minus k factorial.
When order doesn't matter, you're counting combinations: divide out the k factorial ways to arrange each group. That's n choose k.

How many ways to pick two people from six for a project? Six choose two: six times five over two, fifteen. And look at Pascal's triangle, where each number is the sum of the two above it. Row six, position two, is fifteen. Every entry is a combination.

And a famous one: picking six numbers out of forty nine, which is how many lotteries work. Forty nine choose six is almost fourteen million. So each ticket has about a one in fourteen million chance. Counting is also the foundation of probability, which you'll study in engineering statistics.

slides.h: Permutation or combination? Ask one question
pts: (written on the whiteboard) Rearrange the choices: a different outcome?
(written on the whiteboard) yes → permutation (order matters)
(written on the whiteboard) no  → combination (order does not)
(written on the whiteboard) ordered: AB BA AC CA AD DA BC CB BD DB CD DC = 12
(written on the whiteboard) teams: A,B A,C A,D B,C B,D C,D = 6
(written on the whiteboard) C(4,2) = (P(4,2))/(2!) = (12)/(2) = 6
(written on the whiteboard) president + VP of 10: P(10,2) = 90
(written on the whiteboard) 2-person committee: C(10,2) = 45
(written on the whiteboard) 4-digit PIN (repeats OK): 10^4
(written on the whiteboard) Three counting formulas
(written on the whiteboard) order matters, repeats allowed:  n^k
(written on the whiteboard) order matters, no repeats:  P(n,k) = (n!)/((n-k)!)
(written on the whiteboard) order ignored, no repeats:  C(n,k) = (n!)/(k! (n-k)!)
say: The most common question in counting: is this a permutation or a combination? Ask one thing. If I rearrange my choices, do I get a different outcome? If yes, order matters, and it's a permutation. If no, it's a combination.

Let's see it with four people, A, B, C, D, choosing two. As an ordered list there are twelve: A B, B A, A C, C A, and so on. That's P of four, two. But as a team, A B and B A are the same team, so every team was counted twice. Twelve over two factorial is six. That's C of four, two.

Test yourself. Picking a president and a vice president from ten people: swapping them changes the outcome, so it's P of ten, two, ninety. Picking a two person committee: swapping changes nothing, so C of ten, two, forty five. A four digit PIN: digits can repeat, so it's neither. It's the product rule, ten to the fourth.
So there are really three formulas. Order matters with repeats allowed: n to the k. Order matters, no repeats: permutations. Order doesn't matter, no repeats: combinations.

slides.h: Worked example: PINs with no repeated digit
pts: (written on the whiteboard) All PINs: 10 times 10 times 10 times 10 = 10,000
(written on the whiteboard) No repeats: 10 times 9 times 8 times 7
(written on the whiteboard) = P(10,4) = (10!)/(6!) = 5040
(written on the whiteboard) At least one repeat = 10,000 - 5040
(written on the whiteboard) = 4960
say: Here's a counting problem worked by hand. How many four digit PINs are there in total? Each of the four positions can be any of ten digits, so by the product rule it's ten to the fourth, ten thousand.

Now, how many have no repeated digit? The first digit has ten choices. The second can't match the first, so nine. The third has eight, and the fourth has seven. Ten times nine times eight times seven is five thousand and forty. That's a permutation: P of ten, four.

And how many PINs have at least one repeated digit? Counting those directly is messy, so count the complement: all PINs minus the ones with no repeats. Ten thousand minus five thousand and forty is four thousand nine hundred sixty. Almost half of all PINs repeat a digit. When a direct count is hard, count what you don't want and subtract.

pts: n + 1 pigeons, n holes → some hole has 2+
367 people → two share a birthday (guaranteed)
More possible files than hash values → collisions are certain
Lossless compression can’t shrink every file
say: Here's a deceptively simple idea. If you put more than n pigeons into n holes, at least one hole gets two pigeons. With three hundred sixty seven people in a room, two must share a birthday, because there are only three hundred sixty six possible birthdays. It sounds obvious, but it proves powerful facts. A hash function maps an unlimited number of possible files onto a fixed number of hash values, so collisions must exist. Security depends on making them hard to find, not impossible. And no compression program can shrink every file: there are fewer short files than long ones, so some inputs must get bigger. Whenever someone claims a perfect compression or a collision free hash, the pigeonhole principle says they're wrong.

slides.h: Number theory: divisibility and the GCD
pts: Primes: only divisible by 1 and themselves
GCD: the largest common divisor
Euclid's algorithm (≈ 300 BC): replace (a, b) with (b, a mod b)
gcd(252, 105) = 21 in three steps
say: Number theory studies the integers. A prime is a number greater than one divisible only by one and itself: two, three, five, seven, eleven. Every integer factors uniquely into primes. Twelve is two times two times three.
The greatest common divisor of two numbers is the largest number that divides both. It's how you reduce fractions, like the Fraction class from object oriented programming.

Finding it by factoring is slow for big numbers. Euclid's algorithm, more than two thousand years old, is fast: the GCD of a and b equals the GCD of b and the remainder of a divided by b. Repeat until the remainder is zero.

Let's run it on two fifty two and one oh five. Two fifty two is two times one oh five plus forty two. So find the GCD of one oh five and forty two. One oh five is two times forty two plus twenty one. Forty two is two times twenty one plus zero. The answer is twenty one. Three steps. This ancient algorithm runs inside every secure web connection today.

slides.h: Modular arithmetic: math on a clock
pts: a mod n = remainder after dividing by n
15:00 is 3 o’clock: 15 ≡ 3 (mod 12)
Add and multiply, then take the remainder
Computer integers ARE mod 2ⁿ (overflow wraps)
say: Modular arithmetic is arithmetic that wraps around, like a clock. a mod n is the remainder when a is divided by n.
Fifteen hundred hours is three o'clock, because fifteen mod twelve is three. We write fifteen is congruent to three, mod twelve.

You can add and multiply first and take the remainder at the end, or take remainders along the way, and get the same answer. Nine plus eight is seventeen, which is five mod twelve. Seven times five is thirty five, which is eleven mod twelve.

This isn't just a curiosity. A thirty two bit register in a C P U literally does arithmetic mod two to the thirty two, which is exactly why integers overflow and wrap around. Check digits on credit cards and book I S B Ns use modular arithmetic to catch typos. And hash tables use mod to pick a slot for each key.

slides.h: Worked example: 3²⁰ mod 7 without a calculator
pts: (written on the whiteboard) 3^20 mod 7 = ?
(written on the whiteboard) 3^1 equiv 3
(written on the whiteboard) 3^2 = 9 equiv 2
(written on the whiteboard) 3^4 equiv 2^2 = 4
(written on the whiteboard) 3^8 equiv 4^2 = 16 equiv 2
(written on the whiteboard) 3^16 equiv 2^2 = 4
(written on the whiteboard) 20 = 16 + 4
(written on the whiteboard) 3^20 = 3^16cdot 3^4 equiv 4 cdot 4 = 16
(written on the whiteboard) 3^20 equiv 2 (mod 7)
say: Encryption needs huge powers mod n, so let's see the trick computers use. Find three to the twentieth, mod seven. Three to the twentieth is about three and a half billion, but we never need to compute it.

Square repeatedly, reducing mod seven every time. Three to the first is three. Three squared is nine, which is two mod seven. Three to the fourth is two squared, four. Three to the eighth is four squared, sixteen, which is two. Three to the sixteenth is two squared, four.

Twenty is sixteen plus four, so three to the twentieth is three to the sixteenth times three to the fourth. That's four times four, sixteen, which is two mod seven. Five small multiplications instead of a ten digit number. This is called square and multiply, and it's how R S A handles exponents hundreds of digits long.

slides.h: Putting it together: RSA encryption (toy version)
pts: Public key (n, e) — anyone can encrypt
Private key d — only you can decrypt
c = mᵉ mod n,  m = cᵈ mod n
Security: factoring a 600-digit n is infeasible
say: Here's the payoff of number theory: R S A, one of the public key encryption systems that has secured the internet. You publish a public key so anyone can encrypt a message to you.

But only you hold the private key that decrypts it. Let's build a toy version. Pick two primes, three and eleven. Multiply: n equals thirty three. Compute phi of n, two times ten, which is twenty. Choose e equals three. Find d so that e times d is one, mod twenty: d equals seven, since twenty one mod twenty is one. Two terms to decode. Phi of n counts the numbers below n that share no factor with it, and for a product of two primes it's p minus one times q minus one. And d is called the modular inverse of e. For big numbers, it's found with an extended version of Euclid's algorithm, the same one from two slides ago.

Encrypt the message four: four cubed is sixty four, and sixty four mod thirty three is thirty one. That's the ciphertext. To decrypt, compute thirty one to the seventh, mod thirty three, which comes out to four. The message is back.

Why is it secure? Anyone can see n and e, but finding d requires knowing p and q. With thirty three, that's trivial. With an n that's six hundred digits long, nobody knows how to factor it in any reasonable time. The whole scheme rests on modular arithmetic, Euclid's algorithm, and primes.

pts: Graph = vertices + edges (optionally weighted)
Degree: number of edges at a vertex
Handshake theorem: Σ degrees = 2 × edges
Maps, networks, social media, task dependencies
say: Finally, graphs. Not charts, but networks: a set of vertices connected by edges. Edges can have weights, like travel times between places.
The degree of a vertex is how many edges touch it.
A neat fact, called the handshake theorem: add up all the degrees and you get twice the number of edges, because every edge has two ends. So the number of odd degree vertices is always even.

Graphs model road maps, where your navigation app searches for the shortest path. Here, the fastest route from A to E isn't the direct looking one. Computer networks, social networks, and the order in which files must be compiled are all graphs. You'll learn the algorithms that search them in data structures.

slides.big: Logic to reason precisely, proof to be sure, counting to size problems, number theory to secure them.
say: To wrap up. Logic gives us a precise language, and truth tables, De Morgan's laws and implications are the same rules used in code and circuits. Proofs, direct, by contrapositive, by contradiction and by induction, let us be certain, not just confident. Sets and functions describe collections and mappings. Counting tells us how big a problem is, from passwords to probabilities. And number theory, with modular arithmetic and primes, underlies encryption and hashing. Next, we take those truth tables and build them out of real gates in digital logic. See you there.

L07_egcp180.title: Digital Logic and Computer Structures
L07_egcp180.file: EGCP-180 Digital Logic/Lecture - EGCP 180 Digital Logic and Computer Structures.mp4

say: Welcome to E G C P one eighty, digital logic and computer structures. This is the course where you learn how a computer is built from the bottom up. That little black chip is a seventy four hundred, containing four NAND gates, and believe it or not, you could build an entire computer out of nothing but NAND gates. We'll go from binary numbers, to Boolean algebra, to gates, to memory, and finally to how a C P U fits together.

slides.h: Why digital? Because noise can’t fool a threshold
pts: Analog: every bit of noise changes the value
Digital: only two levels — 0 or 1
Receiver asks one question: above or below threshold?
Copies and long cables stay perfect
say: Why do we build computers out of ones and zeros? Look at the top graph. An analog signal stores information in its exact voltage. Add noise, the orange wiggle, and the value is corrupted. Copy it again and again, and the errors pile up, like a photocopy of a photocopy.
A digital signal uses just two levels. Here, zero volts means zero and five volts means one.
The receiver only asks one question: is the voltage above or below the threshold, the dashed line? Even with plenty of noise, it recovers the exact bits, the green line.

That's why digital information can be copied billions of times, stored for decades and sent across the planet without degrading. Every phone call, photo and video you've ever streamed relies on that idea.
