pts: Each bit position is a power of 2
Hex: each digit = 4 bits (0–9, A–F)
1001 1100 → 9C → written 0x9C
say: In binary, each position is a power of two instead of a power of ten: one, two, four, eight, sixteen, and so on, up to one hundred twenty eight for eight bits.

To convert one zero zero one one one zero zero to decimal, add the place values where there's a one: one twenty eight plus sixteen plus eight plus four is one hundred fifty six. To go the other way, keep subtracting the largest power of two that fits.

Long binary strings are hard for humans to read, so engineers use hexadecimal, base sixteen. Each hex digit stands for exactly four bits, using zero through nine and then A through F for ten through fifteen.

Split the byte into groups of four: one zero zero one is nine, and one one zero zero is twelve, which is C. So the byte is nine C, written zero x nine C. You'll see hex everywhere: memory addresses, color codes like hash F F zero zero zero zero for red, and register values in a debugger.

slides.h: Worked example: 200 in binary and hex, by hand
pts: (written on the whiteboard) 200 ÷ 2 = 100  remainder 0
(written on the whiteboard) 100 ÷ 2 = 50   remainder 0
(written on the whiteboard) 50 ÷ 2 = 25    remainder 0
(written on the whiteboard) 25 ÷ 2 = 12    remainder 1
(written on the whiteboard) 12 ÷ 2 = 6     remainder 0
(written on the whiteboard) 6 ÷ 2 = 3      remainder 0
(written on the whiteboard) 3 ÷ 2 = 1      remainder 1
(written on the whiteboard) 1 ÷ 2 = 0      remainder 1
(written on the whiteboard) read upward: 11001000
(written on the whiteboard) check: 128 + 64 + 8 = 200
(written on the whiteboard) hex: group by 4 bits
(written on the whiteboard) 1100 | 1000
(written on the whiteboard) C  |  8
(written on the whiteboard) 200 = 0xC8
say: Let's convert the decimal number two hundred to binary, the way you would on an exam. Divide by two over and over, and write down each remainder. Two hundred divided by two is one hundred, remainder zero. One hundred over two is fifty, remainder zero. Fifty over two is twenty five, remainder zero.

Twenty five over two is twelve, remainder one. Twelve over two is six, remainder zero. Six over two is three, remainder zero. Three over two is one, remainder one. And one over two is zero, remainder one. We stop at zero.
Now read the remainders from the bottom up: one, one, zero, zero, one, zero, zero, zero. Check it: one twenty eight plus sixty four plus eight is two hundred. Correct.

For hex, split the bits into groups of four. One one zero zero is twelve, which is the hex digit C. One zero zero zero is eight. So two hundred is hex C eight. That's why hex is everywhere in computing: two hex digits are exactly one byte.

pts: (code on the board) weights:  -128  64  32  16   8   4   2   1
(code on the board)  5      =  0000 0101
(code on the board) invert  =  1111 1010
(code on the board) +1      =  1111 1011   = -5
(written on the whiteboard) -128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = -5
(code on the board)    0000 0101   (5)
(code on the board)  + 1111 1011  (-5)
(code on the board)  1 0000 0000   -> drop carry -> 0
(written on the whiteboard) subtract = add the negative
(written on the whiteboard) range (8 bits): −128 … +127
say: Hardware has no minus sign, so how does a computer store negative five? Almost every computer uses two's complement. The trick: in eight bits, the top bit's place value isn't plus one twenty eight. It's minus one twenty eight. Everything else stays positive.

To negate a number, invert every bit, then add one. Five is zero zero zero zero zero one zero one. Invert: one one one one one zero one zero. Add one: one one one one one zero one one. That's negative five.

Check it with the weights: minus one twenty eight, plus sixty four, thirty two, sixteen, eight, two and one. That's minus five. And here's the beautiful part. Add five and negative five with an ordinary binary adder. Every column carries, and the final carry falls off the end of the eight bits, leaving zero.

So the same adder circuit does subtraction: a minus b is just a plus negative b. That's why everyone uses this format. Eight bits hold minus one twenty eight up to plus one twenty seven. Add one to one twenty seven, and you get one zero zero zero zero zero zero zero, which is minus one twenty eight. That's the integer overflow from the programming course: the wheel wraps around.

slides.h: Codes: BCD, ASCII and Gray code
pts: BCD: each decimal digit in 4 bits (calculators, clocks)
ASCII: 7-bit codes for text
Gray code: neighbors differ in exactly one bit
Used in rotary encoders to avoid glitches
say: Bits can encode more than plain numbers. Binary coded decimal stores each decimal digit in its own four bits, which makes driving digit displays easy. ASCII, as you saw in programming, encodes text. And Gray code is a clever ordering where neighboring values differ in exactly one bit. Look at three to four. In normal binary, all three bits flip at once: zero one one becomes one zero zero. In real hardware, those bits never flip at exactly the same instant, so for a moment you might read a garbage value like one one one. In Gray code, three to four is zero one zero to one one zero. Only one bit changes, so there's no in between garbage.

That's why rotary position sensors, like this encoder used to measure the angle of a motor shaft or a robot joint, mark their tracks in Gray code. It's also why the rows and columns of the Karnaugh maps you're about to learn are in Gray order.

slides.h: From transistors to gates: the CMOS inverter
pts: A transistor is a voltage-controlled switch
PMOS connects output to 1; NMOS connects it to 0
Exactly one is on → output = NOT input
Billions of these = a modern chip
say: What's a logic gate made of? Transistors, used as switches. In today's C M O S technology, there are two kinds. A P M O S transistor turns on when its input is zero. An N M O S transistor turns on when its input is one.
Put a P M O S between the power supply and the output, and an N M O S between the output and ground. That's an inverter.

When the input is zero, the top switch closes and the bottom opens, so the output connects to one. When the input is one, it flips, and the output connects to zero. Exactly one switch is on at a time, which means almost no current flows when nothing is switching. That's why C M O S chips use so little power.

Combine a few more transistors in series and parallel, and you get NAND and NOR gates. A modern processor is billions of these tiny switches. You'll study exactly how they work, and how fast they switch, in the electronics courses.

pts: AND, OR, NOT — the basics
NAND, NOR — each one alone can build anything
XOR — true when inputs differ (adders, parity)
say: Here's the full set of basic gates with their symbols. AND outputs one only when both inputs are one. OR outputs one when either is. NOT inverts. NAND and NOR are AND and OR followed by an inverter, and X O R outputs one when its inputs differ, which makes it perfect for adders and parity checks.

NAND and NOR are called universal gates, because you can build every other gate from just one of them. A NAND with its inputs tied together is a NOT. A NAND followed by a NOT is an AND. In C M O S, NAND is also the cheapest and fastest gate to build, so chip designers love it. Chips like this seventy four hundred, with four NAND gates in a fourteen pin package, are what you'd wire up on a breadboard in this course's lab.

pts: Distributive: AB + AC = A(B + C)
Example: AB + AB′ + A′B
= A(B + B′) + A′B = A + A′B = A + B
say: Boolean algebra is the arithmetic of logic, where plus means OR, multiplication means AND, and a prime means NOT. Some rules look like normal algebra, and some don't. A plus not A is always one: something is either true or false. A times not A is always zero. A plus one is one.
The distributive law lets you factor: A B plus A C equals A times B plus C.
Why bother? Because simpler expressions mean fewer gates, which means less area, less power, and more speed. Let's simplify A B plus A B prime plus A prime B.

Factor A out of the first two terms: A times B plus B prime, and B plus B prime is one, so that's just A. Now we have A plus A prime B. A useful identity says that equals A plus B. So three AND gates and an OR gate collapse into a single OR gate. That's a real saving, and the tools that design chips do this kind of simplification millions of times. Why is A plus A prime B equal to A plus B? In Boolean algebra, OR also distributes over AND, which ordinary algebra can't do. So A plus A prime B equals A plus A prime, times A plus B. And A plus A prime is one, leaving A plus B. Or simply check all four rows of the truth table.

slides.h: From a truth table to a circuit
pts: Write the truth table
OR together the rows where F = 1 (minterms)
Simplify
Majority vote: F = AB + AC + BC
say: Any logic function can be built straight from its truth table. Here's a majority function: the output is one when at least two of the three inputs are one.

For each row where the output is one, write an AND term that matches exactly that row. These terms are called minterms. Then OR them all together. That's called sum of products form, and it always works.
But it's rarely the simplest. These four minterms simplify down to three terms.

F equals A B plus A C plus B C: any two agreeing inputs win. This isn't just a toy. Spacecraft and aircraft computers use triple modular redundancy: three copies of the same circuit, with a majority voter on the output, so a single fault, like a radiation strike, gets outvoted.

Algebra works, but it's easy to miss a simplification. A Karnaugh map, or K map, makes it visual. Arrange the truth table in a grid with the rows and columns in Gray code order, so that neighboring cells differ by exactly one variable. Here's a four variable function, with ones in eight cells.

Now circle groups of adjacent ones, in sizes that are powers of two. Within a group, any variable that changes drops out. This orange group of four covers rows where B equals one and columns where D equals one, while A and C both change. So the whole group simplifies to just B D.

Here's the trick that surprises everyone: the map wraps around, like a donut. The four corners are all neighbors. They share B equals zero and D equals zero, so they form the group B prime D prime. The final answer is B D plus B prime D prime. Eight minterms with four variables each became two terms with two variables each. And notice that's actually an X N O R of B and D, which you might never have spotted from the equation.

slides.h: Worked example: a K-map from start to circuit
pts: (written on the whiteboard) F(A,B,C) = sum m(1,3,5,6,7)
(written on the whiteboard) m1 = 001, m3 = 011, m5 = 101
(written on the whiteboard) m6 = 110, m7 = 111
(written on the whiteboard) group of 4: only C stays constant, so it is C
(written on the whiteboard) pair 6, 7: A = 1 and B = 1, so it is AB
(written on the whiteboard) F = C + AB
say: Here's a complete K-map problem. F of A, B, C is one for minterms one, three, five, six and seven. Draw a two by four map. Rows are A. Columns are B C, in Gray code order: zero zero, zero one, one one, one zero.

Fill in the ones. Minterm one is A B C equals zero zero one: row zero, column zero one. Three is zero one one. Five is one zero one. Six is one one zero. And seven is one one one. Everything else is zero.
Now circle the biggest groups of ones, in powers of two. The two middle columns form a block of four. In those columns C is always one, while A and B both change. So this group is just C.
One one is still uncovered: minterm six. Pair it with seven next to it. In that pair, A is one and B is one, while C changes. So the group is A B.

So F equals C plus A B. That's one AND gate and one OR gate, instead of five three-input AND gates. The map did the Boolean algebra for us, just by looking. Two exam tips. Make every group as large as possible, and let groups overlap, because a one may be covered more than once. And if some input combinations can never happen, mark them with an X, a don't care, and treat an X as a one whenever it lets you draw a bigger group.

Real designs aren't built gate by gate. They're built from standard blocks. A multiplexer selects one of several inputs using select lines, like a digital switch. A decoder takes an n bit number and activates exactly one of two to the n outputs, which is how memory chooses a row and how a C P U chooses which register to use. An encoder does the reverse. Adders, built from the full adders you'll meet again in the V H D L course, do arithmetic. Comparators check whether two numbers are equal or which is bigger. All of these are combinational: the output depends only on the current inputs. To build a computer, though, we need something more. We need memory.

slides.h: Memory from feedback: the SR latch
pts: Feed outputs back into inputs → the circuit can remember
S (set) = 1 → Q = 1
R (reset) = 1 → Q = 0
S = R = 0 → hold the last value
say: Here's the most important trick in sequential logic: feedback. Take two NOR gates and connect each one's output to the other's input. The orange wires loop back.
Pulse S, the set input, to one, and Q becomes one. Now let S go back to zero. Q stays at one, because the loop holds it there.
Pulse R, the reset input, and Q flips to zero, and again stays there.

With both inputs at zero, the circuit simply holds whatever it last stored. That's one bit of memory, made from two gates. It's called an S R latch. The one forbidden case is setting S and R to one at the same time, which leaves the latch in an undefined state when they're released.

pts: D flip-flop: copies D to Q on the clock edge
Register: n flip-flops sharing a clock
Counter: register + adder (or toggling flip-flops)
Each bit toggles at half the rate of the one before
say: Latches respond whenever their inputs change, which makes timing tricky. A flip-flop only updates at the instant the clock rises, the edge. A D flip-flop simply copies its D input to Q on each rising edge, then holds it.
Put n flip-flops side by side with a shared clock and you have a register, which stores an n bit number. Every C P U register is exactly this.
Feed a register's output through an adder that adds one, back into its input, and you have a counter. On every clock edge, the count goes up by one.

Look at the timing diagram. Q zero toggles every clock cycle. Q one toggles at half that rate, and Q two at half again. Read the three bits together and they count zero, one, two, up to seven, then wrap around to zero. That halving is also why a counter makes a perfect clock divider.

slides.h: Worked example: drawing a 2-bit counter’s timing diagram
pts: (written on the whiteboard) 2-bit counter
(written on the whiteboard) acts on rising edges
(written on the whiteboard) Q0 toggles on every edge
(written on the whiteboard) f(Q0) = f(clk) / 2
(written on the whiteboard) Q1 toggles when Q0 falls
(written on the whiteboard) f(Q1) = f(clk) / 4
(written on the whiteboard) count: 1, 2, 3, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0
say: Let's draw the timing diagram of a two bit counter, the way you would in lab. Start with the clock: a square wave. The flip-flops only act on the rising edges, where the clock goes from low to high.
Bit zero is a toggle flip-flop: it flips on every rising edge. So it runs at half the clock frequency.
Bit one toggles only when bit zero falls from one back to zero. That's every second edge, so it runs at a quarter of the clock frequency.

Now read the two bits together after each edge, with Q one as the high bit: one, two, three, zero, one, two, three, zero. It counts! And each extra bit halves the frequency again, which is exactly how a clock divider turns one hundred megahertz into one hertz.

pts: Memory = huge grid of storage cells
Address lines pick one word (decoder)
n address bits → 2ⁿ words
2048 × 8 memory: 11 address lines, 8 data lines
say: Scale that up and you get memory chips. A memory is a huge grid of storage cells, organized into words.
To read or write, you send an address. A decoder turns that address into a single selected row, here highlighted in yellow, and that row's bits appear on the data lines.
With n address bits, you can select two to the n words.

Example: a sixteen kilobit memory organized as two thousand forty eight words of eight bits. How many address lines? Two to the eleventh is two thousand forty eight, so eleven. And eight data lines, one per bit. That same arithmetic tells you that a thirty two bit address can reach four gigabytes, which is why older thirty two bit computers couldn't use more than four gigabytes of memory.

slides.h: Worked example: how many address lines?
pts: (written on the whiteboard) 64 KB = 64 times 1024 = 65,536 addresses
(written on the whiteboard) 2^n = 65,536 Rightarrow n = 16 lines (A0 to A15)
(written on the whiteboard) addresses: 0x0000 to 0xFFFF
(written on the whiteboard) two 32 KB chips: each uses A0 to A14 (2^15)
(written on the whiteboard) A15 = 0: chip 0, 0x0000 to 0x7FFF
(written on the whiteboard) A15 = 1: chip 1, 0x8000 to 0xFFFF
(written on the whiteboard) the top address bit selects the chip: address decoding
say: Every memory problem starts with the same question: how many address lines? Take a sixty four kilobyte memory, with one byte per address. Sixty four K is sixty four times one thousand twenty four, or sixty five thousand five hundred thirty six bytes.
With n address lines, you can name two to the n locations. Two to the sixteenth is sixty five thousand five hundred thirty six. So we need sixteen address lines, A zero through A fifteen.

Now suppose we build it from two thirty two kilobyte chips. Each chip needs fifteen lines, A zero to A fourteen. The leftover line, A fifteen, chooses the chip. When A fifteen is zero, the lower chip answers, addresses zero to seven F F F. When it's one, the upper chip answers, eight thousand to F F F F.
That extra line feeding a chip select is called address decoding. It's how every computer's memory map is built, and you'll see it again in the microcontrollers course.

slides.h: Putting it together: the structure of a computer
pts: Datapath: registers + ALU
Control unit: decodes instructions, drives the datapath
Memory holds instructions AND data (von Neumann)
Fetch → decode → execute, forever
say: Now we have every piece needed for a computer. This is the layout of the Intel four zero zero four from nineteen seventy one, the first commercial single chip microprocessor, with about two thousand three hundred transistors.

Every processor has the same main parts. The datapath: registers that hold values, and an arithmetic logic unit, the A L U, that adds, subtracts and does logic operations. The control unit is a big state machine that reads each instruction and drives the datapath.
And memory holds both the program's instructions and its data, an arrangement called the von Neumann architecture.

The C P U runs one loop forever. Fetch: read the instruction at the address in the program counter. Decode: figure out what it means. Execute: do it, using the A L U and registers. Then move to the next instruction. A modern processor does this billions of times per second. You'll design one of these yourself, in V H D L, in the computer design course.

slides.big: Transistors → gates → combinational blocks + flip-flops → registers, counters, memory → a computer.
say: Let's recap the whole tower. Binary and hex represent information. Transistors make gates. Boolean algebra and Karnaugh maps simplify logic into fewer gates. Gates make combinational blocks like multiplexers, decoders and adders. Feedback makes latches and flip-flops, which make registers, counters and memory. And registers, an A L U, memory and a control unit make a computer. Every later digital course builds on this one, so it's worth knowing cold. Next up, Calculus three. See you there.

L08_math250a.title: Calculus III
L08_math250a.file: MATH-250A Calculus III/Lecture - MATH 250A Calculus III.mp4

say: Welcome to Calculus three. So far, our functions have had one input. But the real world has three dimensions, and quantities like temperature, air pressure and electric field vary from point to point in space. This course extends calculus to many variables. You'll learn to see a function of two variables as a landscape, find the steepest direction uphill, add up quantities over areas and volumes, and describe fields that fill space. It's the language you'll need for electricity and magnetism, and, surprisingly, for machine learning.

pts: a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ = |a||b| cos θ
Zero → perpendicular
3D graphics: brightness = normal · light direction
say: Vectors now have three components. The dot product multiplies matching components and adds them. Geometrically, it equals the lengths times the cosine of the angle between them.
So if the dot product is zero, the vectors are perpendicular. It also gives the projection: how much of one vector points along another.

Example: one, two, two dotted with two, zero, one is two plus zero plus two, which is four. The lengths are three and root five, so the cosine of the angle is four over three root five, about point six, and the angle is about fifty three degrees.

Every video game uses this billions of times per second. The brightness of a surface depends on the dot product between its normal vector and the direction to the light. Facing the light, it's bright. Turned edge on, the dot product is zero, and it's dark.

slides.h: Worked example: the angle between two vectors
pts: (written on the whiteboard) vec a = (3,4,0),  vec b = (4,0,3)
(written on the whiteboard) vec acdotvec b = 3(4) + 4(0) + 0(3) = 12
(written on the whiteboard) |vec a| = sqrt9+16+0 = 5
(written on the whiteboard) |vec b| = sqrt16+0+9 = 5
(written on the whiteboard) costheta = (vec acdotvec b)/(|vec a||vec b|) = (12)/(25) = 0.48
(written on the whiteboard) theta = cos^-1(0.48) approx 61.3°
say: Let's compute an angle with the dot product, start to finish. Take a equals three, four, zero, and b equals four, zero, three. Step one: multiply matching components and add. Three times four, plus four times zero, plus zero times three, is twelve.
Step two: the lengths. The length of a is the square root of nine plus sixteen plus zero, which is five. The length of b is the square root of sixteen plus zero plus nine, also five.

Step three: the dot product equals the product of the lengths times cosine of the angle. So cosine theta is twelve over twenty five, point four eight. The inverse cosine gives about sixty one point three degrees. A positive dot product means the angle is less than ninety degrees: the vectors point roughly the same way.

slides.h: The cross product: a perpendicular vector
pts: a × b is perpendicular to both a and b
Length = |a||b| sin θ = parallelogram area
Direction: right-hand rule
Torque τ = r × F · surface normals in graphics
say: The cross product of two 3D vectors produces a third vector perpendicular to both. Its length equals the area of the parallelogram they span, and its direction follows the right hand rule: curl your fingers from a to b, and your thumb points along a cross b. For example, x hat cross y hat is z hat. Torque from mechanics is really a cross product: r cross F. In 3D graphics, the normal vector of each triangle in a model is the cross product of two of its edges. And in electromagnetism, the force on a moving charge is q v cross B. Same operation, everywhere.

slides.h: Worked example: computing a cross product
pts: (written on the whiteboard) vec a = (1,0,2),  vec b = (0,3,1)
(written on the whiteboard) vec atimesvec b = (a_2b_3 - a_3b_2, a_3b_1 - a_1b_3, a_1b_2 - a_2b_1)
(written on the whiteboard) x:\ 0(1) - 2(3) = -6
(written on the whiteboard) y:\ 2(0) - 1(1) = -1
(written on the whiteboard) z:\ 1(3) - 0(0) = 3
(written on the whiteboard) vec atimesvec b = (-6, -1, 3)
(written on the whiteboard) check: (-6,-1,3)cdotvec a = -6+0+6 = 0
(written on the whiteboard) (-6,-1,3)cdotvec b = 0-3+3 = 0
(written on the whiteboard) area = sqrt36+1+9 = sqrt46 approx 6.78
say: Now a cross product, worked by hand. Take a equals one, zero, two, and b equals zero, three, one. Each component of the cross product uses the other two components, in a crisscross pattern.

First component: zero times one minus two times three, negative six. Second: two times zero minus one times one, negative one. Third: one times three minus zero times zero, three. So a cross b is negative six, negative one, three.

Always check it: the result must be perpendicular to both. Dot it with a: negative six plus zero plus six, zero. Dot it with b: zero minus three plus three, zero. Both zero, so it's correct. And its length, the square root of forty six, about six point seven eight, is the area of the parallelogram the two vectors span.

pts: z = f(x, y) is a surface
Contour lines: points with equal height
Like a topographic hiking map
say: A function of two variables, z equals f of x and y, assigns a height to every point on a map. Its graph is a surface, a landscape of hills and valleys.

We can draw it two ways. As a 3D surface, on the left. Or as a contour map, on the right, where each curve connects points with the same height. That's exactly a topographic hiking map: contour lines packed close together mean steep terrain, and lines spread apart mean gentle slopes. Weather maps draw temperature and pressure the same way.

slides.h: Partial derivatives: slope in one direction
pts: ∂f/∂x: change x, hold y fixed
∂f/∂y: change y, hold x fixed
f = x²y + 3y → f_x = 2xy, f_y = x² + 3
say: On a landscape, the slope depends on which direction you walk. A partial derivative measures the slope in one coordinate direction. The partial with respect to x: change x, and treat y as a constant.
The partial with respect to y: change y, and treat x as a constant.
Example: f equals x squared y plus three y. With respect to x, y is just a constant, so the derivative is two x y. With respect to y, x squared is a constant multiplier, so it's x squared plus three.
At the point one, two, both partials equal four. All the single variable rules still work. You just have to be disciplined about which variables you're holding still.

slides.h: The gradient: which way is uphill?
pts: Points in the direction of steepest ascent
Its length = the steepest slope
Always perpendicular to contour lines
say: Collect the partial derivatives into a vector, and you get the gradient, written with an upside down triangle called nabla.
Here's the key fact: the gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent. If you're standing on a hillside in the fog, the gradient tells you which way is straight uphill.
Its length tells you how steep that steepest direction is. The slope in any other direction, called the directional derivative, is the gradient dotted with a unit vector in that direction.

And the gradient is always perpendicular to the contour lines. Look at the red arrows. They cross every contour at a right angle, pointing toward the peaks. Water flows in the opposite direction, straight downhill, which is why streams cross contour lines at right angles on a topographic map.

pts: Want the minimum of an error function?
Step opposite the gradient: x ← x − η∇f
Repeat until the slope is ~0
Neural networks: the same idea with billions of variables
say: Now an application that runs much of modern technology. Suppose you want the lowest point of a function, like the error of a prediction model.
Start anywhere, compute the gradient, and take a small step in the opposite direction, downhill. The step size, eta, is called the learning rate.
Repeat. Here, on the bowl f equals x squared plus three y squared, the orange path zigzags down into the minimum at the center. It zigzags because the bowl is steeper in y than in x.

This is gradient descent, and it's how neural networks are trained. The error is a function of millions or billions of parameters, the gradient is computed with the chain rule, and the computer takes millions of small downhill steps. Every image recognizer and language model you've used was trained this way, using exactly this Calculus three idea.

slides.h: Worked example: two steps of gradient descent
pts: (written on the whiteboard) f = x^2 + 3y^2
(written on the whiteboard) nabla f = (2x,\ 6y)
(written on the whiteboard) start (2, 1), eta = 0.1, f = 7
(written on the whiteboard) nabla f(2,1) = (4,\ 6)
(written on the whiteboard) (2,1) - 0.1(4,6) = (1.6,\ 0.4)
(written on the whiteboard) f = 3.04
(written on the whiteboard) nabla f(1.6,0.4) = (3.2,\ 2.4)
(written on the whiteboard) f approx 1.72
say: Let's run gradient descent by hand on f equals x squared plus three y squared. Its minimum is obviously at the origin, so we can watch the algorithm find it. The gradient is two x, six y. Start at two comma one, with a learning rate of point one.

Step one. At two comma one, the gradient is four comma six. Move opposite to it, scaled by point one: two minus point four, and one minus point six. The new point is one point six comma point four, and f has dropped from seven to about three.

Step two. The gradient at the new point is three point two comma two point four. Subtract a tenth of it: one point two eight comma point one six. Now f is about one point seven. Each step heads downhill, perpendicular to the contour lines. Notice y shrinks faster than x, because the bowl is steeper in y. Training a neural network is exactly this loop, with millions of variables instead of two.

pts: Critical point: ∇f = 0
Second-derivative test: max, min, or saddle
With a constraint g = c: ∇f = λ∇g (Lagrange)
Max xy with x + y = 10 → x = y = 5
say: To find peaks and valleys, look for critical points where the gradient is zero: the surface is flat in every direction. But flat doesn't always mean a peak or a valley. Look at the third surface. It's a saddle: it curves up in one direction and down in the other, like a mountain pass. A second derivative test, using all the second partial derivatives, tells the three cases apart.

Often you're optimizing with a constraint. Maximize the area x y of a rectangle, given that x plus y must equal ten, say because you have twenty meters of fence. Lagrange's insight: at the best point, the contour line of f just touches the constraint curve, so their gradients are parallel. Gradient of f equals lambda times gradient of g. Solving gives x equals y equals five, a square, with area twenty five. Engineers use this to maximize performance subject to power, cost or size limits.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) f(x,y) = x^3 - 3x + y^2
(written on the whiteboard) f_x = 3x^2 - 3 = 0 Rightarrow x = pm 1
(written on the whiteboard) f_y = 2y = 0 Rightarrow y = 0
(written on the whiteboard) D = f_xxf_yy - f_xy^2
(written on the whiteboard) = (6x)(2) - 0^2 = 12x
(written on the whiteboard) (1,0): D = 12 > 0, f_xx > 0 so it's a minimum
(written on the whiteboard) (-1,0): D = -12 < 0 so it's a saddle
say: Let's classify the critical points of f equals x cubed minus three x plus y squared. Step one: set both partial derivatives to zero. f x is three x squared minus three, which is zero at x equals plus or minus one. f y is two y, zero at y equals zero. So there are two critical points: one comma zero, and negative one comma zero.
Step two: the second derivative test. Compute D equals f x x times f y y, minus f x y squared. Here f x x is six x, f y y is two, and f x y is zero. So D equals twelve x.
At one comma zero, D is twelve, positive, and f x x is six, positive. So it's a local minimum, with value negative two.

At negative one comma zero, D is negative twelve. A negative D means a saddle point: it's a peak if you walk along x, but a valley if you walk along y, like a horse's saddle. Gradient descent can stall near saddles like this, which is a real problem when training neural networks.

slides.h: Double integrals: volume under a surface
pts: ∬ f dA adds f over an area
Compute as two nested single integrals
∫₀² ∫₀¹ (x + y) dy dx = ∫₀² (x + ½) dx = 3
Mass from density, total charge, average temperature
say: A double integral adds up a function over a two dimensional region, just like a single integral adds up over an interval. Geometrically, it's the volume under the surface, made of thin columns, like these bars.
You compute it as two nested single integrals: integrate over y with x held fixed, then integrate the result over x.

Example: x plus y over the rectangle from zero to two in x and zero to one in y. The inner integral over y gives x plus one half. Then integrate from zero to two: two plus one, which is three. When the region isn't a rectangle, the inner limits become functions of the outer variable. Over the triangle under the line y equals x, for example, y runs from zero up to x, and then x runs over its range. Always draw the region first, then read the limits off the picture.

Double integrals compute total mass from a density, total charge on a surface, the average temperature over a chip, or the probability that two random variables land in a region, which you'll do in the statistics course.

slides.h: Change of coordinates: polar, cylindrical, spherical
pts: Polar: dA = r dr dθ (the extra r matters!)
Gaussian integral: ∫ e^(−x²) dx = √π
Spherical: dV = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ
Sphere volume (4/3)πr³ falls right out
say: Circular regions are painful in x and y, so we switch coordinates. In polar coordinates, a tiny area element is r d r d theta. That extra r is crucial: the little patches get bigger as you move outward.

Here's a famous trick. The integral of e to the minus x squared has no antiderivative. But square it, turning it into a double integral over the whole plane, and switch to polar. The extra r makes it easy: the answer is pi. Take the square root, and the integral of e to the minus x squared is root pi. That's why root pi appears in the normal distribution's formula.
In three dimensions, cylindrical and spherical coordinates do the same job, with their own volume elements. In spherical coordinates, it's rho squared sine phi.
Integrate one over a ball in spherical coordinates, and the volume of a sphere, four thirds pi r cubed, falls right out in a couple of lines.

slides.h: Worked example: a double integral in polar coordinates
pts: (written on the whiteboard) iint_disk (x^2 + y^2) dA
(written on the whiteboard) x^2 + y^2 = r^2
(written on the whiteboard) dA = r dr dtheta
(written on the whiteboard) = int_0^2piint_0^2 r^2 cdot r dr dtheta
(written on the whiteboard) int_0^2 r^3 dr = (2^4)/(4) = 4
(written on the whiteboard) int_0^2pi 4 dtheta = 8pi approx 25.1
say: Here's why polar coordinates are worth it. Integrate x squared plus y squared over a disk of radius two. In x and y, the limits are square roots and the algebra gets ugly. In polar, x squared plus y squared is just r squared, and the disk is simply r from zero to two, theta from zero to two pi.
Don't forget the extra r: a little patch of area is r d r d theta, because patches farther from the center are wider. So the integrand becomes r squared times r, r cubed.

The inner integral of r cubed is r to the fourth over four, which from zero to two is four. The outer integral of four, over a full turn, is four times two pi. Eight pi, about twenty five point one. Two short lines, instead of a page of square roots.

pts: Vector field: an arrow at every point (wind, E, B)
Divergence ∇·F: is stuff flowing out? (sources)
Curl ∇×F: is it swirling? (rotation)
Maxwell’s equations are written with these
say: A vector field attaches an arrow to every point in space: wind velocity on a weather map, water flow in a pipe, the electric field around a charge.
Divergence measures whether a field is spreading out from a point, like the electric field of a positive charge on the left. A positive divergence means a source. Negative means a sink.
Curl measures how much the field swirls around a point, like the magnetic field circling a wire carrying current, on the right.

These aren't abstract. Maxwell's equations, the four equations of electricity and magnetism, say: the divergence of E is proportional to charge density, the divergence of B is zero, the curl of E comes from a changing magnetic field, and the curl of B comes from current and a changing electric field. You'll meet them next year in physics.

slides.h: One symbol, three operations: grad, div, curl
pts: (written on the whiteboard) nabla = ((partial)/(partial x),\ (partial)/(partial y))
(written on the whiteboard) nabla f : scalar in, VECTOR out (gradient)
(written on the whiteboard) nablacdotvec F = (partial P)/(partial x) + (partial Q)/(partial y) : vector in, NUMBER out
(written on the whiteboard) vec F = (x, y): 1 + 1 = 2 > 0 source
(written on the whiteboard) curl: (partial Q)/(partial x) - (partial P)/(partial y) : measures rotation
(written on the whiteboard) vec F = (-y, x): curl = 1 - (-1) = 2
(written on the whiteboard) div = 0 − 0 = 0
say: The nabla symbol confuses everyone, because it shows up three ways. Think of nabla as a vector of derivative instructions: d by d x, d by d y. What you get depends on what you combine it with. Apply it to a scalar function, and you get the gradient, a vector.

Dot it with a vector field, and you get the divergence, a single number at each point: d P d x plus d Q d y. For the field x comma y, every arrow points outward. The divergence is one plus one, two, positive everywhere: a source.

Cross it with the field, and you get the curl, which measures rotation. In two dimensions, it's d Q d x minus d P d y. For the field minus y comma x, the arrows circle the origin. The curl is one minus negative one, two, so it swirls counterclockwise. And its divergence? Zero minus zero, zero. Pure rotation, nothing spreading.

slides.h: Line integrals and the big theorems
pts: Line integral ∫ F·dr: work along a path
Conservative fields: only the endpoints matter
Green, Stokes, Divergence: inside ⇄ boundary
All are cousins of the Fundamental Theorem
say: A line integral adds up a field along a path. The work done moving through a force field is the integral of F dot d r along the path.
For conservative fields, like gravity, the work depends only on the starting and ending points, not on the route. That's exactly why we can define potential energy, and in circuits, voltage.

Then come the three great theorems of vector calculus. Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem and the divergence theorem all say the same thing in different dimensions: adding up a derivative over the inside of a region equals adding up the field over its boundary.

Look at the first row: the fundamental theorem of calculus is the one dimensional version, where the boundary of an interval is just its two endpoints. The divergence theorem is what turns Maxwell's equations into Gauss's law, which says the electric flux out of any closed surface equals the charge inside. It's one beautiful idea, from Calculus one all the way to electromagnetism.

slides.h: Worked example: work along two different paths
pts: (written on the whiteboard) vec F = (y,\ x),  W = int vec Fcdot dvec r
(written on the whiteboard) vec r = (t,t), dvec r = (1,1) dt
(written on the whiteboard) int_0^1 (t,t)cdot(1,1) dt = int_0^1 2t dt = 1
(written on the whiteboard) vec r = (t,t^2), dvec r = (1,2t) dt
(written on the whiteboard) int_0^1 (t^2 + 2t^2) dt = int_0^1 3t^2 dt = 1
(written on the whiteboard) vec F = nabla(xy) so W = f(1,1) - f(0,0) = 1
say: Let's actually compute a line integral, and see path independence happen. The field is F equals y comma x. We'll move from the origin to the point one comma one, along two different paths.

Path one: the straight line y equals x. Write it as r of t equals t comma t, with t from zero to one. Then d r is one comma one, d t, and F along the path is t comma t. The dot product is two t. Integrate from zero to one: one.

Path two: the parabola y equals x squared. r of t is t comma t squared, so d r is one comma two t, d t. F along it is t squared comma t. The dot product is t squared plus two t squared, three t squared. Integrate: again exactly one.

Same answer, different paths. That's because this field is conservative: it's the gradient of f equals x y. So the work is just f at the end minus f at the start, one minus zero. That's the fundamental theorem of calculus again, and it's exactly why voltage is well defined in circuits.

slides.big: The gradient points uphill. Multiple integrals add up over areas and volumes. Divergence & curl describe fields — the language of E&M.
say: To recap. Dot and cross products measure angles, projections, areas and perpendicular directions. Functions of two variables are landscapes, partial derivatives measure slopes along each axis, and the gradient points straight uphill, which is the engine of machine learning. Critical points and Lagrange multipliers find the best designs. Double and triple integrals add up quantities over regions, often in polar or spherical coordinates. And vector fields, with divergence, curl and the big theorems, are the language of electricity and magnetism. Next, linear algebra and differential equations. See you there.

L09_math250b.title: Linear Algebra & Differential Equations
L09_math250b.file: MATH-250B Differential Equations & Linear Algebra/Lecture - MATH 250B Linear Algebra & Differential Equations.mp4

say: Welcome to Math two fifty B, linear algebra and differential equations. These two subjects look different at first, but they turn out to be one subject. Differential equations describe how things change: a cooling cup of coffee, a charging capacitor, a car's suspension. Linear algebra handles many equations at once with matrices. By the end, you'll see that eigenvalues of a matrix decide whether a system settles down or blows up, which is the core idea of every circuit and control system you'll ever design.
Part one. First order differential equations.

slides.h: A differential equation describes how something changes
pts: Unknown is a function, not a number
dT/dt = −k(T − T_room): cools faster when hotter
Slope field: the slope at every point
Solutions follow the arrows; equilibrium where slope = 0
say: In algebra, you solve for a number. In a differential equation, you solve for a whole function, given a rule for how it changes. Take a hot cup of coffee. Newton's law of cooling says it loses heat at a rate proportional to how much hotter it is than the room.
Written as an equation: d T d t equals minus k times T minus twenty, for a room at twenty degrees. Hot coffee cools fast. Lukewarm coffee cools slowly.
Even before solving it, we can draw it. A slope field puts a little arrow at every point, showing the slope the equation demands there.

Every solution is a curve that follows the arrows. Start at ninety degrees, the orange curve, and it bends down toward twenty. Start below room temperature, the green curve, and it warms up toward twenty. The flat red line, where the slope is zero, is the equilibrium. Everything is attracted to it.

When a differential equation is separable, put everything with T on one side and everything with t on the other. Integrate both sides: the natural log of T minus twenty equals negative point one t, plus a constant. Exponentiate, and T equals twenty plus some constant A times e to the minus point one t. The initial condition, ninety degrees at time zero, gives A equals seventy. So after ten minutes, the coffee is at twenty plus seventy over e, about forty six degrees. Notice the shape: an exponential decay toward a final value. That's exactly the formula for a capacitor charging or discharging through a resistor, which you'll use constantly in circuits. Same equation, different physics. The other main technique, for linear first order equations, is the integrating factor, which handles equations with a forcing term like a changing outside temperature or an input voltage.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) y' + 2y = 4,  y(0) = 0
(written on the whiteboard) form: y' + p y = q
(written on the whiteboard) mu = e^int 2 dt = e^2t
(written on the whiteboard) e^2ty' + 2e^2ty = (e^2t y)' = 4e^2t
(written on the whiteboard) e^2ty = 2e^2t + C
(written on the whiteboard) y = 2 + Ce^-2t,  y(0) = 0 Rightarrow C = -2
(written on the whiteboard) y(t) = 2 (1 - e^-2t)
say: Separation doesn't work when there's an input term, so here's the integrating factor, worked out. Take y prime plus two y equals four, starting at zero. It's the shape of a capacitor charging toward a supply voltage.
Multiply both sides by e to the integral of p, here e to the two t. Why that? Because now the left side is exactly the product rule result for e to the two t times y. That's the whole trick.
Integrate both sides: e to the two t times y equals two e to the two t, plus C. Divide by e to the two t: y equals two plus C e to the minus two t. The starting value zero gives C equals minus two.

So y equals two times one minus e to the minus two t. It starts at zero and rises toward two, fast at first, then slowly. That's exactly the voltage on a charging capacitor, with a time constant of one half.
Part two. Linear algebra.

slides.h: Systems of equations and row reduction
pts: Write as A x = b
Row-reduce the augmented matrix
Outcomes: one solution, infinitely many, or none
Circuit analysis produces exactly these systems
say: Many problems give you several linear equations in several unknowns. We write them compactly as A x equals b, where A is a matrix of coefficients.

To solve, row reduce the augmented matrix: swap rows, scale rows, and add multiples of one row to another, until it's triangular. Here, subtracting half of row one from row two eliminates x. Then back substitute: y equals one, so x equals two.
There are only three possible outcomes. Exactly one solution, infinitely many solutions with free variables, or no solution at all, which shows up as a row saying zero equals something nonzero.

In circuits, nodal analysis writes Kirchhoff's current law at each node, and you get exactly this kind of system. A circuit with fifty nodes is a fifty by fifty matrix, and circuit simulators like SPICE solve systems like this millions of times.

slides.h: Worked example: solving three equations by elimination
pts: (written on the whiteboard) (1) x + y + z = 6
(written on the whiteboard) (2) 2y + 5z = -4
(written on the whiteboard) (3) 2x + 5y - z = 27
(written on the whiteboard) (3) - 2(1): 3y - 3z = 15
(written on the whiteboard) y - z = 5 Rightarrow y = z + 5
(written on the whiteboard) 2(z+5) + 5z = -4
(written on the whiteboard) 7z = -14 Rightarrow z = -2
(written on the whiteboard) y = 3,   x = 6 - 3 + 2 = 5
(written on the whiteboard) (x, y, z) = (5,\ 3,\ -2)
(written on the whiteboard) check (3): 10 + 15 + 2 = 27
say: Let's solve a system of three equations by hand. x plus y plus z equals six. Two y plus five z equals negative four. Two x plus five y minus z equals twenty seven.

Step one: eliminate x from equation three. Subtract two times equation one. Two x cancels, five y minus two y is three y, minus z minus two z is minus three z, and twenty seven minus twelve is fifteen. Divide by three: y minus z equals five.
Step two: substitute y equals z plus five into equation two. Two times z plus five, plus five z, equals negative four. That's seven z plus ten equals negative four, so z equals negative two.

Back substitute. y is z plus five, which is three. And x is six minus y minus z: six minus three plus two, which is five. Always check in the equation you didn't use last: two times five plus five times three minus negative two is ten plus fifteen plus two, twenty seven. Correct. This is exactly what circuit simulators do, with thousands of equations instead of three.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) A = genfrac[]001 23 4,  B = genfrac[]000 11 0
(written on the whiteboard) entry (i, j) = row i of A · column j of B
(written on the whiteboard) top-left: 1(0) + 2(1) = 2
(written on the whiteboard) top-right: 1(1) + 2(0) = 1
(written on the whiteboard) AB = genfrac[]002 14 3
(written on the whiteboard) BA = genfrac[]003 41 2
(written on the whiteboard) AB neq BA
say: Before we treat matrices as transformations, let's make sure the multiplication itself is clear, because it isn't done entry by entry. Each entry of the product is a row of the first matrix times a column of the second: multiply matching entries and add.

Top left of A B: row one of A, one two, times column one of B, zero one. One times zero plus two times one: two. Top right: one two times one zero: one. The bottom row the same way gives four and three.

Now swap the order. B A comes out as three, four, one, two. Different! A B swapped A's columns, but B A swapped its rows. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so order always matters. And for A times a vector x, it's the same rule: each row of A dotted with x.

pts: Multiplying by A moves every point
Columns of A = where the basis vectors land
det A = area (or volume) scaling factor
det A = 0 → space gets squashed → not invertible
say: Here's the most useful way to think about a matrix: it's a machine that moves every point in space. Multiply a vector by A and you get a new vector. These pictures show the unit square, in blue, transformed into the orange shape.

The columns of A tell you where the basis vectors land. The first column is where the x direction goes, the second is where the y direction goes. That's how 3D graphics rotate and scale every point of a model: one matrix multiply per point.
The determinant is the factor by which areas get scaled. Stretching x by two doubles areas, so the determinant is two. Rotations and shears keep area the same, so their determinant is one.

And if the determinant is zero, the matrix squashes the plane flat onto a line. Information is lost, so you can't undo it: the matrix has no inverse. This connects a dozen facts into one theorem. A is invertible exactly when the determinant isn't zero, exactly when the columns are independent, exactly when A x equals b always has a unique solution.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) A = genfrac[]004 72 6, b = genfrac[]0012
(written on the whiteboard) det A = (4)(6) - (7)(2) = 10
(written on the whiteboard) A^-1 = (1)/(10)genfrac[]006 -7-2 4
(written on the whiteboard) x = A^-1b = (1)/(10)genfrac[]006(1) - 7(2)-2(1) + 4(2) = (1)/(10)genfrac[]00-86
(written on the whiteboard) x = (-0.8,\ 0.6)
(written on the whiteboard) check: 4(-0.8) + 7(0.6) = 1,  2(-0.8) + 6(0.6) = 2
say: Let's solve A x equals b using an inverse. A is four, seven, two, six, and b is one, two. For a two by two matrix, the inverse has a shortcut. First the determinant: a d minus b c, four times six minus seven times two, which is ten. It's not zero, so A can be inverted.
The shortcut: swap the two diagonal entries, negate the other two, and divide by the determinant. So the inverse is one tenth of six, negative seven, negative two, four.

Now x equals A inverse times b. Top row: six times one minus seven times two is negative eight. Bottom row: negative two times one plus four times two is six. Divide by ten: x is negative point eight, point six.

Check it in the original equations. Four times negative point eight plus seven times point six is one. Two times negative point eight plus six times point six is two. Both match. In practice, computers solve by elimination rather than computing inverses, because it's faster and more accurate, but the inverse is the cleanest way to see what's happening.

pts: Vector space: anything you can add and scale
Rⁿ, polynomials, solutions of linear ODEs, signals
Basis: independent vectors that build everything
Rank + nullity = number of columns
say: Linear algebra generalizes far beyond arrows. A vector space is any collection of objects you can add together and multiply by numbers, following the usual rules.
That includes ordinary vectors, but also polynomials, matrices, the solutions of a linear differential equation, and audio signals. That's why the same tools work in so many places.

A basis is a minimal set of vectors from which you can build every vector in the space, using combinations. The number of vectors in a basis is the dimension. Sine and cosine waves at different frequencies form a basis for signals, which is the idea behind the Fourier series you'll study in signals and systems.

And the rank nullity theorem: the dimension of the output space a matrix reaches, plus the dimension of the inputs it crushes to zero, always equals the number of columns. Nothing is lost without being accounted for.

slides.h: Least squares: fitting a line to noisy data
pts: More equations than unknowns → no exact solution
Find the closest one: minimize squared error
Normal equations: AᵀA x = Aᵀb
Calibration, trend lines, machine learning
say: Real measurements are noisy. If you have twelve data points and want the best line through them, you have twelve equations and only two unknowns, the slope and intercept. There's no exact solution.
So we find the closest one: the line that minimizes the sum of the squared vertical gaps, the red dotted lines.
Linear algebra solves this in one step with the normal equations: A transpose A x equals A transpose b. Geometrically, it projects the data onto the space of possible lines.
Engineers use least squares to calibrate sensors, fit trend lines, estimate positions from GPS signals, and it's the starting point of machine learning. Linear regression is literally this slide.

slides.h: Worked example: the best-fit line through three points
pts: (written on the whiteboard) data: (0,1),\ (1,3),\ (2,4)
(written on the whiteboard) bar x = 1,  bar y = (8)/(3)
(written on the whiteboard) x - bar x:\ -1,\ 0,\ 1
(written on the whiteboard) m = (sum (x-bar x) y)/(sum (x-bar x)^2)
(written on the whiteboard) b = bar y - mbar x = (8)/(3) - 1.5 = (7)/(6)
(written on the whiteboard) y = 1.5x + 1.17
say: Let's fit a line to three measurements by hand: zero comma one, one comma three, and two comma four. No straight line passes through all three, so we want the one that minimizes the squared errors.
Compute the averages. The average x is one. The average y is eight thirds, about two point six seven. Then subtract the averages: the x deviations are negative one, zero, one.

The best slope is the sum of the x deviations times the y values, over the sum of the squared x deviations. On top: negative one times one, plus zero, plus one times four, which is three. On the bottom: one plus zero plus one, two. So the slope is one point five.

The line always passes through the averages, so the intercept is eight thirds minus one point five times one, which is seven sixths, about one point one seven. Look at the dashed orange errors: two points sit above the line and one below, and the squared errors are as small as any line can make them.

slides.h: Eigenvalues: directions a matrix only stretches
pts: A v = λ v: v keeps its direction, scaled by λ
Solve det(A − λI) = 0
Google’s PageRank is an eigenvector
say: Most vectors get turned when you multiply by a matrix. Look at the light blue arrows: their directions change. But a few special directions only get stretched. Those are eigenvectors, and the stretch factor is the eigenvalue.
To find them, solve the determinant of A minus lambda I equals zero. For this matrix, that's two minus lambda squared, minus one, equals zero.

So lambda is three or one. The eigenvector for three is one, one: multiplying gives three, three, the same direction tripled. The eigenvector for one is one, negative one, which comes back unchanged. Those are the orange arrows.

Eigenvectors are everywhere. Google's original PageRank algorithm ranked web pages by finding the main eigenvector of an enormous matrix of links between pages. Vibration engineers find the eigenvectors of a structure to learn its natural shapes of vibration. And as we'll see in a moment, eigenvalues decide whether a system is stable.

slides.h: Worked example: finding eigenvalues and eigenvectors
pts: (written on the whiteboard) A = genfrac[]004 12 3
(written on the whiteboard) det(A - lambda I) = (4-lambda)(3-lambda) - 2 = 0
(written on the whiteboard) lambda^2 - 7lambda + 10 = 0
(written on the whiteboard) (lambda - 5)(lambda - 2) = 0
(written on the whiteboard) lambda = 5,\ \ lambda = 2
(written on the whiteboard) lambda=5: -x + y = 0 Rightarrow v_1 = (1,\ 1)
(written on the whiteboard) lambda=2: 2x + y = 0 Rightarrow v_2 = (1,\ -2)
say: Let's find the eigenvalues of A equals four, one, two, three. Subtract lambda from the diagonal and set the determinant to zero. Four minus lambda, times three minus lambda, minus one times two, equals zero.

Multiply out: lambda squared minus seven lambda plus twelve minus two, so lambda squared minus seven lambda plus ten. That factors as lambda minus five, times lambda minus two. The eigenvalues are five and two.

For lambda equals five, solve A minus five I times v equals zero. The first row says negative x plus y equals zero, so v is one, one. Check: A times one, one is five, five. Same direction, stretched by five.

For lambda equals two, the first row says two x plus y equals zero, so v is one, negative two. A times that is two, negative four, which is exactly twice v. On the drawing, these two directions are special: A only stretches them. Every other vector gets turned.
Part three. Where the two halves of the course meet.

slides.h: Second-order equations: springs, suspensions and RLC circuits
pts: a y″ + b y′ + c y = 0 → try y = e^(rt)
Real roots: overdamped · repeated: critical
Complex α ± iβ: rings at β while decaying at α
Car suspensions aim for near-critical damping
say: A mass on a spring with friction, a car's suspension, and a resistor, inductor and capacitor circuit all obey the same equation: a y double prime plus b y prime plus c y equals zero. Guess y equals e to the r t, and you get the characteristic equation, a r squared plus b r plus c equals zero. Its roots decide everything. Two real roots: overdamped. The system creeps back without oscillating, the orange curve. A repeated root: critically damped, the fastest return without overshooting, the green curve. That's what a car's shock absorbers are designed to approach. Complex roots, alpha plus or minus i beta: underdamped. It rings at frequency beta while dying off at rate alpha, the blue curve. Add a forcing term, like a bumpy road or an input voltage, and the full solution is this homogeneous part plus one particular solution.

And when the forcing frequency matches a system's natural frequency, the response can grow huge. That's resonance. The famous nineteen forty collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge is often described as resonance, though engineers today attribute it to a related effect called aeroelastic flutter, where the wind fed energy into the bridge's twisting oscillation. Either way, the lesson is the same: you must know your system's natural modes. In circuits, resonance is a feature: it's how a radio tunes to one station.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) y'' + 5y' + 6y = 0,  y(0)=1,\ y'(0)=0
(written on the whiteboard) try y = e^rt:  r^2 + 5r + 6 = 0
(written on the whiteboard) (r+2)(r+3) = 0 Rightarrow r = -2,\ -3
(written on the whiteboard) y = c_1 e^-2t + c_2 e^-3t
(written on the whiteboard) c_1 + c_2 = 1
(written on the whiteboard) -2c_1 - 3c_2 = 0
(written on the whiteboard) c_1 = 3,\ \ c_2 = -2
(written on the whiteboard) y(t) = 3e^-2t - 2e^-3t
say: Let's solve a second order equation completely. y double prime plus five y prime plus six y equals zero, starting at y equals one, at rest. Guess y equals e to the r t. Every derivative brings down an r, so we get the characteristic equation: r squared plus five r plus six equals zero.
It factors as r plus two times r plus three. Two real, negative roots: negative two and negative three. So the general solution is c one e to the minus two t, plus c two e to the minus three t.

Use the starting conditions. At t equals zero, y is one, so c one plus c two equals one. The starting velocity is zero, so negative two c one minus three c two equals zero. Solve: c one is three and c two is negative two.

So y equals three e to the minus two t minus two e to the minus three t. Because both roots are real, the system just glides back to zero, with no overshoot and no ringing. That's overdamped, like a slow door closer. Complex roots would have made it oscillate.

slides.h: Worked example: complex roots mean oscillation
pts: (written on the whiteboard) y'' + 2y' + 26y = 0
(written on the whiteboard) r = frac-2 pm sqrt4 - 1042 = -1 pm 5i
(written on the whiteboard) e^(-1+5i)t = e^-t(cos 5t + isin 5t)
(written on the whiteboard) y = e^-t (c_1cos 5t + c_2sin 5t)
(written on the whiteboard) alpha pm ibeta to e^alpha t(c_1cosbeta t + c_2sinbeta t)
(written on the whiteboard) y(0)=1,\ y^prime(0)=0:\ \ c_1 = 1,\ c_2 = (1)/(5)
(written on the whiteboard) α: decay rate   β: ringing frequency
say: Now the case students find hardest: complex roots. Take y double prime plus two y prime plus twenty six y equals zero. The characteristic equation r squared plus two r plus twenty six has roots minus one plus or minus five i.

We don't want imaginary numbers in a real answer. Euler's formula fixes it. e to the minus one plus five i, times t, splits into e to the minus t times cosine five t plus i sine five t. The real and imaginary parts are both real solutions.

So the rule is simple. For roots alpha plus or minus i beta, the solution is e to the alpha t, times a cosine and a sine at frequency beta. Starting at one, at rest, gives c one equals one and c two equals one fifth.

Look at the graph. The real part, minus one, sets the shrinking envelope. The imaginary part, five, sets how fast it rings. That's an underdamped spring, or an R L C circuit ringing after a switch closes.

slides.h: Systems of ODEs: eigenvalues decide stability
pts: x′ = A x for a vector of states
Solutions built from e^(λt) v for each eigenpair
All Re(λ) < 0 → everything decays: STABLE
Any Re(λ) > 0 → something blows up: UNSTABLE
say: Real systems have many interacting states: positions and velocities, voltages and currents. We stack them into a vector x and write x prime equals A x.
The solutions are built from e to the lambda t times v, one term for each eigenvalue and eigenvector pair of A. So the eigenvalues of A control the behavior of the whole system.

If every eigenvalue has a negative real part, every term decays, and the system settles down. On the left, the eigenvalues are negative one plus or minus two i, so trajectories spiral inward. That's stable.

If any eigenvalue has a positive real part, some term grows exponentially, and the system runs away, like the trajectories escaping on the right. This is the bridge to signals and systems and to control engineering, where those eigenvalues are called poles, and the first question about any design, from an amplifier to a drone, is: are all the poles in the left half plane?

slides.big: Differential equations describe change; matrices handle many equations at once; eigenvalues decide whether a system settles or explodes.
say: To wrap up. First order differential equations model exponential change, and separation of variables solves them. Linear algebra solves many equations at once, matrices transform space, the determinant measures scaling and invertibility, and least squares fits models to data. Eigenvalues are the special stretch factors of a matrix. Second order equations describe springs and circuits, with damping set by their characteristic roots. And for systems, the eigenvalues decide stability. You'll lean on this course in circuits, signals, control, graphics and machine learning. Next up, electricity and magnetism. See you there.

L10_phys226.title: Electricity & Magnetism
L10_phys226.file: PHYS-226 Electricity & Magnetism/Lecture - PHYS 226 Electricity & Magnetism.mp4

say: Welcome to Physics two twenty six, electricity and magnetism. For a computer engineer, this is the physics of everything. Every bit in your processor is a tiny packet of charge, every wire carries current, every motor and speaker runs on magnetic forces, and every wireless signal is an electromagnetic wave. Circuits class gives you rules. This class explains where those rules come from.

pts: Two kinds of charge: + and −
Like repel, opposites attract
F = k q₁q₂ / r² — inverse square, like gravity
But ~10⁴² times stronger than gravity between electrons
say: Matter is made of positive protons and negative electrons. Charge comes in exactly those two flavors.
Like charges repel, and opposite charges attract.
Coulomb's law gives the force: k times q one times q two, over r squared, with k about nine billion. Double the distance and the force drops to a quarter.

This force is enormous compared to gravity. Between two electrons, the electric force is about ten to the forty two times stronger than their gravitational pull. Even two tiny one microcoulomb charges, a centimeter apart, push on each other with ninety newtons, the weight of nine kilograms. The only reason we don't feel these forces every day is that ordinary matter is almost perfectly neutral.

pts: Field E = force per unit charge, at every point
Field lines leave + and end on −
Potential V = energy per unit charge (volts)
E points “downhill” in V and crosses equipotentials at 90°
say: Instead of computing forces between every pair of charges, we describe the electric field: the force a tiny positive test charge would feel at each point, per coulomb. It's a vector field, like the ones from Calculus three.
Field lines start on positive charges and end on negative ones. Here, the gray lines show the field of a positive and negative pair, called a dipole.
The electric potential, measured in volts, is the potential energy per unit charge. A volt is a joule per coulomb. The orange curves connect points at equal potential.

The field points downhill in potential, from high voltage to low, and always crosses equipotentials at right angles, exactly like the gradient and contour lines from Calculus three. In fact, E is minus the gradient of V. That's the physics behind every voltage in a circuit.

slides.h: Force, field, energy, potential: four look-alikes
pts: (written on the whiteboard) force vec F : newtons, VECTOR
(written on the whiteboard) field vec E = vec F/q : N/C, VECTOR
(written on the whiteboard) potential energy U : joules, scalar
(written on the whiteboard) potential V = U/q : volts, scalar
(written on the whiteboard) ÷ q : one charge → the place itself
(written on the whiteboard) gravity: mg (F)  g (field)  mgh (U)  gh (potential)
(written on the whiteboard) voltage = a DIFFERENCE between two points
say: These four quantities sound alike, and mixing them up is the most common mistake in this course. Let's put them side by side. Force, in newtons, is a vector: the push on a particular charge. Field is force per coulomb, also a vector. It describes the space itself, whether or not a charge is there.

Potential energy, in joules, is a scalar: the energy a particular charge has at that spot. And potential, the voltage, is energy per coulomb: joules per coulomb, volts. Also a scalar. Notice the pattern: divide by the charge, and you go from a property of one charge to a property of the place.

Gravity has the same four. Your weight is a force. g, nine point eight newtons per kilogram, is the field. m g h is the potential energy. And g h alone is the potential. Height is to gravity what voltage is to charge.

And one more thing. Only differences in potential matter, just like only differences in height matter. Where you call zero volts is a choice. That's why a voltage is always measured between two points, and why every circuit needs a ground reference.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) q = pm 2\ mathrmnC,  P is r = 0.3\ mathrmm from each
(written on the whiteboard) E = (kq)/(r^2)
(written on the whiteboard) E_1 = frac(9times 10^9)(2times 10^-9)0.3^2 = (18)/(0.09) = 200\ mathrmN/C
(written on the whiteboard) E_2 = 200\ mathrmN/C, also to the right
(written on the whiteboard) E = E_1 + E_2 approx 400\ mathrmN/C (to the right)
say: Let's add fields from two charges, step by step. A plus two nanocoulomb charge and a minus two nanocoulomb charge sit sixty centimeters apart. What's the electric field at point P, exactly halfway between them?

One charge at a time. The field from a point charge is k q over r squared. For the positive charge: nine times ten to the ninth, times two times ten to the minus ninth, over point three squared. That's eighteen over point zero nine, two hundred newtons per coulomb. It points away from the positive charge, so to the right.
The negative charge has the same size and distance, so its field is also two hundred. Fields point toward negative charges, so this one points to the right as well.

Fields are vectors, so add them with direction. Both point right, so they add: four hundred newtons per coulomb, pointing from plus toward minus. If both charges had been positive, the two fields would have cancelled to zero. Direction matters.

pts: Flux of E through a closed surface = Q_inside / ε₀
Use symmetry to make hard problems easy
Inside a conductor in equilibrium: E = 0
Excess charge sits on the outer surface
say: Gauss's law says the total electric flux out of any closed surface equals the charge enclosed, divided by epsilon naught. It's the divergence theorem from Calculus three applied to the electric field.
When there's symmetry, it turns a hard integral into one line. For example, it shows that a uniformly charged sphere looks exactly like a point charge from outside.
It also proves that inside a conductor in equilibrium, the field is zero. Any field would push the free electrons around until they cancel it.

So excess charge sits on the outer surface. That's why a car, a metal box, is a relatively safe place in a lightning storm, and why sensitive electronics are wrapped in metal shields called Faraday cages.

slides.h: Worked example: Gauss's law finds a field in two lines
pts: (written on the whiteboard) oint vec Ecdot dvec A = fracQ_insidevarepsilon_0
(written on the whiteboard) E (4pi r^2) = (Q)/(varepsilon_0)
(written on the whiteboard) E = (Q)/(4pivarepsilon_0 r^2) = (kQ)/(r^2)
(written on the whiteboard) line of charge: E = (lambda)/(2pivarepsilon_0 r)
(written on the whiteboard) symmetry → constant E → pull it out
say: Gauss's law is a tool, so let's use it. Find the field at distance r from a point charge Q, without Coulomb's law. Step one: draw an imaginary closed surface that matches the symmetry. Here, a sphere of radius r centered on the charge.

Step two: use the symmetry. Every point on the sphere is the same distance from the charge, so the field has the same size everywhere on it, and points straight outward. So the flux integral is just E times the sphere's area, four pi r squared.

Step three: solve for E. E equals Q over four pi epsilon naught r squared, which is exactly k Q over r squared, Coulomb's law. The same three steps, with a cylinder instead of a sphere, give the field of a long charged wire, which falls off as one over r instead of one over r squared.

The recipe: pick a surface where the field is constant and perpendicular, pull E out of the integral, and divide by the area. If the problem has no symmetry, Gauss's law is still true, just not useful for calculation.

pts: C = Q / V
Parallel plates: C = ε₀A/d (bigger, closer → more C)
Energy U = ½CV²
Touchscreens, DRAM bits, camera flashes
say: A capacitor is two conductors separated by a gap. Put a voltage across it and charge piles up, plus on one side and minus on the other. Capacitance is the charge stored per volt.

For parallel plates, C equals epsilon naught times the area over the gap. Bigger plates or a smaller gap store more charge. One square centimeter plates a micrometer apart give about point nine nanofarads. Filling the gap with an insulating material multiplies it by the dielectric constant.
The energy stored is one half C V squared, the same triangle we integrated in calculus two.

Capacitors are everywhere in computer engineering. Every bit in a computer's D RAM memory is a tiny capacitor that's either charged or not. Your phone's touchscreen senses your finger because your finger changes the capacitance of a grid of electrodes. And every chip has capacitors next to it to smooth out its power supply.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) A = (0.1)(0.1) = 0.01\ mathrmm^2,  d = 10^-4\ mathrmm
(written on the whiteboard) C = (varepsilon_0 A)/(d)
(written on the whiteboard) = frac(8.85times 10^-12)(0.01)10^-4
(written on the whiteboard) C approx 885\ mathrmpF
(written on the whiteboard) Q = CV = (885\ mathrmpF)(5\ mathrmV) approx 4.4\ mathrmnC
(written on the whiteboard) U = (1)/(2)CV^2 approx 11\ mathrmnJ
say: Let's size a real capacitor. Two square plates, ten centimeters on a side, separated by a tenth of a millimeter of air. What's the capacitance? The plate area is point one times point one, point zero one square meters.

Use C equals epsilon naught A over d. Epsilon naught is eight point eight five times ten to the minus twelve. Multiply by point zero one and divide by ten to the minus four: about eight point eight five times ten to the minus ten farads, or eight hundred eighty five picofarads.

Connect it to five volts. The charge is C V: about four point four nanocoulombs. The stored energy is one half C V squared: about eleven nanojoules. Tiny! That's why real capacitors use thin insulating films, rolled up or stacked in layers, to get far more area in far less space.

pts: Current I = dq/dt (amperes = coulombs/second)
R = ρL/A — longer, thinner wires resist more
Electrons drift slowly; the field moves fast
Power P = I²R = V²/R → heat
say: Current is the rate at which charge flows: one ampere is one coulomb per second.

A wire's resistance depends on its material, its length and its cross section: R equals rho L over A. A meter of copper wire one square millimeter thick has only about point zero one seven ohms. On a chip, wires are thousands of times thinner, so their resistance matters a lot, as you'll see in advanced electronics.

Here's a surprise. In a wire carrying one amp, the electrons themselves drift at only about seven hundredths of a millimeter per second, slower than a snail. But when you flip a switch, the light comes on instantly, because the electric field that pushes all the electrons travels down the wire at a large fraction of the speed of light.
And resistance turns electrical energy into heat: power equals I squared R. That's how toasters work, and also why processors need fans.

slides.h: Worked example: how much power does a wire waste?
pts: (written on the whiteboard) copper: rho = 1.68times 10^-8\ Omega mathrmm,  L = 10\ mathrmm,  d = 1\ mathrmmm
(written on the whiteboard) A = pi r^2 = pi(5times 10^-4)^2 approx 7.85times 10^-7\ mathrmm^2
(written on the whiteboard) R = (rho L)/(A) = frac(1.68times 10^-8)(10)7.85times 10^-7
(written on the whiteboard) R approx 0.21\ Omega
(written on the whiteboard) V = IR = 10(0.21) approx 2.1\ mathrmV
(written on the whiteboard) P = I^2R = 100(0.21) approx 21\ mathrmW
say: Here's a practical one. A ten meter copper wire, one millimeter in diameter, carries ten amps. What's its resistance, and how much power turns into heat? The cross section is a circle of radius half a millimeter: pi times five times ten to the minus four, squared, about seven point eight five times ten to the minus seven square meters.
Resistance is rho L over A. One point six eight times ten to the minus eight, times ten, divided by seven point eight five times ten to the minus seven. That's about point two one ohms.

At ten amps, the voltage lost along the wire is I R, about two point one volts. The power turned into heat is I squared R: one hundred times point two one, about twenty one watts. That's why high current cables are thick, and why the power grid uses high voltage: for the same power, less current, and the loss drops with the square of the current.

pts: F = q v × B: always perpendicular to motion
Charges circle in a uniform field
Force on a wire: F = I L × B
Current loop in a field feels a torque → motor
say: Magnetic fields push on moving charges with the force q v cross B. Because it's a cross product, the push is always sideways, perpendicular to the velocity. So a magnetic field can bend a charge's path into a circle, but never speed it up or slow it down. The radius is m v over q B. That's how particle accelerators steer beams, and how old tube televisions aimed their electron beam. For the direction, point your right hand's fingers along v, curl them toward B, and your thumb gives the force on a positive charge. For an electron, which is negative, flip it: the force points the opposite way. Forgetting that flip is the classic mistake.

A current carrying wire is just many moving charges, so it feels a force too: I L cross B. Put a loop of wire in a magnetic field, and the forces on opposite sides push in opposite directions, creating a torque. Switch the current direction at the right moments, and the loop keeps spinning. That's an electric motor, like this cutaway industrial motor. Your hard drive, cooling fans, drones and electric cars all depend on this one equation.

pts: Long straight wire: B = μ₀I / (2πr)
Field circles the wire (right-hand rule)
Coil (solenoid): B = μ₀nI — an electromagnet
MRI magnets: 1.5–3 T (≈ 50,000× Earth’s field)
say: The connection runs both ways: currents create magnetic fields. Around a long straight wire, the field forms circles, with strength mu naught I over two pi r. Ten amps, one centimeter away, gives about point two millitesla, a few times stronger than Earth's magnetic field. Point your right thumb along the current, and your fingers curl in the direction of the field.

Wind the wire into a coil, a solenoid, and the fields add up inside to make a strong, uniform field: an electromagnet. Relays, speakers, and the read and write heads of hard drives use this. And an MRI scanner uses a superconducting coil to create a field of one and a half to three tesla, tens of thousands of times stronger than Earth's.

slides.h: Worked example: why compasses fail near wires
pts: (written on the whiteboard) I = 10\ mathrmA,  r = 5\ mathrmcm
(written on the whiteboard) B = (mu_0 I)/(2pi r)
(written on the whiteboard) = frac(4pitimes 10^-7)(10)2pi (0.05)
(written on the whiteboard) B = 4times 10^-5\ mathrmT = 40\ mumathrmT
(written on the whiteboard) Earth: approx 50\ mumathrmT: same size!
say: How strong is the magnetic field near an ordinary wire? Take a wire carrying ten amps, and a point five centimeters away. The field circles the wire, following the right hand rule.

Use B equals mu naught I over two pi r. Mu naught is four pi times ten to the minus seven. The pi's cancel, leaving two times ten to the minus seven, times ten, over point zero five. That's four times ten to the minus five tesla, forty microtesla.

Compare that to the Earth's magnetic field, about fifty microtesla. They're about the same size! So a compass next to a wire carrying ten amps can point the wrong way entirely. That's why electronic compasses in phones and drones are calibrated, and placed away from high current wiring.

pts: Faraday: emf = −dΦ/dt
Lenz: induced current opposes the change
Generators, wireless chargers, induction cooktops
Inductors: v = L di/dt (current can’t jump)
say: In eighteen thirty one, Michael Faraday discovered that a changing magnetic field creates a voltage. Push a magnet into a coil, and a current flows. Hold it still, and the current stops.
