The induced voltage equals minus the rate of change of magnetic flux through the coil. And Lenz's law explains the minus sign: the induced current always flows so as to oppose the change. Push the magnet in, and the coil pushes back. That's energy conservation in action. Almost all the electricity on the grid comes from generators that spin coils past magnets.

Wireless phone chargers use induction directly. A coil in the pad carries alternating current, creating a changing field, which induces a current in a coil inside the phone. No wires touching. Inductors, the circuit component, are coils that resist changes in current, with voltage L d i d t. That's why inductor current can't jump instantly, a rule you'll use in circuits.

slides.h: Worked example: Faraday's law in numbers
pts: (written on the whiteboard) N = 100, A = 0.01\ mathrmm^2, Delta B = 0.5\ mathrmT in 0.1\ mathrms
(written on the whiteboard) DeltaPhi = A Delta B = (0.01)(0.5) = 0.005\ mathrmWb
(written on the whiteboard) mathcalE = N(DeltaPhi)/(Delta t) = 100cdot(0.005)/(0.1)
(written on the whiteboard) mathcalE = 5\ mathrmV
say: Let's put numbers into Faraday's law. A coil of one hundred turns, each with an area of point zero one square meters, sits in a magnetic field that ramps from zero to half a tesla in a tenth of a second. What voltage appears across the coil?
The flux through one turn is B times A. It changes from zero to point five times point zero one, which is point zero zero five webers.

Faraday's law: the voltage equals the number of turns times the rate of change of flux. One hundred times point zero zero five over point one. That's five volts. Flip the field back and forth sixty times a second, and you have the principle of every generator and transformer on the power grid.

slides.h: Transformers: how the power grid works
pts: Two coils sharing an iron core
V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁
Step up for transmission (less current → less I²R loss)
Step down near homes: e.g. 7200 V → 240 V
say: A transformer is two coils wound on a shared iron core. Alternating current in the first coil creates a changing magnetic flux in the core, which induces a voltage in the second coil. The voltage ratio equals the turns ratio. With thirty times fewer turns on the secondary, seven thousand two hundred volts becomes two hundred forty.

Why bother? Power lost in a long transmission line is I squared R. For the same power, raising the voltage by a factor of ten cuts the current by ten, and the losses by a hundred. So power plants step voltage up to hundreds of thousands of volts for long distance transmission, and transformers like this one on a utility pole step it back down near your home. This is also why the grid uses AC: transformers only work when the flux keeps changing.

pts: Gauss (E) · Gauss (B) · Faraday · Ampère–Maxwell
A changing E makes B, a changing B makes E
Self-sustaining wave at c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s
Radio, Wi-Fi, light, X-rays: same physics
say: In the eighteen sixties, James Clerk Maxwell collected everything into four equations: Gauss's law for electric fields, Gauss's law for magnetism, which says there are no magnetic monopoles, Faraday's law, and Ampère's law, to which Maxwell added one crucial term.
That term says a changing electric field creates a magnetic field, just as a changing magnetic field creates an electric field.

Put those together and you get a wave: a changing E makes B, which makes E, and so on, sustaining itself through empty space. Maxwell calculated its speed from two lab constants, one over the square root of mu naught epsilon naught, and got three hundred million meters per second, the measured speed of light. Light is an electromagnetic wave.

And so is everything on this chart. Radio and TV, the microwaves your Wi Fi uses at two point four gigahertz with a wavelength of about twelve centimeters, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, and X rays. Every wireless technology you'll ever design is an application of these four equations.

slides.big: Charges make E fields, currents make B fields, changing fields make each other — and that makes light, motors, transformers and radio.
say: To recap. Charges exert forces through electric fields, and voltage is energy per charge. Gauss's law relates fields to charge. Capacitors store charge and energy, and resistance turns current into heat. Moving charges feel magnetic forces, which drive motors, and currents create magnetic fields. Changing magnetic flux induces voltage, which gives us generators, transformers and wireless charging. And Maxwell's equations unite it all and predict electromagnetic waves. Circuits are the low frequency, simplified version of all this. Next up, waves, optics and modern physics. See you there.

L11_phys227.title: Waves, Optics & Modern Physics
L11_phys227.file: PHYS-227 Physics/Lecture - PHYS 227 Waves, Optics & Modern Physics.mp4

say: Welcome to Physics two twenty seven: waves, optics and modern physics. This is the physics of things that wiggle, from a vibrating guitar string to the light carrying internet traffic through glass fibers. And it ends with the twentieth century revolution: relativity and quantum physics, which explain why semiconductors work at all. Every chip you'll ever design rests on the last part of this lecture.

slides.h: Simple harmonic motion: the universal oscillator
pts: Restoring force F = −kx → x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ)
Spring: ω = √(k/m) · pendulum: ω = √(g/L)
Energy sloshes between kinetic and potential
Quartz crystal: 32,768 Hz = 2¹⁵ → divide 15× → 1 Hz
say: Anything with a restoring force proportional to displacement, like a spring, oscillates as a perfect cosine. That's simple harmonic motion. For a spring, the angular frequency is the square root of k over m: stiffer springs vibrate faster, heavier masses slower. For a small pendulum, it's the square root of g over L. Energy constantly sloshes back and forth, potential at the turning points, kinetic in the middle, with the total constant.

Here's where computer engineers meet it every day. Inside every watch, phone and computer is a tiny quartz crystal that vibrates like a stiff spring when driven electrically. A watch crystal is cut to vibrate at thirty two thousand seven hundred sixty eight hertz. Why that odd number? It's two to the fifteenth. Divide it by two fifteen times with a chain of flip flops, the clock divider from digital logic, and you get exactly one tick per second.

slides.h: Worked example: a mass on a spring
pts: (written on the whiteboard) omega = sqrtk/m = sqrt200/0.5 = sqrt400 = 20\ mathrmrad/s
(written on the whiteboard) f = (omega)/(2pi) approx 3.18\ mathrmHz
(written on the whiteboard) T = (1)/(f) = (2pi)/(omega) approx 0.314\ mathrms
(written on the whiteboard) x(t) = 0.05cos(20t)
(written on the whiteboard) v_max = Aomega = (0.05)(20) = 1\ mathrmm/s
say: Let's work out a spring and mass completely. A half kilogram mass hangs on a spring with stiffness two hundred newtons per meter. How fast does it oscillate? The angular frequency is the square root of k over m: two hundred over point five is four hundred, and its square root is twenty radians per second.
Convert to ordinary frequency by dividing by two pi: about three point one eight cycles per second. The period is one over that: about point three one four seconds per bounce.

Pull it five centimeters and let go. The motion is x equals point zero five cosine twenty t. The fastest it moves, through the middle, is amplitude times omega: point zero five times twenty, one meter per second. Notice the period doesn't depend on how far you pull it. That's exactly why a quartz crystal or a pendulum makes a reliable clock.

slides.h: Damping, resonance — and the RLC connection
pts: Friction → amplitude decays
Drive near the natural frequency → resonance
Mass–spring–damper ≡ inductor–capacitor–resistor
Same differential equation, same behavior
say: Real oscillators lose energy to friction, so the amplitude decays. That's damping.
Push an oscillator periodically, and if you push near its natural frequency, the amplitude grows dramatically. That's resonance, like pushing a child on a swing at just the right moments.

Now look at this table. A mass, spring and damper obey exactly the same differential equation as an inductor, capacitor and resistor in series. Mass corresponds to inductance, spring stiffness to one over capacitance, friction to resistance.

So the natural frequency of an L C circuit is one over the square root of L C, just as a spring's is the square root of k over m. Radios use this resonance to select one station out of thousands. Same physics, same math, different parts.

pts: A wave carries energy, not matter
Transverse (string, light) vs longitudinal (sound)
Middle A, 440 Hz in air: λ = 343/440 ≈ 78 cm
Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz: λ = c/f ≈ 12.5 cm
say: A wave is a disturbance that travels, carrying energy without carrying matter along. A stadium wave moves around the stadium, but each person just stands up and sits down.

In a transverse wave, like a wave on a string or light, the wiggle is perpendicular to the direction of travel. In a longitudinal wave, like sound, the air molecules are pushed back and forth along the direction of travel.

Every wave obeys the simplest formula in physics: speed equals frequency times wavelength. Sound travels at about three hundred forty three meters per second in air. Middle A, at four hundred forty hertz, has a wavelength of about seventy eight centimeters.

Radio waves travel at the speed of light. Wi Fi at two point four gigahertz has a wavelength of about twelve and a half centimeters, which is why Wi Fi antennas are a few centimeters long. Antenna size is set by wavelength.

pts: Waves add: constructive + destructive interference
String fixed at both ends: λₙ = 2L/n
Harmonics f, 2f, 3f … give instruments their tone
Noise-cancelling headphones: add the inverse wave
say: When two waves overlap, their displacements simply add. That's superposition. Crest on crest makes a bigger wave, constructive interference. Crest on trough cancels, destructive interference.
A string fixed at both ends, like a guitar string, can only vibrate in patterns that fit: wavelengths of two L over n. These are standing waves, with fixed points called nodes.

So a string vibrates at its fundamental frequency and at whole number multiples, called harmonics. The mix of harmonics is why a guitar and a piano playing the same note sound different. And the idea that any sound is a sum of sine waves at different frequencies is exactly Fourier analysis, which you'll use in signals and systems.
Destructive interference is also how noise cancelling headphones work: a microphone hears the noise, and the electronics play the inverted wave, so the two cancel at your ear.

slides.h: Worked example: the notes of a guitar string
pts: (written on the whiteboard) L = 0.65\ mathrmm,  f_1 = 110\ mathrmHz
(written on the whiteboard) lambda_1 = 2L = 1.3\ mathrmm
(written on the whiteboard) v = flambda = 110 times 1.3 approx 143\ mathrmm/s
(written on the whiteboard) f_n = n f_1:  110, 220, 330 Hz
say: A guitar string is sixty five centimeters long and plays a fundamental of one hundred ten hertz, the note A. The fundamental fits half a wavelength on the string, so the wavelength is twice the length: one point three meters.

So the wave speed on the string is f times lambda: one hundred ten times one point three, about one hundred forty three meters per second. That speed is set by the string's tension and thickness, which is why tightening a tuning peg raises the pitch.

The string can also vibrate with two half waves, or three. Those harmonics have wavelengths L and two thirds L, so their frequencies are two hundred twenty and three hundred thirty hertz: exactly two and three times the fundamental. The mix of these harmonics is what makes a guitar sound different from a flute playing the same note.

slides.h: Sound: decibels and the Doppler effect
pts: β = 10 log(I/I₀) dB — a logarithmic scale
+10 dB = 10× intensity; +3 dB = 2×
Doppler: moving source → shifted frequency
Radar guns, weather radar, ultrasound blood flow
say: Our ears handle an enormous range of intensities, so sound is measured on a logarithmic scale, in decibels. Every ten decibels is ten times the intensity. A rock concert at one hundred ten decibels is a hundred billion times more intense than the faintest sound you can hear. Engineers use decibels for signal strength and amplifier gain too: plus three decibels means double the power.

And when a source moves, its waves bunch up in front and stretch out behind. That's the Doppler effect. A siren at one thousand hertz moving toward you at thirty meters per second sounds like about one thousand ninety six hertz, then drops to about nine hundred twenty as it passes. Police radar guns, weather radar and medical ultrasound all measure speed by measuring this frequency shift.

slides.h: Worked example: the Doppler shift of a siren
pts: (written on the whiteboard) f = 700\ mathrmHz,  v_s = 30\ mathrmm/s,  v = 343\ mathrmm/s
(written on the whiteboard) f_approach = f (v)/(v - v_s) = 700cdot(343)/(313)
(written on the whiteboard) approx 767\ mathrmHz
(written on the whiteboard) f_away = f (v)/(v + v_s) = 700cdot(343)/(373)
(written on the whiteboard) approx 644\ mathrmHz
say: An ambulance siren sounds at seven hundred hertz and drives at thirty meters per second. Sound travels at three hundred forty three meters per second. What pitch do you hear as it approaches, and as it leaves? Look at the drawing: ahead of the ambulance, the wave crests bunch up.

Approaching, the crests arrive closer together. The formula divides by the speed of sound minus the source speed: seven hundred times three forty three, over three thirteen. That's about seven hundred sixty seven hertz.

Moving away, you add instead: seven hundred times three forty three over three seventy three, about six hundred forty four hertz. So the pitch drops by more than a hundred hertz as it passes you. Police radar and weather radar use the same shift, with radio waves, to measure speed.

slides.h: Decibels by hand: the 10 vs 20 rule
pts: (written on the whiteboard) power: dB = 10log_10(P_2)/(P_1)
(written on the whiteboard) times 100 to 20\ dB   times 2 to 3\ dB   times(1)/(2) to -3\ dB
(written on the whiteboard) P propto V^2:  10log(V_2^2)/(V_1^2) = 20log_10(V_2)/(V_1)
(written on the whiteboard) voltage times 10: 20log 10 = 20\ dB = power times 100
(written on the whiteboard) -3\ dB: power times(1)/(2), voltage times 0.707
(written on the whiteboard) a filter cutoff = the −3 dB point
say: Decibels will follow you into every electronics course, so let's get them exactly right. A decibel compares two powers: ten times the log of the power ratio. A power ratio of one hundred is ten log one hundred, twenty decibels. A ratio of two is about three decibels.
Here's the trap. Engineers often measure voltages, not powers. But power goes as voltage squared. The square comes out of the log as a factor of two, so for voltages, it's twenty log of the ratio.

So an amplifier that multiplies voltage by ten has a gain of twenty decibels, not ten. And it multiplies power by one hundred, which is also twenty decibels. Same answer, as it must be. Use ten for power ratios, twenty for voltage or current ratios.

The most important number: minus three decibels. It's half the power, and one over root two, point seven oh seven, of the voltage. When you meet a filter's cutoff frequency in circuits and signals, it's defined exactly there: the frequency where the output drops three decibels.

slides.h: Light bends: refraction and Snell’s law
pts: Light slows in glass: n = c / v
n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
Air → glass at 30°: bends to 19.5°
n depends on color → prisms split white light
say: Light travels slower in glass or water than in air. The index of refraction, n, is how many times slower. For glass, about one and a half. When light enters at an angle, the change in speed bends it. And since the index depends slightly on the color, a prism bends each color by a different amount, splitting white light into a rainbow.

Snell's law gives the angle: n one sine theta one equals n two sine theta two. From air into glass at thirty degrees, the sine of the new angle is point five divided by one point five, so the light bends to about nineteen and a half degrees, toward the perpendicular, as it slows down.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) n_1 = 1.33,  n_2 = 1.00,  theta_1 = 40°
(written on the whiteboard) n_1sintheta_1 = n_2sintheta_2
(written on the whiteboard) sintheta_2 = 1.33 sin 40° approx 0.855
(written on the whiteboard) theta_2 approx 58.8°
(written on the whiteboard) sintheta_c = (1)/(1.33) Rightarrow theta_c approx 48.8°
say: Light travels from water into air. Water's index is one point three three, air's is one. The light hits the surface at forty degrees from the normal. Where does it go?

Snell's law: n one sine theta one equals n two sine theta two. One point three three times sine forty is about point eight five five. Since air's index is one, that's sine theta two directly. The inverse sine gives fifty eight point eight degrees. It bends away from the normal, because it speeds up.

Tilt the beam more and the outgoing angle grows until it reaches ninety degrees. That happens when sine theta one equals one over one point three three, at about forty eight point eight degrees: the critical angle. Beyond it, all the light reflects back into the water. That's total internal reflection, and it's how optical fiber traps light.

slides.h: Total internal reflection: the internet is made of light
pts: Dense → less dense, beyond the critical angle: 100% reflection
sin θc = n₂/n₁ → 41.8° for glass to air
Optical fiber traps light for kilometers
Undersea cables carry most intercontinental data
say: Going the other way, from glass into air, light bends away from the perpendicular. At a steep enough angle, the critical angle, it can't get out at all. Every bit of it reflects back inside. That's total internal reflection. For glass to air, the sine of the critical angle is one over one point five, about forty two degrees. An optical fiber is a thin glass core surrounded by cladding with a slightly lower index, so light bounces along the core for kilometers.

These fibers carry the backbone of the internet. Undersea fiber cables carry the vast majority of data between continents, with lasers blinking billions of times per second. Every video you stream from another country probably traveled as light through glass, trapped by this one equation.

pts: Thin lens: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i
Camera, f = 50 mm, subject at 2 m → image at 51.3 mm
Focusing = moving the lens a millimeter or so
Phone cameras, microscopes, chip lithography
say: A lens bends light so that rays from one point of an object meet again at one point of an image. The thin lens equation relates the focal length to the object and image distances: one over f equals one over d o plus one over d i.
A camera with a fifty millimeter lens photographing someone two meters away forms the image fifty one point three millimeters behind the lens, right on the sensor.

For something very far away, the image forms at exactly fifty millimeters. So focusing just means moving the lens by about a millimeter. Your phone does that with a tiny motor, often a voice coil like a speaker.
The same optics, scaled up enormously in precision, is how chips are made: lithography machines use lenses and mirrors to project circuit patterns onto silicon wafers.

slides.h: Interference and diffraction: light is a wave
pts: Two slits: bright where d sin θ = mλ
Fringe spacing = λL/d = 13 mm in this example
Diffraction limits how small you can image
Chipmakers use 13.5 nm extreme-UV light to print tiny features
say: Shine a laser through two narrow slits, and instead of two bright lines you get a whole row of bright and dark fringes. Light from the two slits interferes: where the path lengths differ by a whole number of wavelengths, the waves add, and where they differ by half a wavelength, they cancel. This experiment, first done by Thomas Young around eighteen hundred, proved light is a wave.

The fringe spacing is wavelength times distance to the screen, over the slit separation. With a red laser at six hundred fifty nanometers, slits a tenth of a millimeter apart, and a screen two meters away, the fringes are thirteen millimeters apart.

Diffraction also sets a fundamental limit: you can't focus light to a spot much smaller than its wavelength. That's a huge problem for chipmakers, who need to print transistor features just a few tens of nanometers across.

So the most advanced chip factories use extreme ultraviolet light with a wavelength of thirteen and a half nanometers, generated by blasting tiny droplets of tin with a laser. Wave optics directly limits how small transistors can be.

slides.h: Relativity — and why GPS needs it
pts: Speed of light is the same for every observer
Moving clocks run slow: Δt = γΔt₀
Clocks in weaker gravity run fast
GPS: net +38 μs/day — uncorrected, ~10 km error per day
say: In nineteen oh five, Einstein built special relativity on one surprising fact: the speed of light is the same for every observer, no matter how they move. The consequences: moving clocks run slow, by the factor gamma. Moving objects contract. And mass and energy are equivalent, E equals m c squared. His later theory, general relativity, adds that clocks run faster where gravity is weaker.

This isn't abstract. GPS satellites carry atomic clocks and move at about fourteen thousand kilometers per hour. Special relativity makes their clocks lose about seven microseconds per day. But they're high above Earth, in weaker gravity, so general relativity makes them gain about forty five. The net is about thirty eight microseconds per day fast. Since GPS measures distance by timing radio signals at the speed of light, thirty eight microseconds is about eleven kilometers of error, every single day, if engineers didn't correct for it. They do, by deliberately setting the satellite clocks slightly slow before launch.

pts: Light comes in packets: E = hf
Photoelectric effect: only high-enough f frees electrons
Atoms have discrete energy levels → sharp spectral lines
LED color = semiconductor band gap
say: Light is also a particle. Each photon carries energy h times f. Shine dim blue light on certain metals, and electrons pop out. Shine intense red light, and nothing happens, because no single red photon has enough energy. Einstein explained this photoelectric effect in nineteen oh five, and it won him the Nobel Prize. Camera sensors and solar cells work on this principle: each photon can free one electron. And atoms can only hold electrons at specific, discrete energy levels. In hydrogen, they're minus thirteen point six electron volts over n squared. When an electron drops from one level to a lower one, it emits a photon with exactly that energy difference, which is why each element glows with its own fingerprint of colors.

In a solid, those levels blur into bands separated by a gap, and the size of that gap decides whether a material is a conductor, an insulator or a semiconductor. An LED emits photons with energy roughly equal to its band gap. A handy rule: energy in electron volts is about twelve hundred forty divided by the wavelength in nanometers. So a red LED's band gap is about one point nine electron volts, and a blue LED's about two point eight. That's the bridge to the electronics course, where band gaps make diodes and transistors work.

slides.h: Worked example: counting photons in a laser pointer
pts: (written on the whiteboard) red laser: P = 5\ mathrmmW,  lambda = 650\ mathrmnm
(written on the whiteboard) E = (hc)/(lambda)
(written on the whiteboard) E = frac(6.63times 10^-34)(3times 10^8)650times 10^-9
(written on the whiteboard) approx 3.06times 10^-19\ mathrmJ approx 1.91\ mathrmeV
(written on the whiteboard) (P)/(E) = frac5times 10^-33.06times 10^-19 approx 1.6times 10^16 photons/s
say: How many photons does a red laser pointer emit? Take a five milliwatt laser at six hundred fifty nanometers. First, the energy of one photon: E equals h c over lambda.

Plug in Planck's constant, six point six three times ten to the minus thirty four, times the speed of light, three times ten to the eighth, over six fifty times ten to the minus nine. That's about three point oh six times ten to the minus nineteen joules. In electron volts, about one point nine one.

The laser emits five thousandths of a joule every second. Divide by the energy per photon: about one point six times ten to the sixteen photons per second. Sixteen quadrillion! Each photon is tiny, which is why light looks smooth and continuous. And that one point nine electron volts is no accident: it matches the band gap of the semiconductor in a red laser diode or LED.

slides.h: Matter waves and the quantum world
pts: de Broglie: particles have wavelength λ = h / p
Electron microscopes resolve atoms
Tunneling: electrons can pass through thin barriers
Flash memory stores bits by tunneling charge onto a floating gate
say: One more twist. If waves can act like particles, particles can act like waves. Louis de Broglie proposed that every particle has a wavelength, h over its momentum.
Electrons have wavelengths far shorter than visible light, which is why electron microscopes can image individual atoms, and why chipmakers use them to inspect their transistors.
Waves can also leak through thin barriers that a classical particle could never cross. That's quantum tunneling.

And you're using tunneling right now. Flash memory, in your phone and in every S S D, stores each bit by forcing electrons to tunnel through a very thin insulating layer onto an isolated floating gate, where they stay trapped for years. Quantum mechanics isn't just theory. It's in your pocket.

slides.big: Oscillators keep time, waves carry energy and data, light bends and interferes, and quantum energy levels make semiconductors possible.
say: To recap. Simple harmonic motion describes every oscillator, from quartz clocks to L C circuits. Waves obey v equals f lambda, superpose, and form standing waves and harmonics. Light refracts, reflects, and interferes, which gives us fiber optics, cameras and the limits of chip manufacturing. Relativity keeps GPS accurate. And quantum physics, with photons and discrete energy levels, explains LEDs, solar cells, flash memory and the semiconductors at the heart of computing. Next, back to software, with data structures. See you there.

L12_cpsc131.title: Data Structures
L12_cpsc131.file: CPSC-131 Data Structures/Lecture - CPSC 131 Data Structures.mp4

say: Welcome to C P S C one thirty one, data structures. Before computers, libraries organized millions of cards in drawers like these, so you could find any book in minutes. A data structure is the same idea: a way of organizing data so that the operations you need are fast. In this lecture you'll learn how to measure speed with big O notation, and the core structures every programmer uses: arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, heaps and graphs.

slides.h: Big-O: how does the cost grow?
pts: Count steps as a function of input size n
Keep only the fastest-growing term
O(log n) ≪ O(n) ≪ O(n log n) ≪ O(n²) ≪ O(2ⁿ)
An algorithm choice can mean 1 ms vs 17 minutes
say: To compare data structures, we need a way to measure speed that doesn't depend on the computer. So we count steps as a function of the input size, n.

And we only care about how that count grows for large n. If a loop takes three n plus five steps, we just say it's order n, written big O of n. Constants and smaller terms don't matter when n is a billion.

Here are the common growth rates, on a log log chart. Logarithmic barely grows. Linear grows in step with n. n log n is a bit worse. n squared shoots up. And two to the n is hopeless beyond tiny inputs.

The difference is dramatic. For a million items, on a computer doing a billion steps per second, a linear algorithm takes about a millisecond, n log n about twenty milliseconds, and n squared about seventeen minutes. Choosing the right algorithm often matters far more than buying a faster computer.

slides.h: Reading big-O straight off the code
pts: (code on the board) for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)  sum += a[i];
(written on the whiteboard) to O(n)
(code on the board) for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
(code on the board)   for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)  check(a[i], a[j]);
(written on the whiteboard) n times n to O(n^2)
(code on the board) for (int k = n; k > 1; k = k / 2)  step();
(written on the whiteboard) n,\ (n)/(2),\ (n)/(4),\ ldots,\ 1: log_2 n steps to O(log n)
(code on the board) for (x : items)  BinarySearch(sorted, x);
(written on the whiteboard) n times log n to O(nlog n)
(written on the whiteboard) in sequence: add, keep the biggest: O(n) + O(n^2) = O(n^2)
say: Knowing the definition isn't enough. On exams and at work you have to read the big O right off the code. Rule one: a single loop over n items is order n. The body runs n times.
Rule two: nested loops multiply. For each of the n values of i, the inner loop runs n times, so the body runs n times n. Comparing every pair of items is order n squared.
Rule three: a loop that halves its range each time is logarithmic. Starting from n, how many halvings until you reach one? Log base two of n. That's binary search.

Combine them. A loop over n items with a binary search inside is n times log n. Statements one after another add, and then you keep only the biggest term: order n plus order n squared is just order n squared.

pts: Array: contiguous → instant access a[i], cache-friendly
Inserting in the middle: shift everything → O(n)
Linked list: insert/remove anywhere in O(1) (given the node)
But reaching element i means walking → O(n)
say: The two most basic ways to store a sequence. An array, or vector, keeps elements side by side in one block of memory. To get element i, the computer just computes the address, start plus i times the element size. That's instant, order one. Arrays are also cache friendly, because the processor loads neighboring elements together, which makes them very fast in practice.
But inserting at the front means shifting every other element over by one: order n.
A linked list stores each element in its own node, scattered in memory, with a pointer to the next node. To insert, you just rewire two pointers. Order one.

But to reach element i, you have to start at the head and follow i pointers. Order n. Every data structure is a set of tradeoffs like this. The skill is knowing which operations your program does most.

slides.h: Worked example: inserting into a linked list
pts: (code on the board) struct Node {
(code on the board)   int value;
(code on the board)   Node* next;
(code on the board) };
(code on the board) Node* n = new Node{25, nullptr};
(code on the board) n->next = prev->next;   // 25 -> 30
(code on the board) prev->next = n;         // 20 -> 25
(written on the whiteboard) list: 10 → 20 → 25 → 30
(written on the whiteboard) Connect the new node first, then relink!
say: Let's insert the value twenty five into the middle of a linked list, between twenty and thirty. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. We already have a pointer, prev, to the node holding twenty.
Step one: create the new node on the heap, holding twenty five. Right now, it isn't connected to anything.
Step two: point the new node at whatever prev currently points to, which is thirty. Now both twenty and twenty five point to thirty.

Step three: point prev at the new node. The old link from twenty to thirty is replaced, and the list reads ten, twenty, twenty five, thirty. No element moved in memory. That's why insertion is constant time.

The order of those two lines is critical. Swap them, and prev points to twenty five before twenty five knows about thirty. The rest of the list is lost forever. When you edit pointers, always connect the new node first.

pts: push onto the top, pop from the top
Undo history, browser Back button
The call stack for function calls
Checking balanced brackets: ( [ { } ] )
say: A stack is like a stack of plates. You add to the top and take from the top. Last in, first out.
Undo is a stack. Every action you take is pushed: you type hello, then make it bold.
Then you delete a line. That's pushed on top.

Press control Z, and the most recent action is popped off and undone first. The browser's back button works the same way. And the call stack you met in programming is literally a stack of function frames. Compilers also use stacks to check that brackets are balanced: push every opening bracket, and every closing bracket must match the one on top.

slides.h: Worked example: are the brackets balanced?
pts: (written on the whiteboard) input:  [ ( ) ]
(written on the whiteboard) open: push
(written on the whiteboard) close: pop, must match
(written on the whiteboard) input ( ]
(written on the whiteboard) pop "(" but saw "]": NOT balanced
say: Compilers check brackets with a stack. Let's trace the string curly, square, round, close round, close square, close curly. The rule: push every opening bracket. For every closing bracket, pop the top and check that it matches.
Curly: push. Square: push. Round: push. The stack now holds three brackets, with the round one on top.
Close round: pop, and the top was round. A match. Close square: pop square, match. Close curly: pop curly, match.

The stack is empty at the end, so the brackets are balanced. Now try round, then close square. Push round. Then close square pops round, which doesn't match. Error. That's exactly the message your compiler gives you, and it works because the most recent opening bracket must be the first one closed. Last in, first out.

pts: enqueue at the back, dequeue from the front
Print jobs, network packets, task scheduling
Circular buffer: fixed array that wraps around
Used in every UART and keyboard driver
say: A queue is a line at a store: first in, first out. New items join at the back, and items leave from the front.
Print jobs wait in a queue. Network routers queue packets. Operating systems queue processes that are ready to run.
A neat way to build one is a circular buffer: a fixed size array where the head and tail indexes wrap around to the start when they reach the end, using the modulo operator from discrete math.

This matters a lot in embedded systems. When bytes arrive on a serial port faster than your program can handle them, an interrupt routine drops them into a circular buffer, and the main program pulls them out later. You'll write exactly this in the embedded systems course.

pts: Base case + a smaller version of the same problem
factorial(n) = n × factorial(n − 1), factorial(0) = 1
Naive Fibonacci recomputes subproblems → O(2ⁿ)
Memoization (cache answers) → O(n)
say: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem, until it reaches a base case it can answer directly.

Factorial is the classic: n factorial is n times n minus one factorial, and zero factorial is one. Recursion is natural for anything that's defined in terms of smaller pieces of itself, like trees, file directories, and the merge sort we'll see shortly.

But be careful. Fibonacci, where each number is the sum of the two before it, looks perfect for recursion. Yet the naive version recomputes the same values over and over. Look at the tree: fib of three, in red, gets computed again and again. The total work grows exponentially. Fibonacci of fifty would take hours.

The fix is memoization: store each answer the first time you compute it, and look it up afterwards. Now each value is computed once, and the time drops to linear. That idea, solving subproblems once and reusing them, is called dynamic programming.

slides.h: Worked example: tracing a recursive function
pts: (code on the board) int Fact(int n) {
(code on the board)   if (n <= 1) return 1;      // base case
(code on the board)   return n * Fact(n - 1);    // smaller problem
(code on the board) }
(written on the whiteboard) calls go down, waiting...
(written on the whiteboard) ...answers come back up
(written on the whiteboard) no base case = stack overflow
say: Here's factorial written recursively. Every recursive function needs two parts. A base case that stops: if n is at most one, return one. And a recursive case that makes the problem smaller: n times factorial of n minus one.
Call Fact of four. It can't answer yet, so it calls Fact of three, which calls Fact of two, which calls Fact of one. Each call waits on the stack.

Fact of one hits the base case and returns one. Now the answers come back up. Fact of two returns two times one, two. Fact of three returns three times two, six. And Fact of four returns four times six, twenty four.
Forget the base case, and the calls never stop, until the stack runs out of memory. That's a stack overflow, and it's the classic recursion bug.

slides.h: Binary search: halve the problem every step
say: If the data is sorted, you can search it incredibly fast. Let's find thirty seven in this sorted array. Check the middle element: forty one. Thirty seven is smaller, so it must be in the left half. Throw away the right half entirely.
Check the middle of what's left: seventeen. Thirty seven is bigger, so keep the right half.
Middle again: twenty nine. Still smaller than thirty seven, keep the right part.

Middle: thirty seven. Found it, in four steps out of fifteen elements. Each step halves the range, so a billion items take only about thirty steps, because two to the thirtieth is about a billion. That's logarithmic time, and it's why sorting data first often pays off.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) find 21
(written on the whiteboard) mid = 5: 34 > 21
(written on the whiteboard) so hi = 4
(written on the whiteboard) mid = 2: 15 < 21
(written on the whiteboard) so lo = 3
(written on the whiteboard) mid = 3: found!
(written on the whiteboard) log_2(10^9) approx 30 steps
say: Let's find twenty one in this sorted array of eleven numbers. Low starts at index zero, high at index ten. The middle is index five, which holds thirty four. Thirty four is bigger than twenty one, so twenty one must be in the left half.
Now low is zero, high is four, and the middle is index two, holding fifteen. Fifteen is smaller than twenty one, so move low up to three.
Low is three, high is four, and the middle is index three. It holds twenty one. Found it, in three comparisons.

A linear scan could take up to eleven comparisons. Binary search halves the range every step, so even a billion sorted items need only about thirty comparisons. That's the power of log n. The catch: the data must be sorted first.

slides.h: Sorting: from O(n²) to O(n log n)
pts: Insertion sort: simple, O(n²) — fine for small n
Merge sort: split in half, sort each, merge
log n levels × n work each = O(n log n)
Quicksort / std::sort: O(n log n) in practice
say: Sorting is one of the most studied problems in computing. The simple approach, insertion sort, takes each item and slides it into place among the ones already sorted. It's easy and fine for small lists, but it's order n squared.

Merge sort uses divide and conquer. Split the list in half, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front element. Look at the picture: we split down to single elements, then merge back up.
There are log n levels of splitting, and each level does order n work merging. So the total is n log n. For a million items, that's the difference between about twenty million steps and a trillion.

In practice, you'll usually call the library's sort, like s t d sort in C plus plus, which uses a carefully tuned hybrid of quicksort and other methods, and runs in n log n time. But knowing why it's fast helps you recognize when your own code accidentally isn't.

slides.h: Hash tables: look things up in O(1)
pts: Hash function turns a key into a bucket number
Lookup, insert, delete: O(1) on average
Collisions: two keys, same bucket → chain them
Python dicts, std::unordered_map, caches, databases
say: What if you want to find things by name, not by position? A hash table runs each key through a hash function that scrambles it into a number, then takes that number mod the table size to pick a bucket. Store the item in that bucket.
To look it up later, hash the key again and go straight to the same bucket. No searching. On average, lookup, insert and delete are all order one, no matter how big the table is.

By the pigeonhole principle, some keys must collide in the same bucket. Here, alice and carol both land in bucket three. The usual fix is chaining: each bucket holds a short list. As long as the table isn't too full, those lists stay tiny. If they don't, say a bad hash function sends every key to the same bucket, a lookup degrades into scanning one long list: order n. That's why the order one is always quoted as average case. Real hash tables grow and rehash automatically when they get too full to keep it that way.

Hash tables are everywhere: Python dictionaries, C plus plus unordered maps, web caches, compilers' symbol tables, and the indexes inside databases. If you only remember one data structure from this course, make it this one.

slides.h: Worked example: filling a hash table
pts: (written on the whiteboard) h(key) = key mod 7
(written on the whiteboard) 14 mod 7 = 0
(written on the whiteboard) 23 mod 7 = 2
(written on the whiteboard) 9 mod 7 = 2  collision!
(written on the whiteboard) 31 mod 7 = 3,  6 mod 7 = 6
(written on the whiteboard) lookup: hash, then check one bucket: O(1)
say: Let's insert five keys into a hash table with seven buckets. The hash function is the key mod seven: the remainder after dividing by seven.
Fourteen mod seven is zero, so fourteen goes in bucket zero. Twenty three mod seven is two: bucket two.
Nine mod seven is also two. A collision! Two keys want the same bucket. With chaining, we simply add nine to a small list hanging off bucket two.

Thirty one mod seven is three, and six goes in bucket six. To look up a key later, we compute its hash and only search that one bucket. With a good hash function and enough buckets, the chains stay short, and lookups take constant time on average.

pts: Left subtree smaller, right subtree larger
Search, insert, delete: O(height)
Balanced → height ≈ log₂ n
std::map, databases (B-trees), file systems
say: A binary search tree keeps data sorted while still allowing fast inserts. Each node has up to two children. Everything in the left subtree is smaller, and everything in the right subtree is larger.
To find forty, start at the root, fifty. Forty is smaller, go left to thirty. Forty is bigger, go right. Found it. The cost is the height of the tree.

If the tree stays balanced, the height is about log base two of n, so a million items need only about twenty comparisons. But insert items in sorted order into a plain BST and it degenerates into a long chain, as slow as a linked list. Self balancing trees, like red black trees, rotate nodes to stay balanced automatically.

The C plus plus s t d map is a red black tree. Databases and file systems use a wide, shallow cousin called a B tree, designed so that each node fills one disk block. You'll see B trees in the databases course.

slides.h: Worked example: building and searching a BST
pts: (written on the whiteboard) insert: 50 30 70 20 40 60 80
(written on the whiteboard) search 60:
(written on the whiteboard) 60 > 50: right
(written on the whiteboard) 60 < 70: left
(written on the whiteboard) found!
(written on the whiteboard) sorted input makes a "stick": O(n)
say: Let's build a binary search tree by inserting fifty, thirty, seventy, twenty, forty, sixty, eighty, in that order. Fifty becomes the root. Thirty is smaller, so it goes left. Seventy is bigger, so it goes right.
Twenty: smaller than fifty, go left. Smaller than thirty, go left again. Forty: left of fifty, but bigger than thirty, so right. Sixty: right of fifty, left of seventy. Eighty: right, then right.

Now search for sixty. Compare with fifty: bigger, go right. Compare with seventy: smaller, go left. Sixty. Found in three comparisons. Each comparison throws away half of what's left, just like binary search.

But watch out: insert the same numbers already sorted, ten, twenty, thirty, and every node goes right. The tree becomes a linked list, and search slows to order n. That's why real libraries use self balancing trees.

pts: Always know the smallest (or largest) item
Insert and remove-min: O(log n)
Stored compactly in an array
OS schedulers, Dijkstra, event simulations
say: Sometimes you don't need everything sorted. You just need to repeatedly grab the most urgent item. That's a priority queue, usually built as a heap.

In a min heap, every parent is smaller than its children, so the smallest item is always at the top. Inserting or removing the top takes order log n, by swapping an item up or down one level at a time.
A heap is stored compactly in a plain array, with no pointers at all. The children of position i live at two i plus one and two i plus two.

Operating systems use priority queues to decide which task runs next. Network routers use them to prioritize traffic. And the shortest path algorithm on the next slide uses one to always explore the closest location first.

pts: Store as adjacency lists (sparse) or a matrix (dense)
BFS explores level by level (queue)
DFS goes deep first (stack / recursion)
Dijkstra: shortest weighted paths — how map apps route you
say: A graph is a set of nodes connected by edges, like the road map from discrete math. In code, we usually store it as adjacency lists: for each node, a list of its neighbors. For dense graphs, an adjacency matrix works too.
Breadth first search explores a graph level by level using a queue: all neighbors first, then their neighbors. On an unweighted graph, it finds shortest paths in number of hops.
Depth first search dives as deep as possible before backing up, using a stack or recursion. It's how you'd solve a maze, detect cycles, or order tasks that depend on each other.

For weighted graphs, Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths. Using a priority queue, it repeatedly settles the closest unsettled node and updates its neighbors' distances. Here, from A, the shortest path to F costs thirteen, going A, C, B, D, E, F, which is not the most direct looking route. Your phone's navigation app runs refined versions of this on a graph with millions of road segments.

Here's the summary table to keep. Need fast access by position? An array or vector. Undo, recursion or parsing? A stack. First come, first served? A queue. Look things up by a key? A hash table, with order one average time. Need things kept in sorted order with fast search? A balanced binary search tree, like s t d map. Always need the smallest or largest item next? A heap. Modeling connections, networks or routes? A graph, with breadth first search or Dijkstra. The standard libraries of every major language provide all of these, so in practice your job is mostly choosing well, and understanding the costs well enough to avoid accidentally writing an n squared program.

slides.big: Data structures trade costs. Measure with Big-O, then pick the structure whose fast operations match what your program does most.
say: To wrap up. Big O notation measures how cost grows with input size. Arrays give instant access, and linked lists give cheap insertion. Stacks and queues order work. Recursion and divide and conquer give us binary search and merge sort. Hash tables give constant time lookup. Trees keep data sorted, heaps keep the minimum handy, and graphs model connections, searched with B F S, D F S and Dijkstra. Next, we drop down to the hardware itself, programming microcontrollers in assembly language. See you there.

Welcome to E G C P two eighty, microcontrollers. A microcontroller is a whole small computer on one chip, and it's the most common computer on Earth. In this lecture you'll see what's inside one, how its processor executes instructions, how to program it in assembly language, and how it controls the physical world through pins, timers, analog inputs and serial links. This is where software meets hardware.

slides.h: What is a microcontroller — and where are they?
pts: CPU + flash + RAM + peripherals on one chip
Costs cents to a few dollars, sips power
Tens of billions shipped every year
A modern car contains dozens to over a hundred
say: Your laptop's processor needs separate memory chips, storage and a lot of supporting hardware. A microcontroller puts a small processor, flash memory for the program, RAM for data, and a collection of input and output hardware all on one chip. Boards like this Arduino and the TI LaunchPad made them popular with students and hobbyists, but the real market is in products. Tens of billions of microcontrollers are shipped every year. They're in your microwave, thermostat, TV remote, washing machine and keyboard. A modern car contains dozens of them, often over a hundred, running the engine, brakes, airbags, windows and seats.

Here's what's inside. The CPU core executes instructions. Flash memory holds the program even with the power off. SRAM holds variables and the stack. An interrupt controller lets hardware events grab the CPU's attention. Timers keep time and generate signals. And along the bottom, the peripherals connect to the outside world: general purpose input output pins, an analog to digital converter, and serial ports like UART, SPI and I squared C. All of them connect through an internal bus. We'll visit each of these today.

pts: Registers: tiny, ultra-fast storage inside the CPU
ARM Cortex-M: R0–R12 general purpose (32 bits)
SP = stack pointer, LR = return address, PC = next instruction
Flags N Z C V record results of the last operation
say: To program in assembly, you need the programmer's model: the registers the instructions can see. Registers are tiny storage slots inside the CPU itself, much faster than memory.

We'll use the ARM Cortex M family as our example, since it's the most widely used microcontroller architecture today. It has thirteen general purpose registers, R zero through R twelve, each thirty two bits wide. Older courses and many 8 bit chips use fewer, smaller registers, but the ideas are identical.

Three registers are special. The stack pointer marks the top of the stack in memory. The link register holds the return address when you call a subroutine. And the program counter holds the address of the next instruction to execute. Change the PC, and you've jumped somewhere else in the program.

Finally, the status flags. After an arithmetic or compare instruction, N says the result was negative, Z says it was zero, C records a carry out, and V signals signed overflow, the same overflow you met in two's complement. Branch instructions read these flags to make decisions.

pts: One 32-bit address space (4 GB)
Flash at the bottom, SRAM at 0x2000 0000
Peripheral registers at 0x4000 0000 and up
Controlling hardware = writing to an address
say: A thirty two bit processor can address four gigabytes, and a microcontroller divides that address space into regions.
On ARM Cortex M chips, the program in flash starts at address zero, and SRAM, holding variables and the stack, starts at hex two zero zero zero, zero zero zero zero.

Here's the key idea of this whole course. The hardware peripherals also live at addresses, starting around hex four zero zero zero, zero zero zero zero. Each pin, timer and serial port is controlled by registers that look exactly like memory locations.

So to turn on an L E D, you don't call a special instruction. You store a number at a particular address. That's called memory mapped I O, and it's why C pointers to fixed addresses are so common in embedded code.

slides.h: Memory-mapped I/O in C: one line, decoded
pts: (code on the board) #define LED_PORT  (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x48000014)
(code on the board) LED_PORT |= (1u << 5);     // pin 5 high: LED on
(written on the whiteboard) 1. 0x48000014 : an address from the datasheet
(written on the whiteboard) 2. (uint32_t *) : make it a pointer to a 32-bit value
(written on the whiteboard) 3. * in front : the register itself, not its address
(written on the whiteboard) 4. volatile : never optimize these reads/writes away
(written on the whiteboard) 5. |= (1u << 5) : set only bit 5
say: Here's the line that confuses everyone the first time they open real embedded code. It turns on an L E D by writing to a hardware register at a fixed address. Let's take it apart from the inside out.

Start with the number, hex four eight zero zero zero zero one four. That's just an address from the chip's memory map, where the reference manual says the output register of a port lives. On its own, it's only an integer.

The cast in front, open paren, volatile u int thirty two star, says: treat that integer as a pointer to a thirty two bit value. Then the star on the far left dereferences it: not the address, but the thing stored at that address. So LED port now behaves exactly like a variable that lives inside the hardware.

And volatile tells the compiler: this value can change, or must be written, outside your view. Without it, the optimizer may skip a write it thinks is pointless, or read the register once and never again, and your hardware silently stops responding. Finally, the bit mask from earlier sets just pin five.

pts: Arithmetic only on registers: ADD R0, R1, R2
Memory only via LDR (load) and STR (store)
CMP sets flags; B, BEQ, BNE, BGT branch
Assembler turns mnemonics into machine code
say: ARM, like most modern processors, uses a load store design. Arithmetic and logic instructions only work on registers. ADD R zero, R one, R two puts R one plus R two into R zero.
To touch memory, you use separate instructions: L D R loads a word from memory into a register, and S T R stores a register back to memory.

To make decisions, CMP compares two values by subtracting them and setting the flags without keeping the result. Then a conditional branch like B E Q, branch if equal, or B G T, branch if greater, jumps based on those flags. A plain B always jumps.

Each of these human readable mnemonics is translated into binary machine code by a program called the assembler. Then the linker places the code at real addresses, and you flash the resulting image onto the board and run it, usually under a debugger.

slides.h: Example: summing an array in assembly
slides.code:
.text
        .global sum_array
@ R0 = address of array, R1 = count  →  returns sum in R0
sum_array:
        MOV   R2, #0           @ sum = 0
loop:   CMP   R1, #0           @ any elements left?
        BEQ   done             @ if count == 0, finish
        LDR   R3, [R0], #4     @ R3 = *R0; then R0 += 4
        ADD   R2, R2, R3       @ sum += R3
        SUBS  R1, R1, #1       @ count--
        B     loop
done:   MOV   R0, R2           @ return value in R0
        BX    LR               @ return to caller
say: Let's read a real routine. The dot text and dot global lines are assembler directives: they're not instructions, they tell the assembler where the code goes and that other files may call sum array. By convention, the first arguments arrive in R zero and R one: the address of the array and the number of elements.
We clear R two to hold the sum. Then the loop: compare the count with zero, and if it's equal, branch to done.

Otherwise, load the next element. The square brackets mean use R zero as an address, and the comma four after the bracket means: after loading, add four to R zero, so it points to the next thirty two bit element. That's called post increment addressing. Add the element to the sum, decrement the count, and branch back to the top.

At the end, move the sum into R zero, where the caller expects the return value, and B X L R jumps back to the address in the link register, returning to whoever called us. This is exactly what a C compiler produces for a simple for loop. Reading compiler output like this is a real debugging skill.

pts: BL label: jump AND save the return address in LR
Nested calls must save LR on the stack
PUSH {R4, LR} on entry, POP {R4, PC} on exit
Stack overflow = writing past its reserved space
say: To call a subroutine, use B L, branch with link. It jumps to the label and saves the return address in the link register.
But if that subroutine calls another one, the second B L overwrites L R, and the first return address is lost. So functions that call other functions save L R on the stack first.

The standard pattern is push R four and L R on entry, and pop R four and P C on exit. Popping the saved return address straight into the program counter returns in one instruction. The stack lives in SRAM and grows downward, toward lower addresses, and the stack pointer always marks its top.

On a microcontroller with only a few kilobytes of RAM, the stack is small. Deep recursion or big local arrays can run it past its reserved space and silently overwrite other variables, a classic and very confusing embedded bug.

slides.h: GPIO: controlling pins with bit masks
pts: Each pin = one bit in a port register
Set a bit: reg |= (1 << n)
Clear a bit: reg &= ~(1 << n)
Toggle: reg ^= (1 << n) · Read: (reg >> n) & 1
say: General purpose input output pins are the simplest peripheral. Each pin corresponds to one bit in a port register. Write a one and the pin goes high, lighting an L E D. Write a zero and it goes low.

But a port register controls eight, sixteen or thirty two pins at once, so you must change one bit without disturbing the others. That's done with bit masks, straight from Boolean algebra. To set bit zero, OR the register with one shifted left by zero.
To clear bit three, AND it with the complement of one shifted left by three. Every bit stays the same except bit three, which becomes zero.

To toggle bit five, X O R with one shifted left by five. And to read a pin, shift right and AND with one. You'll write these four patterns thousands of times as an embedded engineer. Before a pin can be used, it must also be configured as an input or output, with its own direction register.

slides.h: Worked example: bit masks, one bit at a time
pts: (code on the board) uint8_t reg = 0xA5;          // 1010 0101
(code on the board) reg |=  (1 << 3);            // 1010 1101 = 0xAD
(code on the board) reg &= ~(1 << 0);            // 1010 1100 = 0xAC
(code on the board) reg ^=  (1 << 7);            // 0010 1100 = 0x2C
(code on the board) int b5 = (reg >> 5) & 1;     // 0010 1100 -> 1
(written on the whiteboard) set: |=  clear: &= ~  toggle: ^=  read: >> and & 1
say: Let's practice the four bit mask operations on a real value. A port register holds hex A five: in binary, one zero one zero, zero one zero one. Bit zero is on the right, bit seven on the left.
Set bit three. One shifted left by three is zero zero zero zero, one zero zero zero. Or it in, and bit three turns on, without touching anything else. The result is hex A D.
Clear bit zero. One shifted by zero is just one. Invert it with tilde, so every bit is one except bit zero, then and it in. Only bit zero is forced to zero: hex A C.
Toggle bit seven with exclusive or. Bit seven was one, so it becomes zero: hex two C.

Finally, read bit five. Shift the register right by five, so bit five lands in position zero, and mask with one. Hex two C is zero zero one zero, one one zero zero. Bit five is one. These four idioms, set, clear, toggle and read, are how every embedded C program controls hardware: an LED, a motor enable, a sensor's ready flag.

pts: Polling: loop asking “ready yet?”
Interrupt: hardware taps the CPU on the shoulder
ISR runs, then main code resumes exactly where it was
Keep ISRs short; share data carefully (volatile)
say: How does a program notice a button press? The simple way is polling: loop forever, reading the pin over and over. It works, but the CPU can't do anything else, and it can't sleep to save battery.
The better way is an interrupt. When the button is pressed, the hardware itself signals the CPU.

The CPU finishes its current instruction, saves its registers, looks up the handler's address in a table called the interrupt vector table, and jumps to the interrupt service routine. When the I S R finishes, the CPU restores its registers and resumes the main program exactly where it left off, as if nothing had happened.

Two golden rules. Keep I S Rs short: set a flag or grab a byte, and do the heavy work later in the main loop. And variables shared between an I S R and the main program must be declared volatile, so the compiler doesn't cache them in a register and miss the update. Forgetting volatile is one of the most common embedded bugs, and it often only shows up when you turn on optimizations.

pts: Timer: a hardware counter clocked by the system clock
Periodic interrupts: “run this every 1 ms”
PWM: fast on/off with adjustable duty cycle
Dim LEDs, set motor speed, position servos (1–2 ms pulses)
say: A timer is a hardware counter that ticks with the system clock, completely independent of your code. When it reaches a set value, it can trigger an interrupt, which gives you precise periodic events, like reading a sensor every millisecond.
Timers can also generate pulse width modulation, or P W M. The output switches on and off at a fixed fast rate, and you control the fraction of time it's on, called the duty cycle.

Anything slow, like an L E D seen by your eye or a motor with inertia, responds to the average. Twenty five percent duty gives roughly a quarter of the power. That's how L E Ds are dimmed and how motor speed is controlled efficiently, without wasting energy as heat in a resistor.

Hobby servo motors use P W M as a position command: a pulse every twenty milliseconds, where one millisecond means one end, two milliseconds means the other end, and one and a half means center. The robot arm in senior design will need exactly this.

slides.h: Worked example: choosing timer values for PWM
pts: (written on the whiteboard) f_clk = 48\ mathrmMHz, want 1 kHz
(written on the whiteboard) period = 48times 10^6 times 0.001 = 48,000 counts
(written on the whiteboard) 25% duty: compare = 0.25times 48,000 = 12,000
(written on the whiteboard) servo 50 Hz: 48times 10^6 / 50 = 960,000 too big!
(written on the whiteboard) prescaler 16: 3\ mathrmMHz/50 = 60,000 fits
(written on the whiteboard) 1.5 ms pulse: 0.0015times 3times 10^6 = 4500
say: A timer counts clock cycles. Our clock is forty eight megahertz, and we want a one kilohertz PWM signal to dim an LED. The period is one millisecond, so the timer must count forty eight million times one thousandth: forty eight thousand cycles per period.

For twenty five percent brightness, the output stays high for a quarter of the period. So the compare value is twelve thousand. When the counter passes twelve thousand, the pin goes low until the period restarts.

Now a servo, which needs fifty hertz: twenty milliseconds per period. That's nine hundred sixty thousand counts, too big for a sixteen bit timer, which tops out at sixty five thousand five hundred thirty five. So we add a prescaler that divides the clock by sixteen first: three megahertz, and sixty thousand counts per period. That fits.
The servo's center position is a one point five millisecond pulse. At three megahertz, that's four thousand five hundred counts. Change that one number, and the servo arm turns.

slides.h: Reading the analog world: the ADC
pts: Sensors produce voltages; the CPU needs numbers
n-bit ADC → 2ⁿ levels
12-bit, 3.3 V: ≈ 0.8 mV per step
V = code × V_ref / 4096 → code 2048 ≈ 1.65 V
say: Temperature sensors, microphones, light sensors and potentiometers produce voltages, but the processor only understands numbers. The analog to digital converter, or A D C, bridges the gap.

An n bit A D C divides its input range into two to the n levels. This chart shows a coarse four bit converter with sixteen steps, so you can see the staircase. That staircase error is called quantization error.
Real microcontrollers typically have twelve bit A D Cs: four thousand ninety six levels. With a three point three volt reference, each step is about point eight millivolts.

To convert a reading back to volts, multiply the code by the reference voltage and divide by four thousand ninety six. A reading of two thousand forty eight means about one point six five volts, half scale. The A D C also has a maximum sampling rate, and in signals and systems you'll learn why you must sample at more than twice the highest frequency you care about.

slides.h: Worked example: from ADC code to temperature
pts: (written on the whiteboard) sensor: V = 0.5\ mathrmV + 0.01\ mathrmV/°Ctimes T
(written on the whiteboard) 12-bit ADC, V_ref = 3.3\ mathrmV, reading = 1241
(written on the whiteboard) V = mathrmcodetimesfracV_ref2^12 = 1241times(3.3)/(4096)
(written on the whiteboard) V approx 1.00\ mathrmV
(written on the whiteboard) T = (V - 0.5)/(0.01) = (1.00 - 0.5)/(0.01)
(written on the whiteboard) T = 50\ mathrm°C
(written on the whiteboard) 1 step approx 0.8\ mathrmmV approx 0.08\ mathrm°C
(code on the board) float t = (adc * 3.3f / 4096 - 0.5f) / 0.01f;
say: A temperature sensor outputs ten millivolts per degree Celsius, with an offset of half a volt at zero degrees. It's wired to a twelve bit ADC with a three point three volt reference. The ADC reads one thousand two hundred forty one. What's the temperature?

Step one: code to volts. A twelve bit converter has four thousand ninety six steps across three point three volts. So the voltage is the code times three point three over four thousand ninety six: about one point zero zero volts.

Step two: volts to temperature. Subtract the half volt offset, and divide by ten millivolts per degree. One point zero zero minus point five is point five, divided by point zero one is fifty degrees Celsius.

And the resolution: one ADC step is three point three over four thousand ninety six, about point eight millivolts, which is less than a tenth of a degree. In code, it's one line: float temp equals the reading times three point three over four thousand ninety six, minus point five, all over point zero one.

slides.h: Serial communication: UART, SPI and I²C
pts: UART: start bit, 8 data bits (LSB first), stop bit
9600 baud → 960 bytes per second
SPI: clocked and fast · I²C: two wires, many addressed devices
Logic analyzers decode these on screen
say: Microcontrollers talk to other chips and computers over serial links, sending bits one after another. The classic is the U A R T. The line idles high. A start bit pulls it low, then eight data bits follow, least significant bit first, then a stop bit. Here's the letter capital A, hex forty one. There's no clock wire, so both sides must agree on the speed, called the baud rate. At ninety six hundred baud, each byte takes ten bit times, so you get about nine hundred sixty bytes per second.

Two other buses are everywhere. S P I uses a separate clock, data lines in each direction, and a chip select, and it's fast, which is why S D cards and displays use it. I squared C uses only two wires shared by many devices, each with its own address, which makes it perfect for wiring up lots of sensors. When something doesn't work, a logic analyzer or oscilloscope that decodes these protocols on screen is an embedded engineer's best friend.

slides.h: Worked example: the UART frame for the letter 'K'
pts: (written on the whiteboard) 'K' = 0x4B = 0100 1011
(written on the whiteboard) LSB first: 1 1 0 1 0 0 1 0
(written on the whiteboard) start 0 + 8 data + stop 1
(written on the whiteboard) bit time = 1/9600 approx 104\ mu s
(written on the whiteboard) 10 bits per char: 960 chars/s
say: Let's draw exactly what travels down the wire when a microcontroller sends the letter capital K. The line rests high when idle. Every frame begins with a start bit: the line drops low for one bit time.
Then come the eight data bits, least significant bit first. Hex four B is zero one zero zero, one zero one one. Reading from the right, the bits go out as one, one, zero, one, zero, zero, one, zero.
Finally a stop bit, high, and the line returns to idle. The receiver has no clock wire. It syncs on the falling edge of the start bit, then samples in the middle of each bit time.

At nine thousand six hundred baud, each bit lasts one over nine thousand six hundred seconds, about a hundred and four microseconds. Ten bits per frame means one point oh four milliseconds per character, so about nine hundred sixty characters per second.

pts: Use a hardware debugger: breakpoints, single-step, watch registers & memory
Blink an LED or toggle a pin to trace timing
Read the datasheet & reference manual — register by register
Check clocks and pin configuration first
Measure with a scope or logic analyzer — don’t guess
say: Embedded debugging is different from desktop debugging, because there's often no screen.

Use the hardware debugger. Through a small debug port, you can stop the processor at a breakpoint, step one instruction at a time, and inspect every register and memory location while the chip is running on your bench.
The humble L E D is a debugging tool. Toggle a pin at the start and end of a routine and measure it on a scope to see exactly how long it takes.
Read the datasheet and the reference manual. Every peripheral is controlled by registers documented bit by bit, and most bugs are a single bit set wrong.
When nothing works at all, check the basics first: is the peripheral's clock enabled, and is the pin configured for the right function?
And measure. A scope or logic analyzer shows what's really happening on the wires, which is often not what you think your code is doing.

slides.big: A microcontroller is a computer on a chip. Hardware is memory-mapped, controlled with bit masks, driven by interrupts and timers.
say: To wrap up. A microcontroller combines a C P U, flash, RAM and peripherals on one chip. The programmer's model is registers, flags and a memory map. Assembly language uses loads, stores, arithmetic and branches, and subroutines use the link register and the stack. Peripherals are memory mapped, so you control them by setting and clearing bits. Interrupts let hardware events take over the processor briefly, timers generate precise timing and P W M, the A D C reads the analog world, and serial buses connect to other chips. Next, we'll design hardware itself with V H D L. See you there.

L14_egcp281.title: Designing with VHDL
L14_egcp281.file: EGCP-281 Digital Logic Design (VHDL)/Lecture - EGCP 281 Designing with VHDL.mp4

say: Welcome to E G C P two eighty one, Designing with V H D L. In this lecture you'll learn how engineers describe digital hardware using code, how that code becomes a real circuit on a chip, and who actually does this for a living. We'll go from the very first idea, all the way to adders, state machines, timing, and test benches. That little board on the screen is an F P G A board, and by the end of this lesson you'll understand exactly what's inside that chip and how to program it.

pts: 1971: ~2,300 transistors — drawn by hand
Today: tens of billions per chip
Nobody can draw that. We describe behavior and let tools build the gates
say: Let's start with the why. In nineteen seventy one, Intel's first microprocessor, the four zero zero four, had about two thousand three hundred transistors. Engineers literally drew the circuit by hand on large sheets.
Today, a laptop processor like Apple's M one has sixteen billion transistors. Look at the chart. That's a log scale, so every grid line is ten times more than the one below it.

No human team can draw sixteen billion transistors. So instead, engineers write a precise description of what the hardware should do, in a hardware description language, and software tools turn that description into gates. That's what this course teaches. V H D L is one of the two big hardware description languages, and Verilog is the other.

V H D L stands for V H S I C Hardware Description Language, and V H S I C stands for Very High Speed Integrated Circuit. It was a U S Department of Defense program in the early nineteen eighties. The military was buying chips from many suppliers, and the documentation was written in plain English, which was ambiguous. Worse, when a part became obsolete, nobody could rebuild it exactly.

So the D o D funded a language that could describe a chip so precisely that a computer could simulate it. The syntax was borrowed from the Ada programming language, which is why V H D L is wordy and strict. It became I E E E standard ten seventy six in nineteen eighty seven. Around the same time, a company called Gateway Design Automation created Verilog, which has a shorter, C like syntax. Both languages are still alive, both are I E E E standards, and most professional engineers can read both.

slides.h: Who uses VHDL today — and why?
pts: Telecom: 4G/5G radios and network gear
Aerospace & defense: satellites, rovers, radar
Products: routers, cameras, medical imaging, factory robots
Chip companies: prototype and verify before manufacturing
say: So who writes V H D L for a living? Mostly people who design F P G A based products and custom chips. Let's look at four real examples.

Telecom. Cell towers like these process radio signals in real time, billions of samples per second. Software on a normal processor is too slow, so that processing is done in custom hardware, very often on F P G As, designed in V H D L or Verilog.

Aerospace and defense, which is V H D L's home turf, especially in Europe. Spacecraft need hardware that's reliable and well documented. NASA's Perseverance rover used an F P G A based vision computer to recognize the terrain and steer its own landing on Mars. And the European Space Agency's LEON family of processors, which fly in many satellites, was written in V H D L.

Everyday products. This is the circuit board inside a home internet router. That square chip is a Xilinx Spartan F P G A. Companies use F P G As when they need custom, very fast logic but can't afford to manufacture their own chip.

And chip companies. Before spending millions of dollars to manufacture a chip on a silicon wafer like this one, designers write the whole thing in a hardware description language, simulate it, and often prototype it on F P G As first. A mistake found in simulation costs minutes. A mistake found after manufacturing can cost months.

pts: Field-Programmable Gate Array
Thousands to millions of small logic blocks
Each block: a look-up table + a flip-flop
Programmable wiring connects them
say: Since V H D L is so often used with F P G As, let's open one up. F P G A stands for field programmable gate array. Field programmable means you can reconfigure it after it leaves the factory, right on your desk.

Inside is a grid of small logic blocks, shown in blue. Between them is a mesh of programmable wiring, the orange lines, with switches where wires cross. Around the edge are the input and output pins, in green.

Here's the clever part. Each logic block contains a look-up table, which is just a tiny memory that holds a truth table. This one has three inputs, so it has eight memory cells, one for every input combination. Store the right eight bits and it becomes any three input logic function you want. Here it's programmed as a majority function. Next to each look-up table is a flip-flop, so the block can also remember a bit.

So when you program an F P G A, you're loading a configuration file that fills in all of those truth tables and closes all the right wiring switches. In about a second, this chip becomes your circuit. Change your code, reload, and it becomes a different circuit. That's why F P G As are perfect for learning, prototyping, and products that need updates.

slides.h: From code to chip: the design flow
say: Here's the workflow you'll repeat for every design, whether you're a student or working at a chip company.
Step one, write the V H D L. You describe what the hardware should do.

Step two, simulate. You write a test bench that feeds inputs to your design and checks the outputs, and a simulator shows you waveforms. This is where you catch most bugs, because it's fast and cheap.
Step three, synthesis. The tool reads your code and turns it into a netlist, which is a list of gates or look-up tables and flip-flops, plus how they connect.
Step four, place and route. The tool decides which physical logic blocks on the chip to use and which wires connect them, while trying to meet your timing goals.
Step five, generate the bitstream, the configuration file for the F P G A.

And step six, load it onto the board and test it in the real world. The tools you'd use are Vivado from Xilinx, which is now part of A M D, Quartus from Intel's Altera, ModelSim or Questa for simulation, and GHDL, which is a free, open source V H D L simulator you can install today.

slides.h: The big mindset shift: everything runs at once
say: Now the single most important idea in this course. On the left is ordinary C code. The computer runs line one, then line two, then line three. Order matters, and each line happens once.

On the right is the same logic as hardware. In V H D L, each of those statements becomes a physical gate. The AND gate, the NOT gate, and the OR gate all exist at the same time, and they're all working continuously, forever. If input a changes, the output z changes a few nanoseconds later, automatically. There's no program counter stepping through lines.

So here's the rule I want you to carry for the rest of your career. Before you write a line of hardware description code, picture the circuit it will become. If you can't picture the gates or flip-flops, you don't really understand that line yet. Code is just a way to draw a schematic.

slides.h: Anatomy of a design: entity + architecture
say: Every V H D L design has the same skeleton. First, we include the I E E E library, which gives us the standard logic type we'll use for wires.

Next is the entity. Think of it as the outside of the chip: its name, and its ports, which are the pins. Each port has a direction, in or out, and a type. Our full adder has three inputs, a, b and carry in, and two outputs, sum and carry out. Look at the diagram on the right: the entity is exactly that black box with five pins.

Then the architecture describes what's inside the box. Here we use two concurrent assignment statements, one for the sum and one for the carry. The arrow made of a less than sign and an equals sign means: this signal is driven by this logic. Remember, both lines are hardware that exists at the same time. The order you write them in doesn't matter at all.

slides.h: Designing a full adder, step by step
pts: Add three bits: a + b + carry-in
Sum is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1 → XOR
Carry is 1 when two or more inputs are 1
Check: 1 + 1 + 0 = binary 10 = 2 ✓
say: But where did those equations come from? Let's derive them, the way you would on an exam. A full adder adds three single bits: a, b, and a carry coming in from the previous column. The result is two bits, a carry out and a sum.

Here's the full truth table, all eight combinations. Look at the sum column. It's one whenever an odd number of the inputs are one. That's exactly what X O R does, so the sum is a X O R b X O R carry in.

Now the carry column. It's one when at least two inputs are one. You can write that as: a AND b, OR carry in AND, a X O R b. Here's that circuit drawn as gates. Two X O R gates make the sum.
