Inside integrated circuits, where matched transistors are easy to make side by side, current mirrors are everywhere, biasing almost every analog stage, including the inputs of op amps.

slides.h: Lab: stable bias that doesn’t depend on β
pts: β varies 2–3× between parts and with temperature
Fixed base bias: I_C ∝ β — unreliable
Stiff divider + R_E: I_C set by resistors
Rule of thumb: R₂ ≤ 0.1 β R_E · bypass R_E for AC gain
say: Here's the most important design lesson of the lab. Beta varies a lot: two transistors with the same part number can differ by a factor of two or three, and beta also changes with temperature.

With simple fixed base bias, a single resistor feeding the base, the collector current is proportional to beta. Swap the transistor and the operating point moves wildly, as the red bars show, and your amplifier may clip or even saturate.

With the four resistor divider bias and an emitter resistor from the electronics course, the base voltage is set by the divider, and the emitter current by that voltage and R E. Beta hardly matters: the green bars barely move from beta fifty to beta three hundred. The trick is a stiff divider, one whose current is large compared to the base current. A rule of thumb is R two at most a tenth of beta times R E.

The emitter resistor reduces the AC gain, so designers often bypass it with a capacitor: it disappears for AC signals but still stabilizes the DC bias. In the bias stability lab, students design exactly this and test it with transistors of different beta.

slides.h: Writing a lab report engineers trust
pts: State what you expected before measuring
Show data with units, uncertainty and plots
Compare theory vs measurement: % error
Explain differences: tolerances, meter loading, temperature
say: A lab report is how engineers convince other engineers. The structure is always similar: objective, theory and pre lab calculations, procedure, data, analysis and conclusion.
The most important habit is predicting before measuring. If you calculate first, you'll notice immediately when a measurement doesn't make sense.
Present data in tables and plots with units, and compute the percent error between theory and measurement.

Then explain the differences honestly. Resistors are typically plus or minus five percent. Beta varies. Meters load circuits. Temperature drifts. A report that says the measured gain was eight percent below the prediction, mostly because the transistor's beta was lower than the datasheet's typical value, is worth far more than one with perfect looking numbers. This course carried part of the engineering writing requirement for exactly this reason.

slides.big: Predict, then measure. Respect meter loading and ground. Design so the circuit works with any transistor off the shelf.
say: To recap. Instruments are part of the circuit, so choose them so they barely disturb it, and be careful where the scope's ground goes. Power supplies are rectifier, filter and regulator. Diodes clip and clamp signals. Transistors switch loads when driven into saturation, act as current sources in the active region, and mirrors copy currents. Good bias design makes a circuit work regardless of beta. And a good lab report predicts, measures, compares and explains. Next, we move to probability and statistics, the math of uncertainty and noise. See you there.

L18_egee323.title: Engineering Probability & Statistics
L18_egee323.file: EGEE-323 Probability & Random Variables/Lecture - EGEE 323 Engineering Probability & Statistics.mp4

say: Welcome to E G E E three twenty three, engineering probability and statistics. This board, called a Galton board, drops balls through a field of pins. Each ball bounces randomly, yet together they pile up into a smooth bell curve, every time. That's the magic of probability: individual events are unpredictable, but large numbers of them behave very predictably. Engineers rely on that for noise in circuits, error rates in communication, manufacturing yield, reliability and machine learning.

pts: Sample space S: all possible outcomes
Event: a subset of S
Axioms: P ≥ 0, P(S) = 1, disjoint events add
P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A) · P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
say: Probability starts with a sample space, the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment. Roll two dice, and there are thirty six equally likely outcomes. An event is any subset of outcomes, like the sum is seven.

Everything follows from three axioms: probabilities are never negative, the whole sample space has probability one, and probabilities of events that can't happen together add up. From those, we get rules like the complement, one minus P of A, and inclusion exclusion from discrete math. Six of the thirty six outcomes sum to seven, so the probability of rolling a seven is one sixth, the most likely sum.

pts: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)
Bayes: P(A | B) = P(B | A) P(A) / P(B)
2% defective, test catches 95%, false alarm 10%
A flagged chip is bad only ≈ 16% of the time!
say: Conditional probability is the probability of A given that we know B happened: the probability of both, divided by the probability of B. Knowing B shrinks the sample space.

Bayes' rule flips a conditional around: the probability of A given B equals the probability of B given A, times the probability of A, divided by the probability of B. It's how you update a belief after seeing evidence.

Here's an engineering example that surprises almost everyone. Two percent of chips from a production line are defective. A quick test catches ninety five percent of bad chips, but it also falsely flags ten percent of good ones. A chip gets flagged. What's the chance it's actually bad?

Count it out with a thousand chips. Twenty are bad, and the test flags nineteen of them. Nine hundred eighty are good, and the test falsely flags ninety eight. So a hundred seventeen chips are flagged, and only nineteen are actually bad: about sixteen percent. When the condition is rare, even a good test produces mostly false alarms. The same math applies to medical tests, spam filters, and fraud detection.

slides.h: Worked example: should you trust the alarm?
pts: (written on the whiteboard) P(F) = 0.05, P(A|F) = 0.9, P(A|mathrmok) = 0.1
(written on the whiteboard) P(F cap A) = 0.05 times 0.9 = 0.045
(written on the whiteboard) P(mathrmok cap A) = 0.95 times 0.1 = 0.095
(written on the whiteboard) P(A) = 0.045 + 0.095 = 0.14
(written on the whiteboard) P(F|A) = (0.045)/(0.14) approx 0.32
(written on the whiteboard) rare events: most alarms are false
say: A factory machine develops a fault five percent of the time. A sensor sounds an alarm for ninety percent of real faults, but it also false alarms ten percent of the time when nothing is wrong. The alarm just went off. What's the probability there's really a fault? Draw a tree. First branch: fault, five percent, or okay, ninety five percent.

Second branch: alarm or quiet. Multiply along each path. Fault and alarm: point zero five times point nine, point zero four five. Okay and alarm: point nine five times point one, point zero nine five.
Now we know an alarm happened, so only the two alarm paths matter. Together they total point one four. The fault path is point zero four five of that.

Only thirty two percent! Most alarms are false, because faults are rare, so false alarms from the many healthy cases outnumber the true ones. This exact reasoning appears in medical tests, spam filters, and the object detector in senior design.

pts: Independent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B)
Knowing B tells you nothing about A
NOT the same as mutually exclusive!
Reliability: 3 independent parts at 99% → 0.99³ ≈ 97%
say: Two events are independent if the probability of both equals the product of their probabilities. Knowing that one happened tells you nothing about the other, like two separate dice.
Equivalently, the conditional probability of A given B is just P of A.

A common mistake: independent is not the same as mutually exclusive. If two events can't happen together and both are possible, then knowing one happened tells you the other definitely didn't. That's maximum dependence.

Independence makes reliability calculations easy. A system that works only if all three of its independent components work, each with ninety nine percent reliability, works with probability point nine nine cubed, about ninety seven percent. Add more components in series and reliability drops quickly. Put them in parallel, with redundancy, and it rises.

slides.h: Bernoulli trials and the binomial distribution
pts: n independent trials, success probability p
P(k successes) = C(n,k) pᵏ (1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ
Batch of 20 chips, 5% defect rate → P(no defects) ≈ 36%
Large n, small p → Poisson with λ = np
say: Repeat an experiment n times independently, each with the same success probability p. The number of successes follows the binomial distribution. The formula combines the counting from discrete math, n choose k ways to pick which trials succeed, with the probability of each such sequence.

Example: chips are defective with probability five percent. In a batch of twenty, what's the probability of zero defects? Point nine five to the twentieth, about thirty six percent. Exactly one defect: about thirty eight percent. The chart shows the full distribution.

When n is large and p is small, the binomial is well approximated by the Poisson distribution, with parameter lambda equals n p. Poisson describes counts of rare events in an interval: packets arriving per millisecond, photons hitting a sensor pixel, or radiation induced bit flips in memory per day.

slides.h: Worked example: bit errors in a 10-bit message
pts: (written on the whiteboard) n = 10, p = 0.1
(written on the whiteboard) P(k) = binom10k 0.1^k 0.9^10-k
(written on the whiteboard) P(0) = 0.9^10 approx 0.349
(written on the whiteboard) P(1) = 10(0.1)(0.9^9) approx 0.387
(written on the whiteboard) P(k leq 1) approx 0.736
(written on the whiteboard) mean = np = 1 error
say: A noisy link flips each bit independently with probability point one. We send ten bits. What's the chance of at most one error? The number of errors follows the binomial distribution.

Zero errors: every bit survives, point nine to the tenth, about point three four nine. Exactly one error: ten choices for which bit fails, times point one, times point nine to the ninth, about point three eight seven.

Add them: about seventy four percent. So one time in four, the message has two or more errors. The expected number of errors is n p, exactly one. That's why real links add error correcting codes, like the Hamming code you'll meet in hardware security.

pts: Random variable: a number assigned to each outcome
CDF F(x) = P(X ≤ x): rises from 0 to 1
PDF f(x) = dF/dx: area under it = probability
Mean E[X] = ∫ x f(x) dx · variance σ² = E[X²] − E[X]²
say: A random variable assigns a number to each outcome: the voltage of a noisy signal, the lifetime of a component, the number of errors in a packet.
The cumulative distribution function, or CDF, gives the probability that X is at most x. It rises from zero to one.

Its derivative is the probability density function, or PDF. For continuous variables, probability is area under the PDF. The probability that X lands between a and b is the integral from a to b. This is where Calculus pays off.

Two numbers summarize a distribution. The mean, or expected value, is the integral of x times f of x: the center of mass. The variance measures spread: the expected squared distance from the mean, and its square root is the standard deviation, sigma.

slides.h: Worked example: mean and variance, by hand
pts: (written on the whiteboard) die: E[X] = sum x p(x) = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/(6) = 3.5
(written on the whiteboard) E[X] = long-run average, not a likely outcome
(written on the whiteboard) uniform on [0,2]: f(x) = (1)/(2)
(written on the whiteboard) E[X] = int_0^2 xcdot(1)/(2) dx = 1
(written on the whiteboard) E[X^2] = int_0^2 x^2cdot(1)/(2) dx = (4)/(3)
(written on the whiteboard) sigma^2 = (4)/(3) - 1^2 = (1)/(3),  sigma approx 0.58
(written on the whiteboard) f(x) can exceed 1: only AREA is probability
say: Let's actually compute an expected value, starting with a fair die. Multiply each outcome by its probability and add: one through six, each times one sixth. That's twenty one sixths, three point five.
Notice you can never roll a three point five. The expected value is the long run average, the balance point of the distribution, not a value you expect to see on any single roll.

Now a continuous one: X uniform between zero and two. The density is one half across that range, so the total area is one. The mean is the integral of x times one half, from zero to two: one. Then E of X squared is the integral of x squared times one half: four thirds.

Variance is E of X squared minus the mean squared: four thirds minus one, one third. The standard deviation is its square root, about point five eight. And one warning: a density can be bigger than one. Uniform on zero to one half has height two. Only areas are probabilities.

pts: Bell curve with mean μ and standard deviation σ
68% within 1σ, 95% within 2σ, 99.7% within 3σ
Standardize: z = (x − μ)/σ, then use tables or Q(z)
Thermal noise, measurement error, manufacturing spread
say: The most important distribution in engineering is the Gaussian, or normal, distribution: the bell curve, set by its mean and its standard deviation.
Memorize the 68, 95, 99.7 rule. About sixty eight percent of values fall within one sigma of the mean, ninety five percent within two sigma, and ninety nine point seven percent within three.
For any other question, standardize: subtract the mean and divide by sigma to get z, then look up the probability in a table or with the Q function, which gives the tail area beyond z.

Example: one kilohm resistors with a one percent tolerance, modeled with sigma of ten ohms. Ninety five percent fall between nine hundred eighty and one thousand twenty ohms. Thermal noise in every resistor, measurement errors, and variations in transistor thresholds across a wafer are all approximately Gaussian, which is why this curve is everywhere.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) mu = 1000\ Omega,  sigma = 20\ Omega
(written on the whiteboard) 980 to 1020: within 1sigma so 68%
(written on the whiteboard) z = (1040 - 1000)/(20) = 2
(written on the whiteboard) P(R > 1040) = P(Z > 2) approx 2.3\%
(written on the whiteboard) 23 of every 1000 boards out of spec
say: A factory makes one kilohm resistors. The actual values are Gaussian, with a mean of one thousand ohms and a standard deviation of twenty ohms.
What fraction lands between nine eighty and ten twenty? That's within one standard deviation of the mean, which is always about sixty eight percent.

What fraction is above ten forty? Standardize: z equals x minus the mean over sigma, forty over twenty, two. The area beyond z equals two, from a table or a calculator, is about two point three percent.

So if a design breaks above ten forty ohms, about twenty three out of every thousand boards would fail. Engineers use exactly this calculation to choose component tolerances, and to decide between one percent and five percent parts.

slides.h: Why the bell curve is everywhere: the Central Limit Theorem
pts: Add many independent random effects…
…and the sum becomes Gaussian, whatever the originals were
Sum of 12 uniforms ≈ Gaussian already
Noise = sum of countless tiny random kicks
say: Why does the Gaussian show up everywhere? Look at the Galton board. Each ball's final position is the sum of many small random left or right bounces. And the pile is a bell curve.

The central limit theorem says that the sum of many independent random effects is approximately Gaussian, no matter what each individual effect's distribution looks like. On the left, a single uniform random number is flat. Add two and you get a triangle. Add twelve, and it's already almost indistinguishable from a bell curve. Electrical noise is the combined effect of enormous numbers of electrons jiggling randomly, so it's Gaussian. Measurement error is the sum of many small disturbances, so it's Gaussian too.

pts: Constant failure rate λ → lifetime is exponential
Mean time to failure MTTF = 1/λ
P(survive past t) = e^(−λt)
Memoryless — plus “burn-in” to weed out early failures
say: Reliability engineering asks how long things last. Chips are tested at the wafer level with probe cards like this one, and samples are stress tested to estimate failure rates. When a part fails at a constant rate, lambda, its lifetime follows the exponential distribution.

The mean time to failure is one over lambda, and the probability of surviving past time t is e to the minus lambda t. Surprisingly, only about thirty seven percent of parts survive past their mean time to failure, and only thirteen and a half percent past twice that. The exponential is also memoryless: a part that has worked for a year is no more likely to fail next week than a new one. Real electronics also have a burst of early failures, called infant mortality, so manufacturers run new parts hot for a while, a process called burn in, to weed out the weak ones before shipping.

slides.h: Two random variables: joint distributions and correlation
pts: Joint PDF f(x, y); marginals by integrating out
Independent ⇔ f(x, y) = f(x) f(y)
Covariance and correlation ρ ∈ [−1, 1]
Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y + 2 Cov(X, Y)
say: With two random variables, we describe them together with a joint PDF. Integrate out one variable to get the other's own distribution, called the marginal.
They're independent exactly when the joint PDF factors into the product of the marginals.

Correlation measures how they move together, from minus one to plus one. On the left, rho is zero: a round cloud, no relationship. In the middle, rho of point seven: when one is high, the other tends to be high. On the right, rho of minus point nine: a strong inverse relationship. Remember that correlation measures linear relationship only, and it doesn't imply causation.

And for sums: the variance of X plus Y is the sum of the variances plus twice the covariance. For independent noise sources, variances simply add, so two independent noise sources with equal power give root two times the noise voltage, not double.

pts: PDF of X + Y (independent) = f_X ∗ f_Y
Uniform + uniform = triangle
Same operation as LTI systems in Signals & Systems
Repeated convolution → Gaussian (CLT again)
say: What's the distribution of the sum of two independent random variables? It's the convolution of their PDFs: slide one across the other, multiply and integrate.
Two uniform variables on zero to one add up to a triangle on zero to two, the same shape you saw with the dice and the central limit theorem demo.

Convolution is exactly the operation that describes linear time invariant systems in signals and systems, where the output is the input convolved with the impulse response. So you'll see it again very soon.
Convolve many distributions together, and the result tends to a Gaussian. That's the central limit theorem from a different angle.

slides.h: Engineering example: bit errors in noisy channels
pts: Send 0 → 0 V, 1 → A volts; noise is Gaussian (σ)
Receiver decides with a threshold at A/2
P(error) = Q(A / 2σ)
A = 4σ → 2.3% · A = 12σ → 1 in a billion
say: Let's combine everything into the core problem of digital communication. A transmitter sends zero volts for a zero and A volts for a one. The channel adds Gaussian noise with standard deviation sigma. So a received zero is a bell curve centered at zero, and a received one is a bell curve centered at A.
The receiver decides with a threshold halfway between, at A over two.
An error happens when noise pushes a signal across the threshold, the red areas. The probability is Q of A over two sigma: the tail of a Gaussian beyond a distance of A over two.

If A is four sigma, the error rate is Q of two, about two point three percent: terrible. Triple the signal to twelve sigma, and the error rate drops to about one in a billion. That's why signal to noise ratio is everything in communications, and why a few extra decibels of signal can cut error rates by orders of magnitude. Wi Fi, cellular, Ethernet and USB are all designed around exactly this calculation.

slides.big: Probability makes uncertainty predictable: Bayes updates beliefs, the Gaussian models noise, and Q(z) turns signal-to-noise into error rates.
say: To recap. Probability rests on sample spaces and three axioms. Conditional probability and Bayes' rule update beliefs, and base rates matter enormously. Independence simplifies reliability calculations. The binomial and Poisson distributions count successes and rare events. PDFs and CDFs describe continuous random variables, and the mean and variance summarize them. The Gaussian is everywhere because of the central limit theorem. The exponential models lifetimes. Sums of random variables convolve. And noise plus a threshold gives you bit error rates. Next, signals and systems. See you there.

L19_egcp371.title: Signals & Systems
L19_egcp371.file: EGCP-371 Signals & Systems/Lecture - EGCP 371 Signals & Systems.mp4

slides.h: Modeling & Simulation of Signals and Systems
say: Welcome to E G C P three seventy one, signals and systems. Audio equalizers, noise cancelling headphones, cell phone radios, image compression, sensor filtering and control systems all rest on the ideas in this course. You'll learn to describe signals and systems mathematically, to see signals in terms of their frequencies, to sample them correctly, and to predict whether a system is stable, using MATLAB to simulate it all.

pts: Continuous x(t) vs discrete x[n] = x(nT)
Building blocks: step, impulse, exponential, sinusoid
Impulse δ(t): infinitely brief, area 1
Sifting: ∫ x(t) δ(t − t₀) dt = x(t₀)
say: A signal is any quantity that varies with time: a voltage, a sound pressure, a temperature. Continuous time signals are defined at every instant. Discrete time signals are sequences of samples, x of n, like the numbers an A D C produces.
A few building blocks describe almost everything. The unit step turns on at time zero. The decaying exponential describes capacitor discharges. Sinusoids describe anything periodic.
The strangest and most useful is the impulse, delta of t: an infinitely brief spike with an area of exactly one. Think of it as an idealized hammer tap.

Its key property, called sifting: integrating any signal times a shifted impulse picks out the signal's value at that instant. That's why, if you know how a system responds to one impulse, you can predict its response to anything.

slides.h: Systems and the magic of LTI
pts: Linear: scale & add inputs → outputs scale & add
Time-invariant: behaves the same at any time
Causal (no peeking at the future) · BIBO stable
LTI → completely described by its impulse response h(t)
say: A system takes an input signal and produces an output signal: an amplifier, a filter, a room's echo, a car's suspension.

The most important class is linear and time invariant, L T I. Linear means superposition holds: double the input, double the output, and the response to a sum is the sum of the responses. Time invariant means the system behaves the same today as tomorrow.
We also care whether a system is causal, meaning the output doesn't depend on future inputs, which every real time system must be, and whether it's stable: bounded inputs always give bounded outputs.

Here's why L T I systems are so special. Any input can be written as a sum of shifted, scaled impulses. So if you know the response to one impulse, h of t, you know the response to everything. The output is the input convolved with h. And in the frequency domain, convolution becomes simple multiplication: Y equals H times X. That single fact is the reason transforms exist.

Convolution sounds intimidating, so let's watch it. The input x is a one second rectangular pulse, in blue. The system's impulse response is a decaying exponential, like an R C circuit. To find the output at time t, flip h around and slide it to position t, the orange curve. Multiply the two, and add up the overlapping area. At t equals point three, there's only a small overlap.
Slide further. At point eight, the overlap is bigger, so the output keeps rising.
At one point five, the pulse has ended, and the overlap is shrinking. The output is now decaying.

By two and a half, it's almost gone. Plot the area at every position, and you get the purple output: the R C circuit charging during the pulse and discharging afterward, exactly what you'd measure on a scope. In discrete time it's the same idea with sums instead of integrals: y of n equals the sum over k of x of k times h of n minus k. Every digital filter computes exactly that.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) x = [1, 2, 1]
(written on the whiteboard) h = [1, 1]
(written on the whiteboard) y[n] = sum_k x[k] h[n-k]
(written on the whiteboard) y[0] = 1·1 = 1
(written on the whiteboard) y[1] = 1 + 2 = 3
(written on the whiteboard) y[2] = 2 + 1 = 3
(written on the whiteboard) y[3] = 1
(written on the whiteboard) y = [1, 3, 3, 1]
(written on the whiteboard) length = 3 + 2 − 1 = 4
say: Let's convolve two short signals by hand. The input x is one, two, one. The system's impulse response h is one, one: it adds each sample to the one before it.

The output at time n is the sum of x of k times h of n minus k. Flip h, slide it along x, multiply the overlapping samples, and add. At n equals zero, only x zero overlaps: one times one, so y zero is one.
At n equals one, two samples overlap: x zero plus x one, one plus two, three. At n equals two: x one plus x two, two plus one, three. At n equals three, only x two remains: one.

So y is one, three, three, one. Notice the output is one sample longer than the input: three plus two minus one. And it's the same arithmetic as multiplying polynomials: one plus two z plus z squared, times one plus z. That connection is exactly why transforms turn convolution into multiplication.

slides.h: Fourier series: any periodic signal is a sum of sines
say: In the early eighteen hundreds, Joseph Fourier claimed that any periodic signal can be written as a sum of sines and cosines at whole number multiples of a fundamental frequency, called harmonics. Mathematicians doubted him at first. He was right.
Let's build a square wave. Start with one sine wave at the fundamental frequency. It's a rough approximation.
Add the third harmonic, at one third the amplitude, and the fifth at one fifth. The edges sharpen.
Nine terms, and it's clearly square.

Twenty five terms, and it hugs the square wave closely. A square wave contains only odd harmonics, with amplitudes falling off as one over k. But notice the little spikes at each edge, about nine percent of the jump. They get narrower with more terms, but never shorter. That's the Gibbs phenomenon. This is why a digital clock signal, which is roughly a square wave, has energy at many harmonics, and why fast digital signals can cause radio interference at multiples of their clock frequency.

pts: X(ω) = ∫ x(t) e^(−jωt) dt
Time domain ⇄ frequency domain: same signal, two views
Convolution in time = multiplication in frequency
Frequency response H(jω): gain & phase per frequency
say: For signals that aren't periodic, the Fourier transform generalizes the series. It measures how much of each frequency is present in a signal.

Look at this signal. In the time domain, on top, it's a messy wiggle. In the frequency domain, on the bottom, it's obvious: three tones, at four hundred forty, eight hundred eighty and thirteen twenty hertz, the note A and two of its harmonics. Same information, two views. Engineers switch between them constantly.
The most important property: convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency. So to understand a filter, look at its frequency response, H, and multiply.

The frequency response tells you, for each frequency, how much the system amplifies or attenuates it, and how much it shifts its phase. An audio equalizer, like the sliders on a mixing console, is just a system whose frequency response you can shape by hand.

slides.h: Modulation: how radio shares the air
pts: Multiply a message by a carrier cos(2πf_c t)
Its spectrum shifts up to ±f_c
Different stations → different f_c → no overlap
AM radio: 540–1700 kHz; Wi-Fi: 2.4 / 5 GHz
say: Here's a beautiful application of the Fourier transform. Multiply a message signal by a high frequency cosine, the carrier. On top, you can see the message, in orange, as the envelope of the fast carrier. That's amplitude modulation, or A M.
In the frequency domain, multiplying by a cosine simply shifts the message's spectrum up to plus and minus the carrier frequency.

So many stations can share the air at the same time, each shifted to its own carrier frequency, as long as their shifted spectra don't overlap. A radio receiver uses a band pass filter to pick out one station, then shifts it back down.

A M radio stations sit between about five hundred forty and seventeen hundred kilohertz. Wi Fi uses carriers around two point four and five gigahertz, with far more sophisticated modulation, but the same principle. In this course's second assignment, students generate a carrier, a message and the modulated signal in MATLAB and look at their spectra.

pts: Sampling at f_s repeats the spectrum every f_s
Nyquist: need f_s > 2 f_max
Too slow → high frequencies masquerade as low ones
Anti-alias low-pass filter before every ADC
say: When an A D C samples a signal f s times per second, the sampled signal's spectrum repeats every f s. If the signal contains frequencies above half the sampling rate, those copies overlap.

So the Nyquist sampling theorem says: to capture a signal whose highest frequency is f max, you must sample faster than two times f max. That's why audio CDs sample at forty four point one kilohertz, a bit more than twice the twenty kilohertz upper limit of human hearing.

Break the rule and something sneaky happens. Here, a nine hertz signal is sampled at only ten hertz. The red samples fit a one hertz sine wave perfectly, so that's what you'd reconstruct. The high frequency has disguised itself as a low one. That's aliasing, and it's the same reason wagon wheels in movies appear to spin backwards.

Once aliasing happens, it can't be undone, because the samples are identical. So every A D C needs an analog low pass filter in front of it, an anti aliasing filter, to remove frequencies above half the sampling rate before sampling.

slides.h: Worked example: a 7 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz
pts: (written on the whiteboard) f = 7\ mathrmkHz, f_s = 10\ mathrmkHz
(written on the whiteboard) need f_s > 14\ mathrmkHz!
(written on the whiteboard) alias = |7 - 10| = 3\ mathrmkHz
(written on the whiteboard) filter BEFORE the ADC
say: Here's aliasing in action. A seven kilohertz tone is sampled at ten kilohertz. Nyquist says we need more than twice the highest frequency, fourteen kilohertz. We're too slow.
Take a sample every tenth of a millisecond. These red dots are all the computer ever sees.

But a three kilohertz cosine passes through every single dot. The computer can't tell them apart, so the seven kilohertz tone shows up as three kilohertz: the sampling rate minus the signal frequency.
Once sampled, the damage can't be undone. That's why every A D C has an analog low pass filter in front of it, to remove anything above half the sampling rate before sampling.

slides.h: The Laplace transform: poles decide stability
pts: X(s) = ∫₀^∞ x(t) e^(−st) dt, s = σ + jω
Derivatives become multiplication by s → ODEs become algebra
H(s) = N(s)/D(s); poles = roots of D(s)
All poles in the left half-plane → stable
say: The Laplace transform generalizes Fourier by using a complex frequency, s, equals sigma plus j omega. Its superpower: differentiation becomes multiplication by s, so the differential equations from math two fifty B turn into algebra. Solve for the output, then transform back with partial fractions, the technique from Calculus two.

Every L T I system gets a transfer function, H of s, a ratio of polynomials. The roots of the denominator are the poles, and they're exactly the eigenvalues from linear algebra. Each pole contributes a term to the impulse response. A pole at minus two point two gives a smooth exponential decay. A pair at minus one plus or minus two j gives a decaying oscillation: the real part sets the decay rate, the imaginary part sets the ringing frequency. A pole at plus one gives exponential growth: an unstable system. So the rule is simple: a system is stable if and only if all its poles are in the left half of the s plane. Every amplifier, power supply, drone flight controller and cruise control is designed around this picture.

slides.h: Worked example: solving a circuit with Laplace
pts: (written on the whiteboard) v' + v = u(t),  v(0) = 0
(written on the whiteboard) mathcalL\v'\ = sV - v(0),  mathcalL\u(t)\ = (1)/(s)
(written on the whiteboard) sV + V = (1)/(s)
(written on the whiteboard) V(s) = (1)/(s(s+1)) = (A)/(s) + (B)/(s+1)
(written on the whiteboard) A = 1,  B = -1
(written on the whiteboard) v(t) = 1 - e^-t
(written on the whiteboard) pole at s = -1 to e^-t, tau = 1\ mathrms
say: Let's actually use the Laplace transform, start to finish. An R C circuit with R C equal to one second, starting empty, is hit by a one volt step at time zero. Its equation is v prime plus v equals one.
Step one: transform every term. The derivative becomes s V minus the initial value, which is zero. v becomes capital V. And the unit step becomes one over s. Calculus has turned into algebra.

Step two: solve for V. V equals one over s times s plus one. Step three: partial fractions, from Calculus two. Plug s equals zero to get A equals one, and s equals minus one to get B equals minus one.

Step four: transform back using the table. One over s is a step, one. One over s plus one is e to the minus t. So v of t equals one minus e to the minus t. That's the same charging curve we found with an integrating factor in math two fifty B, and notice the pole at s equals minus one sets the time constant.

pts: Evaluate H(s) at s = jω
RC low-pass: H = 1 / (1 + jωRC)
1 kΩ, 100 nF → f_c ≈ 1.6 kHz, then −20 dB/decade
Bode: magnitude in dB and phase vs log frequency
say: To get a system's frequency response, evaluate its transfer function on the imaginary axis, at s equals j omega. Take the simple R C low pass filter: H equals one over one plus j omega R C. With one kilohm and one hundred nanofarads, the corner frequency is one over two pi R C, about one point six kilohertz. Below that, signals pass almost unchanged. At the corner, the gain is minus three decibels, half power, and the phase is minus forty five degrees. Above it, the gain falls by twenty decibels for every factor of ten in frequency, and the phase approaches minus ninety degrees. A Bode plot shows exactly this: gain in decibels and phase, against frequency on a log scale. Engineers sketch Bode plots by hand from the poles and zeros, a skill you'll use for filters, amplifiers and feedback control. And watch the units, because this trips up everyone. Omega is in radians per second, and f is in hertz, cycles per second. Omega equals two pi f. The corner is at omega equals one over R C, which is f equals one over two pi R C. Forgetting the two pi is the most common mistake in this course.

slides.h: Worked example: an RC low-pass filter
pts: (written on the whiteboard) H(jomega) = (1)/(1 + jomega RC)
(written on the whiteboard) f_c = (1)/(2pi RC) = frac12pi(10^3)(10^-7) approx 1.6\ mathrmkHz
(written on the whiteboard) |H| = frac1sqrt1 + (f/f_c)^2
(written on the whiteboard) 1 kHz: |H| = 0.85 to -1.4\ mathrmdB
(written on the whiteboard) 10 kHz: |H| = 0.16 to -16\ mathrmdB
(written on the whiteboard) −20 dB per decade above fc
say: Take an RC low pass filter with one kilohm and one hundred nanofarads. Its frequency response is one over one plus j omega R C. The cutoff frequency, where the output falls to minus three decibels, is one over two pi R C: about one point six kilohertz.
The magnitude is one over the square root of one plus f over f c squared. At one kilohertz, that's point eight five, or minus one point four decibels. Barely touched.

At ten kilohertz, it's point one six, or minus sixteen decibels. Above the cutoff, the response falls about twenty decibels for every factor of ten in frequency. That's how a filter keeps the signal you want and removes high frequency noise.

pts: X(z) = Σ x[n] z⁻ⁿ; z⁻¹ = one-sample delay
Stable iff all poles inside the unit circle
Connect: z = e^(sT)
say: For discrete time signals, the Z transform plays the role of Laplace. Its key idea: multiplying by z to the minus one means delay by one sample.
So a difference equation, like y of n equals x of n plus a times y of n minus one, becomes H of z equals one over one minus a z to the minus one. That has a pole at z equals a.

In discrete time, the stability boundary is the unit circle. A pole inside it, like point eight, gives an impulse response of point eight to the n, decaying. A pole outside it, like one point two, grows forever.

The two worlds are connected by z equals e to the s T, which maps the left half of the s plane to the inside of the unit circle. In the course assignments, students compute Z transforms and plot poles and zeros in MATLAB, exactly like this.

slides.h: Worked example: a one-line digital filter
pts: (code on the board) y[n] = x[n] + a * y[n-1];
(written on the whiteboard) impulse in, a = 0.5
(written on the whiteboard) y = 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, ...
(written on the whiteboard) H(z) = frac11 - a z^-1: pole at z = a
(written on the whiteboard) |a| < 1: stable  |a| > 1: blows up
say: Here's a digital filter in one line of code: y of n equals x of n, plus a times y of n minus one. Feed it a single one, an impulse, with a equals one half.
The output is one, then half of that, then a quarter, an eighth, decaying forever. That's an infinite impulse response. Its z transform is one over one minus a z inverse, with a pole at z equals a.

The pole at one half is inside the unit circle, so it's stable. Now change a to one point five. The output grows: one, one point five, two point two five, three point three seven five, forever. A pole outside the unit circle means the filter is unstable. One number decides it.

slides.h: Digital filters, the DFT and the FFT
pts: FIR: weighted sum of recent inputs — always stable
IIR: feeds back old outputs — sharp, cheap, can go unstable
DFT: spectrum of N samples; FFT computes it in O(N log N)
Frequency resolution = f_s / N
say: Digital filters are just difference equations running on a processor. A finite impulse response, or F I R, filter is a weighted sum of recent inputs. The simplest is a moving average: here, averaging nine samples smooths a noisy sensor reading. F I R filters are always stable and can have perfectly linear phase.

An infinite impulse response, or I I R, filter also feeds back old outputs. This one blends eighty five percent of the previous output with fifteen percent of the new input. With just one multiply per sample, it smooths as well as a long F I R filter. The trade off: I I R filters have poles, so a bad design can be unstable.

To analyze sampled data, we use the discrete Fourier transform, the D F T, which computes the spectrum of N samples. Done directly, it takes N squared operations. The fast Fourier transform, the F F T, computes the same result in N log N, the divide and conquer trick from data structures. It's been called one of the most important algorithms of the twentieth century.

The frequency resolution is the sample rate divided by N: one second of audio at forty four point one kilohertz resolves frequencies one hertz apart. F F Ts run in every phone, Wi Fi chip, M P 3 encoder and spectrum analyzer.

slides.big: LTI systems are defined by h(t). Convolution in time = multiplication in frequency. Sample above 2 f_max. Keep poles in the stable region.
say: To recap. Signals are built from steps, impulses, exponentials and sinusoids. L T I systems are completely described by their impulse response, and the output is a convolution. Fourier series and transforms reveal the frequencies inside signals, and turn convolution into multiplication. Modulation shifts spectra to share the airwaves. Sampling must be faster than twice the highest frequency, or aliasing corrupts the data. Laplace and Z transforms turn differential and difference equations into algebra, and their poles decide stability. And digital filters and the F F T bring all of this into software. Next, we design a C P U. See you there.

L20_egcp381.title: Computer Design and Organization
L20_egcp381.file: EGCP-381 Computer Architecture (VHDL Processor)/Lecture - EGCP 381 Computer Design and Organization.mp4

say: Welcome to E G C P three eighty one, computer design and organization. That's a photograph of a real processor die, an A M D Zen chip under a microscope. By the end of this lecture, you'll know what the major blocks on a chip like that do. We'll cover the instruction set as a contract between hardware and software, how a datapath executes instructions, how to measure performance, how pipelining makes processors fast and what goes wrong with it, and how caches hide slow memory. In this course's labs, students build and extend a small sixteen bit processor in V H D L, all the way to a pipelined version with hazard handling.

slides.h: The ISA: the contract between hardware and software
pts: ISA = registers, instructions, encodings, memory model
Many implementations of one ISA
RISC (ARM, RISC-V, MIPS): simple, fixed-length, load/store
CISC (x86): complex variable-length — decoded into RISC-like micro-ops
say: The instruction set architecture, or I S A, is the contract between software and hardware. It defines what a programmer or compiler can see: the registers, the instructions, how they're encoded in bits, and how memory behaves.

Underneath, the implementation, called the microarchitecture, can be anything. A tiny microcontroller and a high end desktop chip can run the same programs if they implement the same I S A, which is exactly why software doesn't need to be rewritten for every new processor.

There are two broad philosophies. RISC, reduced instruction set computers, like ARM, RISC five and MIPS, use simple, fixed length instructions, lots of registers, and only loads and stores touch memory. That makes them easy to decode and pipeline. ARM chips power nearly every phone.

CISC, complex instruction set computers, mainly x86 from Intel and A M D, have variable length instructions that can operate directly on memory. Modern x86 chips translate those instructions internally into simple, RISC like micro operations. So today, almost everything is RISC on the inside.

pts: R-type: register operands (add, sub, and)
I-type: a 16-bit immediate (loads, stores, branches)
J-type: a 26-bit jump target
Accumulator machines use one implicit register — fewer bits, more instructions
say: Every instruction is just a binary number, with fields. MIPS style instructions are thirty two bits, in three formats. R type instructions name three registers: two sources and a destination, plus a function code that picks the operation. Add t zero equals s one plus s two is R type.

I type instructions carry a sixteen bit constant, an immediate. Loads and stores use it as an offset from a base register, like load word t zero from eight bytes past the stack pointer. Branches use it as a distance from the current instruction.
J type instructions are jumps with a twenty six bit target address.

Simpler machines, like the accumulator machines in early labs, use a single implicit register, the accumulator, for every operation. Instructions get shorter, but you need more of them to do the same work. Choosing instruction formats is a constant trade off between code size, decoding simplicity and flexibility.

slides.h: Worked example: encoding an instruction by hand
pts: (code on the board) add $t0, $s1, $s2
(written on the whiteboard) R-type: op rs rt rd shamt funct
(written on the whiteboard) op = 0, rs = s1 = 17, rt = s2 = 18
(written on the whiteboard) rd = t0 = 8, shamt = 0, funct = 32
(written on the whiteboard) = 0x02324020
say: Let's turn one assembly instruction into the thirty two bits the processor actually fetches. The instruction is add t zero, s one, s two: add registers s one and s two, and put the result in t zero. Add is an R type instruction, with six fields.

Fill in the numbers. Opcode zero for all R type instructions. The source registers: s one is register seventeen, s two is eighteen. The destination t zero is register eight. Shift amount zero. And the function code for add is thirty two.

Now write each field in binary, with exactly its bit width. Zero is six zeros. Seventeen is one zero zero zero one. Eighteen is one zero zero one zero. Eight is zero one zero zero zero. Then five zeros, and thirty two is one zero zero zero zero zero.

Group the thirty two bits by fours and convert to hex: zero two three two, four zero two zero. Hex zero two three two four zero two zero is exactly what sits in memory, and the control unit decodes it by slicing out these same fields.

pts: PC → instruction memory → register file → ALU → data memory → write back
Control unit decodes the opcode into control signals
One instruction per (long) clock cycle
Clock period set by the slowest instruction (load)
say: Here's how a processor actually executes instructions. The program counter holds the address of the current instruction. Instruction memory delivers it. The register file reads the two source registers. The A L U computes, for example, a sum, or an address for a load. Data memory is read or written for loads and stores. And the result is written back to a register, the orange path.

The control unit looks at the opcode and sets the control signals: whether to write a register, whether the A L U's second input is a register or an immediate, whether to read or write memory, and so on. In a single cycle design, control is just a combinational truth table, the kind you'd write in V H D L with a case statement.
In a single cycle processor, every instruction completes in one clock cycle.

The catch: the clock period must be long enough for the slowest instruction, a load, which uses every block. Simple instructions waste most of that time. In this course's labs, students first build exactly this single cycle datapath and control, then extend it with new instructions and a register file.

pts: CPU time = instruction count × CPI × clock period
CPI: average clock cycles per instruction
A higher GHz chip can still be slower
Amdahl: speeding up 40% of the work by 10× → only 1.56× overall
say: How do you compare processors? The iron law of performance: C P U time equals the number of instructions, times the average cycles per instruction, C P I, times the clock period. All three matter.

Example: processor A runs a program in one billion instructions, at a C P I of two, with a one gigahertz clock: two seconds. Processor B needs one point two billion instructions, but has a C P I of one point two and an eight hundred megahertz clock: one point eight seconds. B is faster despite the slower clock. Megahertz alone is a terrible way to compare processors.
C P I depends on the microarchitecture, the instruction count depends on the I S A and the compiler, and the clock depends on the circuit design and technology.

And Amdahl's law, which you'll meet again in operating systems, limits every speedup. The overall speedup is one over the fraction you didn't improve, plus the fraction you did improve divided by its speedup. If you make forty percent of a program ten times faster, that's one over point six plus point four over ten, point oh four: only about one point five six times. Speed up the common case.

pts: Split execution into 5 stages: IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB
Start a new instruction every cycle
Ideal speedup ≈ number of stages
Throughput improves; one instruction’s latency doesn’t
say: In nineteen thirteen, Ford's moving assembly line cut the time to build a car from about twelve hours to about an hour and a half, not by making any single step faster, but by working on many cars at once, each at a different station. Processors do the same thing. It's called pipelining.

Think of laundry: wash, dry, fold. Done one load at a time, two loads take six steps. Pipelined, you start the second wash while the first load is drying. Each load still takes three steps, that's latency, but a load finishes every step, that's throughput.

The classic RISC pipeline has five stages: instruction fetch, instruction decode and register read, execute, memory access, and write back. Each stage is separated by pipeline registers, and a new instruction starts every cycle. In cycle five, five instructions are in flight at once, outlined in red. Ideally, the speedup equals the number of stages, because each stage can use a clock about five times shorter. In the labs, students convert their single cycle processor into a pipelined one.

pts: Next instruction needs a result that isn’t written back yet
Forwarding: route the ALU result straight back to the ALU input
Load-use hazard: data only ready after MEM → 1 stall (bubble)
Compilers reorder code to fill the gap
say: Overlapping instructions creates hazards. The most common is a data hazard. Add writes t zero, and the very next instruction, subtract, reads t zero. But add won't write its result back until the fifth stage, while subtract wants it in the third.

The fix is forwarding, also called bypassing. The result exists at the end of add's execute stage, so extra wires and multiplexers route it straight back to the A L U input for subtract, the red arrow. No waiting.

But a load is different. Its data only arrives at the end of the memory stage, one cycle too late for an immediately following instruction that uses it. That's the load use hazard, and the hardware must insert one bubble, a stall, delaying the dependent instruction by a cycle.

Good compilers reorder instructions to put something independent in that slot. In the lab on hazards, students implement forwarding and stall logic in V H D L for their pipelined processor and test it with programs that deliberately create these hazards.

slides.h: Worked example: a pipeline diagram with a load-use stall
pts: (written on the whiteboard) rows: instructions
(written on the whiteboard) columns: cycles
(written on the whiteboard) load-use: 1 stall
(written on the whiteboard) forwarding: MEM to EX
(written on the whiteboard) compiler fills the slot
say: Let's draw a pipeline diagram. Each row is an instruction, each column is a clock cycle. The load word goes through the five stages in cycles one through five.
The add needs t zero, which the load is still fetching from memory. Without hazards, add would be in its execute stage in cycle four.
And the sub follows one cycle behind. But there's a problem with the add.
The load's data only appears at the end of the memory stage, cycle four. Forwarding can't send data back in time, so the add must wait one cycle: a bubble. The sub behind it waits too.

Then forwarding carries the loaded value straight from the memory stage into the add's execute stage in cycle five, without waiting for write back. One lost cycle instead of two. And a smart compiler will try to move an independent instruction into that slot, so no cycle is lost at all.

pts: Branch outcome isn’t known until EX
Predict, keep fetching, flush if wrong
2-bit saturating counter per branch
Modern predictors: > 95% accurate
say: Branches cause control hazards. The processor doesn't know whether a branch is taken until it reaches the execute stage, but it has already fetched the next instructions by then.

Waiting would waste cycles on every branch, and roughly one in six instructions is a branch. So processors predict, keep fetching down the predicted path, and if the prediction turns out wrong, flush the wrongly fetched instructions.

A classic predictor uses a two bit saturating counter for each branch: a tiny state machine with four states. Two taken outcomes push it toward predicting taken, and it takes two surprises in a row to change its mind. That works beautifully for loops, which are taken many times and then not taken once.

Modern processors use far more elaborate predictors that learn patterns across many branches, and they're right over ninety five percent of the time. It matters for programmers too: code with unpredictable branches, like checking random data, can run several times slower than code with predictable ones.

slides.h: Putting numbers on it: CPI with hazards
pts: Ideal pipeline CPI = 1
Loads 25%, 40% followed by a use → +0.10
Branches 15%, 20% mispredicted, 2-cycle penalty → +0.06
Effective CPI = 1.16
say: Let's put numbers on hazards. An ideal pipeline finishes one instruction per cycle, a C P I of one.

Suppose twenty five percent of instructions are loads, and forty percent of those are immediately followed by an instruction that uses the loaded value. Each causes one stall. That adds point two five times point four times one, which is point one cycles per instruction.

Suppose fifteen percent of instructions are branches, the predictor is wrong twenty percent of the time, and each misprediction costs two cycles. That adds point one five times point two times two, point oh six.

So the effective C P I is one point one six. Still far better than an unpipelined design, but it shows exactly where to invest: better instruction scheduling to hide load delays, and better branch prediction.

pts: Fast memory is small and expensive; big memory is slow
DRAM ≈ 100× slower than the CPU cycle
Locality: temporal (reuse soon) + spatial (neighbors next)
Caches keep the working set close to the CPU
say: Here's a problem pipelines can't fix on their own. A processor cycle takes about a third of a nanosecond, but main memory, D RAM, takes around eighty nanoseconds to respond. If every load went to D RAM, the processor would spend almost all its time waiting.
The solution is a hierarchy. Registers are tiny and instant. Then small, fast caches built from S RAM right on the chip: level one, level two, level three. Then D RAM, then the S S D.

It works because of locality. Temporal locality: data you used recently, you'll probably use again soon, like a loop counter. Spatial locality: data near what you just used, you'll probably use next, like the next element of an array.
So caches keep recently used data, and fetch it in blocks of neighbors, typically sixty four bytes. In those die photos, a large fraction of the chip area is cache. That's how important it is.

slides.h: Worked example: average memory access time
pts: (written on the whiteboard) AMAT = hit time + miss rate times miss penalty
(written on the whiteboard) = 1 + 0.05 times 100 = 6 cycles
(written on the whiteboard) misses dominate: 6× slower than a hit!
(written on the whiteboard) add L2: hit 10 cycles, local miss rate 20%
(written on the whiteboard) L1 miss penalty = 10 + 0.2 times 100 = 30
(written on the whiteboard) AMAT = 1 + 0.05 times 30 = 2.5 cycles
say: Average memory access time is the hit time, plus the miss rate times the miss penalty. Take a cache that hits in one cycle, misses five percent of the time, and costs one hundred cycles to reach DRAM on a miss.

Six cycles on average, even though ninety five percent of accesses take one. The rare misses dominate. Now add a second level cache between them: it hits in ten cycles, and only twenty percent of the requests that reach it miss to DRAM.

The L one miss penalty becomes ten, plus point two times one hundred: thirty cycles instead of a hundred. So AMAT is one plus point zero five times thirty, two and a half cycles. More than twice as fast, by adding a cache level. That's why every modern processor has two or three levels.

pts: Address = tag | index | offset
Index picks a cache line; tag checks it’s the right block
Direct-mapped, set-associative, fully associative
AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty
say: A cache splits each memory address into three fields. The offset picks the byte within a block. With sixty four byte blocks, that's six bits.

The index picks which cache line to look in. A thirty two kilobyte cache with sixty four byte blocks has five hundred twelve lines, so nine index bits. The remaining seventeen bits are the tag, stored alongside the data and compared on every access to check that the line really holds the block you want. Match: a hit. No match: a miss, and the block is fetched from the next level.

In a direct mapped cache, each block can live in exactly one line, so two blocks that share an index keep kicking each other out. Set associative caches allow a few choices per index, and replace the least recently used one.

Performance is measured by average memory access time: hit time plus miss rate times miss penalty. With a one nanosecond hit, a five percent miss rate and a hundred nanosecond penalty, that's six nanoseconds. Cut the miss rate to two percent, and it drops to three. That's why the order in which your code walks through arrays can change its speed dramatically.

slides.h: Worked example: splitting an address for a cache
pts: (written on the whiteboard) 16 KB, direct-mapped, 64 B blocks
(written on the whiteboard) offset: 64 = 2^6 so 6 bits
(written on the whiteboard) lines: 16384 / 64 = 256 = 2^8 so 8 bits
(written on the whiteboard) tag: 32 − 8 − 6 = 18 bits
(written on the whiteboard) address 0x1234ABCD:
(written on the whiteboard) offset 13, index 175, tag 0x48D2
say: A sixteen kilobyte direct mapped cache uses sixty four byte blocks, with thirty two bit addresses. How does the cache split each address? Start at the right. The offset picks a byte inside a block. Sixty four is two to the sixth, so six offset bits.
The index picks which line of the cache. Sixteen kilobytes over sixty four bytes is two hundred fifty six lines, two to the eighth, so eight index bits.
Everything left over is the tag: thirty two minus eight minus six, eighteen bits. The tag is stored next to the data, to check that the line holds the address we want.

Try a real address: hex one two three four A B C D. The low six bits give offset thirteen. The next eight give index one seventy five. The rest is the tag, hex four eight D two. So the cache goes straight to line one seventy five, compares tags, and on a match returns byte thirteen. One lookup, no searching.

pts: Superscalar: issue several instructions per cycle
Out-of-order execution + register renaming
Multicore + cache coherence (MESI)
SIMD and GPUs: one instruction, many data
say: Real processors go much further. This is the Pentium two from nineteen ninety seven, one of the first widely used out of order x86 processors. Superscalar processors fetch and issue several instructions per cycle. Out of order execution lets later, independent instructions run while an earlier one waits for memory, with register renaming removing false dependencies, and a reorder buffer making sure results still appear in program order.

Today's chips, like this A M D Zen design, put several such cores on one die. Each core has private caches, so the hardware must keep them consistent with a coherence protocol such as MESI, which tracks whether each cache line is modified, exclusive, shared or invalid. And SIMD instructions and G P Us apply one instruction to many data elements at once, which is what makes graphics and machine learning fast. All of it is built on the ideas in this course: datapaths, pipelines, hazards and caches.

slides.big: Time = instructions × CPI × period. Pipelines overlap work; forwarding, stalls and prediction handle hazards; caches hide slow memory.
say: To recap. The I S A is the contract between software and hardware, and many implementations can share one I S A. A datapath fetches, decodes, executes, accesses memory and writes back, under the direction of a control unit. Performance is instruction count times C P I times clock period. Pipelining overlaps instructions for throughput, and hazards are handled with forwarding, stalls and branch prediction. And the memory hierarchy, with caches exploiting locality, hides the enormous gap between processor and memory speeds. Next, operating systems. See you there.

L21_cpsc351.title: Operating Systems Concepts
L21_cpsc351.file: CPSC-351 Operating Systems/Lecture - CPSC 351 Operating Systems Concepts.mp4

say: Welcome to C P S C three fifty one, operating systems. The operating system is the program that runs all other programs. Whether it's Linux, mascotted by this penguin, Windows, mac O S, Android or the tiny real time kernels in embedded devices, every O S solves the same problems: sharing one machine among many programs, safely and efficiently. In this lecture we'll cover processes and threads, scheduling, synchronization and deadlock, and virtual memory, with the C and POSIX examples this course uses on Linux.

pts: Resource manager: CPU, memory, storage, devices
Abstraction: files, processes, sockets
Protection: user mode vs kernel mode
System calls are the only door into the kernel
say: In nineteen sixty nine, Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie, pictured here, began writing Unix at Bell Labs, and soon rewrote it in the new C language they created for the purpose. Its ideas, processes, files and a small set of system calls, live on in Linux, mac O S, Android and i O S.

An operating system does three jobs. It manages resources: deciding which program gets the C P U, how memory is divided, and who can use the disk and network. It provides abstractions: instead of disk sectors you get files, instead of a raw C P U you get processes. And it protects programs from each other. The processor itself enforces this with two modes. Applications run in user mode, unable to touch hardware directly. The kernel runs in kernel mode. The only way across is a system call, like open, read or fork, which traps into the kernel, does the privileged work, and returns.

pts: Process = program in execution + its own address space
PCB: PID, state, registers, PC, memory map, open files
Context switch: save one PCB, load another
Unix: fork() clones · exec() replaces · wait() reaps
say: A process is a program in execution: its code, data, heap and stack, plus the kernel's bookkeeping record, the process control block, which holds its I D, state, saved registers, program counter, memory map and open files. A process moves through states. It's admitted as ready, gets scheduled to running, and goes back to ready when its time slice expires. If it starts a disk read or waits for input, it moves to waiting, and when the I O completes, back to ready. Switching the C P U from one process to another is a context switch: save one P C B, load another. It's pure overhead, so schedulers try not to do it too often.

On Unix, new processes are made with fork, which clones the calling process. Fork returns twice: zero in the child, and the child's I D in the parent. The child usually calls exec, which replaces its program with a new one, and the parent calls wait to collect the child's exit status. If the parent never waits, the finished child lingers as a zombie. Every time you type a command in a shell, this is exactly what happens. In this course, students write a time utility this way: fork a child, exec a command, and measure how long it takes.

slides.h: Worked example: creating a process with fork()
pts: (code on the board) int main(void) {
(code on the board)   pid_t pid = fork();
(code on the board)   if (pid == 0) {
(code on the board)     printf("child: my pid is %d\n", getpid());
(code on the board)   } else {
(code on the board)     wait(NULL);           // block until the child exits
(code on the board)     printf("parent: child %d done\n", pid);
(code on the board)   }
(code on the board) }
(program output) $ ./forkdemo
(program output) child: my pid is 4012
(program output) parent: child 4012 done
(written on the whiteboard) shell = fork + exec + wait
say: Here's how every Unix program starts another process. Call fork. It creates an almost exact copy of the running process. Both copies continue from the very next line.
The only difference is fork's return value. In the child it returns zero. In the parent it returns the child's process I D. So one if statement splits the two paths.

The parent calls wait, so it blocks until the child finishes. That guarantees the order of the output: the child's line, then the parent's. Without wait, the two lines could come out in either order, depending on the scheduler. A shell runs every command you type with exactly this pattern: fork, then exec in the child, then wait in the parent.

pts: Threads share code, heap and files; each has its own stack
Cheaper to create & switch than processes
pthread_create / pthread_join
Amdahl’s law caps the speedup
say: A thread is a lighter unit of execution inside a process. Threads share the process's code, global data, heap and open files, but each has its own stack and registers. They're cheap to create and switch, and on a multicore C P U, they truly run at the same time. In C on Linux, you create them with p thread create and wait for them with p thread join. A classic course exercise: two worker threads each sort half of an array, and a third thread merges the results.

But parallelism has limits, captured by Amdahl's law. If a fraction S of a program is inherently serial, the speedup on N cores is at most one over S plus one minus S over N. With ten percent serial code, even infinitely many cores give at most a ten times speedup. With half the program serial, you never get past two times. So the serial parts, often the parts protected by locks, end up dominating.

pts: FCFS: simple, but short jobs wait behind long ones
SJF: optimal average wait (needs burst estimates)
Round robin: time slices → responsive
Real OSes: multilevel feedback queues + priorities
say: When several processes are ready, the scheduler picks which runs next. First come, first served is simplest. But look what happens when a twenty four millisecond job arrives just before two three millisecond jobs. The waits are zero, twenty four and twenty seven milliseconds, an average of seventeen. The short jobs are stuck behind the long one, called the convoy effect.

Run the shortest job first, and the waits become zero, three and six: an average of three milliseconds, for exactly the same work. Shortest job first is provably optimal for average waiting time, but the O S can't know the future, so real systems estimate burst lengths from past behavior.

Round robin gives each ready process a short time slice in turn, which keeps interactive programs responsive. A tiny slice means lots of context switches. A huge one turns back into first come, first served.

Real operating systems combine these ideas with priorities and multilevel feedback queues: interactive tasks that block often stay at high priority, while long C P U bound jobs drift down. Priorities need aging, so low priority tasks don't starve forever.

slides.h: Worked example: three schedulers, one workload
pts: (written on the whiteboard) P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3 ms
(written on the whiteboard) FCFS: (0 + 24 + 27)/3 = 17
(written on the whiteboard) SJF: (0 + 3 + 6)/3 = 3
(written on the whiteboard) RR: (6 + 4 + 7)/3 ≈ 5.7
say: Three processes arrive at time zero: P one needs twenty four milliseconds of CPU, P two and P three need three each. First come, first served runs them in arrival order. P one waits zero, P two waits twenty four, P three waits twenty seven. Average: seventeen milliseconds.

Shortest job first runs the short ones first. Waits: zero, three and six. Average: three milliseconds. Same work, almost six times less waiting. That's why shortest job first is provably optimal for average wait.

But the OS can't know the future. Round robin with a four millisecond slice gives each process a turn. P one runs four, P two finishes at seven, P three at ten, then P one gets the rest. Average wait: about five point seven. Nearly as good, and nobody is stuck behind a long job, which is why interactive systems use time slices.

pts: count++ is really load → add → store
Interleaving can lose updates
Critical section: one thread at a time
Mutex lock / unlock around shared data
say: Here's the bug that makes concurrent programming hard. Count plus plus looks like one step, but the machine does three: load count into a register, add one, store it back.

Suppose count is five, and two threads increment it. Thread one loads five. Before it stores, thread two also loads five. Both add one, and both store six. Two increments happened, but count is six, not seven. The result depends on timing, which is called a race condition. It might work perfectly a million times and fail on the million and first.
The fix is to make the read modify write a critical section, a region of code only one thread may execute at a time.

The standard tool is a mutex lock: lock before touching the shared data, unlock after. In this course, students make a linked list stack thread safe exactly this way. Semaphores, condition variables and monitors build on the same idea, and solve classic problems like the bounded buffer between a producer and a consumer.

slides.h: Worked example: losing an update, then fixing it
pts: (code on the board) count++;   =>   reg = count;  reg = reg + 1;  count = reg;
(code on the board) T1: reg1 = count      // 5
(code on the board) T2: reg2 = count      // 5   (switched in!)
(code on the board) T2: count = reg2 + 1  // 6
(code on the board) T1: count = reg1 + 1  // 6   <- T2's update is lost
(code on the board) pthread_mutex_lock(&m);
(code on the board) count++;                 // critical section
(code on the board) pthread_mutex_unlock(&m);
(written on the whiteboard) T2 waits at lock → loads 6 → stores 7
(written on the whiteboard) keep critical sections SHORT
say: Let's trace the lost update one machine step at a time, because seeing it written out is what makes it click. Count starts at five. Each thread's count plus plus is really three steps: load, add, store.

Thread one loads five into its register. Then the scheduler switches. Thread two loads count, still five. Thread two adds one and stores six. Back to thread one: it adds one to its own copy, five, and stores six too.
Two increments, and count went up by one. The fix: wrap the read, modify, write in a mutex. Lock, increment, unlock.

Now if thread two tries to lock while thread one holds the mutex, thread two simply waits. Thread one finishes all three steps, unlocks, and only then does thread two load count, which is now six. The answer is seven, every time. Keep critical sections as short as possible, because every thread waiting on a lock is a thread not running in parallel.

pts: Four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait
Break any one → no deadlock
Simplest: global lock ordering
Classic puzzle: the dining philosophers
say: Locks bring a new danger. Thread one holds lock A and waits for lock B. Thread two holds lock B and waits for lock A. Neither can proceed, ever. That's deadlock. It requires four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, holding while waiting, no forced preemption, and a circular wait. Break any one and deadlock is impossible. The most practical fix is to break circular wait: assign every lock a global order, and always acquire locks in that order. If everyone takes A before B, the cycle can't form.

The classic illustration is the dining philosophers. Five philosophers sit around a table with one fork between each pair, and each needs both neighboring forks to eat. If everyone picks up their left fork at the same moment, everyone waits for the right fork forever. Ordering the forks, or allowing at most four to sit down at once, solves it. Operating systems mostly prevent deadlock by design and leave detection to tools, because full deadlock avoidance algorithms, like the Banker's algorithm, are too expensive to run all the time.

pts: Every process sees its own private address space
Address = page number + offset (4 KB pages)
Page table maps pages → physical frames
TLB caches recent translations
say: Every process believes it has a huge private memory starting at address zero. That's virtual memory, and it's one of the most important ideas in computing.

Memory is divided into fixed size pages, typically four kilobytes. A virtual address splits into a page number and an offset within the page. With four kilobyte pages, the low twelve bits are the offset. Here, hex one A two B is page one, offset A two B.

The page table, maintained by the O S, maps each virtual page to a physical frame. Page one maps to frame four, so the physical address is hex four A two B. The hardware memory management unit does this translation on every single access.

Because looking up the page table would double every memory access, the processor caches recent translations in a translation lookaside buffer, the T L B. Virtual memory gives each process isolation, since it can't even name another process's memory, and it lets the O S load only the pages a program actually uses.

slides.h: Worked example: translating a virtual address
pts: (written on the whiteboard) 4 KB page = 2^12: 12-bit offset
(written on the whiteboard) 0x3A7F: page 3, offset 0xA7F
(written on the whiteboard) page table[3] = frame 7
(written on the whiteboard) physical = 0x7A7F
say: A small system uses sixteen bit virtual addresses and four kilobyte pages. Four K is two to the twelfth, so the low twelve bits are the offset within a page, and the top four bits are the page number. Translate hex three A seven F. Each hex digit is four bits, so the page is three and the offset is A seven F.
Look up page three in this process's page table. It says page three lives in physical frame seven.

The offset never changes. Glue frame seven onto offset A seven F: the physical address is hex seven A seven F. Another process could use the same virtual address three A seven F and land in a completely different frame. That's how processes are isolated from each other, and the T L B caches these lookups so they cost almost nothing.

pts: Page not in RAM → page fault → load it from disk
Memory full → evict a page (LRU ≈ best practical)
FIFO can suffer Belady’s anomaly
Too little RAM → thrashing
say: If a program touches a page that isn't currently in memory, the hardware raises a page fault. The O S finds a free frame, loads the page from disk, updates the page table, and restarts the instruction. The program never knows. This is demand paging.

When memory is full, the O S must evict a page. The optimal choice is the page that won't be needed for the longest time, but that requires knowing the future. Least recently used is an excellent approximation, and real systems use cheap versions of it, like the clock algorithm.

Simple first in, first out replacement has a strange flaw called Belady's anomaly: for some access patterns, giving it more memory produces more page faults. In this course, students analyze a virtual memory simulation where doubling physical memory cut page faults from five hundred thirty nine to two hundred forty four.

But starve a system of memory, and it thrashes: the working sets of the running programs don't fit, so it spends almost all its time moving pages to and from disk, and almost none doing useful work. The cure is more memory, or running fewer programs at once.

slides.h: Worked example: LRU page replacement, step by step
pts: (written on the whiteboard) 3 frames
(written on the whiteboard) refs: 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4
(written on the whiteboard) LRU: 6 faults
(written on the whiteboard) FIFO: 7 faults
say: Three frames of RAM, and the program touches pages seven, zero, one, two, zero, three, zero, four. Let's run least recently used. The first three references fill empty frames: three page faults. Then page two arrives. Memory is full, so we evict the page used longest ago, seven. Four faults.
Page zero is already in memory: a hit. Then page three. The least recently used page is now one, so one goes. Five faults.
Zero: another hit. Then four replaces two, the least recently used. Six faults in total.

First in, first out ignores recent use. It throws out zero just before zero is needed again, and ends with seven faults. Every fault costs a disk access, millions of times slower than RAM, so a smarter policy pays off enormously.

slides.h: Storage, files and the rest of the OS
pts: Files & directories; inodes point to data blocks
Free-space management, journaling for crash safety
Disk scheduling: SCAN (elevator); SSDs: wear leveling, TRIM
RAID 0 (stripe) · 1 (mirror) · 5 (striped parity)
IPC: shared memory (fast) vs message passing (simple, networkable)
say: A few more pieces complete the picture. File systems organize disk blocks into files and directories. On Unix style systems, an inode records each file's metadata and points to its data blocks.
The file system tracks free space, and modern ones keep a journal, logging changes before making them, so a crash can't leave the disk inconsistent.

For spinning disks, the O S reorders requests to reduce head movement, for example the elevator algorithm. S S Ds have no moving parts, but their flash cells wear out, so they spread writes around, called wear leveling, and the O S tells them which blocks are free with the TRIM command.
RAID combines disks: level zero stripes data for speed, level one mirrors it for safety, level five stripes with parity so any single disk can fail without losing data.

And processes communicate either through shared memory, which is fast but needs synchronization, or by message passing through pipes, queues and sockets, which is simpler and works across machines. Choosing between them for a mission critical system is a classic design question in this course.

slides.big: The OS shares one machine safely: processes & threads for the CPU, locks for shared data, virtual memory for isolation.
say: To recap. The operating system is a resource manager, an abstraction layer and a protector, entered only through system calls. Processes are isolated programs in execution, created with fork, exec and wait. Threads share a process and run in parallel, limited by Amdahl's law. Schedulers trade off average wait, fairness and responsiveness. Shared data needs locks to avoid races, and lock ordering avoids deadlock. And virtual memory gives each process a private address space, with paging, the T L B and page replacement making it efficient. Next, software engineering. See you there.

L22_cpsc362.title: Foundations of Software Engineering
L22_cpsc362.file: CPSC-362 Software Engineering/Lecture - CPSC 362 Foundations of Software Engineering.mp4

say: Welcome to C P S C three sixty two, foundations of software engineering. That's Margaret Hamilton in nineteen sixty nine, standing next to printouts of the Apollo guidance software her team at M I T wrote. She popularized the term software engineering, insisting that building software deserved the same discipline as building bridges. This course is about that discipline: how teams decide what to build, design it, test it and deliver it, reliably, again and again.

pts: Most failures: wrong requirements, poor communication, unmanaged change
Ariane 5 (1996): reused code overflowed → rocket lost
Defects cost far more to fix the later they’re found
Build the right thing, reliably, as a team
