say: Most software failures aren't caused by someone forgetting a semicolon. They come from building the wrong thing, from teams misunderstanding each other, and from changes nobody tracked. A famous example is the first flight of the Ariane five rocket in nineteen ninety six. Its guidance code was reused from the smaller Ariane four. On the new rocket's faster trajectory, a sixty four bit floating point value was converted into a sixteen bit integer and overflowed. The software shut down, and the rocket broke apart about forty seconds after launch. The code had been tested, but against the old rocket's requirements.

The economics push the same way. A mistake caught while writing requirements costs almost nothing to fix. The same mistake found after release can cost a hundred times more, because by then it's tangled into the design, the code, the tests, the documentation and the users' data. So software engineering puts heavy effort into the early stages: understanding the problem, communicating clearly, and catching defects as early as possible.

pts: Waterfall: phases in order — clear, but rigid
Agile/Scrum: 1–4 week sprints, working software each time
Roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master, team
Backlog, daily stand-up, sprint review, retrospective
say: A process model describes how a team moves from idea to product. The classic waterfall model runs each phase once, in order: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment. It's easy to plan and works when requirements are stable, as in some aerospace or medical projects. But if you discover in testing that the requirements were wrong, going back upstream is very expensive. Agile methods instead deliver in short loops. In Scrum, the most common one, work happens in sprints of one to four weeks. Each sprint the team picks items from a prioritized product backlog, builds them, demonstrates working software at a sprint review, and then holds a retrospective to improve how it works.

The product owner decides what matters most, the scrum master removes obstacles, and the team meets briefly every day in a stand up. Progress is often tracked on a board like this, with columns such as to do, in progress and done. Kanban uses the same kind of board and limits how much work is in progress at once. In this course, students work in teams through several sprints to build a complete mobile app, writing the sprint documents along the way.

slides.h: Requirements: user stories and use cases
pts: Functional (what it does) vs non-functional (speed, security, usability)
User story: As a… I want… so that…
Acceptance criteria make it testable
Use case: actor, main flow, alternate flows
say: Requirements come in two kinds. Functional requirements say what the system does: log a workout, sign in with Google. Non functional requirements say how well: it must load in under two seconds, protect personal data, and be usable one handed. Agile teams capture functional requirements as user stories in a simple template: as a gym member, I want to log a workout in under thirty seconds, so that I keep a streak without breaking my routine. The so that part matters, because it explains the value. Acceptance criteria then make the story testable: saving takes at most three taps, it works offline, and the streak updates immediately. Good stories follow INVEST: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small and testable.

Use cases add more detail. A use case diagram shows the actors outside the system, here a member and the Google sign in service, and the goals they accomplish inside it. Each use case is then written out with preconditions, the main success scenario step by step, and alternate flows for errors, like what happens when there's no network.

slides.h: Worked example: turning a wish into a testable requirement
pts: (written on the whiteboard) "The arm should respond quickly."
(written on the whiteboard) ✗ untestable: how fast? measured how?
(written on the whiteboard) "The arm shall begin moving within 500 ms
(written on the whiteboard) of a recognized voice command,
(written on the whiteboard) in at least 95 of 100 trials."
(written on the whiteboard) As a user with limited hand mobility,
(written on the whiteboard) I want to say "pick up the cup",
(written on the whiteboard) so that I can drink without help.
(written on the whiteboard) GIVEN the cup is in view and within reach
(written on the whiteboard) WHEN the user says "pick up the cup"
(written on the whiteboard) THEN the arm grasps it and lifts 5 cm, no spill
say: Here's a requirement from a real first draft: the robot arm should respond quickly. It sounds fine, but it can't be tested. Quickly compared to what? Measured how? Let's fix it.

A testable requirement names a measurable quantity, a limit, and how it will be checked. The arm shall begin moving within five hundred milliseconds of a recognized voice command, in at least ninety five of one hundred trials.
The same need, written as a user story: as a user with limited hand mobility, I want to say pick up the cup, so that I can drink without help. The story explains who and why.

And acceptance criteria make the story testable. Given the cup is within reach and in view, when the user says pick up the cup, then the arm grasps it and lifts it five centimeters without spilling. At the end of the project, these sentences become your test plan.

pts: Class diagram: classes, attributes, methods, relationships
Multiplicity: 1, 0..*, 1..*
Composition ◆ · aggregation ◇ · inheritance △
Sequence diagram: messages between objects over time
say: The unified modeling language, UML, is the standard notation for software design. A class diagram shows classes with their attributes and methods, and how they relate. Here, one user has zero or more workouts, written one to zero dot dot star. A workout is composed of one or more exercises, shown with a filled diamond: composition means the exercises don't exist without their workout, so deleting the workout deletes them. A hollow diamond, aggregation, would mean the parts can live on their own. And the hollow triangle is inheritance, from object oriented programming: a run is a kind of workout, with its own way of computing calories.

A sequence diagram shows one scenario over time. Objects run across the top, time flows downward, and arrows are messages. The member taps sign in, the login screen calls the auth service, which sends an OAuth request to Google, gets a token back, returns the user's profile, and the screen shows the dashboard. Dashed arrows are returns. Sequence diagrams are great for finding missing steps before writing code. Activity diagrams and state machine diagrams, the same finite state machines from digital logic, complete the toolkit.

slides.h: Worked example: drawing a class diagram
pts: (written on the whiteboard) nouns: member, book, loan
(written on the whiteboard) − private,  + public
(written on the whiteboard) member: 0..5 loans
(written on the whiteboard) book: 0..* loans over time
(written on the whiteboard) rules visible before code
say: Let's model a library system. Start with the nouns from the requirements: member, book, and loan. A Member class has a private name and I D, written with a minus sign, and a public borrow method, written with a plus.
A Book has a title and an I S B N, and can report whether it's available.
A Loan connects one member to one book, with a due date. Now the multiplicities. Each member can hold zero to five loans at a time. Each book can appear in many loans over its lifetime, zero or more.

Notice what the diagram just did: the rule maximum five books per member is now visible to everyone, before any code is written. That's the point of UML: catching design decisions while they're still cheap to change.

pts: High cohesion: each module does one job
Low coupling: modules depend on each other little
SOLID, information hiding, separation of concerns
Architectures: layered, client–server, MVC/MVVM, microservices
say: Two words summarize good design: cohesion and coupling. A cohesive module does one well defined job. Loosely coupled modules know as little about each other as possible, so you can change one without breaking the others. On the left, everything talks to everything, so any change ripples everywhere. On the right, the user interface, the logic and the data are separate, with narrow, defined connections. The SOLID principles, starting with single responsibility, are a checklist for achieving exactly this.

At a larger scale, an architecture organizes the whole system. Most mobile and web apps follow model view controller or its cousin, model view view model, which Android recommends. The view only displays and collects input. The controller or view model handles the user's actions. The model holds the data and the business rules, and notifies the view when data changes, using the observer pattern. Design patterns like observer, factory, strategy and adapter are named, reusable solutions to recurring design problems, so a team can say use a strategy here and everyone understands.

pts: Unit → integration → system → acceptance
Many fast unit tests, fewer slow end-to-end tests
Black-box: equivalence classes, boundary values
Regression tests stop old bugs coming back
say: Testing happens at several levels. Unit tests check a single function or class in isolation. Integration tests check that modules work together. System tests check the whole application, and acceptance tests check that it meets the user's actual needs, often written straight from the acceptance criteria. The testing pyramid says to write many fast unit tests and fewer slow end to end tests, because fast tests get run constantly and catch problems within minutes. For choosing test inputs, black box techniques work from the specification. Equivalence partitioning groups inputs that should behave the same, and boundary value analysis tests the edges, where bugs love to hide. If ages from thirteen to one hundred twenty are allowed, test twelve, thirteen, one hundred twenty and one hundred twenty one. White box testing instead looks at the code and aims to cover its branches. And whenever a bug is fixed, add a regression test, so it can never quietly return.

slides.h: Worked example: boundary-value tests catch a real bug
pts: (code on the board) bool IsValidAge(int age) {
(code on the board)   return age > 18 && age <= 65;
(code on the board) }
(written on the whiteboard) test: 17, 18, 40, 65, 66
(code on the board) for (int a : {17, 18, 40, 65, 66})
(code on the board)   std::cout << a << ": " << IsValidAge(a) << "\n";
(program output) 17: 0
(program output) 18: 0    <- should be 1!
(program output) 40: 1
(program output) 65: 1
(program output) 66: 0
(code on the board)   return age >= 18 && age <= 65;   // fixed
(written on the whiteboard) test the edges: 17 | 18 ... 65 | 66
say: The requirement says: ages eighteen through sixty five are valid. Here's an implementation. Look carefully, and see if you can spot the bug before the tests do.
Bugs cluster at boundaries, so boundary value analysis tests just below, on, and just above each edge: seventeen, eighteen, sixty five and sixty six, plus one ordinary value, forty.
Run it. Seventeen is invalid: correct. But eighteen also says invalid! The code wrote greater than, where the requirement means greater than or equal. Forty, sixty five and sixty six are all correct.

Change one character, greater than to greater than or equal, rerun, and all five pass. A random test like twenty five would never have found this. Testing the edges is the cheapest bug hunting there is.

slides.h: Version control, code review and CI
pts: Git: every change recorded, every version recoverable
Feature branches keep main working
Pull requests: code review before merging
Continuous integration runs the tests on every push
say: Teams can't work on the same code without version control. Git records every change, who made it and why, and lets you recover any earlier version.
Developers work on feature branches, so the main branch always stays in a working state. Here, a meal logging feature gets its own branch with several commits.

When it's ready, the developer opens a pull request. Teammates review the code, ask questions and suggest improvements before it's merged. Code review catches bugs, and just as importantly, spreads knowledge across the team.

Continuous integration servers automatically build the project and run the whole test suite on every push, so a broken change is flagged within minutes, while it's still fresh in the author's mind. This is how nearly every professional software team works today.

slides.h: Worked example: a feature-branch workflow in git
pts: (program output) $ git switch -c feature/voice-cmd
(program output) $ git add speech.py
(program output) $ git commit -m "Map 'pick up' to grasp action"
(program output) $ git push -u origin feature/voice-cmd
(written on the whiteboard) pull request: review + CI tests
(program output) $ git log --oneline   # full history
say: Here's the everyday git workflow. The main branch always works. To add a feature, first make a branch.
Work in small steps. After each one, stage the changed files and commit with a message that says why, not just what.

Push the branch and open a pull request. A teammate reviews the code, and continuous integration runs every test automatically. Only when both pass does the branch merge into main. If something breaks, git log and git revert can undo any single change.

pts: Break work down: epics → stories → tasks
Agile: story points and team velocity
Traditional: Gantt charts, critical path, COCOMO
Risk table: probability × impact → mitigation plan
say: Finally, planning. Large goals are broken into epics, epics into user stories, and stories into concrete tasks.

Agile teams estimate stories in relative units called story points, then measure velocity, how many points the team actually completes per sprint. After a few sprints, velocity predicts the future far better than optimism does.
Traditional projects use Gantt charts and critical path analysis to find the chain of tasks that determines the end date, and models like COCOMO estimate effort from the expected size of the code.

And every project keeps a risk table: for each risk, estimate its probability and its impact, multiply them to rank the risks, and plan mitigations for the top ones. A third party API changing, a key team member getting sick, or an app store review delay are classic risks for a mobile project.

slides.h: Worked example: velocity, critical path and risk
pts: (written on the whiteboard) backlog: 120 points
(written on the whiteboard) velocity ≈ (18 + 22 + 20) / 3 = 20
(written on the whiteboard) 120 / 20 = 6 sprints ≈ 12 weeks
(written on the whiteboard) A→B→D = 3 + 5 + 2 = 10 days
(written on the whiteboard) A→C→D = 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 days
(written on the whiteboard) longest path = the earliest finish
(written on the whiteboard) risk exposure = probability × impact
(written on the whiteboard) 0.3 × 10 days = 3 days
say: Let's put real numbers on planning. The backlog holds one hundred twenty story points. The team finished eighteen, twenty two and twenty points in its first three sprints, so its velocity is about twenty. One hundred twenty over twenty is six more sprints. With two week sprints, that's about twelve weeks. Velocity is measured, not hoped for.
Now a dependency chart. Task A takes three days. B and C can start after A. D needs both. Each path from start to finish adds up: A, B, D is ten days. A, C, D is seven.

The longest path is the critical path: it sets the earliest possible finish, ten days. Any delay on A, B or D delays the whole project. C has three days of slack, so it can slip without hurting anything. That tells a manager exactly where to put the best people.

And risk exposure is probability times impact. If there's a thirty percent chance the Google sign in A P I changes, costing ten days, the expected cost is three days. Rank every risk that way, and mitigate the top few first.

slides.big: Build the right thing, reliably, as a team: clear requirements, simple loosely-coupled designs, tests at every level, and short feedback loops.
say: To recap. Software engineering exists because most failures come from requirements, communication and change, and because defects get far more expensive the later they're found. Agile processes deliver working software in short sprints. User stories, acceptance criteria and use cases pin down requirements. UML class and sequence diagrams communicate designs. Good designs have high cohesion and low coupling. Testing happens at every level, and version control, code review and continuous integration keep a team's work safe. Next, databases. See you there.

L23_cpsc332.title: File Structures & Database Systems
L23_cpsc332.file: CPSC-332 Database Systems/Lecture - CPSC 332 File Structures & Database Systems.mp4

say: Welcome to C P S C three thirty two, file structures and database systems. Almost every app you use, from banking to social media to the university's class registration, is a user interface sitting on top of a database. In this lecture you'll learn how to model data, how relational tables and SQL work, how to design tables that can't contradict themselves, and how databases stay fast and correct when thousands of people use them at once.

pts: Separate files → redundancy and inconsistency
DBMS: one schema, declarative queries
Integrity constraints, concurrent access, crash recovery
Security: who may see and change what
say: This is the I B M three fifty RAMAC from nineteen fifty six, the first commercial hard disk drive: fifty spinning platters storing about five megabytes. Random access storage made it possible to look up any record directly, and the question quickly became how to organize that data well.

Without a database, each program keeps its own files. Payroll has one copy of an employee's details, H R another, the badge system a third. Soon the same person has three different phone numbers, and nobody knows which is right. A database management system stores each fact once, in one schema shared by all programs. You ask questions declaratively, saying what you want rather than how to find it. And the D B M S enforces rules, lets many users work at the same time without corrupting data, recovers after crashes, and controls who can see what.

pts: Entities (rectangles) with attributes (ovals)
Key attribute underlined: uniquely identifies
Relationships (diamonds) with cardinality 1:1, 1:N, M:N
Relationships can have attributes (grade)
say: Before creating tables, designers draw an entity relationship diagram. Entities are the things you store data about, drawn as rectangles: students and courses.
Their attributes are drawn as ovals. The key attribute, underlined, uniquely identifies each entity: a student I D, a course I D.

Relationships are diamonds. A student enrolls in courses. The cardinality says how many: one to one, one to many, or many to many. Here it's many to many, since each student takes many courses and each course has many students.

Notice that grade belongs to the relationship, not to either entity. It's not a property of a student or of a course, but of one student taking one course. That observation tells us exactly how to build the tables.

slides.h: The relational model: tables and keys
pts: Relation = table of rows (tuples) and columns
Primary key: unique, never NULL
Foreign key: refers to a primary key elsewhere
M:N relationship → its own table
say: In the relational model, invented by Edgar Codd at I B M in nineteen seventy, all data lives in tables, formally called relations. Each row is one record and each column one attribute. Every table has a primary key, a column or set of columns that's unique and never empty, like the student I D. Mapping our E R diagram is mechanical. Each entity becomes a table. The many to many relationship becomes its own table, enrolls, whose columns are foreign keys pointing to a student and a course, plus the grade. Its primary key is the pair: student I D and course I D together. Foreign keys enforce referential integrity: the database refuses an enrollment for a student who doesn't exist, and you choose what happens when a referenced row is deleted, for example cascading the delete or blocking it. For a one to many relationship, there's no extra table: just put a foreign key on the many side, like a department number in each employee row.

slides.h: Relational algebra: the math under SQL
pts: σ select rows · π project columns
⋈ join tables on matching values
Set operations ∪, −, ∩
The optimizer rewrites SQL into algebra plans
say: Under SQL sits relational algebra, a small set of operations on tables, each producing another table. Selection, sigma, keeps the rows that satisfy a condition. Projection, pi, keeps chosen columns.
Join, the bowtie symbol, combines rows from two tables whose values match, like each employee with their department.
And the set operations from discrete math, union, difference and intersection, combine tables with the same columns.

Because these operations have algebraic laws, such as filtering before joining gives the same answer as joining before filtering, the database's query optimizer can rewrite your query into a much faster equivalent plan. That's why you can write SQL declaratively and still get good performance.

slides.code:
SELECT d.Dname, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(e.Salary) AS avg_sal
FROM Employee e
  JOIN Department d ON e.Dno = d.Dnumber
WHERE e.Salary > 50000
GROUP BY d.Dname
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC;
say: Here's a typical SQL query. Read it in the order the database logically evaluates it. From the employee table, join each employee to their department where the department numbers match.
WHERE filters individual rows first, before any grouping.

GROUP BY collapses the remaining rows into one group per department, and aggregate functions like count and average summarize each group. HAVING then filters whole groups, keeping only departments with more than two qualifying employees. That's the key difference: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after.
Finally, SELECT picks the output columns and ORDER BY sorts them, highest average salary first.

slides.h: Running the query on real rows
pts: WHERE drops Gus (45,000)
GROUP BY → one row per department
HAVING keeps groups with > 2 rows
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC
say: Let's run it on seven employees. WHERE removes Gus, who earns forty five thousand. Grouping leaves Engineering with Ana, Ben and Chen, averaging ninety five thousand, and Sales with Dev, Eli and Fay, averaging about sixty thousand six hundred sixty seven. Both have three employees, so both pass the HAVING test, and sorting puts Engineering first. Support disappears completely, because its only employee was filtered out before grouping. Tracing a query on a handful of rows like this is the best way to check that it means what you think it means.

pts: INNER: only matching rows
LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER: keep unmatched rows, fill with NULL
NULL = unknown: use IS NULL, not = NULL
EXISTS, IN, window functions, recursive CTEs
say: Joins come in flavors. An inner join keeps only rows that match in both tables: employees who have a department.

A left outer join keeps every row from the left table, filling the right side's columns with NULL where there's no match: every department, even one with no employees. Right and full outer joins work the same way for the other side, or both sides.

NULL means unknown, and it's tricky. Any comparison with NULL is neither true nor false but unknown, so WHERE phone equals NULL never matches anything. You must write IS NULL. NULLs also catch people in aggregates. COUNT star counts every row, but COUNT of a column skips the NULLs, and AVG ignores them too. So if three of ten employees have no bonus recorded, COUNT star is ten, COUNT bonus is seven, and the average bonus is over those seven only.

SQL goes much further: subqueries with EXISTS and IN, set operations, window functions like ROW NUMBER and RANK that compute per row rankings or running totals without collapsing groups, and recursive common table expressions that can walk hierarchies like an org chart or a graph. In this course's assignments, students write self joins, ranking queries with window functions, and even a breadth first search over a tree table.

slides.h: Worked example: a join, row by row
pts: (code on the board) SELECT o.order_id, c.name, p.name, p.price
(code on the board) FROM Orders o
(code on the board) JOIN Customers c ON o.cust_id = c.cust_id
(code on the board) JOIN Products  p ON o.prod_id = p.prod_id
(written on the whiteboard) order 1: C1 → Ana, P1 → Arduino 25
(written on the whiteboard) order 2: C1 → Ana, P2 → Servo 12
(written on the whiteboard) order 3: C2 → Ben, P1 → Arduino 25
(code on the board) WHERE p.price > 20
(code on the board) ORDER BY c.name;
(program output) order_id | name | name    | price
(program output) 1        | Ana  | Arduino | 25
(program output) 3        | Ben  | Arduino | 25
say: Using our normalized tables, let's list each order with the customer's name and the product's price. That data lives in three tables, so we join them on matching keys.

Read the joins like this: for each order, find the customer whose I D matches the order's customer I D, and the product whose I D matches. Each order row picks up exactly one customer and one product.
Add a WHERE clause to filter, for example only products costing more than twenty, and an ORDER BY to sort. The database decides the fastest way to do this; we only describe what we want.

pts: Functional dependency X → Y: X determines Y
1NF: atomic values · 2NF: no partial dependency on the key
3NF: no transitive dependency · BCNF: every determinant is a key
Avoid update, insert and delete anomalies
say: Normalization is a systematic way to design tables that can't contradict themselves. It's built on functional dependencies: X determines Y means that whenever two rows agree on X, they must agree on Y. A student I D determines the student's name.

Look at the red table. Its key is student I D plus course I D. But name depends only on the student I D, and title only on the course I D. Those are partial dependencies, which violates second normal form. The symptoms: Ana's name is stored twice, so an update could change one copy and not the other, and you can't even add a new course until someone enrolls in it.

The fix is to decompose: a student table, a course table, and an enrollment table holding only the grade. Third normal form goes further and removes transitive dependencies, where a non key column depends on another non key column, like a department name depending on a department I D stored in a course row. Boyce Codd normal form requires every determinant to be a key.

The decomposition must be lossless: joining the tables back together must reproduce exactly the original data. Designers sometimes denormalize on purpose for read speed, but they do it knowingly, accepting the cost of keeping copies in sync.

slides.h: Worked example: normalizing an orders table
pts: (written on the whiteboard) one big table
(written on the whiteboard) update anomaly
(written on the whiteboard) customer → city (not order → city)
(written on the whiteboard) each fact stored once
(written on the whiteboard) orders hold foreign keys
(written on the whiteboard) 3NF: the key, the whole key,
(written on the whiteboard) and nothing but the key
say: Here's a spreadsheet-style orders table. Each row repeats the customer's name and city, and the product's price.

Look at Ana: her city is stored twice. If she moves, we must update every one of her orders. Miss one, and the database contradicts itself. That's an update anomaly. The root cause: city depends on the customer, not on the order.

The fix is to give each fact its own table. Customers stores each name and city once. Products stores each price once. Orders keeps only keys pointing to them: foreign keys. Now Ana's move is a single update, and a price change is a single update.
This is third normal form: every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key. To get the original view back, we join the tables in a query.

slides.h: Storage and indexing: the B+ tree
pts: Data lives in fixed-size disk pages
Without an index: scan every page
B+ tree: wide, shallow, balanced — 3–4 levels for millions of rows
Hash indexes for equality; column stores for analytics
say: On disk, a table is stored in fixed size pages, typically a few kilobytes each. Without an index, finding one row means scanning every page of the table.

The default index structure is the B plus tree, the wide, shallow cousin of the binary search tree from data structures. Each node is a whole disk page holding hundreds of keys, so the tree is extremely shallow: three or four levels can index hundreds of millions of rows. A lookup reads just three or four pages.
All the data pointers live in the leaves, and the leaves are linked together, so a range query, like ages between thirty and fifty, finds the first match and then just walks along the leaves.

Hash indexes are even faster for exact matches but can't do ranges. And analytics databases often store data by column instead of by row, so a query that averages one column reads only that column. One of the papers reviewed in this course proposes a hybrid layout that groups each column together inside a page, for better cache performance.

slides.h: Worked example: why an index is so fast
pts: (written on the whiteboard) 10^9 rows, 100 rows per page
(written on the whiteboard) no index: 10^7 page reads
(written on the whiteboard) fan-out approx 200 keys per node
(written on the whiteboard) 200^3 = 8times 10^6,  200^4 = 1.6times 10^9
(written on the whiteboard) log_200(10^9) approx 3.9 so 4 levels
(written on the whiteboard) 4 reads instead of 10,000,000
say: A table has one billion rows, about a hundred rows per disk page. Without an index, finding one customer means scanning every page: ten million page reads.

A B plus tree node fills one page and holds about two hundred keys, so each level multiplies the reach by two hundred. One level reaches two hundred pages, two levels forty thousand, three levels eight million, four levels one point six billion.

So four levels are enough for a billion rows: log base two hundred of a billion is about three point nine. Four page reads instead of ten million. And the top levels stay cached in memory, so in practice it's often just one or two disk reads. That's why adding the right index can turn a minutes-long query into milliseconds.

pts: A transaction: a unit of work that commits or aborts
Atomicity · Consistency · Isolation · Durability
Concurrency: locking (2PL) or multiversioning (MVCC)
Recovery: write-ahead log, undo/redo, checkpoints
say: Moving a hundred dollars from checking to savings takes two updates. If the system crashes between them, money vanishes. So databases group the updates into a transaction.

Transactions guarantee four properties, ACID. Atomicity: all of it happens, or none of it. Consistency: every constraint holds before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's half finished work. Durability: once committed, it survives a crash.

Isolation is provided by concurrency control. Two phase locking acquires locks as it goes and releases them only at the end. Multiversion concurrency control instead keeps old versions of rows, so readers never block writers. Weaker isolation levels trade some correctness, allowing anomalies like non repeatable reads, for more speed.

Durability and atomicity come from the write ahead log: every change is recorded in the log, on disk, before the data pages are updated. After a crash, the database redoes committed transactions and undoes uncommitted ones from the log. Checkpoints keep recovery short.

slides.h: Worked example: a transfer, a crash, and the log
pts: (code on the board) BEGIN;
(code on the board) UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id = 1;
(code on the board) UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 100 WHERE id = 2;
(code on the board) COMMIT;
(code on the board) LOG: T7 acct1  old 500  new 400
(code on the board) LOG: T7 acct2  old 200  new 300
(code on the board) LOG: T7 COMMIT
(written on the whiteboard) crash before COMMIT → UNDO with old values
(written on the whiteboard) crash after COMMIT → REDO with new values
(written on the whiteboard) write-ahead: log first, data later
say: Here's the bank transfer as real SQL. Begin a transaction, subtract a hundred from checking, add a hundred to savings, commit. Until the commit, none of it is permanent.

Before touching any data page, the database writes each change to the log on disk: transaction seven, account one, old value five hundred, new value four hundred. Then account two, old two hundred, new three hundred. Then a commit record.

Now suppose the power fails after the first update, before the commit. On restart, the database reads the log. Transaction seven has no commit record, so it's undone using the old values: account one goes back to five hundred. Atomicity: no money vanished.

If the crash comes after the commit record is on disk, but before the data pages were written, the database redoes the change from the new values. Durability: a committed transfer is never lost. That's the whole trick: log first, data later.

pts: Key-value (Redis), document (MongoDB)
Wide-column (Bigtable, Cassandra), graph (Neo4j)
Scale out across many machines
CAP: during a partition, choose consistency or availability
say: At internet scale, other data models appear. Key value stores like Redis are giant distributed hash tables, perfect for caches and sessions. Document databases like MongoDB store flexible JSON like records.

Wide column stores, descended from Google's Bigtable, another paper reviewed in this course, store enormous sparse tables across thousands of servers. Graph databases store relationships directly, for social networks and recommendations.
These systems scale out by splitting and replicating data across many machines.

But distribution brings a fundamental trade off, the CAP theorem: if the network splits the cluster in two, each side must choose either to keep answering, possibly with stale data, or to stay consistent by refusing some requests. Banks lean toward consistency. Shopping carts and social feeds lean toward availability. Relational databases remain the default for most applications, and SQL is one of the most transferable skills in all of computing.

slides.big: Model with ER, store in normalized tables, query with SQL, find fast with B+ trees, stay correct with ACID.
say: To recap. A database management system stores each fact once and serves many programs safely. E R diagrams model entities and relationships, which map mechanically to tables with primary and foreign keys. Relational algebra underlies SQL, where WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY and HAVING summarize groups, and joins combine tables. Normalization prevents contradictions. B plus tree indexes make lookups fast, and ACID transactions keep data correct through concurrency and crashes. Next, engineering economics and ethics. See you there.

L24_egee401.title: Engineering Economics & Professionalism
L24_egee401.file: EGEE-401 Engineering Economics/Lecture - EGEE 401 Engineering Economics & Professionalism.mp4

say: Welcome to E G E E four oh one, engineering economics and professionalism. Engineers don't just ask whether something will work. They ask whether it's worth it: should we build this solar farm, buy that test equipment, or lease it instead? And they carry a responsibility to the public that can outweigh their employer's wishes. This lecture covers both: the mathematics of money over time, and the ethics of engineering practice. The money math is also directly useful for your own car loans, mortgages and retirement savings.

pts: A dollar today > a dollar later
Simple interest: F = P(1 + i·n)
Compound interest: F = P(1 + i)ⁿ
Effective rate: 12% compounded monthly = 12.68%/yr
say: The foundation of the whole course: a dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year, because today's dollar can be invested and earn interest.
With simple interest, you earn interest only on the original amount. Ten thousand dollars at six percent earns six hundred dollars every year.

With compound interest, interest earns interest. The future value is the present value times one plus i, to the n. Ten thousand dollars at six percent becomes seventeen thousand nine hundred eight dollars in ten years, and over forty years, more than one hundred thousand dollars, versus thirty four thousand with simple interest. That's the exponential growth from calculus.

Watch out for how rates are quoted. Twelve percent per year compounded monthly means one percent per month, and one point oh one to the twelfth power gives an effective annual rate of twelve point six eight percent. Credit card rates hide this effect all the time.

slides.h: Worked example: compounding monthly for ten years
pts: (written on the whiteboard) P = \1000, 6%/yr compounded monthly, 10 yr
(written on the whiteboard) i = 0.06/12 = 0.005 per month
(written on the whiteboard) n = 10 times 12 = 120 months
(written on the whiteboard) F = P(1+i)^n = 1000(1.005)^120
(written on the whiteboard) F approx \1,819.40
(written on the whiteboard) effective: 1.005^12 - 1 = 6.17\%
say: You deposit one thousand dollars at six percent per year, compounded monthly, and leave it for ten years. Always start with the cash flow diagram: money out today is an arrow down at year zero.
Monthly compounding means the rate per period is six percent over twelve, half a percent, and there are one hundred twenty periods.
F equals P times one plus i, to the n. One thousand times one point zero zero five to the one hundred twentieth: about one thousand eight hundred nineteen dollars. That's the arrow up at year ten.

The effective annual rate is one point zero zero five to the twelfth, minus one: six point one seven percent, a little more than the six percent advertised, because interest earns interest within each year. That's why lenders must state both the nominal annual percentage rate and the effective rate.

slides.h: Cash-flow diagrams and the interest factors
pts: Draw the cash-flow diagram first — every time
Arrows down = costs, up = receipts
Factors move money through time: (P/F), (P/A), (A/P)…
Excel: PV, FV, PMT, RATE, NPV, IRR
say: Every problem starts with a cash flow diagram. Time runs along the axis in years. Costs point down, receipts point up. Here, a company considers a new automated test machine: it costs fifty thousand dollars now, saves fifteen thousand dollars a year in labor for five years, and can be sold for five thousand at the end. The company's minimum attractive rate of return, the MARR, is ten percent, the return it could earn on other investments.

To compare money at different times, we move it all to one point with a handful of interest factors. F over P moves a lump sum forward, P over F brings it back. P over A converts a uniform yearly series into one present amount, and A over P does the reverse: it's the loan payment formula. These are just sums of the geometric series from calculus two, tabulated for convenience. Spreadsheets have them built in as P V, F V, P M T, N P V and I R R.

pts: Total paid $28,999 → $3,999 interest
Early payments are mostly interest
say: Let's use the capital recovery factor on something real. You borrow twenty five thousand dollars for a car at six percent per year, paid monthly over five years. The monthly rate is half a percent, and there are sixty payments.
Plugging into A equals P times i times one plus i to the n, over one plus i to the n minus one, gives a payment of four hundred eighty three dollars and thirty two cents.
Over sixty months, you pay about twenty nine thousand dollars in total, so the loan costs about four thousand dollars in interest.

The chart shows how each payment splits. Early on, a big chunk, in orange, is interest on the large balance. As the balance falls, more of each payment goes to principal. That's why extra payments early in a loan or mortgage save so much interest.

slides.h: Comparing alternatives: present worth and rate of return
pts: PW: discount everything to today at the MARR
IRR: the rate where PW = 0 → ≈ 17.2%
Accept if PW > 0, equivalently IRR > MARR
say: Back to the test machine. The present worth method discounts every cash flow back to today at the MARR, and adds them up.

At ten percent, the five years of fifteen thousand dollar savings are worth fifty six thousand eight hundred sixty two dollars today, and the salvage value is worth about three thousand one hundred. Subtract the fifty thousand dollar cost, and the present worth is about plus nine thousand nine hundred sixty six dollars. Positive means the investment beats the company's ten percent alternative.

The internal rate of return is the interest rate that makes the present worth exactly zero, where the curve crosses the axis. For this machine, about seventeen point two percent. It's the effective return the investment earns.

The decision rules agree: accept if the present worth at the MARR is positive, or equivalently if the rate of return exceeds the MARR. One caution: when choosing between mutually exclusive projects, compare the rate of return of the extra investment, the incremental cash flow, not each project's rate on its own, or you can pick the wrong one.

slides.h: Worked example: present worth, factor by factor
pts: (written on the whiteboard) -50,000 now, +15,000/yr for 5 yr, +5,000 at yr 5, i = 10\%
(written on the whiteboard) 15,000 times 3.791 = 56,862
(written on the whiteboard) (P/F) = (1)/((1+i)^n) = 0.6209:  5,000 times 0.6209 = 3,105
(written on the whiteboard) PW = -50,000 + 56,862 + 3,105 approx +\9,967
(written on the whiteboard) only add money that sits at the SAME time
say: Students often see the plus nine thousand nine hundred sixty six and wonder where it came from. Let's compute it by hand. Cost fifty thousand now, savings of fifteen thousand a year for five years, salvage five thousand at year five, at a MARR of ten percent.

The uniform series uses the P over A factor: one plus i to the n, minus one, over i times one plus i to the n. One point one to the fifth is one point six one zero five. So the factor is point six one zero five over point one six one zero five: three point seven nine one. Fifteen thousand times that is fifty six thousand eight hundred sixty two.
The salvage is a single future amount, so use P over F: one over one point six one zero five, which is point six two zero nine. Five thousand times that is three thousand one hundred five.

Add everything at time zero: minus fifty thousand, plus fifty six thousand eight hundred sixty two, plus three thousand one hundred five. Plus nine thousand nine hundred sixty seven, the same as the slide, give or take rounding. Positive, so buy the machine. And the sign convention matters: costs are negative, receipts positive, everything moved to the same moment before adding.

pts: Convert everything to an equivalent annual cost
Pump A: $12k, 6 yr → $4,096/yr
Pump B: $20k, 12 yr → $3,554/yr — cheaper
Payback period: quick, but ignores time value
say: When alternatives last different lengths of time, present worth needs a common study period. The annual worth method sidesteps that. Convert each option to an equivalent uniform annual cost. Pump A costs twelve thousand dollars, lasts six years, and costs fifteen hundred a year to run. Spreading the purchase over six years at eight percent with the A over P factor, then adding the operating cost, gives about four thousand ninety six dollars per year. Pump B costs twenty thousand but lasts twelve years and is cheaper to run: about three thousand five hundred fifty four dollars per year. Despite the higher price tag, B is the better buy. The simple payback period, how many years until savings repay the cost, is popular because it's easy, three point three years for our test machine, but it ignores the time value of money and everything after the payback point, so use it only as a rough screen.

pts: Depreciation: non-cash expense that reduces taxable income
Straight-line: (cost − salvage) / life = $18,000/yr
MACRS: faster, fixed IRS percentages
Real vs market rates: (1 + i) = (1 + i_real)(1 + f)
say: Equipment wears out, and tax law lets companies deduct that loss in value over time as depreciation. It's not a cash payment, but it reduces taxable income, which saves real tax dollars.
Straight line depreciation spreads the cost evenly. A one hundred thousand dollar machine with a ten thousand dollar salvage value over five years depreciates eighteen thousand dollars per year.

The U S tax system uses MACRS, which front loads the deductions with fixed percentages per year. Because a tax saving today is worth more than one later, faster depreciation increases a project's present worth. After tax cash flow equals before tax cash flow minus taxes, where taxes are the tax rate times the before tax cash flow minus depreciation.

And inflation erodes money too. The market interest rate combines a real return and inflation: one plus the market rate equals one plus the real rate, times one plus inflation. Analyze in either real or market dollars, but never mix them. For example, with eight percent market interest and three percent inflation, the real rate is one point oh eight over one point oh three, minus one: about four point nine percent, close to the shortcut of eight minus three.

slides.h: Worked example: a straight-line depreciation schedule
pts: (written on the whiteboard) cost \50,000, salvage \5,000, 5 years
(written on the whiteboard) D = frac50,000 - 5,0005 = \9,000/yr
(written on the whiteboard) tax saving = 0.25 times 9,000 = \2,250/yr
say: A company buys a test machine for fifty thousand dollars. It will last five years, then sell for five thousand. Straight line depreciation spreads the lost value evenly.
Each year's depreciation is the cost minus salvage, divided by the life: forty five thousand over five, nine thousand dollars a year.
Book value drops by nine thousand each year: forty one thousand, thirty two, twenty three, fourteen, and finally five thousand, exactly the salvage value.

Depreciation isn't cash leaving the company, but it is a tax deduction. At a twenty five percent tax rate, nine thousand of depreciation saves two thousand two hundred fifty dollars in taxes each year. That's why depreciation shows up in every after-tax comparison of alternatives.

slides.h: Engineering ethics: lessons written in failures
pts: Codes (NSPE, IEEE): public safety, health and welfare come first
Challenger, Hyatt Regency, Ford Pinto, I-35W
Common threads: pressure, poor communication, silence
Your duty: speak up, document, escalate
say: Professional codes of ethics, from the National Society of Professional Engineers and from the I E E E, put the safety, health and welfare of the public first, above an employer's or client's interests. The case studies show why. In January nineteen eighty six, the space shuttle Challenger launched on an unusually cold morning. Engineers at the booster manufacturer had warned that the rubber O rings sealing the booster joints might not seal in the cold, and recommended against launching. Under schedule pressure, the recommendation was reversed. Seventy three seconds after launch, a failed joint led to the breakup of the shuttle and the loss of all seven crew members.

In two thousand seven, the I 35 W bridge in Minneapolis collapsed during rush hour, killing thirteen people. Investigators found gusset plates, the steel plates connecting the truss members, had been undersized in the original design decades earlier, and the bridge was carrying extra weight from later modifications and from construction materials stored on it that day.

Other classic cases follow the same pattern. At the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City, a seemingly minor change to how suspended walkways were connected doubled the load on one connection, and the walkways fell, killing one hundred fourteen people. In the Ford Pinto case, a cost benefit analysis effectively placed a dollar value on lives lost to a known fuel tank problem. The common threads are cost and schedule pressure, communication failures, and warnings that weren't heard or weren't escalated. As an engineer, your duty is to speak up clearly, put concerns in writing, and escalate when public safety is at stake.

slides.big: Move money through time with (1 + i)ⁿ, compare options by PW, AW or IRR at the MARR — and put public safety first.
say: To recap. Money has time value, and compound interest grows exponentially. Draw the cash flow diagram, then use the interest factors to move money through time. Present worth, annual worth and rate of return compare alternatives against the minimum attractive rate of return, and give the same decision. Depreciation, taxes and inflation change the numbers in predictable ways. And above the economics sits ethics: engineers hold paramount the safety of the public. Next, we go inside the chips: CMOS circuit design. See you there.

L25_egcp441.title: Advanced Electronics for Computer Engineers
L25_egcp441.file: EGCP-441 Advanced Electronics (CMOS)/Lecture - EGCP 441 Advanced Electronics for Computer Engineers.mp4

say: Welcome to E G C P four forty one, advanced electronics for computer engineers. In digital logic, gates were ideal boxes that switched instantly and cost nothing. In this course we open the boxes. Every gate is built from MOS transistors, and their physics decides how fast a chip can run, how much power it burns, and how small it can be. Chips like the ones made in clean rooms like this are designed from the ideas in this lecture: the CMOS inverter, static logic gates, delay and power, interconnect, and physical layout.

slides.h: MOSFETs as switches: NMOS and PMOS
pts: NMOS: on when gate high — good at pulling DOWN
PMOS: on when gate low — good at pulling UP
Threshold V_t: below it, (mostly) off
In this course’s labs: measure V_t and I–V curves of real MOSFETs
say: Recall the MOSFET from electronics. An N channel MOSFET conducts when its gate is high. It passes a strong zero, pulling a node all the way to ground, but only a weak one, because it turns off as the output rises to within a threshold voltage of the gate.
A P channel MOSFET is the mirror image. It conducts when its gate is low, and it passes a strong one but a weak zero.

So CMOS, complementary MOS, uses each where it's strong: PMOS transistors to pull outputs up to the supply, and NMOS transistors to pull them down to ground. Below the threshold voltage, a transistor is mostly off, though a small leakage current still flows.

In this course's first labs, students characterize real MOSFETs on the bench, measuring threshold voltages and current voltage curves for both N and P channel devices, to see the square law models from electronics in actual hardware.

pts: PMOS on top, NMOS on bottom, gates tied together
IN = 0 → PMOS on → OUT = V_DD; IN = 1 → NMOS on → OUT = 0
Switching threshold V_M set by PMOS/NMOS strength
Noise margins: how much noise an input can tolerate
say: The simplest CMOS gate is the inverter: a PMOS transistor from the supply to the output, an NMOS from the output to ground, and both gates tied to the input. When the input is low, the PMOS is on and the NMOS is off, so the output is pulled up to V D D. When the input is high, the NMOS is on and the PMOS is off, so the output is pulled to ground. In either steady state, one transistor is always off, so there's no path from supply to ground and almost no current flows. That's why CMOS took over the industry.

Sweep the input slowly and plot the output, and you get the voltage transfer characteristic. The switching threshold, V M, is where input equals output. It depends on the relative strength of the two transistors. Holes move more slowly than electrons, so designers make the PMOS two to three times wider to center V M at half the supply. The noise margins measure how much noise an input can tolerate and still be read correctly. They're set by the points where the curve's slope is minus one, V I L and V I H. A steep curve, like this one, means large noise margins, which is why digital logic is so robust. In the labs, students measure exactly this curve, then the inverter's switching delay.

slides.h: Worked example: building an inverter from two transistors
pts: (written on the whiteboard) PMOS: ON when its gate is LOW
(written on the whiteboard) NMOS: ON when its gate is HIGH
(written on the whiteboard) IN = 0: PMOS on, NMOS off so OUT = 1
(written on the whiteboard) IN = 1: NMOS on, PMOS off so OUT = 0
(written on the whiteboard) never a path VDD to GND in steady state
say: Let's draw the most important circuit in digital electronics. Put a P M O S transistor at the top, with its source connected to the supply, V D D.
Below it, an N M O S transistor, with its source at ground. Their drains meet in the middle, and that's the output.

Tie both gates together as the input. Now, input low: the P M O S turns on and the N M O S turns off, so the output connects to V D D. A one. Input high: the N M O S turns on, the P M O S off, and the output connects to ground. A zero. It's a NOT gate.

Here's the magic. In either steady state, one transistor is always off, so there's no path from the supply to ground. A CMOS gate burns almost no power while it sits still. That one property is why CMOS won, and why your phone can have billions of these.

slides.h: Static CMOS gates: NAND and NOR
pts: Pull-down network (NMOS) + complementary pull-up (PMOS)
Series in one ⇔ parallel in the other
NAND: NMOS in series, PMOS in parallel
CMOS gates invert naturally; AND = NAND + inverter
say: Every static CMOS gate follows one recipe. Build a pull down network of NMOS transistors that conducts exactly when the output should be zero. Then build the complementary pull up network of PMOS transistors: wherever the NMOS network has transistors in series, the PMOS network has them in parallel, and vice versa. It's De Morgan's law in silicon.

Look at the NAND gate. The output should be zero only when A and B are both one, so the two NMOS transistors are in series: both must be on to pull the output down. The PMOS transistors are in parallel: if either input is zero, its PMOS pulls the output up. A NOR gate is the opposite, with NMOS in parallel and PMOS in series.
Because NMOS transistors are faster, NAND gates, with their series NMOS, are usually preferred over NOR gates, whose slow PMOS transistors end up in series.

Notice that CMOS gates naturally invert. An AND gate is really a NAND followed by an inverter, costing six transistors instead of four. That's why logic synthesis tools love NAND and NOR. In this course's labs, students build NOT, NAND, NOR, and three input versions as transistor level schematics and physical layouts.

slides.h: Worked example: any inverting expression is one gate
pts: (written on the whiteboard) Y = overlineAcdot B + C
(written on the whiteboard) pull-down conducts when A·B + C = 1
(written on the whiteboard) AND → series,  OR → parallel
(written on the whiteboard) pull-up = the dual: swap series ↔ parallel
(written on the whiteboard) A=B=1, C=0: down path on, up path off → Y = 0
(written on the whiteboard) 6 transistors, 1 stage of delay
say: Students usually ask: what if the function isn't just NAND or NOR? The same recipe builds any inverting expression as a single gate. Take Y equals not of A and B, or C. This is called an and or invert gate.
Step one, the pull down network: it must conduct when the expression inside the bar is true. AND means series, OR means parallel. So A in series with B, and that pair in parallel with C.

Step two, the pull up network is the dual: swap series and parallel. A in parallel with B, and that pair in series with C. Check one case: A equals B equals one, C equals zero. The series A B chain conducts, pulling Y low, and in the pull up, C's PMOS is on but both A and B PMOS are off, so there's no path up. Y is zero. Correct.

Six transistors, one gate delay. Built from separate AND, OR and NOT gates, it would take more transistors and three levels of delay. That's why standard cell libraries are full of these compound gates.

slides.h: Worked example: a CMOS NAND gate, transistor by transistor
pts: (written on the whiteboard) NAND: OUT = 0 only if A = B = 1
(written on the whiteboard) series in one network ⇔ parallel in the other
(code on the board) A B | OUT
(code on the board) 0 0 |  1
(code on the board) 0 1 |  1
(code on the board) 1 0 |  1
(code on the board) 1 1 |  0
say: A NAND output should be zero only when A and B are both one. Build the pull up network first: two P M O S transistors in parallel from V D D to the output. If either input is low, at least one of them conducts, and the output is pulled high.
The pull down network is the complement: two N M O S transistors in series from the output to ground. Current only gets through if both are on, which needs A and B both high.

Check every row. Zero zero: both P M O S on, output one. Zero one, and one zero: one P M O S on, and the series N M O S chain is broken, so output one. One one: both P M O S off, both N M O S on, output zero. That's NAND, with just four transistors.

slides.h: Delay: it’s all R and C
pts: On transistor ≈ resistor R; everything it drives ≈ capacitor C
t_p ≈ 0.69 RC (time to cross 50%)
Wider transistor → lower R, but more input C
Logical effort: size stages ≈ 4× apart (fanout-of-4)
say: Why does a gate take time to switch? Model the on transistor as a resistor, and everything the output drives, the gates of the next stage, the wire, and the transistor's own diffusion regions, as a capacitor.

When the input switches, the output charges or discharges through that resistor, the R C exponential from the circuits course. The propagation delay is the time to cross fifty percent of the swing, which is the natural log of two, about point six nine, times R C. Average the rising and falling delays, t P L H and t P H L, to get the gate's delay.
To go faster, make the transistor wider to lower its resistance. But a wider transistor also has a bigger gate capacitance, which slows down whatever drives it. There's no free lunch.

The method of logical effort optimizes this trade off. One famous result: to drive a big load, use a chain of inverters that grow by about a factor of four at each stage, called the fanout of four rule. Chip designers use F O four delays as a technology independent unit of speed.

slides.h: Worked example: how long does a gate take?
pts: (written on the whiteboard) R_on approx 10\ mathrmkOmega,  C_load approx 10\ mathrmfF
(written on the whiteboard) t_p = 0.69 RC = 0.69(10^4)(10^-14)
(written on the whiteboard) t_p approx 69\ mathrmps
(written on the whiteboard) fan-out 4: C = 40\ mathrmfF Rightarrow t_p approx 276\ mathrmps
(written on the whiteboard) wider: lower R, but more input C
(written on the whiteboard) size each stage about 4× the previous
say: Model an on transistor as a resistor, about ten kilohms for a small one in this example, and everything it drives as a capacitor, say ten femtofarads for one gate input plus wire.

The output is an RC circuit charging or discharging. It crosses the halfway point after point six nine times R C. Ten thousand times ten femtofarads is a hundred picoseconds, so the delay is about sixty nine picoseconds.
Now make this gate drive four others, a fan out of four. The load capacitance quadruples to forty femtofarads, and so does the delay: two hundred seventy six picoseconds.

The fix is to make the driving transistor wider, which lowers its resistance. But a wider transistor has more gate capacitance, which slows down whatever drives it. That trade off is exactly what logical effort and gate sizing are about.

pts: Dynamic: P = α C V_DD² f
Voltage is the biggest lever (squared!)
Short-circuit power during transitions
Leakage (static) dominates at nanometer scales
say: Every time a node switches, its capacitance is charged from the supply and then dumped to ground, burning energy C V squared per full cycle. Multiply by how often nodes switch, the activity factor alpha, and the clock frequency, and you get dynamic power: alpha C V D D squared f.

Voltage is the biggest lever, because it's squared. With an activity factor of point one, ten nanofarads of total switched capacitance and a three gigahertz clock, a one point two volt chip burns over four watts. Drop to point eight volts and it's under two watts, less than half. That's why phones constantly scale voltage and frequency up and down, called D V F S.
During each transition, both networks are briefly on at once, so a little short circuit current flows straight from supply to ground.

And in modern nanometer transistors, which can't fully turn off, leakage current flows all the time, even when nothing switches. Leakage is a major part of a modern chip's power, which is why unused blocks are power gated, switched off completely. In this course's labs, students measure the power and energy of their gates in simulation.

slides.h: Worked example: the power equation in numbers
pts: (written on the whiteboard) P = alpha C V_DD^2 f
(written on the whiteboard) alpha = 0.1, C = 1\ mathrmnF, V = 1.0\ mathrmV, f = 2\ mathrmGHz
(written on the whiteboard) P = 0.1times 10^-9times 1^2times 2times 10^9 = 0.2\ mathrmW
(written on the whiteboard) V = 0.8\ mathrmV: P = 0.2times 0.8^2 = 0.128\ mathrmW
(written on the whiteboard) 20% less voltage = 36% less power
(written on the whiteboard) DVFS: lower V and f together when idle
say: Dynamic power is alpha times C times V squared times f. Take a chip whose switched capacitance totals one nanofarad, with ten percent of nodes switching each cycle, at one volt and two gigahertz.
Point one times ten to the minus nine times one squared times two times ten to the ninth: point two watts.
Now lower the supply to point eight volts. Voltage is squared, so power drops to point six four of the original: point one two eight watts, thirty six percent less, for a twenty percent voltage cut.

That's why phones and laptops constantly scale voltage and frequency together, running slow and low when idle, and only boosting when you need speed. The quadratic dependence on voltage is the biggest power lever in chip design.

slides.h: Interconnect: wires are the new bottleneck
pts: Wires have distributed resistance and capacitance
Unbuffered delay grows with length² (Elmore)
Fix: insert repeaters → roughly linear
Crosstalk couples neighboring wires
say: Transistors have shrunk enormously, but the wires connecting them haven't kept up. A wire has resistance along its length and capacitance to everything around it, distributed all along it.

For a long wire, both resistance and capacitance grow with length, so the delay grows with length squared. The Elmore delay of a distributed R C line is about point three eight times r times c times L squared. Double a wire's length, and its delay quadruples.
The fix is to break long wires into segments with buffers, called repeaters, in between. Each segment is short, so the total delay grows roughly linearly with length instead.

Wires also couple to their neighbors. When one switches, it can inject noise into the wire next to it, called crosstalk. In many modern chips, the critical path is dominated by wires, not transistors. In the interconnect lab, students model exactly this R C wire delay.

slides.h: Transmission gates and other logic styles
pts: Transmission gate: NMOS ∥ PMOS with complementary controls
Passes both 0 and 1 cleanly
Ideal for multiplexers, XORs and latches
Other styles: pass-transistor, pseudo-NMOS, dynamic/domino
say: A single NMOS transistor passes zeros well but ones poorly, and a PMOS the opposite. Put them in parallel, with complementary control signals, and you get a transmission gate, a nearly ideal switch that passes both values cleanly.

Two transmission gates make an elegant two to one multiplexer. When the select signal is zero, the top gate passes A. When it's one, the bottom gate passes B. Just four transistors, plus an inverter for the complemented select, far fewer than building a mux from NAND gates.

Transmission gates are also the heart of efficient X O R gates and of latches and flip flops. As a final project in this course, student teams design a CMOS multiplexer from transmission gates and trade off its power, area and delay.

Other logic styles exist for special needs. Pseudo N MOS uses a weak always on pull up, which is small but burns static power. Dynamic, or domino, logic precharges a node and then conditionally discharges it, which is very fast but sensitive to noise. Static CMOS remains the default because it's robust.

slides.h: From schematic to silicon: layout and fabrication
pts: Photolithography: pattern one layer at a time
Layers: wells, active, poly (gates), contacts, metals
Design rules (λ) guarantee manufacturability
DRC, LVS, extraction → back to SPICE
say: Chips are manufactured by photolithography. A light sensitive resist is exposed through a patterned mask, using machines like this mask aligner in a university lab, or vastly more advanced scanners in commercial fabs. Each exposure defines one layer, and a modern chip is built up from dozens of them.

A designer draws the layout, the actual shapes on each layer. Here's an inverter. The PMOS sits in an n well at the top, where the red polysilicon gate crosses the p plus active region. The NMOS sits at the bottom where the same gate crosses the n plus active region. Black squares are contacts, and blue metal connects the supply, ground and the output. Design rules, often expressed in units of lambda, set minimum widths and spacings so the chip can actually be manufactured. Tools then check the layout against the rules, called D R C, verify that it matches the schematic, called L V S, and extract the real resistances and capacitances back into SPICE for accurate simulation. In this course, students draw layouts like this in the Magic layout tool and simulate them in LT spice.

slides.big: CMOS = complementary pull-up and pull-down networks. Speed is RC, power is α C V² f, and long wires need repeaters.
say: To recap. NMOS transistors pull down and PMOS transistors pull up, so CMOS gates combine complementary networks that draw almost no static current. The inverter's transfer curve gives noise margins. NAND and NOR follow the series parallel duality. Delay comes from charging capacitance through transistor resistance, power from charging it at all, scaled by voltage squared, and leakage adds static power. Long wires are slow and need repeaters. Transmission gates make efficient muxes, and layout turns schematics into manufacturable silicon. Next, advanced digital design with Verilog. See you there.

L26_egcp446.title: Advanced Digital Design using Verilog
L26_egcp446.file: EGCP-446 Advanced Digital Design (Verilog)/Lecture - EGCP 446 Advanced Digital Design using Verilog.mp4

say: Welcome to E G C P four forty six, advanced digital design using Verilog. You've already designed hardware in V H D L. Verilog describes the same hardware with a compact, C like syntax, and together with its successor SystemVerilog, it's the most widely used hardware description language in the chip industry. In this lecture you'll learn Verilog's essentials, the one rule that prevents most simulation and synthesis surprises, finite state machines, and the real world problems every F P G A design faces: dividing clocks, debouncing buttons, synchronizing inputs, driving displays, and closing timing.

pts: Same hardware ideas, different syntax
Verilog: C-like and compact, but weakly typed
module = entity + architecture
SystemVerilog adds powerful verification features
say: V H D L and Verilog describe exactly the same hardware: signals, concurrent logic, processes triggered by clock edges. The difference is style.

Verilog looks like C and is far less verbose. The trade off is weak typing: assign a sixteen bit value to an eight bit wire and Verilog silently truncates it, where V H D L would refuse to compile. Lint tools and careful habits make up for that.
A Verilog module combines what V H D L splits into an entity and an architecture: the ports and the implementation in one place.

Most American and Asian chip companies use Verilog and SystemVerilog, while V H D L remains strong in aerospace, defense and in Europe. SystemVerilog adds object oriented testbenches, constrained random stimulus and assertions, the basis of the UVM verification methodology used across the industry. Knowing both languages covers the job market.

Here's a complete Verilog module: a counter whose width is a parameter, defaulting to four bits. The port list declares a clock and reset as inputs, and q as an N bit output. Wire means a continuously driven connection. Reg means a value assigned inside an always block. Despite its name, reg doesn't automatically mean a register.

The always block runs on every rising clock edge. If reset is high, q becomes zero, otherwise q increments, wrapping around after two to the N minus one. Because it's assigned on a clock edge, q does become a bank of flip flops, with an adder in front. Notice the arrow shaped operator, less than equals. That's a non blocking assignment, and we'll see why it matters next.
To use the module, instantiate it, here as an eight bit counter driving the board's L E Ds, connecting ports by name. Parameters and generate loops let one module describe a whole family of circuits.

slides.h: The rule to memorize: blocking vs. non-blocking
pts: Clocked always @(posedge clk): use <= (non-blocking)
Combinational always @(*): use = (blocking)
Assign every output in every branch → no latches
Never mix both on one variable
say: Verilog has two assignment operators, and confusing them is the number one source of designs that simulate one way and synthesize another. Inside a clocked always block, use non blocking assignments. All the right hand sides are evaluated first, then all the left hand sides update together, exactly like real flip flops that all sample on the same clock edge. So a gets b and b gets a really does swap them.

With blocking assignments, statements execute in order like software. A becomes two, and then b copies the new a, so both end up two. Use blocking assignments for combinational logic, inside always at star blocks, where you want that step by step evaluation.

In combinational blocks, assign every output in every branch, or set defaults at the top. If some path leaves an output unassigned, the tool must remember its old value, and it infers a latch you never wanted.
And never assign the same variable with both kinds of operators. Follow these three rules and your simulation will match your hardware.

slides.h: Worked example: the latch you never asked for
pts: (code on the board) always @(*) begin
(code on the board)   if (sel) y = a;
(code on the board) end
(written on the whiteboard) sel = 0: y = ?  → "keep old value" → LATCH
(code on the board) always @(*) begin
(code on the board)   if (sel) y = a;
(code on the board)   else     y = b;
(code on the board) end
(code on the board) always @(*) begin
(code on the board)   y = 0;            // default first
(code on the board)   if (sel) y = a;
(code on the board) end
(written on the whiteboard) every output, every path
say: The latch rule is easier to see than to hear. This combinational block sets y to a when select is one. But what should y be when select is zero? The code doesn't say.

Hardware can't leave a question unanswered, so the tool assumes y must keep its old value. Keeping a value means memory, and a memory controlled by a level, not a clock edge, is a latch. The synthesis report will warn: inferring latch for y. Latches cause timing headaches and glitchy behavior, and they're almost never what you meant.
Fix one: add an else branch, so every path assigns y. Now it's a plain two to one multiplexer.

Fix two, the habit professionals use: put a default assignment at the very top of the block. Then any branch you forget simply falls back to the default. This matters most in big case statements for state machines, where it's easy to miss one output in one state.

slides.h: Worked example: why "=" vs "<=" changes the hardware
pts: (code on the board) always @(posedge clk) begin
(code on the board)   a = b;
(code on the board)   b = a;
(code on the board) end
(written on the whiteboard) start: a = 1, b = 2
(written on the whiteboard) a = b so a = 2
(written on the whiteboard) b = a so b = 2 (old a lost!)
(code on the board)   a <= b;
(code on the board)   b <= a;
(written on the whiteboard) a = 2, b = 1: swapped
(written on the whiteboard) clocked: <=   combinational: =
say: Here's the classic trap. We want two registers to swap values on every clock edge. Version one uses blocking assignments, the plain equals sign. Start with a equal to one and b equal to two.

Blocking assignments execute in order, like software. a becomes two. Then b gets the new a, which is also two. Both are two: the old value of a is lost forever, and the synthesizer builds hardware that does exactly that.

Version two uses non-blocking assignments, less than equals. All right-hand sides are sampled at the clock edge, then every register updates together. a gets the old b, two, and b gets the old a, one. A true swap, just like two real flip flops wired to each other.
So the rule: inside clocked always blocks, use non-blocking. Inside combinational always blocks, use blocking. Follow it every time and simulation will match the real hardware.

pts: State register: always @(posedge clk) with <=
Next-state + output logic: always @(*) with =
Moore: outputs from state · Mealy: from state + inputs
ASM charts add datapath actions (counters, registers)
say: Finite state machines are written in a standard two process style. One clocked always block holds the state register, updated with non blocking assignments. A second combinational block computes the next state and the outputs from the current state and inputs, using a case statement. States get names with local parameters, so the code reads like the diagram.

Here's a Moore machine that detects two ones in a row on input x. In a Moore machine, the outputs depend only on the current state, so the output turns on in state S two and stays clean for the whole clock cycle.

A Mealy machine computes outputs from the state and the current inputs. It often needs fewer states and reacts one cycle sooner, but its output can glitch when inputs change. In this course's labs, students build a Moore machine that animates an L E D pattern, with a testbench that checks every transition.

Algorithmic state machine charts extend state diagrams with datapath operations, like increment a counter or load a register, the standard way to design a controller together with the datapath it drives.

slides.h: Worked example: a Verilog FSM from diagram to code
pts: (written on the whiteboard) output 1 after two 1s in a row
(code on the board) localparam S0 = 2'd0, S1 = 2'd1, S2 = 2'd2;
(code on the board) reg [1:0] state, next;
(code on the board) always @* begin
(code on the board)   case (state)
(code on the board)     S0: next = x ? S1 : S0;
(code on the board)     S1: next = x ? S2 : S0;
(code on the board)     S2: next = x ? S2 : S0;
(code on the board)     default: next = S0;
(code on the board)   endcase
(code on the board) end
(code on the board) always @(posedge clk) state <= rst ? S0 : next;
(code on the board) assign y = (state == S2);
(written on the whiteboard) register + next-state + output
say: Design a machine that outputs one after it sees two ones in a row on input x. Three states: S zero, nothing seen. S one, one one seen. S two, two or more ones: output one.
Draw the arrows for input one: S zero to S one, S one to S two, and S two stays in S two. Then code the next state logic in a combinational always block, using blocking assignments.
Any zero sends us back to S zero. The default branch covers the unused fourth state code, so the machine can never get stuck there.

Finally, the state register, clocked with non-blocking assignment and a reset, and the Moore output, which depends only on the state. Three blocks: state register, next state logic, output logic. Every FSM you write in this course has this exact shape.

slides.h: Real FPGA problem 1: clocks and buttons
pts: 100 MHz → 1 Hz: count 50,000,000 cycles per toggle
Better: a 1-cycle enable pulse, one global clock
Buttons bounce for milliseconds → debounce
Async inputs → two-flip-flop synchronizer
say: F P G A boards typically run a one hundred megahertz clock, far too fast to see an L E D blink. To make a one hertz signal, count fifty million clock cycles, then toggle, which takes a twenty six bit counter. Good practice is not to use that slow signal as a new clock, but to generate a one cycle enable pulse and keep every flip flop on the main clock. Mixing derived clocks causes timing problems the tools can't analyze. Mechanical push buttons have another problem: when pressed, the metal contacts bounce, opening and closing many times over a few milliseconds. A counter would see one press as a dozen. The fix is debouncing: accept a new button value only after it has stayed stable for several milliseconds, then detect the edge to get a single clean pulse. In the A S M lab, students build exactly this: a clock divider and a push button debouncer.

There's a subtler danger. A button changes at random times relative to the clock. If it changes right as a flip flop samples, the flip flop can enter a metastable state, hovering between zero and one for an unpredictable time. The standard fix is a synchronizer: pass the signal through two flip flops in a row. The first may go metastable, but it almost always settles within a clock cycle, before the second samples it. Every asynchronous input in a real product goes through a synchronizer.

slides.h: Worked example: a synchronizer and one-pulse circuit
pts: (code on the board) reg sync1, sync2, prev;
(code on the board) always @(posedge clk) begin
(code on the board)   sync1 <= btn;     // may be metastable
(code on the board)   sync2 <= sync1;   // clean
(code on the board)   prev  <= sync2;
(code on the board) end
(code on the board) assign pulse = sync2 & ~prev;
say: A push button can change at any instant, with no relation to the clock. If it changes right at a clock edge, the flip flop that samples it can go metastable: stuck between zero and one for a while.
The fix is two flip flops in a row. The first one may go metastable, but it has a whole clock period to settle before the second one samples it.
The second flip flop's output is clean and synchronized to our clock. Everything else in the design should only ever look at sync two.

A held button would look like thousands of presses to a fast counter. So compare sync two with its value one clock ago: the pulse is high only when it is one now and was zero before. Exactly one clock cycle per press. Add a debounce counter, and you have the input stage of nearly every F P G A lab.

slides.h: Real FPGA problem 2: driving a multi-digit display
pts: 4 digits share the same 7 segment lines
Enable one digit (anode) at a time
Switch every ~1 ms → persistence of vision
Decoder: hex digit → 7-segment pattern (case)
