say: Seven segment displays are everywhere on F P G A boards. A four digit display would need twenty eight segment wires, so instead all four digits share the same seven segment lines, and each digit has its own enable line, called its anode.

The trick is time multiplexing. Turn on digit zero and drive its pattern, then one millisecond later switch to digit one with its pattern, and so on. Each digit is lit only a quarter of the time, but it refreshes two hundred fifty times per second, much faster than the eye can follow, so all four appear steadily lit. A case statement decodes each hex digit into its segment pattern. In this course's project, students first show a counter on one digit, then build the full time multiplexed multi digit display.

slides.h: Memories: ROM and RAM that map to block RAM
say: Memories are just arrays. This declares two hundred fifty six bytes. On each clock edge, if write enable is high, the input byte is stored at the address, and the byte at the address is read out. Written in this synchronous pattern, the synthesis tool recognizes it and maps it to the F P G A's dedicated block RAM, instead of building it from two thousand individual flip flops and a giant multiplexer. Write it slightly differently, with an asynchronous read for example, and you may lose that mapping, so follow the vendor's coding templates.

A ROM can be a case statement, or an array initialized from a file of hex values with read mem h, which is handy for lookup tables like one period of a sine wave. In the memory lab, students build ROM and RAM modules and show the RAM's contents on the seven segment display.

slides.h: From RTL to bitstream: implementation and timing
pts: Simulate first: testbenches with self-checking
Synthesis → LUTs, flip-flops, block RAM, DSP slices
Constraints (.xdc): pins and clock period
Static timing analysis: worst negative slack must be ≥ 0
say: The design flow always starts with simulation. A testbench drives inputs with initial blocks and delays, and a good one checks the outputs automatically, printing an error instead of making you stare at waveforms.

Synthesis translates the R T L into the F P G A's resources: lookup tables, flip flops, block RAM and D S P multiplier slices. Then place and route decides where each one goes on the chip and how to wire them.
A constraints file tells the tools which package pin each port connects to, and what the clock period is. One hundred megahertz means ten nanoseconds.

Finally, static timing analysis checks every path from one flip flop to the next against that period, just like the maximum frequency calculation from the V H D L course. The key number is worst negative slack. If it's negative, some path is too slow and the design won't work reliably at that clock rate. You fix it by pipelining long paths, simplifying logic, or lowering the clock frequency. Only then is the bitstream generated and loaded onto the board.

slides.h: Worked example: reading a timing report
pts: (written on the whiteboard) T = 10 ns, t_cq = 0.5, t_logic = 8.0, t_su = 0.4
(written on the whiteboard) slack = T - (t_cq + t_logic + t_su)
(written on the whiteboard) = 10 - 8.9 = +1.1 ns
(written on the whiteboard) t_logic = 10: slack = 10 - 10.9 = -0.9 ns
(written on the whiteboard) pipeline: 10 ns → 5 + 5 ns (+1 cycle latency)
(written on the whiteboard) or slow the clock: T = 12 ns ≈ 83 MHz
say: What is slack, exactly? Follow one path between two flip flops on a one hundred megahertz clock: ten nanoseconds per cycle. The launching flip flop takes half a nanosecond to change its output. The logic and wires take eight. And the capturing flip flop needs its input steady for point four nanoseconds of setup time before the next edge.
Slack is the time to spare: the period minus everything the path needs. Ten minus point five minus eight minus point four: one point one nanoseconds. Positive, so this path is fine.

Now someone adds a multiplier and the logic grows to ten nanoseconds. The slack becomes ten minus ten point nine: minus point nine. The worst negative slack is negative, so this design may fail in hardware at one hundred megahertz, even though the simulation looked perfect, because simulation doesn't model delays.

The cure is pipelining: put a register in the middle, splitting the ten nanoseconds into two paths of five. Each now has plenty of slack, at the cost of one extra cycle of latency. Or lower the clock: with a twelve nanosecond period, about eighty three megahertz, the original path fits too.

slides.big: Use <= in clocked blocks and = in combinational ones. One global clock with enables, debounce and synchronize inputs, and check slack.
say: To recap. Verilog describes the same hardware as V H D L with a compact syntax, organized into modules with parameters. Non blocking assignments model flip flops, blocking assignments model combinational logic, and assigning every output avoids latches. Finite state machines use a clocked state register and combinational next state logic. Real designs divide clocks with enables, debounce and synchronize inputs, multiplex displays, and use memory templates that map to block RAM. And static timing analysis decides whether it all runs at speed. Next, embedded systems on an ARM microcontroller. See you there.

L27_egcp450.title: Embedded Processor Interfacing
L27_egcp450.file: EGCP-450 Embedded Systems (MSP432 ARM)/Lecture - EGCP 450 Embedded Processor Interfacing.mp4

say: Welcome to E G C P four fifty, embedded processor interfacing. This is where computer architecture meets real hardware. Using a Texas Instruments M S P four thirty two LaunchPad, a board much like this one but built around a thirty two bit ARM Cortex M four F processor, students write assembly and C that blinks L E Ds, reads switches, keeps precise time, runs a traffic light controller, plays music through a homemade digital to analog converter, and talks over serial links. The microcontrollers course introduced many of these ideas. Here we build complete systems with them.

pts: Wearables, thermostats, drones, car ECUs, medical devices
Cortex-M4F: 32-bit, Thumb-2, hardware floating point
AAPCS: arguments in R0–R3, result in R0
Callee must preserve R4–R11 (PUSH/POP)
say: ARM Cortex M processors are the workhorses of embedded computing: fitness watches like this one, thermostats, drones, electronic control units in cars, insulin pumps and industrial sensors. The M four F adds signal processing instructions and a hardware floating point unit, useful for filters and control loops. It runs the compact Thumb two instruction set, which mixes sixteen and thirty two bit instructions to save memory.

To let C and assembly work together, everyone follows the ARM procedure call standard, AAPCS. The first four arguments go in R zero to R three, and the result comes back in R zero. Those registers, plus R twelve, can be overwritten freely by the called function. But R four to R eleven belong to the caller: a function that uses them must push them on entry and pop them before returning. Follow these rules, and an assembly routine can be called from C, or a C function from assembly, with no surprises. Each call gets its own stack frame, which is also why recursion works, until the stack runs out.

slides.h: GPIO for real: LEDs and switches
pts: PxDIR: 1 = output · PxIN / PxOUT: read / write
LED needs a series resistor: R = (3.3 − 1.8) / 6 mA ≈ 250 Ω → 270 Ω
Switch needs a pull-up (PxREN + PxOUT) and debouncing
C idioms: P1->OUT |= BIT0; if (P1->IN & BIT1)
say: Each port on the M S P four thirty two has a set of registers. The direction register makes each pin an input or an output. The input register reads pins, the output register drives them, and the select registers route a pin to a peripheral like a UART or timer instead.

An L E D needs a series resistor to limit its current. The pin provides three point three volts, a red L E D drops about one point eight volts, and we want around six milliamps. Ohm's law gives one point five volts over six milliamps, two hundred fifty ohms. Round up to the next standard value, two hundred seventy ohms.

A switch to ground needs a pull up resistor, so the pin reads one when the switch is open, instead of floating at a random value. The M S P four thirty two has internal pull resistors, enabled with the resistor enable register, with the output register choosing up or down. And mechanical switches bounce, so software must debounce them, just like on the F P G A.

In C, it's the same bit masking from the microcontrollers course: P one arrow OUT or equals BIT zero to turn on the L E D, and if P one arrow IN and BIT one to test the switch. In the first labs, students do all of this in ARM assembly first, then in C.

slides.h: Worked example: an LED and a switch, in C
pts: (code on the board) P1->DIR |=  BIT0;     // P1.0 = output (LED)
(code on the board) P1->DIR &= ~BIT1;     // P1.1 = input (switch)
(code on the board) P1->REN |=  BIT1;     // enable its resistor...
(code on the board) P1->OUT |=  BIT1;     // ...as a pull-UP
(code on the board) while (1) {
(code on the board)   if ((P1->IN & BIT1) == 0)   // pressed reads 0
(code on the board)     P1->OUT |=  BIT0;         // LED on
(code on the board)   else
(code on the board)     P1->OUT &= ~BIT0;         // LED off
(code on the board) }
(written on the whiteboard) set |= mask  clear &= ~mask  test & mask
say: Wire a red L E D through two hundred seventy ohms to pin P one point zero. Make that pin an output by setting bit zero of the direction register. Or equals sets one bit and leaves the other seven untouched.

Wire a switch from P one point one to ground. Clear its direction bit to make it an input. With the switch open, the pin would float, so enable the internal resistor and set the output bit to make it a pull up.
Now the loop. Pressing the switch connects the pin to ground, so pressed reads as zero. That's called active low. If the bit is zero, turn the L E D on; otherwise, turn it off.
Notice the bit masking pattern: or equals with a mask to set, and equals with the inverted mask to clear, and with a mask to test. These three idioms are ninety percent of all embedded register code.

pts: Busy-wait loops: imprecise and waste the CPU
SysTick: 24-bit down-counter at the bus clock
RELOAD = period × f_clk − 1 → 1 ms = 47,999 at 48 MHz
Max one wrap ≈ 349 ms; count wraps for longer delays
say: Delay loops, counting down a register in software, are imprecise, change when the compiler or clock changes, and waste the processor's time.

Every Cortex M has a simple built in timer called SysTick: a twenty four bit counter that counts down once per bus clock cycle. When it reaches zero, it reloads, sets a flag, and can trigger an interrupt.

To get a one millisecond tick on a forty eight megahertz clock, you need forty eight thousand counts, so the reload value is forty seven thousand nine hundred ninety nine, since the count includes zero. The chart shows the counter sawtoothing down, wrapping exactly once per millisecond.

Twenty four bits limits a single wrap to about sixteen point eight million counts, about three hundred forty nine milliseconds at forty eight megahertz, so longer delays count multiple wraps. For P W M and measuring input pulses, the chip's more capable Timer A peripherals take over.

slides.h: Worked example: a millisecond delay with SysTick
pts: (code on the board) void Delay_ms(uint32_t n) {
(code on the board)   SysTick->LOAD = 48000 - 1;   // 1 ms at 48 MHz
(code on the board)   SysTick->VAL  = 0;           // start a fresh period
(code on the board)   SysTick->CTRL = 5;           // ENABLE + CPU clock
(code on the board)   while (n--)
(code on the board)     while ((SysTick->CTRL & (1u << 16)) == 0) {}
(code on the board) }
say: Let's write a precise delay. At forty eight megahertz, one millisecond is forty eight thousand clock cycles. SysTick counts from the reload value down to zero inclusive, so load forty eight thousand minus one.
Clear the current value so the first period is a full one, then enable the counter with the processor clock as its source.

Every time the count wraps from zero back to the reload value, hardware sets the count flag, bit sixteen of the control register. Reading the register clears it. So wait for the flag n times, and you've waited exactly n milliseconds, no matter what the compiler does with your code.

pts: NVIC: nested vectored interrupt controller
Hardware stacks R0–R3, R12, LR, PC, xPSR automatically
So an ISR is a plain C function
Shared data: volatile + disable interrupts around critical sections
say: Cortex M interrupts are handled by the nested vectored interrupt controller, the NVIC. Each interrupt source has a priority, and a higher priority interrupt can preempt a lower priority one, which is the nested part.

When an interrupt is accepted, the hardware automatically pushes eight registers onto the stack: exactly the ones the calling convention says a function may destroy. Then it fetches the handler's address from the vector table.

Because the hardware already saved the caller saved registers, an interrupt service routine is just an ordinary C function. No special assembly wrapper is needed, an elegant design choice by ARM. On return, the hardware unstacks everything and the main program resumes.

The concurrency lessons from operating systems apply directly. Variables shared between an I S R and main must be volatile, and if main does a read modify write on shared data, it must briefly disable interrupts or use atomic operations, or an interrupt arriving in the middle creates exactly the race condition from the count plus plus example.

slides.h: Worked example: an ISR, and why "volatile" matters
pts: (code on the board) volatile uint32_t ticks = 0;     // shared with the ISR
(code on the board) void SysTick_Handler(void) {     // every 1 ms
(code on the board)   ticks++;
(code on the board) }
(code on the board) uint32_t start = ticks;
(code on the board) while (ticks - start < 500) {}   // wait 500 ms
(written on the whiteboard) no volatile: compiler reads ticks once, hangs forever
(code on the board) __disable_irq();     // critical section
(code on the board) count++;             // load, add, store
(code on the board) __enable_irq();
say: Set SysTick to interrupt every millisecond. The handler is a plain C function with a special name: it just adds one to a global counter.

Main waits half a second by watching the counter. Now delete the word volatile. The optimizer sees that nothing inside this loop changes ticks, so it reads ticks once into a register and loops forever. Volatile tells the compiler: this can change behind your back, so read it from memory every time.

Second danger. If main also changes a shared variable, count plus plus is really three instructions: load, add, store. An interrupt between the load and the store loses an update. Protect it by disabling interrupts for those few instructions.

slides.h: Finite state machines in C: a traffic light
pts: Moore FSM: each state = outputs + wait time + next states
Store it as a table: an array of structs
Loop: output → wait (SysTick) → read inputs → next state
Adding a state = adding a table row
say: Traffic lights are a classic embedded control problem: lights that must never show green both ways, sensors that detect waiting cars, and a pedestrian button.

The clean way to build one is a table driven Moore machine. Each state stores its light outputs, how long to wait, and its next state for every combination of inputs. The program is a tiny loop: write the outputs, wait using SysTick, read the sensors, and jump to the next state from the table. Here, go north holds for three seconds. If a car is waiting east or a pedestrian presses the button, it moves to a half second yellow, then go east, and so on, with a walk state that blinks a warning before handing control back. The logic lives in data, not tangled if statements, so it's easy to verify and easy to change: adding a state means adding a row. In this course's lab, students build exactly this controller, with pedestrian walk and blink states, in C on the LaunchPad.

Here's the core of that design, simplified to four states. Each state is a struct: the output pattern for the lights, the time to wait, and an array giving the next state for each of the four combinations of two sensor inputs.

The whole controller is this constant table, stored in flash. Read a row: in go north, the lights are pattern hex twenty one, wait three seconds, then stay in go north if no car waits east, or move to wait north if one does.

And the engine is three lines: output the lights, wait, then index the next array with the current sensor reading. That's the entire program. The same pattern runs vending machines, elevator controllers and washing machines.

slides.h: Making sound: a DAC and a sine table
pts: Binary-weighted resistors sum 4 GPIO bits into one voltage
Store one period of a sine wave in a table
Output one sample per SysTick interrupt
Tone = interrupt rate / table length: 14,080 / 32 = 440 Hz
say: To make sound, a microcontroller needs a digital to analog converter. The simplest is built from resistors. Four output pins drive resistors whose values double: twelve, twenty four, forty eight and ninety six kilohms. The most significant bit has the smallest resistor and contributes the most current, so the summed output voltage is proportional to the binary number on the pins: sixteen levels.

To play a note, store one period of a sine wave as a table of thirty two four bit values, and output one entry per SysTick interrupt. The frequency of the tone is the interrupt rate divided by the table length. For the note A at four hundred forty hertz, that's fourteen thousand eighty interrupts per second, a SysTick reload of about three thousand four hundred eight at forty eight megahertz. Change the reload value and you change the note, which is how students build a digital piano with buttons as keys in this course's labs. The staircase is quantization, the same effect an A D C has in reverse, and the sample rate easily satisfies Nyquist from signals and systems for a four hundred forty hertz tone.

slides.h: Worked example: playing a 440 Hz tone
pts: (code on the board) const uint8_t Sine[32] = {
(code on the board) void SysTick_Handler(void) {
(code on the board)   DAC_Out(Sine[i]);     // 4 bits to the resistor DAC
(code on the board)   i = (i + 1) & 0x1F;   // 0..31, wrap
(code on the board) }
(written on the whiteboard) 440 times 32 = 14,080 interrupts/s
(written on the whiteboard) LOAD = frac48times 10^614,080 - 1 approx 3408
say: Store one period of a sine wave as thirty two four bit values, from zero to fifteen.

Each SysTick interrupt sends the next value to the four bit D A C, and wraps the index back to zero after thirty one. And-ing with thirty one is a fast way to wrap, because thirty two is a power of two.

One full sine period takes thirty two interrupts. For four hundred forty hertz, we need four hundred forty times thirty two: fourteen thousand eighty interrupts per second. The reload is forty eight million over fourteen thousand eighty, minus one: about three thousand four hundred eight. Pass the staircase through a simple RC low pass filter and it sounds like a smooth tone.

pts: UART 115200 baud, SPI for displays, I²C for sensors
Blind cycle → busy-wait → interrupts + FIFO → DMA
FIFO = the circular-buffer queue from data structures
Lab: serial link + 7-segment display
say: The final labs connect the microcontroller to other devices over serial links: UART for a console at speeds like one hundred fifteen thousand two hundred baud, S P I for fast displays, and I squared C for sensors.

Just as important is how software synchronizes with an I O device. A blind cycle simply waits a fixed time and hopes the device is ready. Busy waiting, also called gadfly polling, loops on a status flag. Both are simple and fine for slow, rare events, but they tie up the processor.

The scalable approach is interrupt driven with a FIFO. When a byte arrives, the receive interrupt drops it into a circular buffer queue, the very structure from data structures, and the main program pulls bytes out whenever it's ready. Nothing is lost, and the C P U is free in between.

For high data rates, direct memory access hardware copies whole blocks between a peripheral and memory with no C P U involvement at all. Choosing the right strategy for each device is a core embedded design skill.

slides.h: Worked example: what "115200 baud" really means
pts: (written on the whiteboard) 'A' = 0x41 = 0100 0001
(written on the whiteboard) start + 8 data (LSB first) + stop = 10 bits
(written on the whiteboard) bit time = 1/115200 = 8.68\ mu s
(written on the whiteboard) 115200 / 10 = 11,520 bytes/s
(written on the whiteboard) 48\ mathrmMHz times 86.8\ mu s approx 4,170 cycles per byte
(written on the whiteboard) divisor = (48times 10^6)/(16 times 115200) = 26.04
(written on the whiteboard) round to 26: 0.16% error
(written on the whiteboard) mismatched baud → garbage characters
say: Students configure a UART at one hundred fifteen thousand two hundred baud without knowing what that buys them. Here's one character, capital A, hex forty one, on the wire. The line idles high. A start bit pulls it low, then eight data bits go out, least significant bit first, then a stop bit returns it high.

Baud is bits per second on the wire. So each bit lasts one over one hundred fifteen thousand two hundred, about eight point six eight microseconds. Ten bits per character means eighty six point eight microseconds per byte, or about eleven thousand five hundred bytes per second, not one hundred fifteen thousand.

Why does this matter? At forty eight megahertz, that's over four thousand C P U cycles per byte. Busy waiting for each byte wastes all of them, which is exactly why a receive interrupt and a FIFO pay off.

And both ends must agree on the rate, because there's no clock wire: the receiver times each bit from the start bit's falling edge. The baud divisor, forty eight million over sixteen times one fifteen two hundred, is twenty six point oh four. Rounding to twenty six gives an error of a sixth of a percent, well under the roughly two percent a UART can tolerate. Wrong settings at the two ends are why a serial console prints garbage.

slides.big: Embedded systems = registers + timing + interrupts. Keep ISRs short, put logic in tables, and pick the right I/O synchronization.
say: To recap. Cortex M microcontrollers run everything from watches to cars. The AAPCS calling convention lets C and assembly cooperate. GPIO needs the right resistors and debouncing. SysTick gives precise timing from a simple reload calculation. The NVIC stacks registers in hardware, so I S Rs are plain C functions, but shared data still needs care. Table driven finite state machines make controllers clear and verifiable. A resistor DAC and a sine table turn a microcontroller into a musical instrument, and serial I O scales with interrupts, FIFOs and DMA. Next, how to secure these cyber physical systems. See you there.

L28_egcp447.title: Cyber-Physical Systems Security
L28_egcp447.file: EGCP-447 Cyber-Physical Systems Security/Lecture - EGCP 447 Cyber-Physical Systems Security.mp4

say: Welcome to E G C P four forty seven, introduction to cyber physical systems security, with a focus on hardware. Most security courses assume the hardware is trustworthy and defend the software. This course asks what happens when the chip itself is the problem: when it was modified by someone in the supply chain, when it's a counterfeit, or when its power consumption leaks the secret key on a credit card chip like this one. You'll learn how these attacks work, how engineers detect them, and how to design hardware that resists them.

pts: Chips pass through many untrusted hands
Malicious logic, overproduction, cloning, recycling
Hardware flaws can’t be patched like software
Physical access enables new attacks
say: A modern chip passes through many hands before it reaches a product. Designers license third party I P cores, use commercial design tools, send the layout to a foundry that is often overseas, then to separate test and assembly houses, then through distributors. Every one of those steps is a party you have to trust. Any of them could insert hidden malicious logic, manufacture extra chips to sell on the side, clone the design, or sell old chips pulled from electronic waste as new. And unlike software, you can't push an update to fix silicon. A flaw in the hardware is there for the life of the product. Finally, cyber physical systems, like cars, medical devices and power grid controllers, are often physically accessible, which opens attacks that never apply to a server in a locked data center.

pts: Trigger: rare input pattern, counter, or physical condition
Payload: flip outputs, leak secrets, deny service
Designed to escape functional testing
Detection: rare-node testing, side-channel fingerprints, reverse engineering
say: A hardware Trojan is a malicious modification to a circuit. It has two parts. The trigger decides when it activates, and it's designed to be rare: here, three internal nodes that are almost never all one at the same time, perhaps a one in a million event. A sequential trigger might instead count events, activating only after the thousandth occurrence.
The payload is what it does: flip an output, as this X O R gate does, leak a secret key through an unused pin or a subtle power pattern, shut the chip down, or quietly reduce its reliability.

Because the trigger is so rare, ordinary functional testing almost never activates it. The Trojan sits silently through verification and manufacturing tests. In this course, students design Trojans themselves, including a counter triggered Trojan inserted into a standard benchmark circuit in V H D L, to understand exactly why they're hard to find.

Detection methods include test generation that deliberately drives rarely activated nodes, comparing a chip's power and timing fingerprint against a trusted golden chip, and in the extreme, destructively reverse engineering samples layer by layer. Prevention includes design for trust techniques and on chip monitors.

pts: Recycled, remarked, overproduced, out-of-spec, cloned
Detect: X-ray, decapsulation, electrical tests, aging sensors
PUFs: chip fingerprints from manufacturing variation
Buy through trusted, authorized supply chains
say: Counterfeits are a huge problem, especially for military and aerospace systems that need parts long after they're out of production. These microSD cards were opened up by a researcher: from the outside they look similar, but the dies inside reveal genuine, questionable and fake parts. Counterfeits come in many forms: recycled chips pulled from old boards and sanded and remarked as new, chips remarked as a faster or higher temperature grade, overproduced chips sold out the back door of a foundry, out of spec rejects, and outright clones. Detection uses physical inspection, X rays, decapsulation, electrical testing, and on chip aging sensors that reveal a used part. A powerful defense is the physically unclonable function, or PUF. Tiny random manufacturing variations make every chip slightly different, for example in which way each S RAM cell settles at power up, or which of two identical ring oscillators runs faster. That gives each chip a fingerprint that even the manufacturer can't copy, usable for authentication and for generating keys.

slides.h: Protecting the design: locking, camouflage, split manufacturing
pts: Logic locking: key gates; chip works only with the secret key
SAT attack breaks naive locking → Anti-SAT, SFLL
Camouflaging: look-alike cells defeat image-based RE
Split manufacturing: untrusted fab never sees the full design
say: How do you stop a foundry from overproducing or pirating your design? Logic locking inserts extra key gates, like an X O R on an internal wire. With the correct key bit, the signal passes unchanged. With the wrong one, it's inverted. Insert a hundred and twenty eight of these, load the key into tamper resistant memory only after manufacturing, and the foundry holds a chip that doesn't work.

Researchers found a powerful attack: if you have one working chip as an oracle, a SAT solver can choose inputs that eliminate large groups of wrong keys at a time, recovering the key surprisingly quickly. That led to SAT resistant schemes like Anti SAT and S F L L, a classic attack and defense arms race.
Camouflaging uses cells that look identical under a microscope but implement different functions, defeating reverse engineering from layout images.

And split manufacturing sends the transistor layers and lower wiring to an untrusted foundry, and adds the top metal layers at a trusted one, so the untrusted foundry never sees how the circuit is actually connected.

slides.h: Worked example: logic locking with a key gate
pts: (written on the whiteboard) original: F = AB
(written on the whiteboard) K = 0: F = AB correct
(written on the whiteboard) K = 1: F = overlineAB wrong
(written on the whiteboard) 128 key gates: 2^128 guesses
(written on the whiteboard) but: SAT attacks, so research continues
say: Logic locking hides a design from an untrusted factory. Start with a simple function: F equals A and B.

Insert an XOR gate on the wire, with a secret key bit as its other input. With K equals zero, XOR passes the signal unchanged: the chip works. With K equals one, the output is inverted: the chip computes garbage.

The key is programmed into tamper-proof memory only after the chip returns from the foundry. A real design uses a hundred or more key gates, so guessing means two to the hundred twenty eight possibilities. Researchers then try clever attacks, like the SAT attack, which is why this is still an active research area.

pts: Secrets leak through power, timing, EM, even sound
SPA: read operations straight off one trace
DPA/CPA: statistics over many traces → AES key
Defenses: constant time, masking, hiding
say: Side channel attacks don't break the math. They watch the hardware. Every operation draws a slightly different amount of power and takes a slightly different time. Here's simple power analysis on R S A implemented with square and multiply. For each key bit, the chip squares, and if the bit is one, it also multiplies. On a single power trace, the pattern is visible: square multiply means one, square alone means zero. You can literally read the key off the oscilloscope.

Differential and correlation power analysis are subtler and more powerful. Collect thousands of traces while the chip encrypts known inputs. For each guess of one key byte, predict the power the chip should draw, using the Hamming weight of an intermediate value, and correlate the prediction with the measurements. Wrong guesses give near zero correlation, the right guess stands out clearly, here hex three C. Repeat for each byte and you have the whole A E S key. Defenses include constant time code, masking, which randomizes intermediate values so they don't correlate with the key, and hiding, which adds noise or shuffles operations. Fault injection, glitching the clock or voltage, and timing attacks on caches, like Spectre and Meltdown, belong to the same family.

slides.h: Worked example: correlation power analysis on a toy chip
pts: (written on the whiteboard) chip computes v = p oplus k
(written on the whiteboard) power ≈ Hamming weight of v (number of 1s)
(code on the board) p:          0000  1111  0011  0101
(code on the board) measured:    1.1   2.9   1.0   1.2
(code on the board) guess 0000:  0     4     2     2
(code on the board) guess 0001:  1     3     1     1
(written on the whiteboard) best correlation → k = 0001
(written on the whiteboard) AES: 16 bytes × 256 guesses each, not 2^128
say: Correlation power analysis sounds like magic, so let's do it by hand on a toy four bit chip. The chip computes p X O R k, a plaintext with a secret key. Driving more ones onto the wires costs more power, so the power is roughly the Hamming weight, the number of ones, of that result.
We send four known plaintexts and measure the power each time. The numbers are noisy: one point one, two point nine, one point oh, one point two.

Now guess the key. If k were zero zero zero zero, v would equal p, with weights zero, four, two, two. That doesn't track the measurements at all. Try k equals zero zero zero one: v becomes zero zero zero one, one one one zero, zero zero one zero, zero one zero zero, with weights one, three, one, one. That rises and falls exactly with the measured power.

The guess with the highest correlation is the key: zero zero zero one. We never broke the math. A real attack does this for each byte of an A E S key, with two hundred fifty six guesses per byte and thousands of traces to beat the noise. That's why masking, which randomizes v so its weight no longer depends on the key, is the standard defense.

slides.h: Testing: stuck-at faults and test vectors
pts: Model: any net stuck at 0 or stuck at 1
A test must activate the fault and propagate it
Fault coverage = detected / total faults
Scan chains: testable — and an attack surface
say: Security and manufacturing test share tools. To check that a chip was built correctly, engineers use the stuck at fault model: assume any wire might be stuck permanently at zero or one.

A test vector detects a fault only if it activates the fault, driving the wire to the opposite value, and propagates the difference to an output you can observe. Here, to test the AND gate's output stuck at zero, set a and b to one so the good circuit produces a one there, and c to zero so the OR gate doesn't mask it. The good circuit outputs one, the faulty circuit outputs zero. Detected.

Automatic test pattern generators find small sets of vectors that cover nearly all possible faults, and fault coverage measures the fraction detected. In this course's first homework, students identify fault sites and test vectors for a small circuit.

For sequential chips, scan chains link all the flip flops into a long shift register, so testers can load and read internal state directly. But that same access lets an attacker dump the internal state of a crypto engine, so secure chips lock down or scramble their scan chains.

slides.h: Worked example: finding a test vector for a stuck-at fault
pts: (written on the whiteboard) F = AB + C
(written on the whiteboard) activate: AND output = 1 so A = B = 1
(written on the whiteboard) propagate: C = 0 (non-controlling)
(written on the whiteboard) test vector ABC = 110
say: Here's a tiny circuit: F equals A and B, or C. Suppose a manufacturing defect shorts the AND gate's output to ground. That's a stuck at zero fault. Which input pattern will reveal it?

Two jobs. First, activate the fault: drive the faulty wire to the opposite of its stuck value. To make the AND output one, A and B must both be one. Second, propagate it: make the difference visible at F. The OR gate passes its first input through only if its other input is zero, so C must be zero.

So the test vector is A B C equals one one zero. A good chip outputs one; the faulty chip outputs zero. Different answers, so the tester catches it. Automatic test pattern generators do exactly this reasoning, for millions of wires, before a chip ships.

pts: 4 data bits + 3 parity bits at positions 1, 2, 4
Parity bit k covers positions with bit k set
Syndrome = position of a single-bit error
SECDED (ECC RAM) adds an overall parity bit
say: Not every error is malicious. Radiation, noise and aging flip bits too, and error correcting codes fix them. The classic is the Hamming seven four code. Four data bits are placed at positions three, five, six and seven, and three parity bits at the power of two positions one, two and four.

Each parity bit covers the positions whose binary index has that bit set. Parity one covers one, three, five and seven. Parity two covers two, three, six and seven. Parity four covers four through seven. To send data one zero one one, the parity bits come out zero, one and zero, giving the codeword zero one one zero zero one one.

Now suppose bit six flips in transit. The receiver recomputes the three parity checks. Check one passes, checks two and four fail, so the syndrome, read as a binary number, is one one zero: six. The syndrome literally points at the bad bit, so the receiver flips it back. If the syndrome is zero, there was no error.

Hamming codes correct any single bit error, or detect two. Adding one more overall parity bit gives SECDED, single error correct, double error detect, which is exactly what E C C memory in servers uses. In this course's project, students implement a Hamming encoder and decoder in V H D L.

slides.h: Worked example: Hamming(7,4) finds and fixes a flipped bit
pts: (written on the whiteboard) data: 1011
(written on the whiteboard) parity at positions 1, 2, 4
(written on the whiteboard) p1: 1,3,5,7 (1+0+1) p1 = 0
(written on the whiteboard) p2: 2,3,6,7 (1+1+1) p2 = 1
(written on the whiteboard) p4: 4,5,6,7 (0+1+1) p4 = 0
(written on the whiteboard) sent 0110011, received 0110001
(written on the whiteboard) s1 = 0, s2 = 1, s4 = 1
(written on the whiteboard) syndrome = 110 = 6: flip bit 6
say: Protect the four data bits one zero one one. Put them in positions three, five, six and seven. Positions one, two and four, the powers of two, will hold parity bits.

Each parity bit makes its group even. P one covers positions one, three, five and seven: data one, zero, one, so p one is zero. P two covers two, three, six, seven: one, one, one, so p two is one. P four covers four through seven: zero, one, one, so p four is zero.
Send zero one one zero zero one one. Noise flips position six. The receiver gets zero one one zero zero zero one.

The receiver rechecks each group. Group one: even, so s one is zero. Group two: odd, s two is one. Group four: odd, s four is one. Read the checks as binary, s four s two s one: one one zero, which is six. The syndrome is the exact position of the error. Flip bit six back, and the data is recovered with no retransmission.

pts: Constrained devices, long lifetimes, physical access
Mirai (2016): default passwords → huge botnet
Secure boot + root of trust + hardware crypto
PUF keys, signed updates, network segmentation
say: The internet of things puts small computers everywhere: cameras, thermostats, door locks, medical devices, factory sensors. They're hard to secure. They have little processing power or energy for heavy cryptography, they stay deployed for years, often with no update mechanism, and attackers can get their hands on them physically. In two thousand sixteen, the Mirai malware scanned the internet for cameras and routers still using factory default passwords, took over hundreds of thousands of them, and used them to launch some of the largest denial of service attacks ever seen, knocking major websites offline. The defenses start in hardware: secure boot, which only runs firmware signed by the manufacturer, anchored in an immutable root of trust; hardware crypto accelerators; keys derived from PUFs instead of stored in memory; signed over the air updates; lightweight cryptography; and network segmentation so a compromised camera can't reach anything important. A term paper in this course explores hardware Trojans in IoT devices specifically.

slides.big: Hardware is part of the attack surface: trust the supply chain carefully, assume physical leakage, and build security in from the root of trust.
say: To recap. Chips pass through many untrusted hands, and hardware can't be patched. Hardware Trojans hide behind rare triggers. Counterfeits are detected by inspection, testing and PUF fingerprints. Logic locking, camouflaging and split manufacturing protect designs, while SAT attacks keep defenders honest. Side channels leak keys through power and timing, countered by constant time code, masking and hiding. Stuck at fault testing and Hamming codes catch accidental errors, and IoT security starts with secure boot and a hardware root of trust. Next, senior design. See you there.

L29_egcp470.title: Senior Design I
L29_egcp470.file: EGCP-470 Senior Design I/Lecture - EGCP 470 Senior Design I.mp4

say: Welcome to E G C P four seventy, senior design one, the first half of the capstone. For the first time, nobody hands you a problem with a known answer. A team picks a real need, and over two semesters designs, builds and demonstrates a working system. This first semester is about doing the engineering before the building: understanding the need, writing requirements you can test, choosing between concepts, planning the work, and budgeting. As a running example, we'll use one kind of project teams take on: a voice commanded robotic arm assistant that recognizes small tools and fetches them, designed especially to help people with limited mobility, built around a Raspberry Pi and a camera.

pts: Need → research → requirements → concepts → choose
Then detailed design → build → test → iterate
Research prior art, markets and standards first
Every loop is cheaper on paper than in hardware
say: Engineering design follows a loop. Start with a clear statement of the need: who has the problem, and why do current solutions fall short? Then research: existing products and patents, the market, and relevant standards, such as electrical safety or accessibility guidelines. From that research come requirements, then several candidate concepts, and a reasoned choice between them.

Only then comes detailed design, building and testing, where every test is judged against the requirements. Results feed back into the loop. The point of front loading the thinking is cost: changing a block diagram costs an afternoon, changing a soldered prototype costs a week, and changing a product after release costs a fortune, the same lesson as software engineering.

pts: Specific, measurable, testable
Functional requirements vs constraints vs nice-to-haves
Include safety and accessibility
Requirements become the final acceptance tests
say: The single most important skill in this course is writing good requirements. Recognize tools is a wish, not a requirement: you can never prove you've met it. Detect a stapler at half a meter, in office lighting, with at least ninety percent success, is a requirement. You can set up that test and get a yes or no.
Separate the functional requirements, what the system must do, from constraints, like budget, size, power and weight, and from nice to haves that you'll add only if time allows.

For anything that moves, safety requirements come first: the arm must stop within half a second when a stop button is pressed. For an assistive device, accessibility requirements matter just as much: commands that work for someone with limited speech, or a button fallback.
Write requirements so they turn directly into the acceptance tests at the end of the second semester. A team that does this well knows exactly what done means.

slides.h: Choosing a concept: the decision matrix
pts: List criteria and agree on weights first
Score each concept 1–5 per criterion
Weighted sum ranks the options
Then sanity-check the winner against requirements
say: Teams usually have several ways to solve each sub problem, and opinions get heated. A decision matrix turns the argument into arithmetic. First agree on the criteria and their weights, before looking at the options: say cost twenty five percent, feasibility thirty, performance twenty five and risk twenty. Then score each concept from one to five on each criterion, multiply by the weights and add. For the arm's gripper, a servo driven claw scores three point five five, an electromagnet three point seven five, and a suction cup two point five. The electromagnet wins on cost and simplicity. But the matrix doesn't end the discussion: it makes the trade off explicit. An electromagnet only grabs iron and steel, so if the requirements include plastic objects, the team must either change the requirement or pick the claw. The matrix's real value is that everyone can see, and challenge, exactly why a choice was made.

pts: (written on the whiteboard) weights first, then scores
(written on the whiteboard) B: best accuracy, worst cost and time
(written on the whiteboard) A = 0.4(3) + 0.3(5) + 0.2(5) + 0.1(4) = 4.1
(written on the whiteboard) A wins: 4.1 vs 3.4 vs 3.6
(written on the whiteboard) check the winner against must-haves
say: Our team has three concepts for the arm: A, a servo arm kit; B, a custom stepper motor arm; and C, a gantry on linear rails. Before scoring anything, agree on the criteria and their weights. Accuracy matters most, point four, then cost, build time, and safety.
Now score each concept from one to five on each criterion. The custom arm is the most accurate, a five, but it's expensive and slow to build.

Multiply each score by its weight and add. Concept A: point four times three, plus point three times five, plus point two times five, plus point one times four: four point one. B gets three point four, and C gets three point six. The kit wins, even though B won the most important criterion.

Finally, a sanity check: does A meet every hard requirement? A matrix ranks options, but a concept that fails a must-have requirement is out, no matter its score. Then write down why you chose it. One more professional check, a sensitivity test: nudge the weights a little, say accuracy from point four to point five, and see whether the winner changes. If a small change flips the ranking, the concepts are effectively tied, and you should decide on risk or prototype both. That paragraph goes straight into your design review.

pts: Block diagram: subsystems + data, power, mechanical links
Define interfaces early so the team works in parallel
Example split: voice, vision, path planning, arm control
Watch power: servos need their own supply
say: Next, break the system into subsystems and define exactly what flows between them. In the robotic arm example, a microphone and speech recognition produce a text command. The camera and an object detector produce bounding boxes in pixel coordinates. A path planning block converts a target into joint angles, and the arm controller drives the servos. A Raspberry Pi ties it together. Once the interface of each block is written down, for example, the vision block outputs a list of object names with x and y pixel positions, each team member can build and test their block in parallel, using fake inputs until the real ones exist. Teams typically split the work exactly along these lines.

Don't forget power and mechanics in the block diagram. Servos draw large current spikes when they move, which can make a Raspberry Pi's supply sag and reboot it, so the arm needs its own supply with a common ground. Problems like this live at the interfaces, which is why the architecture deserves careful thought before anything is bought.

slides.h: Worked example: a power budget and battery life
pts: (written on the whiteboard) list every load
(written on the whiteboard) servos: 9.6 times 0.25 = 2.4 W average
(written on the whiteboard) regulators: size for PEAK (16.6 W)
(written on the whiteboard) battery: size for AVERAGE (9.4 W)
(written on the whiteboard) battery draw = 9.4 / 0.85 approx 11.1 W
(written on the whiteboard) 12 mathrmV times 5 mathrmAh = 60 Wh, use 80%
(written on the whiteboard) runtime = 48 / 11.1 approx 4.3 h
say: Before choosing a battery, list every load. The single board computer draws one point two amps at five volts, six watts, all the time.
The four servos draw about point four amps each at six volts: nine point six watts while moving. But the arm only moves about a quarter of the time, so they average two point four watts.
Add the camera and microphone, one watt. Peak is sixteen point six watts, but the average is only nine point four. Size the regulators for the peak, and the battery for the average.

The regulators are about eighty five percent efficient, so the battery supplies nine point four over point eight five, about eleven point one watts. A twelve volt, five amp hour battery stores sixty watt hours. Using only eighty percent of it to protect the battery: forty eight over eleven point one is about four point three hours of runtime.

slides.h: Planning: schedule, risk and design reviews
pts: Work breakdown → Gantt chart with milestones
Critical path and part lead times
Risk register: likelihood × impact → mitigation
PDR and CDR before committing money
say: Break the work down into tasks small enough to estimate, then lay them out on a Gantt chart against the semester's weeks. Mark the milestones, especially the design reviews.

Find the critical path, the chain of tasks with no slack, and pay special attention to part lead times. A component with a six week shipping time can sink a schedule all by itself, so order early and order spares.

Keep a risk register: for each risk, its likelihood, its impact and a mitigation plan. If voice recognition accuracy turns out too low, fall back to selecting objects with buttons. If the object detector is too slow on the Raspberry Pi, reduce the image resolution.

And hold formal design reviews: a preliminary design review to agree on the approach, and a critical design review before committing serious money. Biweekly status reports summarize what was done, what's next, any blockers, and the budget, which is exactly how engineering projects are tracked in industry.

pts: Bill of materials: part numbers, quantities, suppliers, lead times
Include spares, shipping and tax
Track spending against the budget
Follow the purchasing process (reimbursement forms!)
say: Every capstone has a budget, typically a few hundred dollars for a student team. The bill of materials lists every part with its part number, quantity, supplier, price and lead time. Include spares, because small servos and boards do get destroyed during testing, and include shipping, which students reliably forget. This illustrative B O M for an arm project comes to about five hundred seventy dollars against a six hundred dollar budget.

Then track actual spending as you go, and follow the university's purchasing process, which for student teams often means filling out reimbursement or check request forms and keeping every receipt. It's unglamorous, but in industry, a project that's technically brilliant and over budget is still in trouble.

slides.h: Professional habits that make projects succeed
pts: Keep an engineering notebook: decisions and why
Version control for code — and for documents
Write documentation someone else could pick up
Consider standards, safety, ethics and accessibility
Communicate early: a blocker reported on Monday is a small problem
say: A few habits separate successful capstone teams from struggling ones. Keep an engineering notebook recording what you tried, what happened, and why you made each decision.
Put all code in version control from day one, and keep documents versioned too.
Write documentation clear enough that another team could pick up your project. In industry, someone always does.
Think about the standards that apply, about safety for anything that moves or plugs into the wall, about the ethics of what you're building, and about accessibility for the people who will use it.

And communicate. A teammate who reports on Monday that a part hasn't arrived creates a small scheduling problem. One who reports it the night before the demo creates a crisis. Next semester, the team builds it.

slides.big: Design before you build: testable requirements, a justified concept, clear interfaces, and a schedule, risk list and budget you actually track.
say: To recap. Senior design follows the engineering design process, front loading the thinking because changes get more expensive later. Requirements must be specific, measurable and testable, including safety and accessibility. Decision matrices make concept choices explicit. Block diagrams with defined interfaces let a team work in parallel. Gantt charts, risk registers and design reviews keep the project on track, and the bill of materials keeps it on budget. Next, senior design two, where we build the robotic arm with computer vision. See you there.

L30_egcp471.title: Senior Design II
L30_egcp471.file: EGCP-471 Senior Design II (Object Detection)/Lecture - EGCP 471 Senior Design II.mp4

say: Welcome to E G C P four seventy one, senior design two, where the plan from the first semester becomes a working system. We'll follow the robotic arm assistant example through its hardest parts: teaching a small computer to recognize objects in a camera image, working out how to move an arm's joints to reach a point, controlling the motors, and integrating everything so it works on demo day. Along the way, you'll see nearly every earlier course reappear: programming, embedded I O, signals, probability and linear algebra.

pts: Haar feature: bright region minus dark region
Integral image: any rectangle sum in 4 lookups
Cheap enough for a Raspberry Pi in real time
Viola–Jones (2001): the original real-time face detector
say: One classic, lightweight way to detect objects is the Viola Jones method, published in two thousand one as the first real time face detector, and available in OpenCV as Haar cascades. It's built from Haar like features: rectangles where you add up the pixels under the white part and subtract the pixels under the black part. An edge feature responds to a brightness change, a line feature to a thin stripe. In a twenty four by twenty four pixel window there are around one hundred sixty thousand possible features of different sizes and positions.

Computing all those sums directly would be far too slow, so the method uses a trick called the integral image. Each entry stores the sum of every pixel above and to the left. Then the sum of any rectangle, of any size, takes just four lookups: bottom right, minus top right, minus bottom left, plus top left. Here, the blue two by two block sums to seven: the highlighted entries give fourteen, minus three, minus five, plus one, which is seven. Four lookups, for a rectangle of any size. That's what makes Haar features cheap enough to run on a Raspberry Pi in real time.

slides.h: Worked example: a rectangle sum in four lookups
pts: (written on the whiteboard) need: sums of rectangles, fast
(written on the whiteboard) ii(r, c) = sum above and left
(written on the whiteboard) ii(2, 2) = 11
(written on the whiteboard) 11 − 4 − 3 + 1 = 5
(written on the whiteboard) check: 1 + 3 + 1 + 0 = 5
(written on the whiteboard) always 4 lookups, any size
say: Haar features need the sum of pixels inside rectangles, millions of times per frame. Here's a tiny four by four image.

The integral image stores, at each cell, the sum of everything above and to the left, including the cell itself. It's built in one pass. For example, the cell in row two, column two holds one plus two plus one, plus zero plus one plus three, plus two plus one plus zero: eleven.

Now the blue rectangle, rows one and two, columns one and two. Take the corner value eleven, subtract the strip above it, four, subtract the strip to its left, three, and add back the overlap we subtracted twice, one. Eleven minus four minus three plus one: five.

Check by adding the blue pixels directly: one plus three plus one plus zero, five. It matches. And the cost is four lookups whether the rectangle is two pixels or two hundred thousand. That's what made real-time detection possible on our small computer.

pts: AdaBoost picks a few strong features from ~160,000
Cascade: cheap early stages reject most windows
Rates multiply: 0.995¹¹ ≈ 95% detection
0.44¹¹ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ false alarms per window
say: Training uses AdaBoost, a machine learning algorithm that picks, out of all those features, the handful that best separate the object from the background, and weights each one. Each feature alone is a weak classifier, barely better than guessing. Combined, they form a strong one.

The second idea is the cascade. Most windows in an image obviously contain nothing, so the first stage uses just a few features to throw them out quickly. Only windows that pass go on to the next, more thorough stage, and so on. On average, very little work is spent per window.

Here's where probability returns. If each of eleven stages keeps at least ninety nine point five percent of real objects, the overall detection rate is point nine nine five to the eleventh, about ninety five percent.

And if each stage lets through at most forty four percent of background windows, the overall false alarm rate is point four four to the eleventh, about one in eight thousand windows. Those are exactly the kinds of parameters a team sets when training a cascade for a tool like a stapler or a screwdriver.

pts: Positives: the object at many angles, lights, backgrounds
Negatives: the SAME environment without the object
Skip near-duplicate and blurry frames
Hard-negative mining: add false positives back as negatives
say: In practice, the quality of the training data matters more than any algorithm setting. Positive images should show the object from many angles, distances, lighting conditions and backgrounds. Negative images should come from the same environment the robot will work in, just without the object, so the detector learns what the desk, the walls and the clutter look like. A practical trick when collecting data from video: save only every tenth frame to avoid near duplicates, and automatically reject blurry frames using a sharpness measure, the variance of the image's Laplacian. A typical successful cascade might use around twelve hundred positive and a thousand negative samples. And the fastest way to improve a detector is hard negative mining: run it, collect the images where it fired falsely, and add them back as negatives.

At run time, three parameters of OpenCV's detect multi scale function control the trade off. The scale factor sets how finely object sizes are scanned. Min neighbors requires several overlapping detections to agree, trading misses for fewer false alarms. Min size ignores tiny boxes. Exposing them on sliders and tuning while watching the live camera feed is far faster than guessing.

pts: Top: the run-time sliders (scale, min neighbors, min area, brightness)
Magenta box: the stapler cascade
Green box: the screwdriver cascade
White box: a parts bag
Watch for a box that drops out for a frame: a miss
say: Here's real footage from this course's project: the trained cascades running live on a webcam feed. At the top are the run time tuning sliders we just talked about: the scale factor, min neighbors, a minimum box area, and a brightness adjustment. Below, every cascade that fires draws a labeled box: magenta for the stapler, green for the screwdriver, and white for a small parts bag. Now watch the boxes closely as the camera moves. Every so often a box disappears for a frame or two, a missed detection, and then comes right back. That's completely normal for a cascade, and it's why the arm's software should act only when a detection holds for several frames in a row, rather than trusting any single frame.

slides.h: Finding the object: scan and center
pts: Sweep the base servo 0° → 180° in small steps
Run the detector at each step
On a hit: draw the box, center it in the frame
Visual servoing: move until the object is centered
say: With a working detector, the arm needs to find the object. A simple, robust strategy: sweep the base servo across its range in small steps, say three degrees, grabbing a frame and running the detector at each position. When the stapler cascade fires, stop, draw a labeled box on the display, and adjust the base until the object sits in the center of the image. Moving until a visual measurement reaches a target is called visual servoing, and it avoids needing a precise camera calibration. A more advanced approach calibrates the camera, measuring its focal length and lens distortion, and computes a fixed transformation from camera coordinates to arm coordinates, so a pixel position converts directly into a three dimensional target.

slides.h: Inverse kinematics: where do the joints go?
pts: Forward: angles → hand position (trig)
Inverse: position → angles (law of cosines)
Two solutions: elbow up / elbow down
Real arms: Denavit–Hartenberg + 4×4 matrices
say: Forward kinematics asks: given the joint angles, where is the hand? For a two link arm it's just trigonometry: x equals L one cosine theta one, plus L two cosine of theta one plus theta two, and similarly for y.

The robot needs the opposite: given a target, what angles reach it? That's inverse kinematics. For two links, the law of cosines gives the elbow angle directly, and then a couple of arctangents give the shoulder angle.

There are usually two solutions, elbow up and elbow down. For links of ten and eight centimeters and a target at twelve, six, elbow up puts the shoulder at about sixty three degrees with the elbow bent minus eighty four, while elbow down uses about minus ten and plus eighty four. The software picks the one that avoids the table and stays within the servos' ranges.

Real arms with five or six joints use Denavit Hartenberg parameters and four by four homogeneous transformation matrices, multiplying one matrix per joint, the linear algebra from math two fifty B in action.

slides.h: Worked example: solving a two-link arm
pts: (written on the whiteboard) L_1 = L_2 = 10, target (12, 8)
(written on the whiteboard) costheta_2 = (x^2 + y^2 - L_1^2 - L_2^2)/(2L_1L_2)
(written on the whiteboard) = (208 - 200)/(200) = 0.04
(written on the whiteboard) theta_2 = pm 87.7° so pick elbow-up: -87.7°
(written on the whiteboard) theta_1 = mathrmatan2(y, x) - mathrmatan2(L_2sintheta_2,\ L_1 + L_2costheta_2)
(written on the whiteboard) = 33.7° + 43.9° = 77.5°
(written on the whiteboard) forward check: (12.0, 8.0)
say: Our arm has two links, each ten centimeters. The camera says the cup is at x equals twelve, y equals eight. What joint angles put the hand there?

The elbow angle comes from the law of cosines. Cosine theta two equals x squared plus y squared, minus L one squared minus L two squared, over two L one L two. That's two hundred eight minus two hundred, over two hundred: point zero four.
So theta two is plus or minus eighty seven point seven degrees: elbow down or elbow up. We choose the elbow up solution, minus eighty seven point seven, to reach over the table.

Then the shoulder angle: theta one equals the angle to the target, minus the angle the second link adds. That's thirty three point seven degrees minus negative forty three point nine: seventy seven point five degrees. Always check with forward kinematics: these angles land exactly at twelve, eight.

slides.h: Moving the joints: servos and PID control
pts: Hobby servo: 1–2 ms pulse every 20 ms sets the angle
Inside: a motor + a position sensor + a controller
PID: proportional + integral + derivative
Move smoothly; big jumps cause current spikes and wobble
say: Small arms use hobby servos like this one. As we saw with timers, a servo reads a pulse every twenty milliseconds: about one millisecond means one end of travel, two milliseconds the other. Inside is a small motor, a gearbox, a potentiometer that measures the actual angle, and a little controller that drives the motor until the measured angle matches the commanded one.

That controller, and almost every feedback controller in engineering, is a variation of P I D. The proportional term pushes harder the bigger the error. Alone, it may leave a steady error or, with high gain, overshoot and oscillate, as the gray and red curves show. The integral term accumulates past error and removes any steady offset. The derivative term reacts to how fast the error is changing and damps the overshoot. Tuned well, the green curve: fast, with little overshoot and no steady error. In software, command joint moves in small increments rather than big jumps, which keeps the arm smooth and avoids current spikes.

slides.h: Worked example: why P alone leaves an error, and I fixes it
pts: (code on the board) err = target - x
(code on the board) x  += Kp * err            # Kp = 0.5
(code on the board) x  += Kp * err - 5        # gravity pulls down 5°
(written on the whiteboard) balance: 0.5 e = 5 Rightarrow e = 10°, stuck at 80°
(code on the board) integ += err
(code on the board) x     += Kp * err + Ki * integ - 5
(written on the whiteboard) integral grows until e = 0 → reaches 90°
(written on the whiteboard) P = present, I = past, D = future
say: Let's watch a controller step by step instead of trusting the curves. A joint sits at zero degrees and must reach ninety. A proportional controller moves it by K p times the error each step. With K p of one half, it moves half the remaining distance every time.

Now add gravity: the arm's weight drags it down five degrees every step. The joint settles where the controller's push exactly balances gravity: one half times the error equals five, so the error is ten. It stops at eighty degrees, forever. That's steady state error, and turning up K p only shrinks it, never removes it.

The integral term adds up the error over time. While the arm sits ten degrees short, the sum keeps growing, so the push keeps growing, until the arm reaches ninety, where the error is zero and the integral holds just enough push to cancel gravity.
And the derivative term watches how fast the error is shrinking, and eases off before the target to prevent overshoot. Proportional for the present, integral for the past, derivative for the future.

slides.h: Worked example: from an angle to a servo pulse
pts: (written on the whiteboard) pulse = 1\ mathrmms + (theta)/(180°)times 1\ mathrmms
(written on the whiteboard) 45°: 1 + 0.25 = 1.25\ mathrmms
(written on the whiteboard) 1 MHz timer: period 20000, compare 1250
(written on the whiteboard) ramp the compare value: smooth motion
say: A hobby servo reads a pulse every twenty milliseconds. A one millisecond pulse means zero degrees, two milliseconds means one hundred eighty degrees, and in between is linear.

Take a forty five degree command as an example: one plus forty five over one eighty, one point two five milliseconds. Kinematic angles like the minus eighty seven point seven we just found are first shifted by each servo's mounting offset into its zero to one eighty range, then converted the same way.

On a timer ticking at one megahertz, one tick is a microsecond. The period register gets twenty thousand, and the compare register gets twelve hundred fifty. To move smoothly, don't jump straight there: step the compare value a little each period, so the arm doesn't jerk or brown out the supply.

slides.h: Integration and testing: where projects really fail
pts: Problems live at the interfaces
Servo current spikes brown out the computer
Lighting changes break the detector
Integrate one subsystem at a time; keep a demo video
say: Most capstone problems don't appear inside a subsystem. They appear when subsystems meet.
The arm moves, the servos draw a surge of current, the supply voltage sags, and the Raspberry Pi reboots. The fix is a separate, adequately rated servo supply with a shared ground.
The detector works perfectly at home, then fails in the demo room under different lighting. The fix is training data from varied lighting, and testing early in the real location.

So test each subsystem alone, integrate one at a time, keep a known good version in version control, and record demo videos as you go, so a last minute failure doesn't erase the proof that it worked. Today, convolutional neural network detectors like YOLO, running on small accelerators, are far more robust than Haar cascades, and would be the natural upgrade for a project like this.

slides.big: A capstone ties it all together: vision finds the object, kinematics plans the reach, control moves the joints — and integration testing makes it real.
say: To recap. Haar cascades detect objects cheaply using rectangle features, integral images, AdaBoost and a cascade whose rates multiply. Good, varied training data matters more than anything else. The arm scans and centers the object, inverse kinematics turns a target into joint angles, and servos with P I D control move the joints. And integration testing, at the interfaces, is where projects succeed or fail. In the final lecture, we'll step back and see how every course in the degree fits together. See you there.

Congratulations on reaching the end of the series. In this final lecture, we'll step back from the individual courses and look at the degree as a whole: how the courses fit together into one picture of a computer, the handful of ideas that kept coming back in different forms, and where to go next if you want to keep learning.

pts: Physics → devices → circuits → logic
Logic → microarchitecture → ISA → OS → applications
Math supports every layer
Security, economics and ethics cut across them all
say: Remember the abstraction stack from the very first lecture. Now every layer has a name and a course behind it. Physics explained fields, charges and waves. Electronics and CMOS design turned that physics into transistors and gates, with real delay and real power. Circuit analysis gave you the laws that govern them. Digital logic and hardware description languages built combinational and sequential circuits on F P G As. Computer design assembled those into a pipelined processor with caches. Microcontrollers and embedded systems programmed that processor in assembly and C, touching the hardware directly. Operating systems managed it for many programs at once, and databases and software engineering built applications and teams on top. Underneath it all ran the mathematics, and across it all ran security, economics and ethics. Very few people understand every layer. You've now seen all of them.

pts: States + transitions + outputs
Hardware: sequence detectors, controllers
Software: UI flows, protocols, games
Draw the diagram first — every time
say: Some ideas appeared again and again. The first is the finite state machine. You met it in digital logic as a sequence detector, wrote it in V H D L and Verilog, built a table driven traffic light in C, saw it as the control unit of a processor, drew it as a UML state diagram in software engineering, and it's how network protocols like TCP manage connections. Whenever a system's behavior depends on history, the right first step is to draw the states and transitions. The diagram makes the design obvious and the bugs visible.

pts: Superposition: break it into pieces, add the answers
Change to a domain where the problem is easy
Phasors, Fourier, Laplace, Z, eigenvectors
The same trick in circuits, signals, control and ML
say: The second idea is linearity. When a system is linear, you can break a complicated input into simple pieces, solve each one, and add the answers. And often the smartest move is to change domains: phasors turn circuit differential equations into complex algebra, the Fourier transform turns convolution into multiplication, the Laplace transform turns differential equations into polynomials whose poles reveal stability, and eigenvectors turn a coupled system into independent modes. Transform, solve the easy problem, transform back. The same pattern powers filters, control systems, image compression and much of machine learning.

pts: There is rarely a free lunch
Quantify both sides, then decide
Make trade-offs explicit (decision matrices, Big-O, Bode plots)
The best engineers know which constraint matters most
say: The third idea: engineering is the art of trade offs. Faster transistors burn more power and area. More amplifier gain means less bandwidth. A faster clock can mean a higher C P I. A distributed database must choose between consistency and availability during a network split. A detector tuned to catch more objects also raises more false alarms. Memoization trades memory for time. And every project balances cost, benefit and safety. Good engineers don't look for a perfect answer. They quantify both sides of each trade off, make it explicit, and choose based on which constraint matters most for the problem in front of them.

slides.h: Idea 4: concurrency, and measuring instead of guessing
pts: Hardware is inherently parallel
Threads, interrupts and pipelines share state
The hardest bugs are about timing and shared data
Measure: testbenches, scopes, profilers, lab reports
say: Two final ideas. First, concurrency. Hardware is naturally parallel: every gate in an H D L design operates at once.
Software became concurrent too: threads on multicore processors, interrupt handlers on microcontrollers, and overlapping instructions in pipelines, all sharing state.
And the hardest bugs, from race conditions to metastability to data hazards, are always about timing and shared data. Recognizing that pattern is half of fixing it.

Second: measure, don't guess. Testbenches in V H D L, oscilloscopes and logic analyzers on the bench, page fault counts, detector training logs and lab reports with percent error all embody the same habit. Predict, then measure, then explain the difference. That habit, more than any formula, is what makes an engineer.

pts: Pick one layer and go deeper
Build projects: they’re the best teacher
Each next step builds on a specific course
Revisit any lecture when a topic resurfaces
say: If you want to keep going, pick a layer and go deeper with a project. For chip design and verification, learn SystemVerilog and the UVM methodology used across the industry. For computer architecture, build your own RISC five processor core, the natural sequel to computer design. For embedded systems, try the Zephyr real time operating system or embedded Rust on a Cortex M board. For computer vision, run a modern YOLO object detector on an edge A I board, the upgrade to a Haar cascade. For signals, implement filters and F F Ts in Python with NumPy and SciPy. And for hardware security, side channel experiments with an open platform like ChipWhisperer make those attacks real. Whenever a topic resurfaces, come back to the matching lecture.

slides.big: From electrons to applications: understand more than one layer, make trade-offs explicit, and always predict, then measure.
say: That's the end of the series. You've traveled from electrons to applications, through thirty courses. If you remember only three things, remember these: understand more than one layer of the stack, make your trade offs explicit, and always predict, then measure. Thank you for watching, and good luck with whatever you build next.
